Extract A: Organic boom sparks farm shortage
VICTORIAN shoppers are turning to organic food in their droves. Nationwide the demand
for organic produce has leapt by more than 80 percent since 2004. Organic processors
have even issued a plea for more farmers to adopt the techniques needed to meet the
demand.
A national study by New England University shows organic farm numbers have increased
by more than 5 per cent a year over the past five years. Australia has almost 12 million
hectares of certified organic farmland, the largest of any food-producing nation. Organic
farmer Jo Whitsed, of Corryong, believes customer recognition of the logos used by testing
authorities is an important factor in the growth rate.
“Demand has really taken off in the last few years,” she said.
“Consumers are learning about certified organic, and looking for the logo.
“They're concerned about the health benefits, the environment and animal welfare issues.”
Organic farming has been the norm for three generations of the Whitsed family on their
150 ha property in a lush valley on the upper reaches of the Murray River. Jo and Steve
Whitsed are continuing the family tradition.
There’s a chance too that Jo’s daughter, Tahnia, could become a fourth-generation organic
farmer, but at 7 she hasn't decided. No pesticides or chemicals are used, and cattle feed
on pasture rich in treated-waste products from within farm boundaries or on silage grown
and prepared on the farm. The family runs 160 dairy cows to produce organically certified
milk.
“The cows are milking the best they ever have,” said Jo Whitsed.
“We make up our own licks from cider vinegar, dolomite and molasses, and we certainly
don't get the vet out very often.”
There are seven organic certification groups in Australia, using standards established by
the Quarantine Inspection Service. Australian Certified Organic, with its sprouting-bud
logo, claims to certify about two-thirds of the genuine organic produce.
“Shoppers need to look for the certification logo,” said Dr Andrew Monk, of Biological
Farmers Australia. “It is harder to farm organically and the product will cost more.
“Consumers make a conscious decision to choose organic. But don’t buy if it’s not
certified.”
Reading Skills )
Extract B: Gambling with dirt: The odds for farmers is getting longer
Farming has always involved considerable risk, likened to a “gamble with dirt,” but climate
change is amplifying unpredictability in weather patterns and intensifying those risks. In
earlier decades, farmers could generally count on consistent harvest periods in late
November to early December, allowing for reliable planning and pricing.
Today, rising temperatures and erratic rainfall have shifted crop cycles, causing some
crops to ripen earlier yet then face heavy downpours or prolonged wet spells that harm
quality. Although overall annual rainfall totals may remain near average, its distribution has
become more uneven—sometimes triggering droughts followed by floods—complicating
decision-making on planting and harvesting. For instance, despite an El Nifio declaration
in 2023 that would typically imply drier conditions, parts of Australia experienced both
me
severe drought and flooding in the same season. Such extremes exacerbate the “fodder |
drought” in regions where livestock feed becomes scarce, forcing difficult choices like
livestock sales or even culling.
Rising input costs—for fertilisers, chemicals, fuel, and machinery maintenance—
compound the challenge, as farmers must invest more to safeguard yields under volatile
conditions. Much of Australia’s farmland is dedicated to grazing rather than cropping,
meaning the pressure to meet global protein demand remains high even when pasture
growth is threatened by weather swings. Farmers are exploring adaptations such as
altered sowing dates, drought-resistant varieties, diversified enterprises, and on-farm
water management systems to mitigate risks. Government and industry bodies also
emphasise the need for coordinated research into climate-resilient practices and policy
frameworks that support sustainable agriculture.
Despite mounting uncertainties, farmers continue to demonstrate resilience by investing in
new approaches, from precision agriculture technologies to regenerative soil techniques,
underscoring their determination to persist amid changing conditions. Community
awareness and supportive policy measures—such as improved drought relief programs
and incentives for sustainable practices—are vital to help farming remain viable in the long
term.

Extract A: Sea Safety - Letter to the editor
Once again another sea rescue that was completely unnecessary has taken place. Small
craft, sailing vessels and helicopters have been involved in a four-day search of our
coastline, often in appalling weather and dangerous seas because of human stupidity.
| am very pleased that the Haslan family was finally rescued from the serious danger they
were in, but the danger was of their own making. Reports indicate that the minimum safety
requirement and safety kits were not on board. Not to have the correct safety equipment,
sufficient safety floatation devices and communicating equipment and setting off past
Barr's Point into the open sea, can only be described as almost criminal negligence.
The weather forecast on the morning the family set out indicated rising seas and steadily
increasing winds, though only freshening during the afternoon to 17 - 21 knots. The area
outside Barr's Point is well known as a place where the current can run in the opposite
direction to the waves. When this happens the waves can overrun each other and this in
turn generates steep and dangerous rogue waves. In this part of the world, the weather
forecasts for fishermen and the general conditions north and south of Eastview are well
known, widely advertised and most people take the necessary precautions to ensure the
safety of the lives of their family.
What did this rescue cost in terms of official police, rescue personnel and volunteers? A
large sum of money no doubt. It is time people who, through their own ignorance, lack of
responsibility and common sense, were made to pay to our local council at least part of the
overall cost of their rescue.
Extract B: Excerpt from ‘The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean’ by R.M.
Ballantyne
| shall say little about the first part of our voyage. We had the usual amount of rough
weather and calm; also we saw many strange fish rolling in the sea, and | was greatly
delighted one day by seeing a shoal of flying fish dart out of the water and skim through
the air about a foot above the surface. They were pursued by dolphins, which feed on
them, and one flying-fish in its terror flew over the ship, struck on the rigging, and fell upon
the deck. Its wings were just fins elongated, and we found that they could never fly far at a
time, and never mounted into the air like birds, but skimmed along the surface of the sea.
Jack and | had it for dinner, and found it remarkably good.
When we approached Cape Horn, at the southern extremity of America, the weather
became very cold and stormy, and the sailors began to tell stories about the furious gales
and the dangers of that terrible cape. Each story outdid the one before in conjuring fearful
possibilities.
Nevertheless, we passed the dreaded cape without much rough weather, and, in the
course of a few weeks afterwards, were sailing gently, before a warm tropical breeze, over
the Pacific Ocean. Thus we proceeded on our voyage, sometimes bounding merrily before
a fair breeze, at other times floating calmly on the glassy wave and fishing for the curious
inhabitants of the deep - all of which, although the sailors thought little of them, were
strange, and interesting, and very wonderful to me.

The Teams
Henry Lawson
A cloud of dust on the long, white road,
And the teams go creeping on
Inch by inch with the weary load;
And by the power of the green-hide goad
The distant goal is won.
With eyes half-shut to the blinding dust,
And necks to the yokes bent low,
The bests are pulling as bullocks must;
And the shining tires might almost rust
While the spokes are turning slow.
With face half-hid by a broad-brimmed hat,
That shades from the heat's white waves,
And shouldered whip, with its green-hide plait,
The driver plots with a gait like that
Of his weary, patient slaves.
He wipes his brow, for the day is hot,
And spits to the left with spite;
He shouts at Bally, and flicks at Scot,
And raises dust from the back of Spot,
And spits to the dusty right.
He'll sometimes pause as a thing of form
In front of a settler's door
And ask for a drink, and remark "It's warm,"
Or say "There's signs of a thunderstorm";
But he seldom utters more

Hating Alison Ashley (PG)
Directed by Geoff Bennett
Screenplay by Christine Madafferi from the novel by Robin Klein
Rated PG
Cinemas Everywhere
Review by Sandra Hall
it's a girls’ world in this comic and colourful adaptation of a-much-loved children's
novel.
It should come as no surprise that Delta Goodrem doesn't convince as a 14-year-old
schoolgirl. Hiding under a Mona Lisa smile and a Goldilocks wig, she looks like a 20-year-
old pop star on the run from the paparazzi.
Not that it matters. The film of Hating Alison Ashley, Robin Klein's much-read children's
novel, has little to do with the real world. It's set in Ockerdom, a place where we patriotic
filmgoers have spent a lot of time lately, thanks to the run of comedies which have been
trying, with raucous relentlessness, to make themselves loveable in the happy-go-lucky
manner of The Castle.
Hating Alison Ashley is not really Alison's story. As Klein's many fans know, its narrator is
Alison's classmate, Erica Yurken (Saskia Burmeister), a talented self-dramatist, who
fancies she's been stranded in the wrong life. Her refined sensibilities, she thinks, are
more suited to some ivy-covered temple of learning than scungy, working-class Barringa
East, where she's been dumped among the delinquents of 9C. Whenever she can, she
escapes to the sick bay, where her impressive list of imaginary ailments has gained her a
reputation as a creative hypochondriac.
And life at home is no better. Although her sweet-natured mum (Tracy Mann) does her
best, Erica can't forgive her for taking up with Lennie (Richard Carter), a truck driver she
met at Parents Without Partners, or for giving her such unbearable siblings. Her chief
torturer is her elder sister, boy-mad Valjoy (Rachael Carpani), whose boots and big hair
are almost as scary as her interest in martial arts.
School improves for Erica with the arrival of Miss Belmont (Jean Kittson), whose fishnet
stockings and gallows humour give her the air of a semi-respectable dominatrix. Miss
Belmont does the previously unthinkable and keeps 9C in order. She also gives Erica high
marks and makes her fee! special - until the arrival of Goodrem's Alison Ashley.
Alison is perfection incarnate. For a minute or two, Erica fancies she has found a kindred
spirit. But Alison proves to be strangely aloof. And, even worse, the quality of her
classwork eclipses Erica's.

People work out whether or not they want to read a novel by using all sorts of different

Extract A: Excerpt from ‘Brenda is the Night’ by Geoffrey McSkimming
In the great deserts of Egypt, where the hot and golden-grained sands stretch on and on
towards the shimmering, far away ends of the earth, miracles are said still to happen.
Everything out here is wide open and lonely. Nearly all of the desert land is dry, the sand
baked almost rock-hard in places by the sun. Sometimes, if you are travelling through this |
furnace of a place, you might come across an oasis — a small patch where there is a
water-hole, with palm trees and small plants called Lilies of the Nile growing around it.
Here you will find shade, and you will be able to fill your water-bottle and wet your
handkerchief and tie it around your neck to cool yourself. If you find an oasis in the desert,
you will be very lucky, as they are few and most definitely far between.
Not many people live in the desert. Those who do usually travel around a lot, not staying in
the one place for a very long time at all. Sometimes they will camp at an oasis for a few
weeks, but they will always move on, for they are usually fearful of meeting up with a
certain tribe — a tribe which has dwelt under the Egyptian sun for thousands of years. The
people who live out in the desert will do anything to avoid coming into contact with this
tribe (one man, long ago, was said to have glued ibis feathers to his body and a long
curved stick to his mouth, and then stood on one leg in the sand, crowing loudly, just so
the tribe would think he was a bird and maybe leave him alone), and so they keep
constantly on the move.
The reason why everyone avoids this particular tribe has nothing to do with dastardliness,
or with their being murderers or thieves or taxation cheats — because they’re not. Nor do
the tribe members make rude sounds or push people to the ground and sit on them,
actions which would automatically make them disagreeable. As a matter of fact, the tribe is
fairly harmless. As another matter of fact, they're not even human beings. They are, as
everybody who has journeyed through these wide sandy plains and hills knows, one of the
oldest wayfaring groups in all of the African continent: camels.
Extract B: What is a Mirage?
A mirage is an optical illusion. Most commonly observed in desert environments, mirages
arise when the sun-heated ground warms the adjacent layer of air more intensely than
the air above it, producing a steep temperature gradient. Since warmer air is less dense
than cooler air, light traversing these layers undergoes continual refraction—bending
gradually away from regions of lower density.
Travellers crossing arid expanses may glimpse what seems to be a shimmering oasis just
ahead—a patch of glimmering water fringed by palm trees and verdant foliage.
Compelled by thirst and hope, they advance, only to find the vision dissolving as they
approach. In reality, the water and trees lie far beyond the true horizon, their light
refracted upward by the denser, cooler air above the hot surface layer. This type of
mirage, known as an inferior mirage, produces inverted—or “upside-down’—images of
the distant scene directly beneath the upright image, explaining why one might perceive a
waterline or the glint of liquid on the desert floor.
Asimilar process occurs at sea under particular atmospheric conditions, giving rise to
superior mirages, in which cooler air lies closer to the ocean’s surface and warmer air sits
aloft. Light from a ship beyond the horizon can be bent downward into the colder layer,
causing the vessel to appear lifted, elongated or even inverted above its actual position—
sometimes floating eerily above the waterline. Mariners of old recorded such spectral
sightings, attributing them to supernatural forces, yet we now understand them as natural
consequences of atmospheric refraction.

Bushfire Weather
By Jeri Kroll
It’s cool in the hills,
breezes dart through houses like trapped birds
beating glass till they're free.
It’s clean up there. Smog doesn’t rain
Across the garden, smudging the birds of paradise,
fingerprinting the windowsills.
It’s calm in the hills when the frenzied heat
in the town bullies pedestrians.
The north wind eggs it on:
cotton wrapped like a second skin
loosens and billows, even sunglasses can’t screen the grit,
the earth in the driveway’s blown off,
vegetables wilt in the garden,
the city lies like an old dog.
In century heat, in the tinder-dry hills,
air has an edge, too, but shade is kinder.
Children swing across the Onkaparinga
into cool green slime. Cats pant under water tanks,
horse munch prickly grass under rattling trees.
By one o’clock the city has a compress on its head,
no longer looks at the hills

Extract A: On the Darling River
The Darling - which is either a muddy gutter or a second Mississippi - is about six times as
long as the distance, in a straight line, from its head to its mouth. The state of the river is
vaguely, but generally understood to depend on some distant and foreign phenomena, to
which bushmen refer in an offhand tone of voice as "the Queenslan' rains", which seem to
be held responsible, in a general way, for most of the outback trouble.
It takes less than a year to go upstream by boat to Walgett or Bourke in a dry season
because the river is then a string of waterholes. After a while the passengers get sick of
climbing out of the boat while it is carried to the next long waterhole. They get sick of being
stuck in the same sort of place, in the same old way; they grow weary of seeing the same
old timer drop his swag on the bank opposite whenever the boat ties up for wood; they get
tired of lending him tobacco, and listening to his ideas, which are limited in number and
narrow in conception.
It shortens the journey to get out and walk; but then you will have to wait so long for your
luggage - unless you hump it with you.
We heard of a man who determined to stick to a Darling boat and travel the whole length
of the river. He was a newspaper man. He started on his voyage of discovery one Easter in
flood-time, and a month later the captain got bushed between the Darling and the South
Australian border. The water went away before he could find the river again, and he left his
boat in a scrub. They had a cargo of rations, and the crew stuck to the craft while the
tucker lasted; when it gave out they rolled up their swags and went to look for a station, but
didn't find one. The captain would study his watch and the sun, rig up dials and make out
courses, and follow them without success. They ran short of water, and didn't smell any for
weeks; they suffered terrible privations, and lost three of their number, not including the
newspaper man. There were even dark hints of considering the drawing of lots in
connection with something too terrible to mention. They crossed a thirty-mile plain at last,
and sighted a young Aboriginal girl. She led them to a boundary-rider's hut where they
were taken in and provided with rations.
Later on a syndicate was formed to explore the country and recover the boat; but they
found her thirty miles from the river and about eighteen from the nearest waterhole deep
enough to float her so they left her there.
Extract B: The Darling River Run
The Darling River Run is one of Australia’s most celebrated outback self-drive adventures,
tracing the course of the Darling River through western New South Wales. Depending on
where you begin—Walgett or Brewarrina—the journey covers roughly 730 km, though
extensions and detours (for example, starting upriver at Brewarrina or including side trips
to sites like White Cliffs) can stretch the itinerary to around 950 km in total. Most travellers
allow between ten days and two weeks to savour the full experience, though shorter or
longer road-trip variations are common.
Starting in the north at Walgett, drivers follow the Barwon River south to its junction with
the Darling at Bourke. From Bourke, the road clings to the riverbank, winding through the
tiny settlements of Louth and Tilpa, then beyond Wilcannia and Menindee—before finally
reaching Wentworth, where the Darling merges with the Murray River at the Victoria-New
South Wales border. Along this route, bitumen alternates with well-graded dirt tracks; after
rain, certain stretches can become impassable without a four-wheel-drive vehicle.
At every turn, the Darling River Run reveals layers of history and culture. In Brewarrina,
just south of Walgett, you can explore the ancient Aboriginal fish traps on the Barwon
stone weirs and pools, believed to be among the oldest human-made structures. Bourke
itself embodies “back o’ Bourke” outback character, with its river-front museums and walk-
through exhibits that chart colonial exploration and pastoral life. Further downstream,
historic pubs in Tilpa and the art-lined streets of Wilcannia speak to both hardship and
resilience in the remote bush.
The road skirts five national parks—Gundabooka, Toorale, Paroo-Darling, Kinchega and
Mungo—each offering its own spectacle of red dunes, coolabah woodlands and, at Mungo,
ancient lunette formations etched with millennia-old Indigenous footprints. Menindee
Lakes provide opportunities for birdwatching, canoeing and camping beside serene
floodplain lagoons. Thermal springs, river red gums and sweeping floodplains reveal the
Darling’s changing moods, from dusty drought to sudden inundation.
Practical planning is essential. A high-clearance 4WD is strongly recommended—not only
for unsealed road sections but also to ensure safe passage when river levels rise. Fuel,
water and supplies can be scarce: town-based fuel stations are found in Walgett,
Brewarrina, Bourke, Wilcannia, Menindee and Wentworth, but it’s wise to carry extra jerry
cans and drinking water. Mobile reception is intermittent; travellers should equip
themselves with a satellite phone or emergency beacon (EPIRB), plus spare tyres and
basic recovery gear. Before setting out, check in at local Visitor Information Centres for the
latest road-condition updates and insider tips

Elizabeth Halley: What do you do on radio?

an analysis of what is happening in Australia and the rest of the world.

people like the Treasurer personally and ask a favour because I’ve been around

personalities.

very valuable to ‘PM’?

On 3 May 1978, Gary Thuerk (USA) sent the first ‘spam’ (an unsolicited e-mail,
usually advertising a product or service) via ARPAnet, a system seen as the
predecessor to the internet.
Why exactly did you send your first spam e-mail?
| wanted to reach people in western USA to tell them about our mainframe-class server.
How many people were on your mailing List?
Over 400, which was about 25% of everyone online in the world at that time. We took the
names from a printed phone book and typed them in!
What do think of spam today?
| don’t get a lot of spam because | don’t leave my contact details on the Internet — chat
room, etc. Also, when people forward jokes to friends, they leave the e-mail list in there
and spammers can eventually get hold of it.
Does anybody ever blame you for the current volumes of spam today?
Oh yes — | get people who blame me but if | talk to them we normally end up smiling or
laughing about it.
Do you feel guilty?
No. of course not. If you take a plane flight and the airline loses your luggage, you don’t
blame the Wright brothers!
Why exactly are unsolicited e-mails called ‘spam’?
It came from a Monty Python’s Flying Circus sketch. Somebody who just watched it was
going through his unsolicited e-mails and complained that he was being spammed — and
everyone around him began singing the Monty Python spam song!

This is the beginning of a poem written by Henry Lawson.
Ah, better the thud of the deadly gun, and the crash of the bursting shell,
Than the terrible silence where drought is fought out there in the western hell;
And better the rattle of rifles near, or the thunder on deck at sea,
Than the sound — most hellish of all to hear — of a fire where it should not be.
On the runs to the west of the Dingo Scrubs there was drought, and ruin and death,
And the sandstorm came from the dread north-east with the blast of a furnace breath;
Till at last one day, at the fierce sunrise, a boundary-rider woke,
And saw, in the place of the distant haze, a curtain of light blue smoke.
There is saddling-up by the Cockey’s Hut, and out in the station yard,
And away to the north, north-east, north-west, the Bushmen are riding hard.
The pickets are out and many a scout, and many a mulga wire,
While Bill and Jim, with their faces grim, are riding to meet the fire.
it roars for days in the hopeless scrub, and across, where the ground seems bare,
With a crackle and hiss, like the hissing of snakes, the fire is travelling there;
Till at last, exhausted by sleeplessness, and the terrible toil and heat,
The squatter is crying, “My God! the wool!” and the farmer, "My God! the wheat!”
But there comes a drunkard (who reels as he rides), with the news from the roadside pub:-
“Pat Murphy, - cockey — cut off by the fire! - way back in the Dingo Scrub!
Let the wheat and the woolshed go to “— Well, they do as each great heart bids;
They are riding a race for the Dingo Scrub - for Pat and his wife and kids.

The Silver Sword
This is an extract from a very exciting adventure story by lan Serraillier about
refugee children during the Second World War. It tells of their struggle to survive,
avoid capture, and of their seemingly hopeless search for their parents.
The current was swift. In the darkness the great wooded hills swept by. For a moment the
moon peeped from a cloud and turned the rippling surface of the stream to silver.
‘Stay away, moon’ Ruth muttered. ‘Don’t come out again until we’ve passed the village.’
Side by side the two canoes sped on.
On the left bank the line of hills curved downwards. Were those dim shapes houses? Had
they reached the village?
Again, the moon appeared. It had chosen quite the wrong moment, for this was indeed the
village, with houses crowded about both banks, and the left bank suddenly an open space
with lorries in it, they were so close together that they were almost touching, and there
were several rows of them. These must be the lorries that were to take the Polish refugees
back to Poland. With a tightening of fear in her throat, Ruth realised if they were spotted
now, they would be taken back, too.
‘Look out for the bridge’ said Edek.
He and Jan shot ahead, aiming for the centre of the three arches. Edging away from the
square, Ruth paddled towards the right-hand arch.
The water was noisy and Ruth did not hear the footsteps on the bridge. But she saw a
man’s shadow on the water and it was moving. She paddled frantically to get free.
‘The water’s coming in, | can feel it under me,’ said Bronia.
Aman shouted and his shadow leaned far out over the water.
The canoe was still across the base of the arch, with the water thrusting against each end,
threatening to break its back. She jabbed hard with the paddle and managed to ease it a
little.
The man was right overhead, shouting and waving, but she could not understand what he
was saying. In the distance a dog was barking.
A pair of legs dangled over the parapet and scraped against the stone. An American soldier.
With a last effort, she thrust at the stonework, and the canoe broke free. But the soldier
had clambered down and jumped into the water where it was shallow at the side. He
caught the paddle and clung on.
Ruth tugged, twisted, and then let go of it, the canoe swung sideways into the shadows
under the arch. The soldier, not expecting her to let go of it, toppled over backwards and
fell with a splash into the river.
As the canoe shot out beyond the bridge, Ruth realised that she was at the mercy of the
current. Bronia had no paddle and could not help.
-— Reading page1

This is an Aboriginal legend.
Very early in the beginning of the Dreamtime there were no kangaroos in this land.
A group of men were out hunting one day, when suddenly they were hit by the worst
oe _ windstorm they had ever experienced: Large trees were blown over, small ones were
carried away into the sky, and huge ‘boulders were tossed around like pebbles in a
children’s game.
The hunters were lucky to reach the safety of a cave. They sat in its shelter and
watched the storm take its course. After a while they were amazed to see a band of
animals being carried across the sky by the wind. They had never seen animals of this
sort before.
The men shook their heads in bewilderment as they discussed this extraordinary
sight, and realised that the creatures must have been brought by the wind from a distant
place that no-one in their group had ever visited.
The animals were quite large and covered in fur. They had small heads and short
front legs. It was obvious that they were very distressed at being blown through the wild
air. Frantically they kept stretching out their hind legs and their tails in an effort to make
contact with the ground.
The hunters watched keenly from their cave as the animals strained and battled
desperately against the wind. At last some of them did manage to find a toehold and
tailhold and anchor themselves to solid earth. The windstorm began to pass, and the
animals, which had forced their way down were left behind.
The watching hunters could now see that the animals had overstretched themselves
in their desperation to reach the ground. Their hind legs and tails were elongated out of
all proportion to the rest of their bodies. It really looked quite strange, but the animals
themselves did not seem particularly upset. Perhaps they were so pleased to be on
steady ground that nothing else mattered.
So far the hunters had been watching all this as an amazing event that would make a
good story. They took it for granted that the animals would run away immediately, trying
to get back to their own land.
It seemed that although the animals were tired and bewildered they were also
induisitive. They began to look for shade, grass and water, and quickly found them
This was exactly the sort of place they liked and it soon became clear that they had
decided to stay.
--— Reading page1

This article comes from a book about insects written by David Suzuki
Spiders are distant cousins of insects. Like insects, they. wear their skeletons on the
outside. But they have only two body parts. Their heads and thoraxes are joined together in
one part called a cephalothorax. They also have an abdomen. And here’s the difference that’s
easiest to spot between insects and spiders — all spiders have.eight legs. (As you already know,
insects get along fine with six.) Spiders belong to a class of animals called arachnida. Some of
the spiders’ relatives are ticks, mites and scorpions
Like insects, spiders lay eggs. But they don’t go through a larval stage. Little spiders
hatch out of the eggs looking just like their parents, except that they’re much smaller. As they
grow bigger, they shed their skins many times. If all the little spiders stayed in the place where
they hatched, they would have to fight each other for food. In fact, they might even eat each
other. They need to travel far away for food. How do you think they do it?
Spiders don’t have wings. But they do have a way to fly through the air when they need
to. They produce fine strong strands of silk from six spinnerets on their abdomens. The silk is
liquid, but it dries as soon as the air touches it. When the spiders want to travel, they raise their
abdomens and send out a strand of silk. The silk thread is caught by the breeze. The spider is
carried off through the air. This is called ballooning. Although most of them only go up a few
hundred metres, ballooning spiders have been found 4200 metres up in the air! Spiders also
use shorter silk strands as bridges from one place to another.
All spiders are hunters. They use their fangs to poison their prey. Then they suck out its
body juices, leaving a little dried husk. When we think of spiders, we think of webs in which
the spider sits waiting for a fly to be caught. But, while all spiders can make silk, not all
spiders spin webs to catch food.
Wolf spiders suddenly jump on their prey. The biggest spiders — the trapdoor spiders —
build burrows with hinged trapdoors, in the ground. The bola spider captures moths by hurling
a silk thread with a sticky glob on the end of it.

This is the beginning of a story called, “Sadako and the Thousand Paper Cranes”, about a girl who
lived in Japan.
Sadako was born to be a runner. Her mother always said that Sadako had learned to run before she could
walk.
One morning in August 1954 Sadako ran outside into the street as soon as she was dressed.
The morning sun of Japan touched brown highlights in her dark hair. There was not a speck of cloud in
the blue sky. It was a good sign. Sadako was always on the lookout for good luck signs.
Back in the house her sister and two brothers were still sleeping on their bed quilts. She poked
her big brother, Masahiro.
“Get up, lazybones!” she said. “It's Peace Day!”
Masahiro groaned and yawned. He wanted to sleep as long as possible but, like most fourteen-
year-old boys, he also loved to eat. When he sniffed the good smell of bean soup, Masahiro got up.
Soon Mitsue and Eiji were awake, too.
Sadako helped Eiji get dressed. He was six, but he sometimes lost a sock or shirt. Afterwards
Sadako folded the bed quilts. Her sister, Mitsue, who was nine, helped put them away in the closet.
Rushing like a whirlwind into the kitchen, Sadako cried, “Oh, Mother! | can hardly wait to go to
the carnival. Can we please hurry with breakfast?”
Her mother was busily slicing pickled radishes to serve with rice and soup. She looked sternly at
Sadako. “You are eleven years old and should know better,” she scolded. “You must not call it a carnival.
Every year on August sixth we remember those who died when the atom bomb was dropped on our city.
It is a memorial day.
Mr Sasaki came in from the back porch. “That's right,” he said. “Sadako chan, you must show
respect. Your own grandmother was killed that awful day.”
“But | do respect Oba chan,” Sadako said, “I pray for her spirit every morning. It's just that I’m so
happy today.”
“As a matter of fact, it's time for our prayers now,” her father said.
The Sasaki family gathered around the little altar shelf. Oba chan’s picture was there in a gold
frame. Sadako looked at the ceiling and wondered if her grandmother's spirit was floating somewhere
above the altar.
“Sadako chan!” Mr Sasaki said sharply.
Sadako quickly bowed her head. She fidgeted and wriggled her bare toes while Mr Sasaki
spoke. He prayed that the spirits of their ancestors were happy and peaceful. He gave thanks for his
barber-shop. He gave thanks for his fine children. And he prayed that his family would be protected from
the atom bomb disease called leukaemia.

This passage is about plants.
Imagine you're standing in one spot and you can't move.
In fact, your feet are buried in the ground. The sun is beating down on your head. Pretty soon, you're
going to get very thirsty. But you can’t go anywhere to get yourself a drink.
This is just the way it is for most plants. While animals walk, run, hop, swim, slither and fly from
place to place, a plant stays in one spot all its life. It is held there by its root — a part of the plant that is
buried in the ground. Roots keep plants from being blown away in the wind. _ If you've ever tried to pull
up a dandelion, you know how well anchored in the earth a root can be.
A root is much more to the plant than’an anchor, though. The root gives the plant that drink it
needs. Water in the soil enters the root’and is carried up through the root, into the stem and out to the
plant's leaves and flowers. In the water are dissolved minerals that the plant needs to grow.
The root is so important to the plant that it is the first part to grow when a seed sprouts. The
. growing tip of the root is protected by a root cap. The moist root cap slips easily among the soil particles.
As roots branch out and spread through the ground, they make a web that holds the soil together.
There are two main kinds of roots. Fibrous roots are thin and have many branches. If you pull
up a fistful of grass you'll see fibrous roots. Tap roots are large thick roots with fine roots called root
hairs branching off them. Many tap roots act as food storage bins — and that food is good for us to eat too.
Carrots, parsnips and beets are tap roots. We pull them up before the plant has a chance to use the
stored food to make leaves, flowers and seeds.
How does the food get down to the roots to be stored? It travels through the stem. While water
and minerals are going up the stem to the leaves, sugary food made by the leaves is going down the stem
to all parts of the plant. lll this liquid flowing through the plant is called sap. Sap keeps the plant alive
the way blood flowing through your body keeps you alive.
You are held upright by a column of bones - your spine. A plant is held upright by its stem. The
stem is not kept stiff by bone, though, but by water. A plant that needs a drink will often droop and fall
over. After it is watered, it will soon stand straight again. Stems hold up the flowers and leaves where
they can get the air and sunlight they need.

These are two extracts taken from a book about volcanoes and earthquakes.
Being in a large earthquake is a terrifying experience.
The shaking of the ground we stand on is profoundly disturbing, both physically and psychologically.
When the shaking starts there is no knowing how long it will go on or how severe it will be. Only when it
stops is there some certainty in life again. The longest tremor ever recorded, the Alaskan earthquake of
23 March, 1964 lasted four minutes. But most quakes last less than a minute. In those brief moments,
homes, shops, even entire cities are destroyed. The earth sometimes seems to undulate. Afterwards,
great cracks may appear in the ground. Even stranger, the rocks may show no sign at all of the intense
undulations they went through in the shaking. People also seem to find the many months of small
earthquakes (after shocks) which follow a big tremor very disturbing.
How do you measure the size of an earthquake? News reports usually give the quake a magnitude on the
Richter scale. Charles Richter invented the Richter Scale during the 1930s in America. The Richter
magnitude is useful because it can be worked out from a recording — called a seismogram - of the
earthquake waves. The waves of a big quake can be recorded on the other side of the globe. So as
long as the distance between the recording device and the quake’s centre is taken into account, the
Richter magnitude can be calculated from anywhere on the planet. But where the shaking is felt, it is
more important to know how intense the shaking was and how it affected buildings and people. Intensity
is purely descriptive and cannot be recorded by a machine. Instead it is compiled by inspecting the
damage and getting the quake’s survivors to fill in questionnaires.

Deadly delight for dogs
Kelly Ryan
ALL the fun of a big backyard Easter egg hunt will count for little if the family dog beats
the children to the chocolates.
Just a small amount of chocolate is potentially fatal to dogs.
Chemicals caffeine and theobromine cause irregular, racing heartbeats in canines, leading
to death.
Dexterous dalmation Elsa’s heart came close to collapsing after she broke into a visitor’s
backpack and wolfed down a 500g block of dark chocolate — seven times the lethal dose
of toxic chocolate for a dog of her size.
“The Animal Emergency Centre sees various cases of chocolate toxicity all year with
spikes at Christmas and Easter,” said veterinary director Cathy Warburton.
“The chemicals in chocolate can increase levels of stress hormones and stimulate dogs’
hearts, potentially leading to a very fast heart beat, irregular rhythm and even death,” Dr
Warburton said.
Elsa’s condition deteriorated quickly and she spent the night in hospital being medicated.

Raccoon
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
The Raccoon (Procyon lotor), also known as Raccoon, North American Raccoon, Northern Raccoon,
Washing Bear or informal Coon, is a medium-sized mammal native to North America and the most
widespread species of the family Procyonidae. Since the mid-20" century they have also been introduced
to the European mainland[1] and in the Caucasus region[2] after having escaped from fur farms or being
deliberately released to the wild.
Two of the most distinctive characteristics of the raccoon are its facial mask around the eyes and extremely
sensitive front paws;[3] they are also know for their good memory.[4] Often raccoons live together in small,
loose groups.[5] Their original habitats are deciduous or mixed forests, but due to their adaptability, they
are also found in urban areas where some house owners consider them to be pests.[6] Furthermore,
raccoons are omnivorous and usually most active during the night. ,

CAN’T FIX A FAULTY CHAN’S MISSION
Jackie Chan’s career has been hovering somewhere between toast and charcoal
for the past few years.
A possible stay of execution looms with a role as the Mr Miyagi-like mentor in the
Karate Kid reboot later this year. But only if enough people don’t get a whiff of his
work in the stinkerly The Spy Next Door.
The latest in a lame line of men-who-couldn’t-babysit-to-save-themselves
comedies sees the Chanster play Bob Ho, a Chinese secret agent who has just
completed a spell on loan with the CIA.
While undercover as a ballpoint pen importer, Bob falls in love with his next-door
“neighbour (Amber Valletta). Now at loose end and wanting to impress his new
girlfriend, Bob puts his hand up to look after her three kids when she suddenly
has to leave town for a few days.
To put it bluntly, two-thirds of Bob’s obnoxious little charges hate his guts. The
other one is too young to make that call, but is not exactly a fan.
And neither shall you be once Bob alternates between klutzing it up all over the
house — Chan works through his repertoire of designer pratfalls very quickly —
and getting on the wrong side of some Russian badskis who want to kill him. And
the kids too.
Which is just lovely for a PG film, when you really think about it, huh?
Inane, unfunny and totally tired, The Spy Next Door is the worst new release of
the holiday period by a wide margin. Parents, you should only go with this ahead
of the wonderful How to Train Your Dragon if you deem your children have been
particularly naughty for a sustained period.

are lost! Launch the boat; try for your lives!” These words went, as it were, through my
heart like a knife: but, as | felt that | ought to cheer my sons, | said to them, “Now is the time
to show that we are brave; we still have life, the land is near, and we know that God helps

hope yet left for us.”
| went at once on deck, and was met by a wave that threw me down, and wet me through

| then thought that our last chance was gone. Still, as | felt that the ship did not sink, |

This extract comes from a story Hans Brinker by Mary Mapes Dodge.
The skating season had commenced unusually early: our boys were by no means
alone upon the ice. The afternoon was so fine that men, women and children, bent upon
enjoying the holiday, had flocked to the grand canal from far and near. St Nicholas had
evidently remembered the favourite pastime: shining new skates were everywhere to be
seen. Whole families were skimming their way to Haarlem, or Leyden, or the neighbouring
villages. The ice seemed fairly alive. Ben noticed the erect, easy carriage of the women, and
their picturesque variety of costume. There were the latest fashions, fresh from Paris,
floating past dingy, moth-eaten garments that had seen service through two generations;
coal-scuttle bonnets perched over freckled faces bright with holiday smiles; stiff muslin caps,
with wings at the sides flapping beside cheeks rosy with health and contentment; furs, too,
encircling the whites of throats; and scanty garments fluttering below faces ruddy with
exercise: in short, every quaint and comical mixture of dry-goods and flesh that Holland
could furnish seemed sent to enliven the scene.
There were belles from Leyden and fishwives from the border villages; cheese-women
from Gouda, and prim matrons from beautiful country seats on the Haarlemmer Meer.
Grey-headed skaters were constantly to be seen; wrinkled old women with baskets upon
their heads; and plump little toddlers on skates, clutching at their mother’s gowns. Some
women carried their babies upon their backs, firmly secured with a bright shawl. The effect
was pretty and graceful as they darted by, or sailed slowly past, now nodding to an
acquaintance, now chirruping and throwing soft baby-talk, to the muffled little ones they
carried.
Boys and girls were chasing each other, and hiding behind the one-horse sleds that,
loaded high with peat or timber pursued their cautious way along the track marked out as
“safe”. Beautiful, queenly women were there, enjoyment sparkling in their quiet eyes.
Sometimes a long file of young men, each grasping the coat of the before him, flew by with
electric speed.

KANGAROOS
Brown out of the brown tussock a darker brown head
rises as if thrust up cautiously on a pole.
A green bird on a feathering grass-stem,
that bends under its weight, flutters
and sinks out of sight. It is the only disturbance
except for the reiterated clicking of castanets
and the fife-notes of insects.
One notices the head gone,
pulled down out of sight, like the vanished bird,
but all over the unfurled
map of the landscape minute brown
figures, dots, jump, all diminishing,
yet each pursuing
lines that intersect, making a maze
of crazy map-lines, meaningless angles.
The skin of the land is a deep fur
maddeningly come alive
with deliberate great fleas.
William Hart-Smith

mole, a rat and a toad who live near a river bank. In this passage Rat and Mole are
going to visit Mr Badger.
They waited patiently for what seemed a very long time, stamping in the snow to keep their
feet warm. At last they heard the sound of slow shuffling footsteps approaching the door
from the inside. It seemed, as the Mole remarked to the Rat, like some one walking in carpet
slippers that were too large for him and down at heel; which was intelli gent of Mole, because
that was exactly what it was.
There was the noise of a bolt shot back, and the door opened a few inches, enough to
show a long snout and a pair of sleepy blinking eyes.
“Now the very next time this happens,” said a gruff and suspicious voice, “I shall be
exceedingly angry. Who is it this time, disturbing people on such a night? Speak up!”
“O Badger,” cried the Rat, “let us in, please. It’s me, Rat, and my friend Mole and we’ve
lost our way in the snow,”
“What, Ratty, my dear little man!” exclaimed the Badger, in quite a different voice. “Come
along in, both of you at once. Why, you must be perished. Well I never! Lost in the
snow! And in the Wild Wood too, and at this time of night! But come in with you.”
The two animals tumbled over each other in their eagerness to get inside, and heard the
door shut behind them with great joy and relief.
The Badger, who wore a long dressing-gown and whose slippers were indeed very
down-at-heel, carried a flat candlestick in his paw and had probably been on his way to bed
when their summons sounded. He looked kindly down on them and patted both their heads.
“This is not the sort of night for small animals to be out,” he said paternally, “I’m afraid
you’ve been up to some of your pranks again, Ratty. Butcome along; come into the kitchen.
There’s a first-rate fire there, and supper and everything.
He shuffled on in front of them, carrying the light, and they followed him, nudging each
other in an anticipating sort of way, down a long, gloomy, and to tell the truth, decidedly
shabby passage, into a sort of central hall, out of which they could dimly see other long
tunnel-like passages branching, passages mysterious and without apparent end.

My Lost Wedding Ring
I’d snorkelled hundreds of times in the lagoon and always loved seeing the beautiful fish and
marine life. This day I had been with my young son. I remember it was quite cold that week
and the waters were far cooler than ever before.
I remember having a few problems with my gear and that I had to readjust my face mask a
number of times. It was letting in water because my youngest son, who was only eight months
old, had been using it as a teether. I later realised it was this that led to the problem.
Anyway, we snorkelled for about an hour in the morning, going up around the point as we'd
earlier discovered these striped sea-horses that were simply ihttiguing. It didn’t take long for
our joy to change to anguish.
When I returned home I realised something was missing. My heart hiccuped as, while I was
removing my flippers, I noticed my wedding ring was gone. I know I had it when I left as I
hadn’t taken it off in the twenty years I’d been married. I couldn’t believe it. I was devastated!
I raced back to the lagoon, dragging along anyone who was available and we scoured the sandy
bottom for hours. Our fingers and toes became wrinkled prunes yet it was all in vain. The colder
water must have made my fingers smaller. The heavy gold ring must have fallen into the soft
sand or lay hidden among the coral and plants.
I never found my ring, despite repeated searches. I am still hopeful one day, perhaps after a
king tide, that it will be exposed and found. I bought another but I am still miserable. It will
never be the same as the one I really was married with.

This is an obituary from the Sydney Morning Herald 10" January 2008.
P.K. Sethi 1927-2008
Millions of amputees in developing countries owe thanks to Dr P.K. Sethi for his invention
of an affordable prosthetic foot, which has enabled them to lead normal lives.
The Jaipur foot, which has never been patented, is available in more than 25 countries,
mostly poor and many with large numbers of landmine victims. Unlike many high-priced
prostheses in developed countries it can be made by traditional craftsmen, last more than five
years and costs-about $34,-_____ - anf.
Pramod Karan Sethi, who has died j in Jaipur, India at 80, was born in the a ancient t northern
Indian city of Benares, on the banks of the Ganges. His father was a professor of physics at
Benares Hindu University. On completing his medical education in India and Britain, Sethi
became a lecturer in surgery at a Medical College in Jaipur.
He became an orthopaedic surgeon by default. In 1958, his institution was about to be
inspected. for accreditation, and since there was no department of orthopaedics, he was asked to
start one at once. He always maintained that not being a qualified orthopaedic surgeon helped him
produce something that was genuinely new.
Sethi came up with his invention after years of research. He was helped by Ramachandra
Sharma, a semiliterate craftsman.
They made a foot of vulcanised rubber but found it too heavy and stiff. So, they filled the
shell with sponge rubber and modified the design.
Since 1971 when Sethi presented the design to British orthopaedic surgeons at Oxford, the
Jaipur foot has revolutionised lives in war-torn countries. It is very flexible, allowing the wearer
to run, climb trees and pedal a bicycle.
The Jaipur foot was first used outside India in Afghanistan, which had the highest number
of amputees in the world after Russian landmines caused thousands of wounds.
Sethi is survived by his wife, Sulochana, a son and three daughters.

The first half of this movie is atrociously bland. Played by TV sitcom stalwart Kevin
James (The King of Queens), the title character is an over-officious, under-achieving
chubster.
Blart covers his beat in a suburban mall with the aid of a motorised upright scooter. He
crashes into things a lot. No one respects him. He is blessed with a good heart. Cursed by a
bad diet. He so wants to be in a relationship. He has a crush on the girl who runs the hair-
extensions kiosk. If only she could see the real him, you know?
That’s enough with the character profiling. Let’s just say that Paul Blart is every Biggest
Loser contestant that has ever lived, stuffed into the body of one man.
The movie improves noticeably after it works off all that sad-sack flab and walks briskly
towards a little low-impact action.
A gang of skateboard-riding youths lay siege to the mall and take hostages. Blart misses
all the initial hubbub because he is playing a video game.
So he becomes the last line of defence against an audacious robbery that could mean
death to innocent bystanders swept along in its wake.
The remainder of Paul Blart: Mall Cop plays out as expected, the door is creaked open
for a sequel, and the film slumps down to rest.
Inessential.

Phar Lap
BEFORE Phar Lap’s second Melbourne Cup, gangsters were sending hitmen to stop him.
He was — and is — the only racehorse to become a national hero, firing the excitement of
Australia with his thundering race wins.
Phar Lap was named after the Thai word pharlap, meaning lightning, but he had a
nickname across the country — The Red Terror.
He seemed to be impossible to beat, and that was very dangerous.
Melbourne gangsters in the racing game were losing fortunes through Phar Lap and
becoming desperate.
Phar Laps’ trainer, Harry Telford, was warned of attacks through fire, acid and poison
darts as the Melbourne Cup of 1930 approached.
Strapper Tommy Woodcock was riding a pony and leading Phar Lap home from exercise
at Caulfield racecourse when he saw two suspicious men in an idling car.
Woodcock placed himself and the pony between the car and Phar Lap. The driver sped
past, blaring the horn as his mate fired a shotgun at the horse.
The shot splattered harmlessly over a high wooden fence, but Telford had had enough.
He took Phar Lap to the safety of Geelong until the race.
But the drama wasn’t over. Two hours before the race, Phar Laps float moved through
heavy rain out of Geelong, escorted by police motorcyclists.
And the engine died.
Telford and Woodcock took it in turns to crank the engine until it sputtered into life. They
reached Flemington racecourse no more than 30 minutes before the race was to start.
On that day four-year-old Phar Lap was carrying 9.12, a weight record for his age with
the odds of 11/8 on (meaning you put 11 units and if you win you only get 8 plus your
original 11). Phar Lap steamed through the race, winning effortlessly.
He was taken to America and he died in April 1932. There were unjustified rumours that
he had been poisoned by American gangsters.
Excerpt from ‘Legends Stories of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

A Special Island
Who doesn't enjoy a stay on a beautiful undeveloped island? Not many I suppose. When
that island is Rottnest Island off the Western Australian coast then there is little doubt. Almost
500,000 people visit this special island each year. The population of the island is about 150
but huge numbers of day trippers make the ninety minute journey from Perth or Fremantle on
ferries or charter boats that regularly carry eager tourists from Western Australia, the rest of
Australia and many countries.
It is an island where progress is measured in creating safe walking trails and ensuring that
the natural environment is protected well.
The total area of the island is about 2,000 hectares with pristine lakes taking up about 200
hectares. The crystal clear waters make for great swimming and boating activities. Snorkelling
with numerous fish and playful sea lions is a favourite activity. During the summer season
there can be as many as 5,000 people visiting at any one time.
The beauty of the island, the absence of high-rise buildings and noisy activities is, of
course, a major drawcard. Rottnest Island is home to a delightful creature - the quokka. It is
certain that this 30-40 centimetre high creature, somewhat like a furry rather overweight
wallaby, thrives well on Rottnest Island because of the absence of feral cats and wild dogs.
It is no wonder that many West Australians consider the island to be their favourite
holiday destination.

From The Raven by Edgar Allen Poe
Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore,
While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping,
As of someone gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door.
“ ‘Tis some visitor,” I muttered, “tapping at my chamber door;
Only this, and nothing more.”
Ah, distinctly I remember, it was in the bleak December,
And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.
Eagerly I wished the morrow; vainly I had sought to borrow
From my books surcease of sorrow, sorrow for the lost Lenore.
For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore,
Nameless here forevermore.
And the silken sad uncertain rustling of each purple curtain
Thrilled me--- filled me with fantastic terrors never felt before;
So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood repeating,
“ “Tis some visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door,
Some late visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door.
This it is, and nothing more.”
Presently my soul grew stronger; hesitating then no longer,
“Sir,” said I, “or madam, truly your forgiveness I implore;
But the fact is, I was napping, and so gently you came rapping,
And so faintly you came tapping, tapping at my chamber door,
That I scarce was sure I heard you. “Here I opened wide the door---
Darkness there, and nothing more.
Deep into the darkness peering, long I stood there, wondering, fearing
Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortals ever dared to dream before;
But the silence was unbroken, and the stillness gave no token,
And the only word there spoken was the whispered word,
Lenore?, This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word,
“Lenore!” Merely this, and nothing more.
Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning,
Soon again I heard a tapping, something louder than before,
“Surely,” said I, “surely, that is something at my window lattice.
Let me see, then, what thereat is, and this mystery explore.
Let my heart be still a moment, and this mystery explore.
“ *Tis the wind, and nothing more”

Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
Whose woods these are I think I know.
His house is in the village though;

To watch his woods fill up with snow.

To stop without a farmhouse near
Between the woods and frozen lake
The darkest evening of the year.
He gives his harness bells a shake
To ask if there is some mistake.
The only other sounds the sweep
Of easy wind and downy flake.
The woods are lovely, dark and deep.
But I have promises to keep,
And miles to go before I sleep,
And miles to go before I sleep.

Harry woke up on Sunday morning to find the dormitory blazing with winter sunlight and
his arm re-boned but very stiff. He sat up quickly and looked over at Colin’s bed, but it had
been blocked from view by the high curtains Harry had changed behind yesterday. Seeing
that he was awake, Madam Pomfrey came bustling over with a breakfast tray and then began
bending and stretching his arm and fingers.
‘All in order,’ she said, as he clumsily fed himself porridge left-handed. ‘When you’ve
finished eating, you may leave.’
Harry dressed as quickly as he could and hurried off to Gryffindor tower, desperate to tell
Ron and Hermione about Colin and Dobby, but they weren’t there. Harry left to look for them,
wondering where they could have got to and feeling slightly hurt that they weren’t interested
in whether he had his bones back or not.
As Harry passed the library, Percy Weasley strolled out of it, looking in far better spirits
than last time they’d met.
‘Oh, hello, Harry’, he said. ‘Excellent flying yesterday, really excellent. Gryffindor have
just taken the lead for the House Cup. You earned fifty points!’
“You haven’t seen Ron or Hermione, have you?’ said Harry.
‘No, I haven’t,’ said Percy, his smile fading. ‘I hope Ron’s not in another girls’ toilet...’
Harry forced a laugh, watched Percy out of sight and then headed straight for Moaning
Myrtle’s bathroom. He couldn’t see why Ron and Hermione would be in there again, but after
making sure that neither Filch nor any prefects were around, he opened the door and heard
their voices coming from a locked cubicle.
‘It’s me,’ he said, closing the door behind him. There was a clunk, a splash and a gasp
from within the cubicle.

It was therefore with some trepidation that I began riding my bicycle to work this year,
but figured I would be fairly safe because most of my journey is on dedicated bicycle tracks.

I have to contend with cyclists who think they own the bike tracks and the roads. They
overtake without warning, cut you off, weave in and out of pedestrians (even elderly
pedestrians or people with prams) and other cyclists.

ambulance would stop for him!

FILM
MONSTERS VS ALIENS (PG)
Lo. @.4
General release (90 minutes)
Jake Wilson Reviewer
WRITTEN and directed by a committee at Dreamworks Pictures, the digitally animated
Monsters vs Aliens replays the nightmares of the Atomic Age as harmless comedy: a sure
recipe for delight.
Reese Witherspoon is the voice of Susan Murphy, who is zapped by a radioactive meteor
on the eve of her wedding and grows into the Fifty Foot Woman, before being hauled to a
secret government compound and blackmailed into saving the Earth from a giant robot from
outer space.
Like Dorothy in The Wizard of OZ (1939), Susan shares her adventures with a trio of zany
male offsiders: a brainless ball of goo (Seth Rogen), a cackling yet soft-hearted giant
cockroach (Hugh Laurie), and a blustering two-legged dinosaur (Will Arnett) who lets others
do the fighting when the chips are down.
In its fusion of boys’ adventure films and chick flicks, the plot also recalls another Seth
Rogen vehicle: Judd Apatow’s pregnancy comedy Knocked Up (2007), which co-starred
Katherine Heigl as a poised entertainment reporter who was forced by her physical
circumstances to join a band of slobs and geeks.
Here, Rogen’s blob steals the show with his rapt idiot grin and habit of harmlessly
engulfing his friends: some of the resulting jokes about gender and identity are quite
sophisticated, but that doesn’t mean small children won’t get the point.
While the animators never strive for painterly beauty, their monsters and aliens all give
highly expressive and precisely timed performances. A central battle sequence in San
Francisco recreates the city in impressively accurate detail, with Susan strapping a car to each
foot and roller skating down one of the steep streets.
Since this is a film for children, we know with virtual certainty that nobody we care about
will come to harm. But there’s no reason this deft fantasy shouldn’t appeal to adults as well.
Once in a while, it’s good to be told that humanity will muddle through, that
transformation is often a blessing — and that monsters can be heroes, even if they’re girls.
The Age April 2"7, 2009

Gracey didn’t sleep much that Saturday night before the final. I know ‘cause I could hear her
talking to Mum in their room along the hall. It was the middle of the night, getting later and
later. No use trying to work out what they were saying, of course, but Gracey was crying for
alittle while, and moving around, sometimes almost shouting, and other times so soft I wasn’t
sure she was speaking. And all the time, Mum’s voice was the same, a gentle murmur, like a
song, calming Gracey down.
I left my room and knocked on their door. Inside, Gracey was sitting on her bed with her
knees up to her chin and her arms wrapped tight round her legs. She always scrunched herself
into a ball like that when she was unhappy or frightened. I didn’t say anything, just sat on the
end of Gracey’s bed. It was sometimes like that when I came to listen to Mum and Gracey
talking. Gracey would look at me and witk, or smile or touch me for a second. It was like
she said, “Hello, Dougy. You can be here, part of us.” But that night Gracey was too upset,
too serious. She was saying, “But it’ll be so obvious if I don’t win. I'll stand out from the
others. Any of those white girls can come last and nobody will say anything, nobody will
even notice. Why do I have to be the one people will talk about?”
“TI know, it’s not fair,” said Mum in the same quiet voice I’d been hearing along the hall.
“That’s what blacks always have to put up with. Lots of noise when you win, lots of noise
when you lose. And they like to see you lose, too. Makes’em feel better. I seen it plenty of
times. They’re worried you might be better than them. That scares ’em inside. They really
don’t think much of you, and it’d be a terrible thing for you to beat ’em at something. That
just the way whities are. You got to worry "bout yourself.”
“It makes me angry,” said Gracey.
“Yes, it makes you angry. I know. But you got to make sure you’re angry at the white
blokes who treat you like that. No good being mad ’cause you’re a black. Just makes you
hate yourself in the end. I seen that too.”
There was lots more said after that. And every time Gracey sounded hopeless, Mum found
a way to change her mind.
Excerpt from ‘Dougy’ By James Moloney

It was quiet in the pines except for the sound of the wind humming through their branches.
Robbie pushed his hands against a tree trunk and straightened one leg, then the other, behind
him. He could feel his calf muscles pulling and the bark digging into his palms. Next he
rested his heel on a stump and bent forward over his outstretched leg until the hamstring
muscle in his thigh warned him to go no further. He swapped legs and repeated the exercise.
His body had ceased revving like a car with the accelerator stuck. Robbie recognized the
calm he usually felt at this time before a race. His heart would pound again when he lined up
with the others at the start, but now he felt almost sleepy. He breathed deeply, shook his arms
and legs, and focused his mind on the course he, Mum and Tid had walked together this
morning.
It was a tight, twisting, hilly trail. A good cross-country course, the parents said. Robbie
remembered the narrow gateway a hundred metres from the start. He would have to be near
the lead if he didn’t want to wait his turn to get through there. Then there was a narrow track
with a barbed-wire fence on one side and a steep drop on the other. The course opened out
after that.
They had walked up a gradual slope, around a marker in a clump of trees and down a
gravel road, where the pebbles skidded under their feet, to a creek crossing. “Go for it up the
hill,” Mum had advised. “Careful coming down this gravel. Not too fast or you’ll go head
over heels into the creek.”

He crawled under the fence. Cold darkness crept over him. Something growled, not far
away. Was this really only a golf course? It felt and sounded like a jungle packed with wild
animals. He took a step, and his foot crunched on crackly twigs and leaves.
The jungle became silent.
Harry reached into a pocket, and got out his only treasure: the Hohner Harmonica, a
mouth organ his Great Aunt Agnes had given him in the week before her death six years
ago.
His parents wouldn’t let him play it in the house, so he practiced at the bottom of the
backyard, beneath the peppercorn tree. Now he played a tune composed specially (by
Harry) to inspire bravery.
It was a marching tune called The Harry March. If you haven’t heard it, please go to
your record store and ask for it. It’s probably world famous by now. Then you’ll understand
how Harry was able to take another step, and another, into the wilds of Rose Bay golf
course.
An owl hooted. An icy breeze curled around Harry’s neck.
Holding tight to his harmonica, he sprinted across a fairway. The grass looked silver.
The trees and bushes were black. He turned around and around.
Which way was Newcastle Street? He had no idea. He was lost.
He pushed through bushes and around trees, but instead of Newcastle Street he came to
another fairway, and stumbled into a bunker. The sand was freezing. He scrambled out,
wiping his hands on his jeans.
“You’re lost, aren’t you?’ came a snobby-sounding voice from behind him.
Harry turned so quickly he nearly fell over.

START BACK ON A GOOD NOTE
THE summer holidays are over (boo hoo!), but returning to school needn’t be a negative

in class.
EAT BREAKFAST

house each morning. The time poor should prepare a sandwich or smoothie the night before.
MAKE FRIENDS

as simple as saying hello to your locker neighbour can help you feel a part of things.

sections.title: Questions 6-9
sections.passage:
Lasseter’s Lost Reef
IN 1897, Harold Bell Lasseter was found unconscious in the desert southwest of Alice
Springs by an Afghan camel-driver — with some interesting rocks.
And the legend grew from there.
Lasseter said he had found a fabulously rich gold reef in the trackless desert out west, but
he would not say where. He wanted to lead an expedition to it.
For a while nobody seemed to be interested, but in 1911 there was an expedition — only
to be beaten back by the toughness of the country.
Lasseter tried one more time, in 1930, with a plane, a six-wheeled lorry and a team of
experts.
The plane crashed and Lasseter said they were over 250 kilometres off course.
The party on the ground battled on but finally decided to go home — except for Lasseter
and a dingo shooter, Paul Johns.
They pressed on, and Lasseter finally said he had found his reef. But he would not show
Johns where it was. They fought in the desert and Johns turned back, leaving Lasseter with
two camels.
The camels bolted from Lasseter, and though an Aboriginal tribe helped him he was
getting weaker and suffering from sandy-blight blindness.
He buried his papers under a tree marked ‘DIG’, crawled into a cave and died.
Nobody has ever found any trace of Lasseter’s reef.
From ‘Legends of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

Saturday was clear and frosty, and the sun felt far away. A freezing gale blew from the south-
west. Robbie stood on the back of the truck and faced like a dog into the wind. It tried to get
under his cap, but he had jammed it down tightly. His eyes watered. His old football jumper
stuck to his chest and billowed from his back as if it were trying to blow away. He could be
in the warm cabin with Mum and Tid while they drove to the first mob of sheep to be fed,
but he liked it on the back. The main range was bright blue today and only its white icing of
snow separated it from the sky. The air felt as cold and clean as mountain water in his lungs.
Funny how in a drought all you can see on the ground is poo, thought Robbie. While the
grass had withered to dry wisps, the balls of horse manure seemed to grow all over the
paddock like some strange fungus. The horses were sheltering from the wind in a clump of
snow gums: Dad’s bay horse, Storm; the old creamy and her filly; dear old Thomas, as shaggy

Tom’s brush with saur teeth
Harbant Gill
SIXTEEN dinosaurs soar two storeys high in Australia’s biggest dinosaur exhibition, which opens at
the Melbourne Museum today.
The biggest creature is as long as six cars parked end to end and has a neck half as long as its
bulking body.
“They would break that roof,” said six-year-old Tom, one of the earliest visitors to the Dinosaur
Walk, which has taken a year to come together with state backing.
Visitors can see the skeletons, which have been gathered from around the world, from below, eye-
to-eye or from a tree-top walkway near the largest flying animal of all time.
There’s a chance to feel their teeth, learn their hunting skills, check out their eggs, measure
yourself against a thigh bone and touch their fossilized dung.
Sundials take visitors back 230 million years to when the earliest dinosaurs appeared, and video
animation brings the creatures to life through a headset viewfinder.
Museum-goers can also meet Australia’s megafauna and the animals that roamed the earth before
and after the dinosaurs.
Arts Minister Lynne Kosky heard the dinosaurs roar and their stomachs rumble before she opened
the permanent exhibition.
“When Iwas achild you could never get this close, let alone touch dinosaur bones,” she said.
“What’s most extraordinary about this is you get a sense of the size — we are quite humble human
beings.”
Herald-Sun April 3 2009

This is the beginning of a book called The Nimbin by Jenny Wagner
“! can’t understand you, Philippa,” her mother said. “All that fresh air outside, and here you
are stuck inside, reading.”
Philippa sighed and sat up on her bunk. “Can't | stay in the caravan? It’s roasting out
there.” a
“Then go for a swim,” her mother said brightly. “It'll do you more good than just
reading.” ,
Philippa stuffed the book in her beach bag and went outside, banging the door
behind her. Her father, sitting in the annexe, looked up as she passed. “Anything wrong?”
“No,” said Philippa shortly, and headed off down the track towards the lagoon.
The dust at her feet spurted up into little clouds as she marched along, and she
watched with satisfaction as her feet got blacker and blacker. Well, you had to have
something your own way now and then. Here they were on holiday, they’d been here a
week or more, and still she hadn’t had a chance to read her book.
At the lagoon she turned off into the dunes and walked towards the ocean till she
found a good spot. There was no shade, but she was reasonably well hidden; if her
parents wanted her for anything they wouldn't find her too easily.
She spread her towel out on the sand and opened her book. But it was a blazing hot
day. The sun shone back off the white sand and the white paper, dazzling her. She pulled
the towel out from under her and hung it over her head instead.
She found her place and started to read, but an irritating little breeze suddenly came up
from nowhere and turned the page before she was ready. She found her place again, and
the same thing happened. She wriggled on to her side and held the book open with her
elbow.
Presently something began to crawl up her leg. She twitched, and the crawling stopped.
After while it started again, and this time when she jerked it didn’t stop, but went on
crawling up her calf. She jumped away in fright, but there was nothing there.
Behind her a dark little shadow leapt to its feet and followed her a little way, then
disappeared into the dunes.

The first place that I can well remember, was a large pleasant meadow with a pond of clear water
in it. Some shady trees leaned over it, and rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep end. Over
the hedge on one side we looked into a ploughed field, and on the other we looked over a gate at
our master’s house, which stood by the roadside; at the top of the meadow was a plantation of fir
trees, and at the bottom a running brook overhung by a steep bank.
‘Whilst I was young I lived upon my mother’s milk, as I could not eat grass. In the day
time I ran by her side, and at night I lay down close by her. When it was hot, we used to stand
by the pond in the shade of the trees, and when it was cold, we had a nice warm shed near the
plantation.
As soon as I was old enough to eat grass, my mother used to go out to work in the day
time, and came back in the evening.
There were six young colts in the meadow besides me; they were older than I was; some
were nearly as large as grown-up horses. I used to run with them, and had great fun; we used to
gallop all together round and round the field, as hard as we could go. Sometimes we had rather
rough play, for they would frequently bite and kick as well as gallop.
One day, when there was a good deal of kicking, my mother whinnied to me to come to
her, and then she said, - ‘’I wish you to pay attention to what I am going to say to you. The
colts who live here are very good colts, but they are carthorse colts, and, of course, they have not
learned manners. You have been well bred and well born; your father has a great name in these
parts, and your grandfather won the cup two years at the Newmarket races; your grandmother
had the sweetest temper of any horse I ever knew, and I think you have never seen me kick or
bite. I hope you will grow up gentle and good, and never learn bad ways; do your work with a
good will, lift your feet up well when you trot, and never bite or kick even in play.”
I have never forgotten my mother’s advice; I knew she was a wise old horse, and our
master thought a great deal of her. Her name was Duchess, but he often called her Pet.

The Rainbow Serpent
IN the Dreamtime a great rainbow shimmered across the flat land.
The spirit of the rainbow slid from the sky to touch the land’s northern edge.
And the spirit became a serpent, gleaming with the red of earth, blue of lake, green of
forest, and the gold of morning.
It kicked up a mountain, slithered south across the land, cutting into the rock and earth,
as it moved. It left patterns of streams, rivers, valleys and gorges.
The rainbow serpent rolled up a range of mountains as long as the land, turning rivers
toward the sea and others away from the sea.
It now rests in a lake, but it likes to swim in the sea. It can be heard at the beginning of
the rains in the north as a whistling sound. The sound is a storm passing through its horns.
A rainbow is the serpent leaping back into the sky, and a shooting star is the serpent
watching you.
From ‘Legends of Australia’ by Allan Baillie

The McDermotts were rich, maybe not filthy rich, but still rich. They’d been coming to the
Port for ages, their shack was one of the first ones here. We called it a shack but it was bigger
and better than our houses. The correct term, I suppose, was holiday house.
You always knew when the Maccas arrived in town for the start of the holidays, you could
hear them. They’d come charging down the main street, in the latest-model Statesman, with
a huge boat behind, and Mr Mac would be learning on the horn — beep, beep, beep all the
way to the jetty.
Mr and Mrs Mac looked like Americans. I don’t know why, they just did. They both had
blond hair with lots of contours. And they wore gold jewellery. Mr Mac spent most of his
time on his boat, churning up the gulf. While Mrs Mac would be out in the back yard, on a
banana lounge, in a bikini, working on her tan.
They had two kids — Andrew, who was my age, and Craig, who was a year older. They
had blond hair too. Which was lucky for them, because they were surfies. They wore board
shorts all the time, they had surfboards and they were always reading magazines like Tracks
and Ripcurl. They did everything, except surf. Not in the Port anyway, because we had no
waves. Didn’t worry those Maccas though. Didn’t worry the local girls either, they all thought
the Maccas were drop-dead gorgeous. Even my own stupid sisters. Especially my own stupid
sisters.
I have to admit, though, that those Maccas had the knack, they knew exactly what to say
to girls. It was uncanny. I used to think that by hanging around with them, I’d learn a thing
or two, I'd get better. No way. I was still as hopeless as ever. In the end I decided chatting up
girls was like rolling your tongue — it was a genetic thing. Either you were born with it, like
those Maccas, or you talked about dead stars, like me.
Excerpt from ‘Deadly Unna?’ ‘by Phillip Gwynne
