I’d sail my ship,
I'd sail my ship
Through Eastern seas;
Down to a beach where the slow waves thunder —

Boom! Boom! Boom!
On the sun-bright sand.

And climb to the trees,
The six dark trees,
Hands and knees
To the coconut trees,
Face to the cliff as the stones patter down,
Up, up, up, staggering stumbling,
Round the comer where the rock is crumbling,
Round this shoulder,
Over this boulder,
Up to the top where the six trees stand.

My chin in my hands, and gaze
At the dazzle of sand below,
And the green waves curling slow,
And the grey-blue distant haze

First Day: Thursday, August 4, 2005
It was only. by the grace of God that the Edgbaston Test match was spared from cancellation after an
astonishing natural disaster. Seven days before the Test was scheduled to begin, a freak tornado roared
in from nowhere to rip through nearby suburbs tearing off roofs, smashing garden sheds. Injuries
were few, but streets were left resembling bombsites, and over at the cricket ground Steve Rouse, the
head groundsman, had his work cut out after several inches of rain interrupted his preparation for the
big match. If the tornado had whooshed a kilometre off its course there would have been no Test
match. Severe damage to the pavilion, the Eric Hollies Stand and much else could not have been made
safe in time.
England remained unchanged from the Lord’s Test, a rare thing and Australia had only the one
enforced change. The pitch, like so many others, defied accurate behavioural prediction, but the sky
was overcast, so that when Ricky Ponting won the toss again he put England in. Among the
adjectives employed were “aggressive”, “crazy”, “complacent”, “defensive” and — from Mike Gatting
29 66 32 66
— “arrogant”. Did the Aussie skipper fear another Harmison onslaught as at Lord’s? Was he trying to
demonstrate that McGrath’s absence didn’t worry him? Was he still reeling from McGrath’s injury
and incapable of clear thought? If England were 70 for six at lunch Ponting would be a bold hero.
England actually went to lunch at 132 for the loss of Strauss after 27 overs. Vaughan and others had
drawn strength after Lord’s by reminding themselves that since 2002-03 England had lost six Test
matches and had bounced back immediately each time to win the next one. This resilience now
seemed to be a vital part of their culture, the result of positive thinking rarely evident in England
teams of recent years.
The Australians, all bedecked in those wonderful baggy green caps (some of them now looking rather
worn — the caps, that is) watched askance as Trescothick cover-drove Lee for three fours in the third

Ms. Jones and Guitar in the Spirit of the Place
The New York Times
By NATE CHINEN - April 2, 2008
“I've never played solo here, ever,” Norah Jones said just after midnight Monday on the
Lower East Side, surveying a capacity crowd with a flicker of a smile. “Much less on guitar,”
she added, fiddling with the strap of her cherry-red Fender Stratocaster. “But I figured in the
spirit of the Living Room, I’d try something new.”
Ms. Jones, the not-so-secret guest on a show celebrating the Living Room’s 10th
anniversary, was appearing in the company of friends. Among them were the singer-
songwriters Jesse Harris, Richard Julian and Sasha Dobson, whose separate sets involved
generous overlap in personnel and style. So in addition to commemorating the first decade
of a club beloved by many — as an incubator of talent, the Living Room can suggest a much
mellower and tidier successor to CBGB — the evening cast warm light on the close-knit
family of folk singers that still counts Ms. Jones as one of its own.
With so many collaborators on hand, her solo set didn’t last long. She sang “Cold, Cold
Heart,” the Hank Williams standard, along with an impish new original about her dog. Then
she welcomed Ms. Dobson for a couple of duets before calling up the Little Willies, her frisky
five- piece vintage-country band, which features Mr. Julian.
Much of their effervescent set recalied the Little Willies’ self- titled debut album, released in
2006. Singing in close but casual harmony, Ms. Jones and Mr. Julian tucked into lighthearted
songs by Jimmy Driftwood, Kris Kristofferson and the band’s namesake, Willie Nelson. The
mood was jaunty, with Ms. Jones at an upright piano and Jim Campilongo playing suitably
twangy electric guitar.
-Reading page 1
In one standout moment, Ms. Jones presented an unpublished Hank Williams song, with his
lyrics set to her melody. Its substance was classic Hank (opening line: “Time after time you’ve
proven untrue”), and its country-waltz setting was easeful and fine, a natural showcase for
Ms. Jones and her gently aerated, coolly intimate style.
Just as satisfying, on the other end of the dynamic spectrum, was Loretta Lynn’s “Fist City.”
It's not the sort of song anyone would immediately associate with Ms. Jones — a threat of
violence, shot through with feisty humor — which is what made it such a delight. Projecting
with a bell-like tone, she sounded gutsy and tough, almost scarily self- assured.
Mr. Julian had exuded a cagier brand of confidence in his own set, backed by a three-piece
band. His songs were terse and often wry, with frequent New York City allusions. And he
sang two of the only remotely political songs of the evening, though his topics, religious
hypocrisy and rampant capitalism, preserved a nonspecific air.
In Ms. Dobson’s set, urbane jazz chords met with a likably unfussy style. She welcomed Ms.
Jones on background vocals for one near-calypso and elsewhere paired off winningly with
Mr. Julian. Her sharp band included Mr. Harris on banjo and Tony Scherr on electric guitar,
and she featured them well.
Mr. Harris, who also played banjo throughout his set, observed that it marked a reunion of
the Ferdinandos, an old Living Room staple. Along with Mr. Scherr, the bassist Tim Luntzel
and the drummer Dan Rieser, he delivered a strong batch of old and new songs. His voice
was reedy, bordering on a whine, but his presence was quietly charismatic.
And his originals, among the best of the evening, whisked the set along. Mr. Harris is another
of this scene’s successes, having written “Don’t Know Why,” the sleeper hit that introduced
Ms. Jones. But he wasn’t afraid to knock the songs around. Twice he ventured something
the band had never touched before. He did this, he said, “in the spirit of the Living Room.”
Both times, the results were impressive. bordering on a whine, but his presence was quietly
charismatic.

This is an obituary from the Sydney Morning Herald 10" January 2008.
P.K. Sethi 1927 — 2008
Millions of amputees in developing countries owe thanks to Dr P.K. Sethi for his invention
of an affordable prosthetic foot, which has enabled them to lead normal lives.
The Jaipur foot, which has never been patented, is available in more than 25 countries,
mostly poor and many with large numbers of landmine victims. Unlike many high-priced
prostheses in developed countries it can be made by traditional craftsmen, last more than five
years and costs about $34.
Pramod Karan Sethi, who has died in Jaipur, India at 80, was born in the ancient northern
Indian city of Benares, on the banks of the Ganges. His father was a professor of physics at
Benares Hindu University. On completing his medical education in India and Britain, Sethi
became a lecturer in surgery at a Medical College in Jaipur.
He became an orthopaedic surgeon by default. In 1958, his institution was about to be
inspected for accreditation, and since there was no department of orthopaedics, he was asked
to start one at once. He always maintained that not being a qualified orthopaedic surgeon helped
him produce something that was genuinely new.
Sethi came up with his invention after years of research. He was helped by
Ramachandra Sharma, a semiliterate craftsman.
They made a foot of vulcanised rubber but found it too heavy and stiff. So, they filled
the shell with sponge rubber and modified the design.
Since 1971 when Sethi presented the design to British orthopaedic surgeons at Oxford,
the Jaipur foot has revolutionised lives in war-torn countries. It is very flexible, allowing the
wearer to run, climb trees and pedal a bicycle.
The Jaipur foot was first used outside India in Afghanistan, which had the highest number
of amputees in the world after Russian landmines caused thousands of wounds.
Sethi is survived by his wife, Sulochana, a son and three daughters.

This extract is taken from a book Minerals and Energy by Brian and Barbara Kennedy.
Gemstones, like other minerals, were mostly formed as a result of tremendous heat below the earth’s
surface. Some gemstones are more valuable than others.
Opals and sapphires are the only gemstones found in large quantities in Australia. Australia produces
almost all of the world’s opal. The main source is Coober Pedy in South Australia, but opals are also
found at Andamooka, South Australia, and at Lightning Ridge in New South Wales.
Opals are used mainly for jewellery and are very popular with overseas tourists, in spite of the fact
that some people believe that they bring bad luck.
Australia also produces half the world’s sapphires. The main fields are at Anakie in Queensland and
at Glen Innes and Inverell in New South Wales. Discoveries of high quality sapphires and an increase
in world demand have caused new interest in the sapphire mining industry in the Glen Innes-Inverell
area. Modern excavating machines are being used by large mining companies on their leases. Small
scale mining for sapphires has been in progress for most of the 20th century. Thailand is by far the
largest customer for Australian sapphires.
Chrysoprase, a green stone, is the most important gemstone after sapphires. It is found mainly in the
Marlborough district of Queensland.
Industrial diamonds exist in all states, especially in Western Australia and in New South Wales in the
Copeton-Bingara district. In the 1970s, the blue clay kimberlite pipes in which diamonds are formed
were discovered in the Kimberleys district of Western Australia. This led to the discovery of rich
diamond fields in the area. Because of their extreme hardness, diamonds can be used in high-speed
tools for cutting and drilling hard materials.
Gemstone fossicking is a very popular pastime for hundreds of Australians and there are many
valuable collections. Collectors are often lapidarists who cut, polish and set their own gemstones.

head groundsman, had his work cut out after several inches of rain interrupted his preparation for the

match. Severe damage to the pavilion, the Eric Hollies Stand and much else could not have been made
safe in time.

enforced change. The pitch, like so many others, defied accurate behavioural prediction, but the sky
was overcast, so that when Ricky Ponting won the toss again he put England in. Among the
adjectives employed were “aggressive”, “crazy”, “complacent”, “defensive” and — from Mike Gatting

drawn strength after Lord’s by reminding themselves that smce 2002-03 England had lost six Test
matches and had bounced back immediately each time to win the next one. This resilience now

worn ~ the caps, that is) watched askance as Trescothick cover-drove Lee for three fours in the third

“Just like a girl,” said Edmund to himself, “sulking somewhere, and won't accept an apology.”
He looked round him again and decided he did not much like this place, and had almost made

and the sound came nearer and nearer and at last there swept into sight a sledge drawn by two
reindeer.
The reindeer were about the size of Shetland ponies and their hair was so white that even
the snow hardly looked white compared with them; their branching horns were gilded and shone
like something on fire when the sunrise caught them. Their harness was of scarlet leather and
covered with bells. On the sledge, driving the reindeer, sat a fat dwarf who would have been
about three feet high if he had been standing. He was dressed in polar bear’s fur and on his
head he wore a red hood with a long gold tassel hanging down from its point; his huge beard
covered his knees and served him instead of a rug. But behind him, on a much higher seat in
the middle of the sledge sat a very different person — a great lady, taller than any woman that
Edmund had ever seen. She also was covered in white fur up to her throat and held a long
straight golden wand in her right hand and wore a golden crown on her head. Her face was white
— not merely pale, but white like snow or paper or icing-sugar, except for her very red mouth. It
was a beautiful face in other respects, but proud and cold and stern.
The sledge was a fine sight as it came sweeping towards Edmund with the bells jingling and
the dwarf cracking his whip and the snow flying up on each side of it.
“Stop!” said the Lady, and the dwarf pulled the reindeer up so sharp that they almost sat
down. Then they recovered themselves and stood champing their bits and blowing. In the frosty
air the breath coming out of their nostrils looked like smoke.

This is the beginning of a book called ‘The Nimbin’ by Jenny Wagner
“| can’t understand you, Philippa,” her mother said. “All that fresh air outside, and here you
are stuck inside, reading.”
Philippa sighed and sat up on her bunk. “Can't | stay in the caravan? It’s roasting out
there.”
“Then go for a swim,” her mother said brightly. “It'll do you more good than just reading.”
Philippa stuffed the book in her beach bag and went outside, banging the door behind
her. Her father, sitting in the annexe, looked up as she passed. “Anything wrong?”
“No,” said Philippa shortly, and headed off down the track towards the lagoon.
The dust at her feet spurted up into little clouds as she marched along, and she
watched with satisfaction as her feet got blacker and blacker. Well, you had to have
something your own way now and then. Here they were on holiday, they'd been here a week
or more, and still she hadn’t had a chance to read her book.
At the lagoon she turned off into the dunes and walked towards the ocean till she found
a good spot. There was no shade, but she was reasonably well hidden; if her parents
wanted her for anything they wouldn't find her too easily.
She spread her towel out on the sand and opened her book. But it was a blazing hot
day. The sun shone back off the white sand and the white paper, dazzling her. She pulled
the towel out from under her and hung it over her head instead.
She found her place and started to read, but an irritating little breeze suddenly came up
from nowhere and turned the page before she was ready. She found her place again, and
the same thing happened. She wriggled on to her side and held the book open with her
elbow.
Presently something began to crawl up her leg. She twitched, and the crawling stopped.
After while it started again, and this time when she jerked it didn’t stop, but went on crawling
up her calf. She jumped away in fright, but there was nothing there.
Behind her a dark little shadow leapt to its feet and followed her a little way, then
disappeared into the dunes.

This is part of a book ‘Black Beauty’ written by Anna Sewell
The first place that I can well remember, was a large pleasant meadow with a pond of clear
water in it. Some shady trees leaned over it, and rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep
end. Over the hedge on one side we looked into a ploughed field, and on the other we
looked over a gate at our master’s house, which stood by the roadside; at the top of the
meadow was a plantation of fir trees, and at the bottom a running brook overhung by a
steep bank.
Whilst I was young I lived upon my mother’s milk, as I could not eat grass. In the
daytime I ran by her side, and at night I lay down close by her. When it was hot, we used
to stand by the pond in the shade of the trees, and when it was cold, we had a nice warm
shed near the plantation.
As soon as I was old enough to eat grass, my mother used to go out to work in the
daytime, and came back in the evening.
There were six young colts in the meadow besides me; they were older than I was;
some were nearly as large as grown-up horses. I used to run with them, and had great fun;
we used to gallop all together round and round the field, as hard as we could go. Sometimes
we had rather rough play, for they would frequently bite and kick as well as gallop.
One day, when there was a good deal of kicking, my mother whinnied to me to
come to her, and then she said, - ‘I wish you to pay attention to what I am going to say to
you. The colts who live here are very good colts, but they are carthorse colts, and, of course,
they have not learned manners. You have been well bred and well born; your father has a
great name in these parts, and your grandfather won the cup two years at the Newmarket
races; your grandmother had the sweetest temper of any horse I ever knew, and I think you
have never seen me kick or bite. I hope you will grow up gentle and good, and never learn
bad ways; do your work with a good will, lift your feet up well when you trot, and never
bite or kick even in play.”
I have never forgotten my mother’s advice; I knew she was a wise old horse, and our
master thought a great deal of her. Her name was Duchess, but he often called her Pet.

This is an article in a book called Why? What? Where?
Nobody knows what the first language was. But scientists feel quite sure that nobody speaks it today,
because all languages change and keep on changing as long as people use them. One language may
change in different ways in different places and grow into several separate languages.
People are always inventing new words. For example, radium was made up as a name for a new
radioactive substance when scientists discovered it over a hundred years ago.
Words even change in one family. Children don’t always use words exactly the way their parents do.
They make small changes in the sounds or in the meaning. In time a lot of these little changes add up
and make big changes. If we could meet the people who spoke English five hundred years ago, we
probably couldn’t understand much of anything they said.
English was originally brought over by the Anglo-Saxons when they invaded Britain in the fifth and
sixth centuries. When Celtic monks came to convert the country, they brought some Latin and Greek
words with them; and in the ninth and tenth centuries Norse invaders from Scandinavia also brought
new words. The Norman invasion of 1066 introduced many new French words, which had originally
come from Latin.
The growth of learning, which began with the discoveries of the fifteenth and sixteenth century
explorers, led to many new words joining our language; and the development of science led to the
adoption of many Greek and Latin names for plants and animals and scientific inventions (e.g.
telephone). As knowledge grows, words are still being added.
Thus, English is a mixture of several languages. Scientists believe that these languages and many
others all grew out of the same ancestor language which they call Indo-European. Nobody speaks
Indo-European now, but some of its descendants, besides English, are German, Latin, French, Greek,
Russian and many of the different tongues spoken in India.
— Reading pagel

The Great Journey
In the thirteenth century, there lived two adventurous brothers, Niccolo and Maffeo Polo.
Niccolo had a young son named Marco. The two brothers set out in 1254, to travel across a
large portion of Asia to China. They travelled along what was called the Silk Road. It was
not a road of course. It was just a set way to go from town to town and oasis to oasis.

questions.stem: It was often very dangerous. Thieves and murderers would sometimes attack the rich camel caravans. Many different products were brought along this route. Silver and glass from Europe was often traded for bales of silk. These goods would change hands many times on the twelve thousand kilometre journey between the capitals of China and Europe.
options: When Niccolo and Maffeo returned to Italy, they had been away from home in Venice for
Niccolo and Maffeo decided to return to China once again and this time to take Marco, who
was seventeen years old, with them. So in the year 1271, the three Polos set out to cross

the vast continent of Asia. Soon they had reached, by ship, the busy port of Ayas. They travelled through Armenia to reach and trade in Baghdad. 23 . Then they moved off through the harsh desert country of Persia to the port of Ormuz. In this important trading town, merchants from Europe came to buy pearls, precious stones, ivory and spices. As they left Ormuz, they found themselves crossing a wild and almost waterless country. On they travelled through Turkestan, into the high snow-covered mountain plateau called the Pamir Plateau. Then the Polos entered the beautiful city of Samarkand, famous for its orchards and gardens. 24 . Near a large, salt lake, Lop Nor, they found this desert strewn with the bones of men and animals. Shortly after crossing this last desert, the hardest part of the journey was over. More than three years after leaving Venice, the Polos reached the Gateway to China, the city of Yumen. Yumen is a Chinese word which means the Jade Gate. By this time, the great ruler of China, Kublai Khan, had heard of their arrival. When the Polos were forty days from Shangtu they, were met by messengers from the Great Khan. The rest of the journey was quite easy, as the messengers helped them all they could. Soon the Polos entered the beautiful valley of Shangtu. In the centre stood the great, white, marble palace of Kublai Khan. This is an Aboriginal legend.
Very early in the beginning of the Dreamtime there were no kangaroos in this land.
A group of men were out hunting one day, when suddenly they were hit by the
worst windstorm they had ever experienced. Large trees were blown over, small ones
were carried away into the sky, and huge boulders were tossed around like pebbles in
a children’s game.
The hunters were lucky to reach the safety of a cave. They sat in its shelter and
watched the storm take its course. After a while they were amazed to see a band of
animals being carried across the sky by the wind. They had never seen animals of this
sort before.
The men shook their heads in bewilderment as they discussed this extraordinary
sight, and realised that the creatures must have been brought by the wind from a distant
place that no-one in their group had ever visited.
The animals were quite large and covered in fur. They had small heads and short
front legs. It was obvious that they were very distressed at being blown through the wild
air. Frantically they kept stretching out their hind legs and their tails in an effort to make
contact with the ground.
The hunters watched keenly from their cave as the animals strained and battled
desperately against the wind. At last some of them did manage to find a toehold and
tailhold and anchor themselves to solid earth. The windstorm began to pass, and the
animals, which had forced their way down were left behind.
The watching hunters could now see that the animals had overstretched
themselves in their desperation to reach the ground. Their hind legs and tails were
elongated out of all proportion to the rest of their bodies. It really looked quite strange,
but the animals themselves did not seem particularly upset. Perhaps they were so
pleased to be on steady ground that nothing else mattered.
So far the hunters had been watching all this as an amazing event that would
make a good story. They took it for granted that the animals would run away
immediately, trying to get back to their own land.
It seemed that although the animals were tired and bewildered they were also
inquisitive. They began to look for shade, grass and water, and quickly found them
This was exactly the sort of place they liked and it soon became clear that they had
decided to stay.
, — Reading page 1

Kites of Many Kinds
Kites have been flown around the world for thousands of years. As early as 3000
years ago, the Chinese built and flew kites. There are many legends in Chinese and
Japanese folklore that tell about a great ‘bird’ that stayed in the air for many days. Buddhist
missionaries are thought to have spread the knowledge and secrets of kite building and
flying, from China to Japan. Some of the tales from Asia tell of man-carrying kites.
In some lands, legends suggest that if a man or woman was thought to have
committed a crime they were strapped onto a kite and thrown out of a tower. If the kite
landed safely, the person was allowed to go free — a safe landing was proof of innocence.

were not to set foot again on the mainland. The father wanted to get his son back to the
mainland so they built a large kite using bamboo and pieces of their clothing. The legend
says that the kite carried the son safely back to the mainland and there he was able to seek

help for his father. Today, kites are painted and decorated as symbols and flown during festivals and celebrations. During the Boys’ Festival held each year in Japan, every family with a baby boy born that year flies a kite shaped like a carp. This fish symbol means that the son, like the carp, will progress through the river of his life. Scientists have used kites for experiments for hundreds of years. Perhaps the most famous of these was Benjamin Franklin. He made a common kite with two crossed sticks covered with silk. 21 . He tied ordinary string into his kite and then tied on a key. Next, he waited for a thunder cloud. His son was helping him with the experiment. They knew that, if they were right, the experiment could be dangerous. They were very careful and took cover inside. 22 When the rain met the kite and string, the key did conduct the electricity, and they knew they were right. Men began to use kites to measure all kinds of things about weather. By 1900, they were able to measure temperature, moisture, wind speed and barometric pressure. Today, many of these measurements are made by using balloons and planes. 23 Engineers used kites to carry ropes and cables across rivers. The kite pulled the cords across the river and settled in trees. By repeating this process, a bridge across the river was gradually formed. Kites have been used for spy missions. 24 . This article comes from a book about insects written by David Suzuki
Spiders are distant cousins of insects. Like insects, they wear their skeletons on the
outside. But they have only two body parts. Their heads and thoraxes are joined together
in one part called a cephalothorax. They also have an abdomen. And here’s the
difference that’s easiest to spot between insects and spiders — all spiders have eight legs.
(As you already know, insects get along fine with six.) Spiders belong to a class of
animals called arachnida. Some of the spiders’ relatives are ticks, mites and scorpions
Like insects, spiders lay eggs. But they don’t go through a larval stage. Little
spiders hatch out of the eggs looking just like their parents, except that they’re much
smaller. As they grow bigger, they shed their skins many times. If all the little spiders
stayed in the place where they hatched, they would have to fight each other for food. In
fact, they might even eat each other. They need to travel far away for food. How do you
think they do it?
Spiders don’t have wings. But they do have a way to fly through the air when they
need to. They produce fine strong strands of silk from six spinnerets on their abdomens.
The silk is liquid, but it dries as soon as the air touches it. When the spiders want to
travel, they raise their abdomens and send out a strand of silk. The silk thread is caught
by the breeze. The spider is carried off through the air. This is called ballooning.
Although most of them only go up a few hundred metres, ballooning spiders have been
found 4200 metres up in the air! Spiders also use shorter silk strands as bridges from
one place to another.
All spiders are hunters. They use their fangs to poison their prey. Then they suck
out its body juices, leaving a little dried husk. When we think of spiders, we think of
webs in which the spider sits waiting for a fly to be caught. But, while all spiders can
make silk, not all spiders spin webs to catch food.
Wolf spiders suddenly jump on their prey. The biggest spiders — the trapdoor
spiders — build burrows with hinged trapdoors, in the ground. The bola spider captures
moths by hurling a silk thread with a sticky glob on the end of it. -
— Reading page

: What is a whale?
Whales and dolphins may look like fish, but they are in fact mammals. Like humans, :
whales and dolphins are warm-blooded. The mothers give birth to their babies and feed the :
babies on milk. Whales, dolphins and porpoises together make a group of sea creatures :
: known as cetaceans.
: Most experts agree that the earliest ancestors of today’s cetaceans were wolf-like 3
creatures which made their homes in estuaries, about fifty million years ago. At first these :
= creatures hunted land animals but grew better at catching fish. They slowly changed as they :
: left the land to live in the sea — all the oceans were theirs to explore. :
Most fish swim by moving their tails and bodies from side-to-side, but cetaceans :
: move through the water with a powerful up-and-down motion. Their sleek and streamlined :
= bodies and their specially shaped fins help these graceful animals to cut through the water :
: at speed. Dolphins are fast swimmers. They can reach speeds of up to 55 kilometres per
: hour —as fast as a speedboat. The larger whales can reach 30 kilometres per hour for short
: bursts. -
Down Under
‘ Whales and dolphins breathe air like we do. However, we can only hold our breath :
= underwater for about three minutes, whereas whales and dolphins can stay underwater for :
: an hour or more. The northern bottlenose whale, for example, can dive for about two hours, :
: without surfacing for a breath of air. :
At the end of a dive whales blow out a stream-like jet of air through a special blowhole ;
at the top of their heads. After a deep breath, the blowhole closes tightly again. Experts :
can tell which whale it is from the size and shape of the ‘blow’ ;
: Senses
As the sea is usually dark, cetaceans do not need good eyesight. However, sounds
travel well through water and cetaceans have an excellent sense of hearing. Sounds pass up :
from the lower jaw to the inner ear inside the head. Their lack of an earflap may prevent :

Toothed cetaceans have a special sense, called echolocation. This sense helps
: cetaceans to find food. A dolphin emits a clicking sound that bounces back off solid objects
like a squid or fish. The echo tells the dolphin where an object is, its size and its shape. A
dolphin even knows if the object is solid or hollow. :

These are two extracts taken from a book about volcanoes and earthquakes.
Being in a large earthquake is a terrifying experience.
The shaking of the ground we stand on is profoundly disturbing, both physically and
psychologically. When the shaking starts there is no knowing how long it will go on or
how severe it will be. Only when it stops is there some certainty in life again. The
longest tremor ever recorded, the Alaskan earthquake of 23 March, 1964 lasted four
minutes. But most quakes last less than a minute. In those brief moments, homes, shops,
even entire cities are destroyed. The earth sometimes seems to undulate. Afterwards,
great cracks may appear in the ground. Even stranger, the rocks may show no sign at
all of the intense undulations they went through in the shaking. People also seem to find
the many months of small earthquakes (after shocks) which follow a big tremor very
disturbing.
How do you measure the size of an earthquake? News reports usually give the quake a
magnitude on the Richter scale. Charles Richter invented the Richter Scale during the
1930s in America. The Richter magnitude is useful because it can be worked out from a
recording — called a seismogram - of the earthquake waves. The waves of a big quake
can be recorded on the other side of the globe. So as long as the distance between the
recording device and the quake’s centre is taken into account, the Richter magnitude
can be calculated from anywhere on the planet. But where the shaking is felt, it is more
important to know how intense the shaking was and how it affected buildings and people.
Intensity is purely descriptive and cannot be recorded by a machine. Instead it is
compiled by inspecting the damage and getting the quake’s survivors to fill in
questionnaires.

sections.title: Questions 11-20

WESTERN SWAMP TURTLE
This turtle, also called the western swamp tortoise, is found only in two swamps in Perth,
Western Australia and is possibly Australia’s most endangered reptile. There are less than
fifty of these animals still living in the wild.
The western swamp turtle is about 15 centimetres long, and has a short neck and a broad,
flat head, which is covered with a rough helmet. It has a square shell, which is brown on top
and olive-brown or yellow underneath.
In November or December, the female lays three to five hard-shelled eggs in a nest dug a
few centimetres below the surface of the ground. The hatchlings emerge between May and
June and may live for more than fifty years.
During the wet winter months, this turtle lives in the swamps. During summer they take
refuge from the sun, spending the hot months in holes in the ground, or under deep leaf litter.
The western swamp turtle feeds on small tadpoles and insect larvae found in and around
the swamp.
To try and ensure that the western swamp turtle does not become extinct, a captive breeding
program has been established at Perth Zoo, and a number of young turtles were born there
in 1989. This breeding program may be the only way that the western swamp turtle will
survive.
The turtle’s natural habitat lies right on the border of the city of Perth and its home has been
destroyed to make way for houses, office blocks and for agriculture. Clay mining has also
destroyed the home of the western swamp turtle.

The skating season had commenced unusually early: our boys were by no means
alone upon the ice. The afternoon was so fine that men, women and children, bent upon
enjoying the holiday, had flocked to the grand canal from far and near. St Nicholas had
evidently remembered the favourite pastime: shining new skates were everywhere to be
seen. Whole families were skimming their way to Haarlem, or Leyden, or the
neighbouring villages. The ice seemed fairly alive. Ben noticed the erect, easy carriage
of the women, and their picturesque variety of costume. There were the latest fashions,
fresh from Paris, floating past dingy, moth-eaten garments that had seen service through
two generations; coal-scuttle bonnets perched over freckled faces bright with holiday
smiles; stiff muslin caps, with wings at the sides flapping beside cheeks rosy with health
and contentment; furs, too, encircling the whites of throats; and scanty garments
fluttering below faces ruddy with exercise: in short, every quaint and comical mixture of
dry-goods and flesh that Holland could furnish seemed sent to enliven the scene.
There were belles from Leyden and fishwives from the border villages; cheese-
women from Gouda, and prim matrons from beautiful country seats on the Haarlemmer
Meer. Grey-headed skaters were constantly to be seen; wrinkled old women with
baskets upon their heads; and plump little toddlers on skates, clutching at their mother’s
gowns. Some women carried their babies upon their backs, firmly secured with a bright
shawl. The effect was pretty and graceful as they darted by, or sailed slowly past, now
nodding to an acquaintance, now chirruping and throwing soft baby-talk, to the muffled
little ones they carried.
Boys and girls were chasing each other, and hiding behind the one-horse sleds
that, loaded high with peat or timber pursued their cautious way along the track marked
out as “safe”. Beautiful, queenly women were there, enjoyment sparkling in their quiet
eyes. Sometimes a long file of young men, each grasping the coat of the before him,
flew by with electric speed.

Baked ratatouille with snags
Stick to Mediterranean vegetables that cook relatively quickly (quartered fennel would
also be good). The oven gives sausages such a crackly-crisp skin, you’ll never fry a
snag again.
INGREDIENTS
2 red onions
1 whole head garlic
2 medium eggplants
2 zacchinis
2 red capsicums
2 tbsp olive oil
400g canned tomatoes
1 tbsp thyme leaves
Sea salt
Black pepper
8 garlicky pork sausages
12 kalamata olives, unpitted
Fresh rosemary and thyme for swerving
METHOD
* Cut the onions into quarters, and the head of garlic in half crosswise.
« Cut the eggplants into rounds, the zucchinis into diagonal slices and the capsicums
into thick rounds, discarding core and seeds.
« Arrange in a large oiled baking tray, burying the garlic halves cut-side down. Add the
canned tomatoes and their juices, and a dash of water.
« Tuck in the pricked sausages, drizzle the lot with olive oil and scatter with thyme and
rosemary, sea salt and pepper.
« Bake for 45 minutes, turning the sausages once, until the veggies are cooked and
snags are browned.
« To serve, scatter with olives, rosemary and thyme. Squeeze the roasted garlic on top,
and drizzle with the pan juices.
Serves 4
Age Epicure, June 24 2008

This is a passage from a book called The Gold Diggers by Belinda Hollyer. It is about the
history of gold mining
The gold miner needed very few tools when he set out on his search for gold. The
basic equipment could be as little as a shovel, a pick, a bucket and a pan for washing
the gold in. The shovel and the pick were needed for digging up the earth and gravel, the
bucket for carrying it in and the pan to wash the dirt away in the stream. Gold was much
heavier than the dirt which held it and it always sank to the bottom of the pan.
However, if the miner used only these few tools, it would take him many hours of
work to uncover just a few particles of gold. To wash the gold in the pan meant that he
had to spend most of the day crouched in a cold mountain stream. To overcome these
problems the miners began to build all sorts of inventions to help them in their search for
riches.
In time the miners came to use the cradle, the long tom and the sluice, although
for the final washing they continued to use their pans to trap the small particles of gold.
All the three inventions still meant that the miners had to work very hard, but by working
in teams they were able to wash far more dirt in a day. As the gold was heavier than the
dirt it became trapped in the slats of the various contraptions. Water washed the dirt away.
This sort of mining for gold is called place mining. It involves washing the dirt, which
contains the gold with water. The water carries the dirt away leaving only the gold.
Long Tom
The long tom was made of two parts, a long trough and at the end of this an iron sheet
with holes in it called a riddle. Gravel was washed down the trough, through the riddle to
the riffle box where the gold was caught by bars as the dirt washed down.
Sluice
The sluice was made of a series of riffle boxes fitted together. Water flowed along it and
the miners shovelled in dirt along the sides. The gold was trapped against bars across
the riffle boxes.
Cradle
The cradle worked like this. Gravel and dirt were shovelled into a hopper, or box, at the
top. Then the miner gently rocked the cradle while pouring water over the dirt. The water
carried the gold through holes in the hopper and it was caught against the bars, which
were called riffles.

This is an article from a newspaper.
Nine gorgeous police puppies stuck to their normal routine with their mother
yesterday, oblivious that a police search to name them had made them stars.
Hundreds of readers struck by photographs of the cute puppies, flooded The Daily
Telegraph with suggestions for names in response to a police appeal.
The police puppies could be taking up names like Ace, Arnie, Apollo and Alice with
everyone from engineers to school children and even CityRail staff making suggestions.
Jordan Roach, 11 was typical of the entrants, saying: “I would love one of your
police dogs to be named Apollo or Ace: while Mikayla Murray, 11, hoped one of the female
puppies could be called Angel because she said her dog recently died.
“Her dog Gypsy recently passed away and she calls her Angel now,” Mikayla’s mum
Michelle wrote.
Superintendent Julie Middlemiss said she was grateful for the huge response after
her squad had a terrible week with the stabbing death of Police Dog Carts.
Many of those who entered the police puppy naming competition yesterday left
messages about Carts and Christmas messages for the dog squad staff.
“| just want to thank everyone very much from here at the dog unit, we are really
looking forward to working out the successful names for the nine little puppies,” Sup
Middlemiss said.
“You often find people focus on the police officer, they realise they have a dog with
them but a lot of people don’t realise they are in the same situation as the police officer
(in terms of danger).”
The competition to give the gorgeous four-week old German shepherd puppies a
name starting with the letter A will continue until Christmas Eve.
Seven-year-old Jaidyn Hutchings came up with the name Aurick because Jaidyn
said it meant “protecting ruler”.
The competition has appealed to all ages, with residents of the Sir Thomas Mitchell
Aged Care Facility in Ilawong coming up with names for all nine dogs.
Their suggestion included Astro-Boy, Arrow, Achilles for the male puppies and Abbie,
Annie and Alex for a girl.’ An engineer suggested they be named after Greek names.
Once the names have been chosen the puppies will be registered with the NSW
Canine Council.
They will spend the next few weeks with their mother Yosi.
The puppies have spent their first weeks of life at a Vineyard vet hospital in
northwest Sydney and will enter a puppy raiser program shortly. Police said the four
female puppies could become police breeding dogs while at least one of the puppies will
follow father Ike into the Queensland police dog squad.

I'd snorkelled hundreds of times in the lagoon and always loved seeing the beautiful fish and

| remember having a few problems with my gear and that | had to readjust my face mask a

When | returned home | realised something was missing. My heart hiccuped as, while | was

This is an extract from “Wind in the Willow” a story by Kenneth Grahame about
a mole, a rat and a toad who live near a river bank. In this passage Rat and Mole
are going to visit Mr Badger.
They waited patiently for what seemed a very long time, stamping in the snow to keep
their feet warm. At last they heard the sound of slow shuffling footsteps approaching
the door from the inside. It seemed, as the Mole remarked to the Rat, like some one
walking in carpet slippers that were too large for him and down at heel; which was
intelligent of Mole, because that was exactly what it was.
There was the noise of a bolt shot back, and the door opened a few inches, enough
to show a long snout and a pair of sleepy blinking eyes.
“Now the very next time this happens,” said a gruff and suspicious voice, “I shall be
exceedingly angry. Who is it this time, disturbing people on such a night? Speak up!”
“O Badger,” cried the Rat, “let us in, please. It’s me, Rat, and my friend Mole and
we’ ve lost our way in the snow.”
“What, Ratty, my dear little man!” exclaimed the Badger, in quite a different voice.
“Come along in, both of you at once. Why, you must be perished. Well I never!
Lost in the snow! And in the Wild Wood too, and at this time of night! But come in
with you.”
The two animals tumbled over each other in their eagerness to get inside, and heard
the door shut behind them with great joy and relief.
The Badger, who wore a long dressing-gown and whose slippers were indeed very
down-at-heel, carried a flat candlestick in his paw and had probably been on his way to
bed when their summons sounded. He looked kindly down on them and patted both
theirheads. “This is not the sort of night for small animals to be out,” he said paternally,
“I’m afraid you’ ve been up to some of your pranks again, Ratty. But come along; come
into the kitchen. There’s a first-rate fire there, and supper and everything.
He shuffled on in front of them, carrying the light, and they followed him, nudging
each other in an anticipating sort of way, down a long, gloomy, and to tell the truth,
decidedly shabby passage, into a sort of central hall, out of which they could dimly
see other long tunnel-like passages branching, passages mysterious and without
apparent end.

Paul Blart: Mall Cop (PG)
Director: Steve Carr (Daddy Day Care)
Starring: Kevin James, Jayma Mays, Keir O’Donnell, Raini Rodriguz, Shirley Knight
**
>My, what a waist
ONE of the weirdest box-office results to come out of the US in a long time is the
spectacular success of Paul Blart: Mall Cop.
Since its premiere in January, this nondescript comedy about a porky security guard
in a shopping centre has taken more than $200 million.
Perhaps in the land of Uncle Sam, the recession afflicts taste in movies before it hits
the hip pocket.
The first half of this movie is atrociously bland. Played by TV sitcom stalwart Kevin
James (The King of Queens), the title character is an over-officious, under-achieving
chubster.
Blart covers his beat in a suburban mall with the aid of a motorised upright scooter.
He crashes into things a lot. No one respects him. He is blessed with a good heart.
Cursed by a bad diet. He so wants to be in a relationship. He has a crush on the girl who
runs the hair-extensions kiosk. If only she could see the real him, you know?
That’s enough with the character profiling. Let’s just say that Paul Blart is every
Biggest Loser contestant that has ever lived, stuffed into the body of one man.
The movie improves noticeably after it works off all that sad-sack flab and walks
briskly towards a little low-impact action.
A gang of skateboard-riding youths lay siege to the mall and take hostages. Blart
misses all the initial hubbub because he is playing a video game.
So he becomes the last line of defence against an audacious robbery that could mean
death to innocent bystanders swept along in its wake.
The remainder of Paul Blart: Mall Cop plays out as expected, the door is creaked
open for a sequel, and the film slumps down to rest.
Inessential.
Herald-Sun March 19", 2009

Mr Bean-Everyone’s Favourite?
Garry Hastings: Thanks for talking to Text Chat Magazine. | hear you are an
expert on Mr Bean and how audiences respond to him.
Jill McGill: Well, | have spent a lot of time researching Rowan Atkinson’s work.
Garry Hastings: So, does everyone love Mr Bean — or is it just everyone | know?
Jill McGill: Well, actually whilst Mr Bean is an amazingly popular character, not
all people find him funny. Instead, my research has found he seems to appeal to
a certain type of viewer.
Garry Hastings: Really? | think he’s hilarious and so do my kids.
Jill McGill: Yes, exactly. He is loved by children. They seem to find his simple
antics very amusing. Since he acts like a child much of the time they can relate to
him. Think of his teddy bear for instance and his inability to carry out multi-staged
tasks. Yet as they know he is an adult they can understand it is silly.
Garry Hastings: So who doesn't like Mr Bean?
Jill McGill: Well, it’s not so much they don’t like him it’s more that they do not
really respond. I’ve found very scientific, fact based people who like clear rules
and logic often find the humour rather lukewarm. They tend to describe the antics
as “stupid” and many even find the shows frustrating. These people do not tend
to enjoy physical humour, you know like slap-stick, but favour more intellectual
humour.
Garry Hastings: Wow? So does that make me a child then?
Jill McGill: No, no, no. There are many lucky people, like yourself, who are able
to appreciate all sorts of humour. You may well like a clever, intellectual satire just
as much.
Garry Hastings: Mmm | do. Well Jill, thanks for speaking with us today. | know
our readers love Rowan Atkinson’s Mr Bean.
, -— Reading page 7

Phar Lap
BEFORE Phar Lap’s second Melbourne Cup, gangsters were sending hitmen to stop him.
He was — and is — the only racehorse to become a national hero, firing the excitement of
Australia with his thundering race wins.
Phar Lap was named after the Thai word pharlap, meaning lightning, but he had a
nickname across the country — The Red Terror.
He seemed to be impossible to beat, and that was very dangerous.
Melbourne gangsters in the racing game were losing fortunes through Phar Lap and
becoming desperate.
Phar Laps’ trainer, Harry Telford, was warned of attacks through fire, acid and poison
darts as the Melbourne Cup of 1930 approached.
Strapper Tommy Woodcock was riding a pony and leading Phar Lap home from exercise
at Caulfield racecourse when he saw two suspicious men in an idling car.
Woodcock placed himself and the pony between the car and Phar Lap. The driver sped
past, blaring the horn as his mate fired a shotgun at the horse.
The shot splattered harmlessly over a high wooden fence, but Telford had had enough.
He took Phar Lap to the safety of Geelong until the race.
But the drama wasn’t over. Two hours before the race, Phar Laps float moved through
heavy rain out of Geelong, escorted by police motorcyclists.
And the engine died. :
Telford and Woodcock took it in turns to crank the engine until it sputtered into life. They
reached Flemington racecourse no more than 30 minutes before the race was to start.
On that day four-year-old Phar Lap was carrying 9.12, a weight record for his age with
the odds of 11/8 on (meaning you put 11 units and if you win you only get 8 plus your
original 11). Phar Lap steamed through the race, winning effortlessly.
He was taken to America and he died in April 1932. There were unjustified rumours that
he had been poisoned by American gangsters.
Excerpt from ‘Legends Stories of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

branches. Robbie pushed his hands against a tree trunk and straightened one leg, then
the other, behind him. He could feel his calf muscles pulling and the bark digging into his
palms. Next he rested his heel on a stump and bent forward over his outstretched leg until

the calm he usually felt at this time before a race. His heart would pound again when he
lined up with the others at the start, but now he felt almost sleepy. He breathed deeply,
shook his arms and legs, and focused his mind on the course he, Mum and Tid had walked
together this morning.
it was a tight, twisting, hilly trail. A good cross-country course, the parents said.

to be near the lead if he didn’t want to wait his turn to get through there. Then there was a
narrow track with a barbed-wire fence on one side and a steep drop on the other. The
course opened out after that.
They had walked up a gradual slope, around a marker in a clump of trees and down a
gravel road, where the pebbles skidded under their feet, to a creek crossing. “Go for it up
the hill,” Mum had advised. “Careful coming down this gravel. Not too fast or you'll go head

Our transport revolution
WHILE views might differ about what should be built first, the massive Victorian
Transport Plan to be announced today is crucial to ensuring our city’s future.
Following almost a decade of promises, and many earlier “plans” to fix greater
Melbourne’s transport woes, this blueprint could finally be a way forward.
It includes a $6 billion link — with tunnels — between the Eastern Freeway at Bulleen and
the Western Ring Road at Greensborough.
Rail would be extended from Epping to South Morang. Footscray and Caulfield would
be linked by underground tracks, and $650 million would be spent on new trains.
Money is allocated to work out how Hoddle St traffic might move faster, and $100 million
over 12 years has been set aside for bicycle paths.
Part of Sir Rod Eddington’s proposed east-west road link is in the mix.
Melbournians are expected to make almost three million extra car trips daily in the next
25 years. More than 900,000 extra trips will be taken on public transport over the same
period.
Transport is a city’s veins and arteries. Without it, we could not work or visit friends or
enjoy ourselves.
And as Melbourne becomes more popular and sprawls ever farther, excellent systems
will be increasingly important.
Aspects of them will always be controversial, but we have no alternative but to build and
pay for them.
Assaults down
THAT CBD assaults on Friday and Saturday nights in October and November dropped
by 24 per cent compared with last year is encouraging.
The Safe Streets Taskforce program begun last month appears to be working, even if
the numbers of drunks remains disturbing.
Police have issued more than 1440 penalty notices for offensive behaviour and urinating
in public. And, despite extra officers on the streets and CCTV vans, Herald Sun reporters
have witnessed this weekend shocking alcohol-fuelled scenes.
Residents of outer suburbs rarely see such things. They are the happiest Melburnians,
according to Leader Newspapers’ annual My Melbourne survey.
If only young people who play — play up — in the CBD could adopt some of the communal
responsibility shown in such places as Eltham and Warrandyte.
Herald Sun (Melbourne, Australia) 12-08-2008

A Special Island
Who doesn't enjoy a stay on a beautiful undeveloped island? Not many | suppose. When
that island is Rottnest Island off the Western Australian coast then there is little doubt. Almost
500,000 people visit this special island each year. The population of the island is about 150
but huge numbers of day trippers make the ninety minute journey from Perth or Fremantle on
ferries or charter boats that regularly carry eager tourists from Western Australia, the rest of
Australia and many countries.
It is an island where progress is measured in creating safe walking trails and ensuring
that the natural environment is well protected.
The total area of the island is about 2,000 hectares with pristine lakes taking up about
200 hectares. The crystal clear waters make for great swimming and boating activities.
Snorkelling with numerous fish and playful sea lions is a favourite activity. During the summer
season there can be as many as 5,000 people visiting at any one time.
The beauty of the island, the absence of high-rise buildings and noisy activities is, of
course, a major drawcard. Rottnest Island is home to a delightful creature - the quokka. It is
certain that this 30-40 centimetre high creature, somewhat like a furry rather overweight
wallaby, thrives well on Rottnest Island because of the absence of feral cats and wild dogs.
It is no wonder that many West Australians consider the island to be their favourite
holiday destination.

FILM
MONSTERS VS ALIENS (PG)
kkk
General release (90 minutes)
Jake Wilson Reviewer
WRITTEN and directed by a committee at Dreamworks Pictures, the digitally animated
Monsters vs Aliens replays the nightmares of the Atomic Age as harmless comedy: a sure
recipe for delight.
Reese Witherspoon is the voice of Susan Murphy, who is zapped by a radioactive meteor
on the eve of her wedding and grows into the Fifty Foot Woman, before being hauled to a
secret government compound and blackmailed into saving the Earth from a giant robot from
outer space.
Like Dorothy in The Wizard of OZ (1939), Susan shares her adventures with a trio of
zany male offsiders: a brainless ball of goo (Seth Rogen), a cackling yet soft-hearted giant
cockroach (Hugh Laurie), and a blustering two-legged dinosaur (Will Arnett) who lets others
do the fighting when the chips are down.
In its fusion of boys’ adventure films and chick flicks, the plot also recalls another Seth
Rogen vehicle: Judd Apatow’s pregnancy comedy Knocked Up (2007), which co-starred
Katherine Heigl as a poised entertainment reporter who was forced by her physical
circumstances to join a band of slobs and geeks.
Here, Rogen’s blob steals the show with his rapt idiot grin and habit of harmlessly
engulfing his friends: some of the resulting jokes about gender and identity are quite
sophisticated, but that doesn’t mean small children won't get the point.
While the animators never strive for painterly beauty, their monsters and aliens all give
highly expressive and precisely timed performances. A central battle sequence in San
Francisco recreates the city in impressively accurate detail, with Susan strapping a car to
each foot and roller skating down one of the steep streets.
Since this is a film for children, we know with virtual certainty that nobody we care about
will come to harm. But there’s no reason this deft fantasy shouldn’t appeal to adults as well.
Once in a while, it’s good to be told that humanity will muddle through, that transformation
is often a blessing — and that monsters can be heroes, even if they're girls.
The Age April 2"4, 2009

We gave this day a name

Lasseter’s Lost Reef
IN 1897, Harold Bell Lasseter was found unconscious in the desert southwest of Alice
Springs by an Afghan camel-driver — with some interesting rocks.
And the legend grew from there.
Lasseter said he had found a fabulously rich gold reef in the trackless desert out west,
but he would not say where. He wanted to lead an expedition to it.
For a while nobody seemed to be interested, but in 1911 there was an expedition — only
to be beaten back by the toughness of the country.
Lasseter tried one more time, in 1930, with a plane, a six-wheeled lorry and a team of
experts.
The plane crashed and Lasseter said they were over 250 kilometres off course.
The party on the ground battled on but finally decided to go home — except for Lasseter
and a dingo shooter, Paul Johns.
They pressed on, and Lasseter finally said he had found his reef. But he would not show
Johns where it was. They fought in the desert and Johns turned back, leaving Lasseter with
two camels.
The camels bolted from Lasseter, and though an Aboriginal tribe helped him he was
getting weaker and suffering from sandy-blight blindness.
He buried his papers under a tree marked ‘DIG’, crawled into a cave and died.
Nobody has ever found any trace of Lasseter’s reef.
From ‘Legends of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

Saturday was clear and frosty, and the sun felt far away. A freezing gale blew from the south-
west. Robbie stood on the back of the truck and faced like a dog into the wind. It tried to get
under his cap, but he had jammed it down tightly. His eyes watered. His old football jumper
stuck to his chest and billowed from his back as if it were trying to blow away. He could be
in the warm cabin with Mum and Tid while they drove to the first mob of sheep to be fed, but
he liked it on the back. The main range was bright blue today and only its white icing of snow
separated it from the sky. The air felt as cold and clean as mountain water in his lungs.

grass had withered to dry wisps, the balls of horse manure seemed to grow all over the
paddock like some strange fungus. The horses were sheltering from the wind in a clump of
snow gums: Dad’s bay horse, Storm; the old creamy and her filly; dear old Thomas, as

SIXTEEN dinosaurs soar two storeys high in Australia’s biggest dinosaur exhibition, which
opens at the Melbourne Museum today.
The biggest creature is as long as six cars parked end to end and has a neck half as
long as its bulking body.
“They would break that roof,” said six-year-old Tom, one of the earliest visitors to the
Dinosaur Walk, which has taken a year to come together with state backing.
Visitors can see the skeletons, which have been gathered from around the world, from
below, eye-to-eye or from a tree-top walkway near the largest flying animal of all time.
There’s a chance to feel their teeth, learn their hunting skills, check out their eggs,
measure yourself against a thigh bone and touch their fossilized dung.
Sundials take visitors back 230 million years to when the earliest dinosaurs appeared,
and video animation brings the creatures to life through a headset viewfinder.
Museum-goers can also meet Australia’s megafauna and the animals that roamed the
earth before and after the dinosaurs.
Arts Minister Lynne Kosky heard the dinosaurs roar and their stomachs rumble before
she opened the permanent exhibition.
“When | was a child you could never get this close, let alone touch dinosaur bones,”
she said.
“What’s most extraordinary about this is you get a sense of the size — we are quite humble
human beings.”

Animal Helpers
When Bernie was fourteen months old, his puppy-walking family took him back to the
training centre. There he was tested to find out if he would be suitable for training as a
guide dog for a blind person. Bernie passed the tests with flying colours - he was
intelligent, healthy, gentle, clever and strong enough to be a guide dog. A dog which does
not pass all the tests may be given back to the puppy-walking family if the family would like
it. Otherwise it is given to someone who needs a pet — a disturbed or disabled child, or a
lonely old person.
Once Bernie was accepted by the training centre, an instructor began the long but
rewarding months of teaching him. Bernie had to learn to see for the blind person he would
guide in the future. To do this, Bernie was taught to guide a person around and under
obstacles, up and down stairs, and across busy streets. He had to learn to judge height as
well as width, so that he could keep his owner from bumping into an overhanging branch
or other obstacle. Bernie was taught how to get on and off public transport and how to get
around in crowded buildings. He was trained to lead at a steady pace while in harness and
to ignore distractions such as cats and other dogs.

Aboard the Wrecked Clipper
Colin Thiele, 1969
Ten minutes went by. Snook felt his father’s forehead and cheeks and they seemed mildly
warm. Then he watched his chest carefully and almost gave a shout. It moved. His father
was still alive; he was breathing. Snook stood up hurriedly. Now he had a job to do — to
bed down his patient somewhere he’d be safe and warm. But first he’d have to go back
below deck and get some blankets.
He peered down the companionway and sniffed tentatively. The ammonia gas was still
there but it hadn’t spread any further; if anything it seemed to have dissipated a little. But
the whiff of gas was enough to wrack his body again; wave after wave of nausea rolled
over him until his throat felt raw and bleeding and his ribs ached. And the pain in his eyes
and nose was unbearable. For a while he stumbled about at the head of the ladder in
deadly danger of pitching down headlong into the gas chamber below. But slowly, very
slowly, the waves passed, the cloud thinned, and he began to think more clearly. His
hopes rose.

sections.passage:
The Silver Sword
This is an extract from a very exciting adventure story by lan Serraillier about refugee
children during the Second World War. It tells of their struggle to survive, avoid
capture, and of their seemingly hopeless search for their parents.
The current was swift. In the darkness the great wooded hills swept by. For a moment the
moon peeped from a cloud and turned the rippling surface of the stream to silver.
‘Stay/away, moon’ Ruth muttered. ‘Don’t come out again until we’ve passed the village.’
Side by side the two canoes sped on.
On the left bank the line of hills curved downwards. Were those dim shapes houses? Had
they reached the village?
Again, the moon appeared. It had chosen quite the wrong moment, for this was indeed the
village, with houses crowded about both banks, and the left bank suddenly an open space
with lorries in it, they were so close together that they were almost touching, and there were
several rows of them. These must be the lorries that were to take the Polish refugees back
to Poland. With a tightening of fear in her throat, Ruth realised if they were spotted now, they
would be taken back, too.
‘Look out for the bridge’ said Edek.
He and Jan shot ahead, aiming for the centre of the three arches. Edging away from the
square, Ruth paddled towards the right-hand arch.
The water was noisy and Ruth did not hear the footsteps on the bridge. But she saw a man’s
shadow on the water and it was moving. She paddled frantically to get free.
‘The water’s coming in, | can feel it under me,’ said Bronia.
Aman shouted and his shadow leaned far out over the water.
The canoe was still across the base of the arch, with the water thrusting against each end,
threatening to break its back. She jabbed hard with the paddle and managed to ease it a
little.
The man was right overhead, shouting and waving, but she could not understand what he
was saying. In the distance a dog was barking.
Apair of legs dangled over the parapet and scraped against the stone. An American soldier.
With a last effort, she thrust at the stonework, and the canoe broke free. But the soldier had
clambered down and jumped into the water where it was shallow at the side. He caught the
paddle and clung on.
Ruth tugged, twisted, and then let go of it, the canoe swung sideways into the shadows
under the arch. The soldier, not expecting her to let go of it, toppled over backwards and fell
with a splash into the river.
As the canoe shot out beyond the bridge, Ruth realised that she was at the mercy of the
current. Bronia had no paddle and could not help.
Reading page 1

Saxophone in a Pawnbroker’s Window
By Andrew Sant
Lost days when cavernous notes
reverberated seismically into the night,
or rose like an exotic flower,
wild and potent, a soloist’s territory,
far from eyes locked
on the instrument’s price.
The neighbours wished for him
and his gleaming saxophone, a gig,
or frozen keys, glad to miss
the magic of his fingertips.
Now it’s a mirror for peering
shoppers, madly skewed,
and at a stretch along its tube,
the street curves weirdly
where the saxophonist
lost control of the one bright
ally with any value —
a beacon among cold rings
and trinkets for him to brave
the crazy way back
to meet his own reflection,
just in time, and get the music out.

Humans hog resources
HUMANS are just one of millions of species on Earth, but we use up almost a quarter of the
sun’s energy captured by plants - the most of any species.
The human dominance of this natural resource is also affecting other species, reducing
the amount of energy available to them by almost 10 per cent, scientists report.
Researchers said the findings showed humans used “a remarkable share” of the Earth’s
plant productivity “to meet the needs and wants of just one species’.
They also warned increased use of biofuels -
such as ethanol and canola - should be viewed cautiously, given the potential for further
pressure on ecosystems.
The scientists, from Austria and Germany, publish their results today in the journal of the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
University of Melbourne agriculture professor Snow Barlow said the paper showed
humans were taking up too much of an important natural resource.
“Here we are, just one species on the Earth, and we're grabbing a quarter of the
renewable resources ... We're probably being a bit greedy.”
CHEE CHEE LEUNG

Extract from The Mysterious Adventures of Sherlock Holmes by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
We were seated at breakfast one morning, my wife and I, when the maid brought in a
telegram. It was from Sherlock Holmes, and ran in this way:
“Have you a couple of days to spare? Have just been wired for from the West of England
in connection with Boscombe Valley tragedy. Shall be glad if you will come with me. Air and
scenery perfect. Leave Paddington by the 11.15.’
“What do you say, dear?’ said my wife, looking across at me. “Will you go?”
“| really don’t know what to say. | have a fairly long list at present.”
“Oh, Anstruther would do you work for you. You have been looking a little pale lately. |
think that the change would do you good, and you are always so interested in Mr Sherlock
Holmes’ cases.”
“I should be ungrateful if | were not, seeing what | gained through one of them,” | answered.
“But if | am to go | must pack at once, for | have only half an hour.”
My experience of camp life in Afghanistan had at least had the effect of making me a
prompt and ready traveller. My wants were few and simple so that in less than the time
stated | was in a cab with my valise, rattling away to Paddington Station. Sherlock Holmes
was pacing up and down the platform, his tall, gaunt figure made even gaunter and taller by
his long grey travelling-clock and close-fitting cloth cap.
“It is really very good of you to come, Watson,” said he. “It makes a considerable difference
to me, having someone with me on whom | can thoroughly rely. Local aid is always either
worthless or else biased. If you will keep the two corner seats | shall get the tickets.”
We had the carriage to ourselves save for an immense litter of papers which Holmes had
brought with him. Among these he rummaged and read, with intervals of note-taking and of
meditation, until we were past Reading. Then he suddenly rolled them all into a gigantic ball,
and tossed them up on to the rack.
: Reading page 7

Ms. Jones and Guitar in the Spirit of the Place
The New York Times
By NATE CHINEN - April 2, 2008
“I've never played solo here, ever,” Norah Jones said just after midnight Monday on the
Lower East Side, surveying a capacity crowd with a flicker of a smile. “Much less on guitar,”
she added, fiddling with the strap of her cherry-red Fender Stratocaster. “But | figured in the
spirit of the Living Room, I'd try something new.”
Ms. Jones, the not-so-secret guest on a show celebrating the Living Room’s 10th
anniversary, was appearing in the company of friends. Among them were the singer-
songwriters Jesse Harris, Richard Julian and Sasha Dobson, whose separate sets involved
generous overlap in personnel and style. So in addition to commemorating the first decade
of a club beloved by many — as an incubator of talent, the Living Room can suggest a much
mellower and tidier successor to CBGB — the evening cast warm light on the close-knit
family of folk singers that still counts Ms. Jones as one of its own.
With so many collaborators on hand, her solo set didn’t last long. She sang “Cold, Cold
Heart,” the Hank Williams standard, along with an impish new original about her dog. Then
she welcomed Ms. Dobson for a couple of duets before calling up the Little Willies, her frisky
five- piece vintage-country band, which features Mr. Julian.
Much of their effervescent set recalled the Little Willies’ self- titled debut album, released in
2006. Singing in close but casual harmony, Ms. Jones and Mr. Julian tucked into lighthearted
songs by Jimmy Driftwood, Kris Kristofferson and the band’s namesake, Willie Nelson. The
mood was jaunty, with Ms. Jones at an upright piano and Jim Campilongo playing suitably
twangy electric guitar.
-Reading page 1
In one standout moment, Ms. Jones presented an unpublished Hank Williams song, with his
lyrics set to her melody. Its substance was classic Hank (opening line: “Time after time you’ve
proven untrue”), and its country-waltz setting was easeful and fine, a natural showcase for
Ms. Jones and her gently aerated, coolly intimate style.
Just as satisfying, on the other end of the dynamic spectrum, was Loretta Lynn’s “Fist City.”
It's not the sort of song anyone would immediately associate with Ms. Jones — a threat of
violence, shot through with feisty humor — which is what made it such a delight. Projecting
with a bell-like tone, she sounded gutsy and tough, almost scarily self- assured.
Mr. Julian had exuded a cagier brand of confidence in his own set, backed by a three-piece
band. His songs were terse and often wry, with frequent New York City allusions. And he
sang two of the’only remotely" political Songs "of the evening, though his topicsmreliqious
hypocrisy and rampant capitalism, preserved a nonspecific air.
In Ms. Dobson's set, urbane jazz chords met with a likably unfussy style. She welcomed Ms.
Jones on background vocals for one near-calypso and elsewhere paired off winningly with
Mr. Julian. Her sharp band included Mr. Harris on banjo and Tony Scherr on electric guitar,
and she featured them well.
Mr. Harris, who also played banjo throughout his set, observed that it marked a reunion of
the Ferdinandos, an old Living Room staple. Along with Mr. Scherr, the bassist Tim Luntzel
and the drummer Dan Rieser, he delivered a strong batch of old and new songs. His voice
was reedy, bordering on a whine, but his presence was quietly charismatic.
And his originals, among the best of the evening, whisked the set along. Mr. Harris is another
of this scene’s successes, having written “Don’t Know Why,” the sleeper hit that introduced
Ms. Jones. But he wasn't afraid to knock the songs around. Twice he ventured something
the band had never touched before. He did this, he said, “in the spirit of the Living Room.”
Both times, the results were impressive. bordering on a whine, but his presence was quietly
charismatic.

So You Think You Can Dance
Channel Ten, 7.30pm
THIS must be just about the best entertainment on telly at the moment. And the really great
thing is, you don’t even have to like dance to enjoy it.
No one could fail to be captivated by the skills of the contestants who — week in , week out
— put on the most tremendous show, in delicious 90-second bites.
And even to a dance ignoramus their excellence is evident in the Monday-night show, where
we’ve seen a succession of performances from some of the top dance companies in the
world, and nothing has eclipsed these enthusiastic amateurs. (With the exception, perhaps,
of the Australian Ballet.)
The talent of the choreographers is just as exhilarating. And girls? If you want to see what a
fabulous young woman’s body should look like, forget the catwalk and check out the pins
(and the abs) on these gals.
Along the way, it's also making a genuine contribution to capital-C culture. Among those
teens screeching for Charlie or chanting for Talia there’s a significant proportion who now
not only know what the Sydney Dance Company or the Australian Dance Theatre are, but
may even spend their hard-earned on a ticket. And that has to be a good thing.
The Age Green Guide April 9 2009

The McDermotts were rich, maybe not filthy rich, but still rich. They’d been coming to the
Port for ages, their shack was one of the first ones here. We called it a shack but it was
bigger and better than our houses. The correct term, | suppose, was holiday house.
You always knew when the Maccas arrived in town for the start of the holidays, you could
hear them. They'd come charging down the main street, in the latest-model Statesman, with
a huge boat behind, and Mr Mac would be learning on the horn — beep, beep, beep all the
way to the jetty.
Mr and Mrs Mac looked like Americans. | don’t know why, they just did. They both had
blond hair with lots of contours. And they wore gold jewellery. Mr Mac spent most of his time
on his boat, churning up the gulf. While Mrs Mac would be out in the back yard, on a banana
lounge, in a bikini, working on her tan.
They had two kids — Andrew, who was my age, and Craig, who was a year older. They
had blond hair too. Which was lucky for them, because they were surfies. They wore board
shorts all the time, they had surfboards and they were always reading magazines like Tracks
and Ripcurl. They did everything, except surf. Not in the Port anyway, because we had no
waves. Didn’t worry those Maccas though. Didn’t worry the local girls either, they all thought
the Maccas were drop-dead gorgeous. Even my own stupid sisters. Especially my own
stupid sisters.
| have to admit, though, that those Maccas had the knack, they knew exactly what to say
to girls. It was uncanny. | used to think that by hanging around with them, I’d learn a thing or
two, I’d get better. No way. | was still as hopeless as ever. In the end | decided chatting up
girls was like rolling your tongue — it was a genetic thing. Either you were born with it, like
those Maccas, or you talked about dead stars, like me.
Excerpt from ‘Deadly Unna?’ ‘by Phillip Gwynne

The ceiling was at least twice as high as the hospital in Sydney, and on the corridor walls
were real oil paintings of important-looking men with beards and stethoscopes.
Famous doctors, thought Colin. The geniuses who gave us modern medicine and all its
wondrous technology. The operating theatre and the X-ray machine and the Band-Aid that
doesn’t leave a sticky black outline when you pull it off.
He moved down the corridor, peeking into rooms. Most of them had big dark wooden
desks in them and ancient leather armchairs. Others were full of gleaming, modern
equipment.
Colin was impressed. You didn’t often come across blokes with those sorts of desks and
those sorts of armchairs who knew how to operate that sort of equipment.
‘You lost?’
Colin spun around. Looking at him was a nurse, her eyebrows raised.
‘No, I’m right thanks,’ said Colin.
She nodded and gave him a kind smile.
‘Looked as though you were lost.’
‘| was just checking that this is the best cancer hospital in London,’ said Colin.
The nurse grinned and leant towards him.
‘Best in London?’ she said. ‘It’s the best in the world. People come in here, their relatives
have already started squabbling over their furniture. When they leave, some of them, they
go round to their Aunty Maud’s, get their sideboard back and carry it home by themselves.’
She grinned again and walked off.
Colin grinned too. He had a vision of Luke, cured and laughing, staggering home from
Bayliss’ Department Store carrying the bunk bed with the built-in cubby house that had been
number two on his Chrissie list.
Colin hurried along the corridor. At the end he turned left and found himself in a huge
ward full of bustling nurses and rows of beds with patients in them.
Then he saw him, standing next to a bed, surrounded by student doctors.
The Best Doctor In The World.
He looked exactly like Colin had imagined he would. Tall and broad-shouldered, with a
wise, important face and thick grey hair just like the dad in Dynasty.
‘Accessibility is paramount,’ he said to the student doctors.
Colin’s chest thumped with excitement.
He even spoke important.
‘In other words,’ said the doctor, ‘the patient must always feel that he can speak to you,
that you’ve got time for him.’
The student doctors scribbled furiously on their notepads, then went back to staring at
the doctor in awe.
Excerpt from ‘Two weeks with the Queen’ by Morris Gleitzman
