This passage is from “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White, a story about a girl who lives ona
farm in America.
The early summer days on a farm are the happiest and fairest days of the year. Lilacs bloom
and make the air sweet, and then fade: Apple blossoms come'with the lilacs and the bees visit
round among the apple trees. The days grow warm and soft. School ends, and children have
time to play and to fish for trout in thé brook. Avery often brought a trout home in-his pocket,
warm and stiff and ready to be fried for supper.
Now that school was over, Fern visited the barn almost every day, to sit quietly on her stool. The
animals treated her as an equal. The sheep lay calmly at her feet.
Around the first of July, the work horses were hitched to the mowing machine, and Mr Zuckerman
climbed into the seat and drove into the field. All morning you could hear the rattle of the
machine as it went round and round, while the tall grass fell down behind the cutter bay in long
green swathes. :
Next day if there was no thunder shower, all hands would help rake and pitch and load, and the
hay would be carried to the barn in the high hay wagon, with Fern and Avery riding at the top of
the load. Then the hay would be hoisted, sweet and warm, into the big loft, until the whole barn
seemed like a wonderful bed of fimothy and clover. It was fine to jump in, and perfect to hide
in. And sometimes Avery would find a little grass snake in the hay and would add it to the other
things in his pocket.
Early summer days are a jubilee time for birds. In the fields, around the house, in the barn, in
the woods, in the swamp — everywhere love and songs and nests and eggs. From the edge of
the woods, the white throated sparrow, (which must come all the way from Boston) calls,” Oh,
Peabody, Peabody, Peabody!” On an apple bough, the phoebe teeters and wags its tail and says,
“Phoebe, phoe-bee!” The song sparrow, who knows how brief and lovely life is, says, “Sweet,
sweet, sweet interlude; sweet, sweet, sweet interlude.” If you enter the barn, the swallows swoop
down from their nests and scold. “Cheeky, cheeky!” they say.
in early summer there are’ plenty of things for a child to eat and drink and suck and chew.
Dandelion stems are full of milk, clover heads are loaded with nectar, the Frigidaire is full of ice-
cold drinks. Everywhere you look is life; even the little ball of spit on the weed stalk, if you poke
it apart, has a green worm inside it. And on the underside of the leaf of the potato vine are the
bright orange eggs of the potato bug.

Tuesday 23 August
Dear Dad,
No wonder you always say you don’t have any photos from when you were a kid!
How much will you pay me if | don’t borrow the negative of one Aunt Winifred has of you
dressed up as a bon-bon for a Sunday School play and send copies to all the men where

| forgot to tell you something very important before | was hustled on to the train and

In my wardrobe there’s a metal cash box with holes drilled in the outside and Sam on

for him (| had to pack to come here etc.). Sam cost $2.75 from Jason Taylor, but Jason

prime of life as |had been told. | checked with the vet’s nurse on the way home from school,

come home? Thanks.

This is an obituary from the Sydney Morning Herald 10" January 2008.
P.K. Sethi 1927-2008
Millions of amputees in developing countries owe thanks to Dr P.K. Sethi for his invention
of an affordable prosthetic foot, which has enabled them to lead normal lives.
The Jaipur foot, which has never been patented, is available in more than 25 countries,
mostly poor and many with large numbers of landmine victims. Unlike many high-priced
prostheses in developed countries it can be made by traditional craftsmen, last more than five
years and costs about $34.
Pramod Karan Sethi, who has died in Jaipur, India at 80, was born in the ancient northern
Indian city of Benares, on the banks of the Ganges. His father was a professor of physics at
Benares Hindu University. On completing his medical education in India and Britain, Sethi
became a lecturer in surgery at a Medical College in Jaipur.
He became an orthopaedic surgeon by default. In 1958, his institution was about to be
inspected for accreditation, and since there was no department of orthopaedics, he was asked
to start one at once. He always maintained that not being a qualified orthopaedic surgeon helped
him produce something that was genuinely new.
Sethi came up with his invention after years of research. He was helped by
Ramachandra Sharma, a semiliterate craftsman.
They made a foot of vulcanised rubber but found it too heavy and stiff. So, they filled
the shell with sponge rubber and modified the design.
Since 1971 when Sethi presented the design to British orthopaedic surgeons at Oxford,
the Jaipur foot has revolutionised lives in war-torn countries. It is very flexible, allowing the
wearer to run, climb trees and pedal a bicycle.
The Jaipur foot was first used outside India in Afghanistan, which had the highest number
of amputees in the world after Russian landmines caused thousands of wounds.
Sethi is survived by his wife, Sulochana, a son and three daughters.
— Reading page3

This is an excerpt from the book Battle for the Ashes 2005
by David Frith
First Day: Thursday, August 4, 2005
It was only by the grace of God that the Edgbaston Test match was spared from cancellation after an
astonishing natural disaster. Seven days before the Test was scheduled to begin, a freak tornado roared
in from nowhere to rip through nearby suburbs tearing off roofs, smashing garden sheds. Injuries
were few, but streets were left resembling bombsites, and over at the cricket ground Steve Rouse, the
head Sroundsman, had his work cut out after several inches of rain interrupted his preparation for the
big match. If the tornado had whooshed a kilometre off its course there would have been no Test
match. Severe damage to the pavilion, the Eric Hollies Stand and much else could not have been made
safe in time.
England remained unchanged from the Lord’s Test, a rare thing and Australia had only the one
enforced change. The pitch, like so many others, defied accurate behavioural prediction, but the sky
was overcast, so that when Ricky Ponting won the toss again he put England in. Among the
adjectives employed were “aggressive”, “crazy”, “complacent”, “defensive” and — from Mike Gatting
— “arrogant”. Did the Aussie skipper fear another Harmison onslaught as at Lord’s? Was he trying to
demonstrate that McGrath’s absence didn’t worry him? Was he still reeling from McGrath’s injury
and incapable of clear thought? If England were 70 for six at lunch Ponting would be a bold hero.
England actually went to lunch at 132 for the loss of Strauss after 27 overs. Vaughan and others had
drawn strength after Lord’s by reminding themselves that since 2002-03 England had lost six Test
matches and had bounced back immediately each time to win the next one. This resilience now
seemed to be a vital part of their culture, the result of positive thinking rarely evident in England
teams of recent years.
The Australians, all bedecked in those wonderful baggy green caps (some of them now looking rather
worn — the caps, that is) watched askance as Trescothick cover-drove Lee for three fours in the third
over on a pitch that showed a certain amount of life but which, after the rude interruption by Nature
a week earlier, did groundsman Rouse proud.

This is an article in a book called Why? What? Where?
Nobody knows what the first language was. But scientists feel quite sure that nobody speaks it today,
because all languages change and keep on changing as long as people use them. One language may
change in different ways in different places and grow into several separate languages.
People are always inventing new words. For example, radium was made up as a name for a new
radioactive substance when scientists discovered it over a hundred years ago.
Words even change in one family. Children don’t always use words exactly the way their parents do.
They make small changes in the sounds or in the meaning. In time a lot of these little changes add up
and make big changes. If we could meet the people who spoke English five hundred years ago, we
probably couldn’t understand much of anything they said.
English was originally brought over by the Anglo-Saxons when they invaded Britain in the fifth and
sixth centuries. When Celtic monks came to convert the country, they brought some Latin and Greek
words with them; and in the ninth and tenth centuries Norse invaders from Scandinavia also brought
new words. The Norman invasion of 1066 introduced many new French words, which had 6figt
come from Latin.
The growth of learning, which began with the discoveries of the fifteenth and sixteenth century
explorers, led to many new words joining our language; and the development of science led to the
adoption of many Greek and Latin names for plants and animals and scientific inventions (e.g.
telephone). As knowledge grows, words are still being added.
Thus, English is a mixture of several languages. Scientists believe that these languages and many
others all grew out of the same ancestor language which they call Indo-European. Nobody speaks
Indo-European now, but some of its descendants, besides English, are German, Latin, French, Greek,
Russian and many of the different tongues spoken in India.

This passage is taken from ‘The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe’, a novel by C. S.
Lewis. Edmund is in a strange land and cannot find his sister Lucy.
“Just like a girl,” said Edmund to himself, “sulking somewhere, and won’t accept an apology.”
He looked round him again and decided he did not much like this place, and had almost made
up his mind to go home, when he heard, very far off in the wood, a sound of bells. He listened
and the sound came nearer and nearer and at last there swept into sight a sledge drawn by two
reindeer.
The reindeer were about the size of Shetland ponies and their hair was so white that even
the snow hardly looked white compared with them; their branching horns were gilded and shone
like Something On fire when the sunrise caught them. Their harness was of scarlet leather and
covered with bells. On the sledge, driving the reindeer, sat a fat dwarf who would have been
about three feet high if he had been standing. He was dressed in polar bear’s fur and on his
head he wore a red hood with a long gold tassel hanging down from its point; his huge beard
covered his knees and served him instead of a rug. But behind him, on a much higher seat in
the middle of the sledge sat a very different person — a great lady, taller than any woman that
Edmund had ever seen. She also was covered in white fur up to her throat and held a long
straight golden wand in her right hand and wore a golden crown on her head. Her face was white
— not merely pale, but white like snow or paper or icing-sugar, except for her very red mouth. It
was a beautiful face in other respects, but proud and cold and stern.
The sledge was a fine sight as it came sweeping towards Edmund with the bells jingling and
the dwarf cracking his whip and the snow flying up on each side of it.
“Stop!” said the Lady, and the dwarf pulled the reindeer up so sharp that they almost sat
down. Then they recovered themselves and stood champing their bits and blowing. In the frosty
air the breath coming out of their nostrils looked like smoke.

This extract is taken from a book Minerals and Energy by Brian and Barbara Kennedy.
Gemstones, like other minerals, were mostly formed as a result of tremendous heat below the earth’s
surface. Some gemstones are more valuable than others.
Opals and sapphires are the only gemstones found in large quantities in Australia. Australia produces
almost all of the world’s opal. The main source is Coober Pedy in South Australia, but opals are also
found at Andamooka, South Australia, and at Lightning Ridge in New South Wales.
Opals are used mainly for jewellery and are very popular with overseas tourists, in spite of the fact
that some people believe that they bring bad luck.
Australia also produces half the world’s sapphires. The main fields are at Anakie in Queensland and
at Glen Innes and Inverell in New South Wales. Discoveries of high quality sapphires and an increase
in world demand have caused new interest in the sapphire mining industry in the Glen Innes-Inverell
area. Modern excavating machines are being used by large mining companies on their leases. Small
scale mining for sapphires has been in progress for most of the 20th century. Thailand is by far the
largest customer for Australian sapphires.
Chrysoprase, a green stone, is the most important gemstone after sapphires. It is found mainly in the
Marlborough district of Queensland.
Industrial diamonds exist in all states, especially in Western Australia and in New South Wales in the
Copeton-Bingara district. In the 1970s, the blue clay kimberlite pipes in which diamonds are formed
were discovered in the Kimberleys district of Western Australia. This led to the discovery of rich
diamond fields in the area. Because of their extreme hardness, diamonds can be used in high-speed
tools for cutting and drilling hard materials.
Gemstone fossicking is a very popular pastime for hundreds of Australians and there are many
valuable collections. Collectors are often lapidarists who cut, polish and set their own gemstones.

This is the beginning of a book called ‘The Nimbin’ by Jenny Wagner
“| can’t understand you, Philippa,” her mother said. “All that fresh air outside, and here you
are stuck inside, reading.”
Philippa sighed and sat up on her bunk. “Can’t | stay in the caravan? It’s roasting out
there.”
“Then go for a swim,” her mother said brightly. “It'll do you more good than just reading.”
Philippa stuffed the book in her beach bag and went outside, banging the door behind
her. Her father, sitting in the annexe, looked up as she passed. “Anything wrong?”
“No,” said Philippa shortly, and headed off down the track towards the lagoon.
The dust at her feet spurted up into little clouds as she marched along, and she
watched with satisfaction as her feet got blacker and blacker. Well, you had to have
something your own way now and then. Here they were on holiday, they’d been here a week
or more, and still she hadn’t had a chance to read her book.
At the lagoon she turned off into the dunes and walked towards the ocean till she found
a good spot. There was no shade, but she was reasonably well hidden; if her parents
wanted her for anything they wouldn’t find her too easily.
She spread her towel out on the sand and opened her book. But it was a blazing hot
day. The sun shone back off the white sand and the white paper, dazzling her. She pulled
the towel out from under her and hung it over her head instead.
She found her place and started to read, but an irritating little breeze suddenly came up
from nowhere and turned the page before she was ready. She found her place again, and
the same thing happened. She wriggled on to her side and held the book open with her
elbow.
Presently something began to crawl up her leg. She twitched, and the crawling stopped.
After while it started again, and this time when she jerked it didn’t stop, but went on crawling
up her calf. She jumped away in fright, but there was nothing there.
Behind her a dark little shadow leapt to its feet and followed her a little way, then
disappeared into the dunes.

This is part of a book ‘Black Beauty’ written by Anna Sewell
The first place that I can well remember, was a large pleasant meadow with a pond of clear
water in it. Some shady trees leaned over it, and rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep
end. Over the hedge on one side we looked into a ploughed field, and on the other we
looked over a gate at our master’s house, which stood by the roadside; at the top of the
meadow was a plantation of fir trees, and at the bottom a running brook overhung by a
steep bank.
Whilst I was young I lived upon my mother’s milk, as I could not eat grass. In the
daytime I ran by her side, and at night I lay down close by her. When it was hot, we used.
to stand by the pond in the shade of the trees, and when it was cold, we had a nice warm
shed near the plantation.
As soon as I was old enough to eat grass, my mother used to go out to work in the
daytime, and came back in the evening.
There were six young Colts in the meadow besides me; they were older than I was;
some were nearly as large as grown-up horses. I used to run with them, and had great fun;
we used to gallop all together round and round the field, as hard as we could go. Sometimes
we had rather rough play, for they would frequently bite and kick as well as gallop.
One day, when there was a good deal of kicking, my mother whinnied to me to
come to her, and then she said, - ‘’I wish you to pay attention to what I am going to say to
you. The colts who live here are very good colts, but they are carthorse colts, and, of course,
they have not learned manners. You have been well bred and well born; your father has a
great name in these parts, and your grandfather won the cup two years at the Newmarket
races; your grandmother had the sweetest temper of any horse I ever knew, and I think you
have never seen me kick or bite. I hope you will grow up gentle and good, and never learn
bad ways; do your work with a good will, lift your feet up well when you trot, and never
bite or kick even in play.”
I have never forgotten my mother’s advice; I knew she was a wise old horse, and our
master thought a great deal of her. Her name was Duchess, but he often called her Pet.

These extracts are from a book called Aboard Endeavour by Bruce Stannard about
Captain Cook’s voyage in 1768 - 1771
26 October 1768
Today we crossed the equator. King Neptune came aboard in the traditional fashion and
demanded tribute — a bottle of rum from all those unable to prove they have been south of the
line. Those who could not pay were tied into a bosun’s chair, hauled up to the mainyard and
dropped into the sea. There was a great deal of laughter. The captain paid Neptune to be
excused from these indignities, and so too did Mr Banks and the other gentlemen. Mr Banks
even paid for his dogs to be ransomed.
13 November 1768
We have reached the Portuguese settlement at Rio de Janeiro. Although we have the royal
crown carved on our catheads, the governor, a stubborn fellow, refuses to believe that so humble
a vessel as Endeavour is a king’s ship on a scientific mission. He suspects us for a smuggler
and, much to the captain's annoyance, has placed an armed guard. We are, he insists, to
purchase the ship’s provisions only through an appointed agent. This fellow has demanded the
highest prices.
25 November 1768
Captain Cook and the governor have exchanged a great many letters, but still the governor
will not bring himself to believe that we are sailing around the world merely to observe an
astronomical event.
The ship’s company is not allowed ashore, but Mr Banks and Mr Parkinson, pretending to
be surgeon's mates seeking the purchase of medical supplies, have managed to botanise on
several occasions. They have brought on board over 300 plants. Many of them, Mr Banks says,
are unknown in Europe.
Mr Thurman, the American impressed at Madeira, received a dozen lashes for refusing to
assist the sailmaker; so did another seaman, who tried to desert; and a marine, who abused the
officer of the watch. John Reading, the boatswain’s mate, was also given a dozen lashes when
it was judged that he flogged the others too lightly.
5 December 1768
As we attempted to leave, a great gun in the fort fired a warning shot, which obliged us to
again come to anchor.
— Reading pagel

This is the beginning of a poem written by Henry Lawson.
Ah, better the thud of the deadly gun, and the crash of the bursting shell,
Than the terrible silence where drought is fought out there in the western hell;
And better the rattle of rifles near, or the thunder on deck at sea,
Than the sound — most hellish of all to hear — of a fire where it should not be.
On the runs to the west of the Dingo Scrubs there was drought, and ruin and death,
And the sandstorm came from the dreaded north-east with the blast of a furnace breath;
Till at last one day, at the fierce sunrise, a boundary-rider woke,
And saw, in the place of the distant haze, a curtain of light blue smoke.
There is saddling-up by the Cockey’s Hut, and out in the station yard,
And away to the north, north-east, north-west, the Bushmen are riding hard.
The pickets are out and many a scout, and many a mulga wire,
While Bill and Jim, with their faces grim, are riding to meet the fire.
It roars for days in the hopeless scrub, and across, where the ground seems bare,
With a crackle and hiss, like the hissing of snakes, the fire is travelling there;
Till at last, exhausted by sleeplessness, and the terrible toil and heat,
The squatter is crying, “My God! the wool!” and the farmer, "My God! the wheat!”
But there comes a drunkard (who reels as he rides), with the news from the roadside pub:-
“Pat Murphy, - cockey — cut off by the fire! - way back in the Dingo Scrub!
Let the wheat and the woolshed go to “— Well, they do as each great heart bids;
They are riding a race for the Dingo Scrub — for Pat and his wife and kids.

This is an Aboriginal legend.
Very early in the beginning of the Dreamtime there were no kangaroos in this land.
A group of men were out hunting one day, when suddenly they were hit by the
worst windstorm they had ever experienced. Large trees were blown over, small ones
were carried away into the sky, and huge boulders were tossed around like pebbles in
a children’s game.
The hunters were lucky to reach the safety of a cave. They sat in its shelter and
watched the storm take its course. After a while they were amazed to see a band of
animals being carried across the sky by the wind. They had never seen animals of this
sort before.
The men shook their heads in bewilderment as they discussed this extraordinary
sight, and realised that the creatures must have been brought by the wind from a distant
place that no-one in their group had ever visited.
The animals were quite large and covered in fur. They had small heads and short
front legs. It was obvious that they were very distressed at being blown through the wild
air. Frantically they kept stretching out their hind legs and their tails in an effort to make
contact with the ground.
The hunters watched keenly from their cave as the animals strained and battled
desperately against the wind. At last some of them did manage to find a toehold and
tailhold and anchor themselves to solid earth. The windstorm began to pass, and the
animals, which had forced their way down were left behind.
The watching hunters could now see that the animals had overstretched
themselves in their desperation to reach the ground. Their hind legs and tails were
elongated out of all proportion to the rest of their bodies. It really looked quite strange,
but the animals themselves did not seem particularly upset. Perhaps they were so
pleased to be on steady ground that nothing else mattered.
So far the hunters had been watching all this as an amazing event that would
make a good story. They took it for granted that the animals would run away
immediately, trying to get back to their own land.
It seemed that although the animals were tired and bewildered they were also
inquisitive. They began to look for shade, grass and water, and quickly found them
This was exactly the sort of place they liked and it soon became clear that they had
decided to stay.

Kites of Many Kinds
Kites have been flown around the world for thousands of years. As early as 3000
years ago, the Chinese built and flew kites. There are many legends in Chinese and
Japanese folklore that tell about a great ‘bird’ that stayed in the air for many days. Buddhist
missionaries are thought to have spread the knowledge and secrets of kite building and
flying, from China to Japan. Some of the tales from Asia tell of man-carrying kites.
In some lands, legends suggest that if a man or woman was thought to have
committed a crime they were strapped onto a kite and thrown out of a tower. If the kite
landed safely, the person was allowed to go free — a safe landing was proof of innocence.

questions.stem: This was taken as proof of the person’s guilt. It was considered to be just punishment.
options: There is a legend that tells of a father and son who were banished to an island. They
were not to set foot again on the mainland. The father wanted to get his son back to the
mainland so they built a large kite using bamboo and pieces of their clothing. The legend
says that the kite carried the son safely back to the mainland and there he was able to seek

help for his father. Today, kites are painted and decorated as symbols and flown during festivals and celebrations. During the Boys’ Festival held each year in Japan, every family with a baby boy born that year flies a kite shaped like a carp. This fish symbol means that the son, like the carp, will progress through the river of his life. Scientists have used kites for experiments for hundreds of years. Perhaps the most famous of these was Benjamin Franklin. He made a common kite with two crossed sticks covered with silk. 21 . He tied ordinary string into his kite and then tied on a key. Next, he waited for a thunder cloud. His son was helping him with the experiment. They knew that, if they were right, the experiment could be dangerous. They were very careful and took cover inside. 22 When the rain met the kite and string, the key did conduct the electricity, and they knew they were right. Men began to use kites to measure all kinds of things about weather. By 1900, they were able to measure temperature, moisture, wind speed and barometric pressure. Today, many of these measurements are made by using balloons and planes. 23 Engineers used kites to carry ropes and cables across rivers. The kite pulled the cords across the river and settled in trees. By repeating this process, a bridge across the river was gradually formed. Kites have been used for spy missions. 24 . The same methods are used in peace-time to photograph cities and cloud formations. During World War ll, a kite was part of the required equipment in life rafts. It was a signal to search parties. There are men alive today who owe their lives to a kite. Even fishermen have used kites to help catch fish. In several parts of the Pacific, kites are used to tow a baited line behind canoes. 25 . The skipping bait attracts fish. The fishing kite is also used by people who want to fish off shore but do not have a boat. The kite is used to carry the bait line far off shore. sections.title: Questions 1-6
sections.passage:
This passage is about plants.
Imagine you’re standing in one spot and you can’t move.
In fact, your feet are buried in the ground. The sun is beating down on your head.
Pretty soon, you’re going to get very thirsty. But you can’t go anywhere to get yourself
a drink.
This is just the way it is for most plants. While animals walk, run, hop, swim,
slither and fly from place to place, a plant stays in one spot all its life. It is held there
by its root — a part of the plant that is buried in the ground. Roots keep plants from
being blown away in the wind. If you’ve ever tried to pull up a dandelion, you know
how well anchored in the earth a root can be.
A root is much more to the plant than an anchor, though. The root gives the
plant that drink it needs. Water in the soil enters the root and is carried up through
the root, into the stem and out to the plant’s leaves and flowers. In the water are
dissolved minerals that the plant needs to grow.
The root is so important to the plant that it is the first part to grow when a seed
sprouts. The growing tip of the root is protected by a root cap. The moist root cap
slips easily among the soil particles. As roots branch out and spread through the
ground, they make a web that holds the soil together. "
There are two main kinds of roots. Fibrous roots are thin and have many
branches. If you pull up a fistful of grass you'll see fibrous roots. Tap roots are large
thick roots with fine roots called root hairs branching off them. Many tap roots act as
food storage bins — and that food is good for us to eat too. Carrots, parsnips and
beets are tap roots. We pull them up before the plant has a chance to use the stored
food to make leaves, flowers and seeds.
How does the food get down to the roots to be stored? It raves through the
stem. While water and minerals are going up the stem to the leaves, sugary food
made by the leaves is going down the stem to all parts of the plant. All this liquid
flowing through the plant is called sap. Sap keeps the plant alive the way blood
flowing through your body keeps you alive.
You are held upright by a column of bones — your spine. A plant is held upright
by its stem. The stem is not kept stiff by bone, though, but by water. A plant that
needs a drink will often droop and fall over. After it is watered, it will soon stand
straight again. Stems hold up the flowers and leaves where they can get the air and
sunlight they need.
— Reading page1

This is the beginning of a story called, “Sadako and the Thousand Paper Cranes”, about a girl who
lived in Japan.
Sadako was born to be a runner. Her mother always said that Sadako had learned to run before she could
walk.
One morning in August 1954 Sadako ran outside into the street as soon as she was dressed.
The morning sun of Japan touched brown highlights in her dark hair. There was not a speck of cloud in the
blue sky. It was a good sign. Sadako was always on the lookout for good luck signs.
Back in the house her sister and two brothers were still sleeping on their bed quilts. She poked
her big brother, Masahiro.
“Get up, lazybones!” she said. “It's Peace Day!”
Masahiro groaned and yawned. He wanted to sleep as long as possible but, like most fourteen-
year-old boys, he also loved to eat. When he sniffed the good smell of bean soup, Masahiro got up. Soon
Mitsue and Eiji were awake, too.
Sadako helped Eiji get dressed. He was six, but he sometimes lost a sock or shirt. Afterwards
Sadako folded the bed quilts. Her sister, Mitsue, who was nine, helped put them away in the closet.
Rushing like a whirlwind into the kitchen, Sadako cried, “Oh, Mother! | can hardly wait to go to the
carnival. Can we please hurry with breakfast?”
Her mother was busily slicing pickled radishes to serve with rice and soup. She looked sternly at
Sadako. “You are eleven years old and should know better,” she scolded. “You must not call it a carnival.
Every year on August sixth we remember those who died when the atom bomb was dropped on our city.
It is a memorial day.
Mr Sasaki came in from the back porch. “That's right,” he said. “Sadako chan, you must show
respect. Your own grandmother was killed that awful day.”
“But | do respect Oba chan,” Sadako said, “I pray for her spirit every morning. It's just that I’m so
happy today.”
“As a matter of fact, it's time for our prayers now,” her father said.
The Sasaki family gathered around the little altar shelf. Oba chan’s picture was there in a gold
frame. Sadako looked at the ceiling and wondered if her grandmother's spirit was floating somewhere
above the altar.
“Sadako chan!” Mr Sasaki said sharply.
Sadako quickly bowed her head. She fidgeted and wriggled her bare toes while Mr Sasaki spoke.
He prayed that the spirits of their ancestors were happy and peaceful. He gave thanks for his barber-shop.
He gave thanks for his fine children. And he prayed that his family would be protected from the atom bomb
disease called leukaemia.

Deadly delight for dogs
Kelly Ryan
ALL the fun of a big backyard Easter egg hunt will count for little if the family dog beats
the children to the chocolates.
Just a small amount of chocolate is potentially fatal to dogs.
Chemicals caffeine and theobromine cause irregular, racing heartbeats in canines, leading
to death.
Dexterous dalmation Elsa’s heart came close to collapsing after she broke into a visitor’s
backpack and wolfed down a 500g block of dark chocolate — seven times the lethal dose
of toxic chocolate for a dog of her size.

spikes at Christmas and Easter,” said veterinary director Cathy Warburton.
“The chemicals in chocolate can increase levels of stress hormones and stimulate dogs’
hearts, potentially leading to a very fast heart beat, irregular rhythm and even death,” Dr
Warburton said.
Elsa’s condition deteriorated quickly and she spent the night in hospital being medicated.

Just then we heard a cry of “Land! Land!” felt a shock, and were thrown down upon
the deck. It was clear that we had struck on a rock, for we heard a loud cry from one
of the men. “Weare lost! Launch the boat; try for your lives!” These words went,

| went at once on deck, and was met by a wave that threw me down, and wet me
through to the skin. When | got up, and went to the side of the ship, | found that all
the boats had been let down, and that the last of the crew had just left it. | cried out
for the men to come back and take us with them, but it was in vain, for the sound of

| then thought that our last chance was gone. Still, as | felt that the ship did not

While the younger boys slept, Fritz, our oldest son said, to me in a low tone, “If

Stick to Mediterranean vegetables that cook relatively quickly (quartered fennel would
also be good). The oven gives sausages such a crackly-crisp skin, you’ll never fry a
snag again.
INGREDIENTS
2 red onions
1 whole head garlic
2 medium eggplants
2 zucchinis
2 red capsicums
2 tbsp olive oil
400g canned tomatoes
1 tbsp thyme leaves
Sea salt
Black pepper
8 garlicky pork sausages
12 kalamata olives, unpitted
Fresh rosemary and thyme for swerving
METHOD
« Cut the onions into quarters, and the head of garlic in half crosswise.
« Cut the eggplants into rounds, the zucchinis into diagonal slices and the capsicums
into thick rounds, discarding core and seeds.
« Arrange in a large oiled baking tray, burying the garlic halves cut-side down. Add the
canned tomatoes and their juices, and a dash of water.
* Tuck in the pricked sausages, drizzle the lot with olive oil and scatter with thyme and
rosemary, sea salt and pepper.
* Bake for 45 minutes, turning the sausages once, until the veggies are cooked and
snags are browned.
« To serve, scatter with olives, rosemary and thyme. Squeeze the roasted garlic on top,
and drizzle with the pan juices.
Serves 4

The skating season had commenced unusually early: our boys were by no means
alone upon the ice. The afternoon was so fine that men, women and children, bent upon
enjoying the holiday, had flocked to the grand canal from far and near. St Nicholas had
evidently remembered the favourite pastime: shining new skates were everywhere to be
seen. Whole families were skimming their way to Haarlem, or Leyden, or the
neighbouring villages. The ice seemed fairly alive. Ben noticed the erect, easy carriage
of the women, and their picturesque variety of costume. There were the latest fashions,
fresh from Paris, floating past dingy, moth-eaten garments that had seen service through
two generations; coal-scuttle bonnets perched over freckled faces bright with holiday
smiles; stiff muslin caps, with wings at the sides flapping beside cheeks rosy with health
and contentment; furs, too, encircling the whites of throats; and scanty garments
fluttering below faces ruddy with exercise: in short, every quaint and comical mixture of
dry-goods and flesh that Holland could furnish seemed sent to enliven the scene.
There were belles from Leyden and fishwives from the border villages; cheese-
women from Gouda, and prim matrons from beautiful country seats on the Haarlemmer
Meer. Grey-headed skaters were constantly to be seen; wrinkled old women with
baskets upon their heads; and plump little toddlers on skates, clutching at their mother’s
gowns. Some women carried their babies upon their backs, firmly secured with a bright
shawl. The effect was pretty and graceful as they darted by, or sailed slowly past, now
nodding to an acquaintance, now chirruping and throwing soft baby-talk, to the muffled
little ones they carried.
Boys and girls were chasing each other, and hiding behind the one-horse sleds
that, loaded high with peat or timber pursued their cautious way along the track marked
out as “safe”. Beautiful, queenly women were there, enjoyment sparkling in their quiet
eyes. Sometimes a long file of young men, each grasping the coat of the before him,

WESTERN SWAMP TURTLE
This turtle, also called the western swamp tortoise, is found only in two swamps in Perth,
Western Australia and is possibly Australia’s most endangered reptile. There are less than
fifty of these animals still living in the wild.
The western swamp turtle is about 15 centimetres long, and has a short neck and a broad,
flat head, which is covered with a rough helmet. It has a square shell, which is brown on top
and olive-brown or yellow underneath.
In November or December, the female lays three to five hard-shelled eggs in a nest dug a
few centimetres below the surface of the ground. The hatchlings emerge between May and
June and may live for more than fifty years.
During the wet winter months, this turtle lives in the swamps. During summer they take
refuge from the sun, spending the hot months in holes in the ground, or under deep leaf litter.
The western swamp turtle feeds on small tadpoles and insect larvae found in and around
the swamp.
To try and ensure that the western swamp turtle does not become extinct, a captive breeding
program has been established at Perth Zoo, and a number of young turtles were born there
in 1989. This breeding program may be the only way that the western swamp turtle will
survive.
The turtle’s natural habitat lies right on the border of the city of Perth and its home has been
destroyed to make way for houses, office blocks and for agriculture. Clay mining has also
destroyed the home of the western swamp turtle.

sections.passage:
This is a passage from a book called The Gold Diggers by Belinda Hollyer. It is about the
history of gold mining
The gold miner needed very few tools when he set out on his search for gold. The
basic equipment could be as little as a shovel, a pick, a bucket and a pan for washing
the gold in. The shovel and the pick were needed for digging up the earth and gravel, the
bucket for carrying it in and the pan to wash the dirt away in the stream. Gold was much
heavier than the dirt which held it and it always sank to the bottom of the pan.
However, if the miner used only these few tools, it would take him many hours of
work to uncover just a few particles of gold. To wash the gold in the pan meant that he
_had to spend most of the day crouched in a cold mountain stream. To overcome these
problems the miners began to build all sorts of inventions to help them in their search for
riches.
In time the miners came to use the cradle, the long tom and the sluice, although
for the final washing they continued to use their pans to trap the small particles of gold.
All the three inventions still meant that the miners had to work very hard, but by working
in teams they were able to wash far more dirt in a day. As the gold was heavier than the
dirt it became trapped in the slats of the various contraptions. Water washed the dirt away.
This sort of mining for gold is called place mining. It involves washing the dirt, which
contains the gold with water. The water carries the dirt away leaving only the gold.
Long Tom
The long tom was made of two parts, a long trough and at the end of this an iron sheet
with holes in it called a riddle. Gravel was washed down the trough, through the riddle to
the riffle box where the gold was caught by bars as the dirt washed down.
Sluice
The sluice was made of a series of riffle boxes fitted together. Water flowed along it and
the miners shovelled in dirt along the sides. The gold was trapped against bars across
the riffle boxes.
Cradle
The cradle worked like this. Gravel and dirt were shovelled into a hopper, or box, at the
top. Then the miner gently rocked the cradle while pouring water over the dirt. The water
carried the gold through holes in the hopper and it was caught against the bars, which
were called riffles.

Nine gorgeous police puppies stuck to their normal routine with their mother
yesterday, oblivious that a police search to name them had made them stars.

Phar Lap
BEFORE Phar Lap’s second Melbourne Cup, gangsters were sending hitmen to stop him.
He was — and is — the only racehorse to become a national hero, firing the excitement of
Australia with his thundering race wins.
Phar Lap was named after the Thai word pharlap, meaning lightning, but he had a
nickname across the country — The Red Terror.
He seemed to be impossible to beat, and that was very dangerous.
Melbourne gangsters in the racing game were losing fortunes through Phar Lap and
becoming desperate.
Phar Laps’ trainer, Harry Telford, was warned of attacks through fire, acid and poison
darts as the Melbourne Cup of 1930 approached.
Strapper Tommy Woodcock was riding a pony and leading Phar Lap home from exercise
at Caulfield racecourse when he saw two suspicious men in an idling car.
Woodcock placed himself and the pony between the car and Phar Lap. The driver sped
past, blaring the horn as his mate fired a shotgun at the horse.
The shot splattered harmlessly over a high wooden fence, but Telford had had enough.
He took Phar Lap to the safety of Geelong until the race.
But the drama wasn’t over. Two hours before the race, Phar Laps float moved through
heavy rain out of Geelong, escorted by police motorcyclists.
And the engine died.
Telford and Woodcock took it in turns to crank the engine until it sputtered into life. They
reached Flemington racecourse no more than 30 minutes before the race was to start.
On that day four-year-old Phar Lap was carrying 9.12, a weight record for his age with
the odds of 11/8 on (meaning you put 11 units and if you win you only get 8 plus your
original 11). Phar Lap steamed through the race, winning effortlessly.
He was taken to America and he died in April 1932. There were unjustified rumours that
he had been poisoned by American gangsters.
Excerpt from ‘Legends Stories of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

One day a student from my class was constantly making noises to annoy the teacher. The

The student stopped for about two minutes then started to make the noise again. Again
the teacher said to stop it, but if the student made the noise again he would be kept in for
five minutes after class.

work as the teacher was busy telling the student off.
Discipline is a huge problem in schools today. Teachers constantly have to tell students
off for mucking around or playing up.
Students have no respect for teachers or their elders as the punishment normally consists
of sitting outside the principal’s office or being kept in a few minutes after class.
If the cane was to be reintroduced into the school system I would be happy with that.
There should be a limit on how many times you could use it.
Research has shown that approximately 3 per cent of teachers and students in schools
are robbed or physically attacked from lack of discipline.
Also minor types of misbehaviour from lack of discipline affects the flow of class
activities and interferes with learning.
Teachers are employed in the school to teach students, not to constantly spend their time
telling the student off for misbehaving.
Reintroducing the cane into schools would not only give the students of today a sense of
discipline but benefit the children of tomorrow.

Director: Steve Carr (Daddy Day Care)
Starring: Kevin James, Jayma Mays, Keir O’Donnell, Raini Rodriguz, Shirley Knight
kk
>My, what a waist
ONE of the weirdest box-office results to come out of the US in a long time is the
spectacular success of Paul Blart: Mall Cop.
Since its premiere in January, this nondescript comedy about a porky security guard
in a shopping centre has taken more than $200 million.
Perhaps in the land of Uncle Sam, the recession afflicts taste in movies before it hits
the hip pocket.
The first half of this movie is atrociously bland. Played by TV sitcom stalwart Kevin
James (The King of Queens), the title character is an over-officious, under-achieving
chubster.
Blart covers his beat in a suburban mall with the aid of a motorised upright scooter.
He crashes into things a lot. No one respects him. He is blessed with a good heart.
Cursed by a bad diet. He so wants to be in a relationship. He has a crush on the girl who
runs the hair-extensions kiosk. If only she could see the real him, you know?
That’s enough with the character profiling. Let’s just say that Paul Blart is every
Biggest Loser contestant that has ever lived, stuffed into the body of one man.
The movie improves noticeably after it works off all that sad-sack flab and walks
briskly towards a little low-impact action.
A gang of skateboard-riding youths lay siege to the mall and take hostages. Blart
misses all the initial hubbub because he is playing a video game.
So he becomes the last line of defence against an audacious robbery that could mean
death to innocent bystanders swept along in its wake.
The remainder of Paul Blart: Mall Cop plays out as expected, the door is creaked
open for a sequel, and the film slumps down to rest.
Inessential.
Herald-Sun March 19", 2009

Garry Hastings: Thanks for talking to Text Chat Magazine. | hear you are an
expert on Mr Bean and how audiences respond to him.
Jill McGill: Well, | have spent a lot of time researching Rowan Atkinson’s work.
Garry Hastings: So, does everyone love Mr Bean — or is it just everyone | know?
Jill McGill: Well, actually whilst Mr Bean is an amazingly popular character, not
all people find him funny. Instead, my research has found he seems to appeal to
a certain type of viewer.
Garry Hastings: Really? | think he’s hilarious and so do my kids.
Jill McGill: Yes, exactly. He is loved by children. They seem to find his simple
antics very amusing. Since he acts like a child much of the time they can relate to
him. Think of his teddy bear for instance and his inability to carry out multi-staged
tasks. Yet as they know he is an adult they can understand it is silly.
Garry Hastings: So who doesn't like Mr Bean?
Jill McGill: Well, it’s not so much they don’t like him it’s more that they do not
really respond. I’ve found very scientific, fact based people who like clear rules
and logic often find the humour rather lukewarm. They tend to describe the antics
as “stupid” and many even find the shows frustrating. These people do not tend
to enjoy physical humour, you know like slap-stick, but favour more intellectual
humour.
Garry Hastings: Wow? So does that make me a child then?
Jill McGill: No, no, no. There are many lucky people, like yourself, who are able
to appreciate all sorts of humour. You may well like a clever, intellectual satire just
as much.

our readers love Rowan Atkinson’s Mr Bean.

Our transport revolution
WHILE views might differ about what should be built first, the massive Victorian
Transport Plan to be announced today is crucial to ensuring our city’s future.
Following almost a decade of promises, and many earlier “plans” to fix greater
Melbourne’s transport woes, this blueprint could finally be a way forward.
It includes a $6 billion link — with tunnels — between the Eastern Freeway at Bulleen and
the Western Ring Road at Greensborough.
Rail would be extended from Epping to South Morang. Footscray and Caulfield would
be linked by underground tracks, and $650 million would be spent on new trains.
Money is allocated to work out how Hoddle St traffic might move faster, and $100 million
over 12 years has been set aside for bicycle paths.
Part of Sir Rod Eddington’s proposed east-west road link is in the mix.
Melbournians are expected to make almost three million extra car trips daily in the next
25 years. More than 900,000 extra trips will be taken on public transport over the same
period.
Transport is a city’s veins and arteries. Without it, we could not work or visit friends or
enjoy ourselves.
And as Melbourne becomes more popular and sprawls ever farther, excellent systems
will be increasingly important.
Aspects of them will always be controversial, but we have no alternative but to build and
pay for them.
Assaults down
THAT CBD assaults on Friday and Saturday nights in October and November dropped
by 24 per cent compared with last year is encouraging.
The Safe Streets Taskforce program begun last month appears to be working, even if
the numbers of drunks remains disturbing.
Police have issued more than 1440 penalty notices for offensive behaviour and urinating
in public. And, despite extra officers on the streets and CCTV vans, Herald Sun reporters
have witnessed this weekend shocking alcohol-fuelled scenes.
Residents of outer suburbs rarely see such things. They are the happiest Melburnians,
according to Leader Newspapers’ annual My Melbourne survey.
If only young people who play — play up —in the CBD could adopt some of the communal
responsibility shown in such places as Eltham and Warrandyte.
Herald Sun (Melbourne, Australia) 12-08-2008

It was quiet in the pines except for the sound of the wind humming through their
branches. Robbie pushed his hands against a tree trunk and straightened one leg, then
the other, behind him. He could feel his calf muscles pulling and the bark digging into his
palms. Next he rested his heel on a stump and bent forward over his outstretched leg until
the hamstring muscle in his thigh warned him to go no further. He swapped legs and
repeated the exercise.
His body had ceased rewving like a car with the accelerator stuck. Robbie recognized
the calm he usually felt at this time before a race. His heart would pound again when he
lined up with the others at the start, but now he felt almost sleepy. He breathed deeply,
shook his arms and legs, and focused his mind on the course he, Mum and Tid had walked
together this morning.
It was a tight, twisting, hilly trail. A good cross-country course, the parents said.
Robbie remembered the narrow gateway a hundred metres from the start. He would have
to be near the lead if he didn’t want to wait his turn to get through there. Then there was a
narrow track with a barbed-wire fence on one side and a steep drop on the other. The
course opened out after that.
They had walked up a gradual slope, around a marker in a clump of trees and down a
gravel road, where the pebbles skidded under their feet, to a creek crossing. “Go for it up
the hill,” Mum had advised. “Careful coming down this gravel. Not too fast or you'll go head
over heels into the creek.”

Irene Murray (of Dunolly)
We gave this day a name
To be remembered evermore.

HOW TO...
START BACK ON A GOOD NOTE
THE summer holidays are over (boo hoo!), but returning to school needn't be a negative
experience. Take advantage of having had a well-earned break and begin the year with
some helpful habits.
CATCH SOME Z22ZZS
Get off on the right foot with a good night’s sleep. Teenagers need at least eight-and-a-half
hours rest, otherwise you may feel yourself drifting off during the day or losing concentration
in class.
EAT BREAKFAST
Your body and brain need energy to get through the day — think off all that learning, running
and concentrating you'll be doing! So dig into a bowl of cereal or toast before you leave the
house each morning. The time poor should prepare a sandwich or smoothie the night before.
MAKE FRIENDS
Whether you're new at school or are returning to the same buildings for the umpteenth time:
take the opportunity to meet new people. Join a club or volunteer at an event. Even
something as simple as saying hello to your locker neighbour can help you feel a part of
things.

Begin the year with a manageable workload. Ask your teachers when important assignments
will be due so you can get a head start on research. More work done at school means less
to take home that night!

Lasseter’s Lost Reef
IN 1897, Harold Bell Lasseter was found unconscious in the desert southwest of Alice
Springs by an Afghan camel-driver — with some interesting rocks.
And the legend grew from there.
Lasseter said he had found a fabulously rich gold reef in the trackless desert out west,
but he would not say where. He wanted to lead an expedition to it.
For a while nobody seemed to be interested, but in 1911 there was an expedition — only
to be beaten back by the toughness of the country.
Lasseter tried one more time, in 1930, with a plane, a six-wheeled lorry and a team of
experts.
The plane crashed and Lasseter said they were over 250 kilometres off course.
The party on the ground battled on but finally decided to go home — except for Lasseter
and a dingo shooter, Paul Johns.
They pressed on, and Lasseter finally said he had found his reef. But he would not show
Johns where it was. They fought in the desert and Johns turned back, leaving Lasseter with
two camels.
The camels bolted from Lasseter, and though an Aboriginal tribe helped him he was
getting weaker and suffering from sandy-blight blindness.
He buried his papers under a tree marked ‘DIG’, crawled into a cave and died.
Nobody has ever found any trace of Lasseter’s reef.
From ‘Legends of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

October 1943
The desert night was almost over, the velvety darkness thinning to pink. At his post, Erich
glanced up, watching the foreign stars beginning to twinkle into obscurity.
“It is cold, yes?”
“Yes.” His companion was talkative. A private named Janz. Twenty-two or three years
old but still wet behind the ears, as far as Erich was concerned.
“You think they will come today?”
Erich shrugged a noncommittal reply. Who knew? Perhaps today, perhaps tomorrow.
Sometimes soon, that was certain.
“They say there are reinforcements on their way from the north.” His companion reached
for a cigarette. “Put that away, idiot! Do you want to bring the whole British army down on
us?”
“Sorry.” Janz’s fingers, numb with cold, fumbled the cigarettes back into his shirt pocket
and the silence of the desert settled again.
Erich stared into the growing dawn, watching the light slowly ooze along the landscape
and across the rolling dunes towards them as the invisible sun climbed towards the horizon.
“At least it will warm up soon, yes?”
“Yes. And then we will burn all day.”
It was the worst thing about this cursed desert — when it wasn’t freezing, it was boiling.
During the day the sun would blaze down on the little encampment, scorching pale
Germanic skin into angry red welts easily inflamed by the sand which seeped its way into
every crack and cranny of the body. It was bad enough that they were there, worse because
none of them had any idea why.

GRAHAM HICKS
Despite being deaf and blind, Graham ‘G-Force’ Hicks (UK) holds
the outright quadbike (PWC) speed records. He achieves his records
with the help of pillion riders who ride behind him and tell him where
to steer using a touch system.
What caused your deafblindness?
My optic nerves were severely damaged at birth leaving me with only a
very small amount of residual vision. My deafness was p ropressive from
age seven and is believed to have been caused by a childhood illness
probably measles.
Why did you settle on motorized challenges as a way of setting
records?
I have always had a great interest and fascination in motorcycles and the
sea. I fixed and rode battered old motorbikes in my late teens. Quadbiking
and jetskiing are my top two passions!
What inspires you to attempt these records?
I’m very committed to proving that, with the right attitude and support, deafblindness is no barrier to
extreme sports. All my challenges are under the auspices of the charity Deafblind UK.
What do your family and friends think about your rather risky pastime?
I think most have got used to the fact I’m a bit mad. My niece once said to me ‘it’s better to die on
your feet than live on your knees.’
What other challenges do you face?
My greatest challenge has nothing to do with my disability directly — it’s all about prejudice from
others and the barriers that result.
What do you do in your free time?
DIY, such as carpentry, plumbing and mains wiring. I also enjoy socializing and reading.
From ‘The Guinness Book of Records’ 2006 Edition

Then it fell like huge hot drops of metal, heavy like the sap of trees or globules of honey. It was
even the colour of honey, sometimes burnt honey, sometimes golden.
The juices of the forest so greedily sucked up, the heady juices of gum and pine and acacia, and the
wind-blown salts of the earth and the sweat of men and the blood of beasts and the steam of ditches
and ponds and creeks and rivers and reservoirs, of tanks and hoses, of irrigated fields and mud puddles,
seemed to have become too heavy a load for the sated heavens to bear, and having weakened, having
allowed the first drops to fall, they seemed to be spilling the lot over.
Black rain, red rain, golden rain, steaming rain, crashed on to the earth, and the sound was real
thunder and the jagged light was real lighting and the giants of north wind and south wind, of the
inferno and of the breadth of the wide cool sea, were locked in conflict.
Peter and Gran Fairhall dragged themselves from the spring, away from the snakes and the other
swimming creatures, and the mammoth flare in the sky had dissolved, had vanished, had become a
tempestuous brown fog.
Gran, confused but revived, awfully battered but conscious, wrapped her huge fleshy arms about
her grandson, as she was often apt to do, and hugged him tight. For years Peter had detested it, had
endured it with a set face and pounding heart; but that had been the way of a boy, not the way of a
man. Gran even sensed the difference herself and faintly heard his voice: ‘It’s all right, Gran.
Everything’s all right now.’
Pippa felt it beating on to her body. At first it came hot like her morning shower and she thought it
was fire; but it did not consume her; it grew cooler; and cooler still.

Q ~~ Why do the tops of some Christmas cakes crack?
I use a fan-forced oven. Val
A Because Christmas cakes are usually dense with fruit,
they take a long time to cook, therefore the top of the cake
is exposed to more direct heat than the rest of the cake.
To prevent this, sprinkle or finely mist water over the top
of the cake before putting it in the oven. After the first
30 minutes baking, cover the top of the cake with foil or
brown paper and place a container of water in the oven to
create a little steam during the cooking. Make sure you
refill it during the cooking process. Fan-forced ovens tend
to dry rich fruit cakes more than conventional cooking.
Cook at a moderately slow temperature and let the cake
cool in the tin for 30 minutes or more before turning out.
As the cake cools, any cracks usually close over.
— KATE McGHIE
Herald-Sun, September 9" 2008

toto
Mere seconds after you first pick up the joypad to play this thrilling racer, you will be hurting off
enormous vertiginous jumps and performing death-defying tricks.
Your steed is a four-wheeled all-terrain vehicle and at all times you are battling 15 aggressive rivals.
The main attraction is the World Tour mode, which visits spectacular locations in countries such as
Italy, New Zealand and Thailand, and offers three different events — races, sprints and freestyle
competitions. Sprints are on very short courses, but the three lap races are long with many jumps and
multiple routes.
The goal in freestyle events is to amass points by performing as many tricks as possible before you
run out of petrol. Chaining wild manoeuvres together is particularly lucrative.
There are four levels of increasingly elaborate tricks, all performed by pressing a button and pushing
the stick in different directions.
Landing a trick earns you boost power, which can be very helpful for catching up to opponents.
Substantially filling your boost meter allows access to higher levels of even more rewarding tricks, so
it is always a tough, strategic decision whether to utilise the boost immediately or conserve the power
for later.
Crashes are common until you learn the best routes and the optimal stunt opportunities on each of
the 12 gorgeous courses, but the consequences are thankfully not too punitive, reducing frustration.
Success is rewarded with access to new events and new parts for your customised vehicles. The tool
for creating your own ride is fiddly though, so it’s much easier to simply let the computer assemble
the best bike for racing or stunt work.
More events, tracks and vehicle types would have given the game more depth and variety, but the
online multiplayer action is certain to be popular.
The Age, October 9" 2008

Haazel Edwards
‘If we win this afternoon, the final will be held at the weekend.’ Miss Ionnides’ voice sliced through
Rachel’s daydreams. In her head she had pitched three perfect strikes while the softball fans cheered.
‘Oh no! Not this Saturday. I’ll be the odd one out AGAIN,’ thought Rachel. ‘And Sunday is no
good either.’
At the sports noticeboard, Miss Ionnides had filled in the names of the softball team. Green ink
made the names stick out. Usually Rachel was the pitcher and Cowen was written in big, green letters
alongside the place of the pitcher. That always gave Rachel a warm feeling of being part of the team.
But today was different.
‘Miss Ionnides, I can’t play this weekend. I’m doing my barmy.’
‘Speak up Rachel. With all that noise from the corridor, I can’t hear you.” Inside the sports
cupboard,Miss Ionnides was sorting the equipment. Bats. Balls. Gloves. She tried to shut the door with
her foot and a box of gloves fell down. Crash!
Rachel went red as she bent to pick up the gloves and muttered, ‘I’m doing my bat mitzvah this
weekend.’
‘Oh,’ Miss Ionnides turned around. ‘I’d forgotten you were Jewish, Rachel. But we’d only need
you for an hour at two o’clock.’
Inside her tummy, Rachel felt the old turning feeling. Everything turned upside down and she
couldn’t stop it. That feeling always came back when she had to explain things.
Why did she always have to explain about being Jewish? And about eating kosher food? She
wasn’t THAT different. She didn’t have three heads or eleven toes. It was just her religion. And that
came from her parents. Family religions weren’t like supermarkets where you could go along and
choose. So Rachel took a deep breath and tried to explain, again.
‘Saturday is Shabbat, our Sabbath. I’m not supposed to work on that day.’

Recruits, returnees and rookies go on show
By GREG BAUM
THE ball fell to Ben Cousins in the middle of the incongruously lush oval at Gosch’s Paddock.
He gathered, arched his back in that familiar way and ran in a wide semi-circle. Now in space,
he paused momentarily, then accelerated again, on a new course, straight towards goal.
Ahead, other players hastily rearranged themselves. “Watch the dish,” urged a man in the
crowd of around 1500, standing three-deep around the fence.
Cousins’ “‘dish” (that is, pass) began wide, but curved as if on an unseen wind, unerringly
onto the chest of the helmeted Graham Polak, leading hard into the forward pocket.
It would be gilding the lily to say that the crowd roared, but it certainly clapped
appreciatively.
Cousins and Polak played together for Richmond yesterday. It was an irresistible turn of
events since one was a drug addict out in the football cold three months ago and the other
was — and still is — rehabilitating from head injuries after being wrong-footed by a tram last
June.
But it was qualified by all these certainties: it was February 5, too early even for March
championship; it was 27 degrees, too sultry for football; the Nylex clock that formed part of
the backdrop said so.
Cousins played half a game, then was whisked away by car, his now customary blaze of
secrecy. Polak played about 40 minutes. Matthew Richardson was long gone, back, bare-
chested, across the scorched parkland to the Tiger’s Punt Road HQ; one, dominant quarter
was enough to clear his few cobwebs.
Excerpt from report I ‘The Age’ newspaper February 6” 2009

Bushfire Weather
by Jeri Kroll
It’s cool in the hills,
breezes dart through houses like trapped birds
beating glass till they’re free.
It’s clean up there. Smog doesn’t rain
Across the garden, smudging the birds of paradise,
fingerprinting the windowsills.
It’s calm in the hills when the frenzied heat
in the town bullies pedestrians.
The north wind eggs it on:
cotton wrapped like a second skin
loosens and billows, even sunglasses can’t screen the grit,
the earth in the driveway’s blown off,
vegetables wilt in the garden,
the city lies like an old dog.
In century heat, in the tinder-dry hills,
air has an edge, too, but shade is kinder.
Children swing across the Onkaparinga
into cool green slime. Cats pant under water tanks,
horse munch prickly grass under rattling trees.
By one o’clock the city has a compress on its head,
no longer looks at the hills
as if they meant afterlife.
The north-east wind dries sweat running down the spine,
belches out yellow clouds, pummeling cyclists,
rocks the lucky sheep trucked from the hills.
Down in the mall the dogged buskers play
till a string snaps.

Martin Luther King
Martin Luther King was born in 15" January, 1929 in Atlanta, Georgia, a southern state of
America. As a child he became aware of how unfairly black people were treated. They
were segregated from white people in schools, restaurants and on transport. Martin
resolved to do what he could to change this state of affairs.
At nineteen, Martin commenced his studies for the ministry. At this time, he became
strongly influenced by Mahatma Gandhi’s philosophy of non-violent protest. After his
ordination, he threw himself into the struggle for black rights. He spearheaded non-violent
demonstrations and in 1963, organised the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
250 000 people converged on Washington on 28" August and Martin Luther King,
standing on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, delivered his most famous speech, “I have
a Dream”.
Gradually, the position of black people in America began to improve. Schools, colleges
and transport systems were integrated. This progress came at a personal Cost to King.
His house was bombed, he was stabbed and once he was jailed for requesting service in
a ‘white only’ restaurant.
In 1963, Martin Luther King was Time Magazine’s “Man of the Year”. The following year,
the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Martin Luther King for his efforts to achieve justice
for the black people of America. Yet, at the time, King was experiencing great difficulties.
His efforts were scorned by the more militant black organisations and at the same time,
his work was being resistance to the war in Vietnam. On 4th April, 1968, Martin Luther
King was assassinated. Although his life was cut short, his achievements were formidable.
He succeeded in greatly advancing the cause of justice and equality for black people.

VANESSA CLELLAND

Start to finish: 1 hours

Makes: about 12

pasta sauce

Bondi of all places!
I have ridden Waimea Bay a number of times, which would have to be considered the largest
surfable surf spot in the world. However, I’d like to tell you about the largest wave I can remember
riding here in Australia.
Surprisingly enough, it was at Bondi of all places. As usual, a large southerly storm created
: huge seas in the Sydney area. Actually, the only way you surf big waves in the Sydney area is when
a storm is on. It was really really big, and Brad Mayes, Paul Manstead and I walked right around
the roadway to the southern end of the point.
There were set waves breaking way out to sea in deep water. We thought we had timed it right
with a safe full, so we jumped off this big flat rock and started paddling like crazy. H
: Out of fear, I was paddling the fastest. As we approached the line-up area, these three waves
were coming in to meet us. The first one was so huge that it seemed as if I was paddling up it for
ages. Paddle, paddle, paddle. :
I quickly focused my attention on the third wave that was just about to break, and I almost i
bailed out at the top, but decided to take the punt and try to get through, which I did.
i As the wave went past me, my heart was going BOOM, BOOM, BOOM, and I said almost
out loud... My God. How am I going to get in?
: I tumed around and saw how far out to sea I was, and thought that maybe it would have been
better to get washed in with my other two friends. They ended up getting washed up the rocks and
scratched up a bit, along with their boards. :
I picked this wave which would have been over four metres. I started going across the face in :
a right slide. I could see this giant left coming from the northern point.
I had to make this decision, as I was going across the top, whether I wanted to try and pull off
one of these bounce-off-the-white-water things you do in small surf. It really looked perfect to try :
to do it... almost inviting me to try.
The moment of truth finally came where I could try it or pull out. But then I noticed that it had
become too late, and I was committed.
I pulled it up and went up, up and away, and got terribly wiped out.
I still think about that one moment often, as it was really a big wave, and a situation that I'd
like to come in contact with again.
BRUCE RAYMOND, Backdoor

FROG enthusiasts have leapt into action for the annual Melbourne Water Frog Census.
The State Government is calling for volunteers to help monitor and record frog croaks at rivers,
creeks and wetlands around Western Port and Port Phillip as part of the 2008-09 frog census.
Melbourne Water will use the information to form a detailed map of the distribution of frogs across
the city.
Volunteers have recorded more than 3000 frog calls and identified 13 species of frogs since the
initial 2001 census.
Last year’s results uncovered what appeared to be a rise in the number of threatened growling grass
frogs and southern brood frogs.
Earlier this year, volunteers managed to record a common spade foot for only the second time in
the history of the census.
Melbourne Water chairman Cheryl Batagol said in previous years volunteers had visited up to 10
sites a night to record frog calls.
“This demonstrates incredible passion and commitment, and we gratefully acknowledge the
contribution of these volunteers,” Ms Batagol said.
Spring and autumn are the most vocal times for frogs.
The Department of Sustainability and Environment intends to study the results of the census to
assess the health of Melbourne’s waterways and the status of threatened species.
To join the water frog census, visit: www.melbournewater.com.au
Herald-Sun, August 2008

Hammocks are difficult to climb into but once in, they are also hard to fallout of. But do you

Well the hammock was invented by the Indians of South America. Their word for the hammock

remember houses were in short supply) that they quickly borrowed the idea. The idea next spread
to sailing ships and the military and of course it didn’t take long for ‘hamaca’ to be changed into the

An excerpt from “My Two — Wheeled Catastrophe” by Patrick McManus
There was a hill about three kilometres from our house called King Hill. By rights it
should have been called Dead Man’s Drop.
Just as I was cresting the hill and starting my descent, one of our neighbour’s wolves
appeared. From fifty metres away, a grin appeared on its face as soon as it spotted me. It
crouched, waiting. The chain chose to eat my trouser leg. I expected to be left by the front
wheel any minute. With one last effort I aimed a kick at the wolf, ripped my trouser leg
free and threw myself into space. I bounced four times, and used my nose as a brake.
Even the wolf was shaken by the impact of the crash. It stared at the wreckage in silent
amazement, forgetting my leg in its jaws.
When I was up and about once more my mother bought a car. She got it from a local
friend who built it with his own three hands. But that’s another story.

sections.passage:
LONE DOG
I’m a lean dog, a keen dog, a wild dog, and lone; -
I’m a rough dog, a tough dog, hunting on my own;
I’m a bad dog, a mad dog, teasing silly sheep;
I love to sit and bay the moon, to keep fat souls from sleep.
I’ll never be a lap dog, licking dirty feet,
A sleek dog, a meek dog, cringing for my meat,
Not for me the fireside, the well-filled plate,
But shut door, and sharp stone, and cuff, and kick, and hate.
Not for me the other dogs, running by my side,
Some have run a short while, but none of them would bide,
O mine is still the lone trail, the hard trail, the best,
Wild wind, and wild stars, and the hunger of the quest!
IRENE R. McLEOD

Kicking an emotional goal
2004 ATHENS IAN THORPE
//// REBECCA WILLIAMS
IAN Thorpe boasted many strengths as a swimmer. But until his 400m freestyle final in 2004, emotion had
never been a weapon he’d used in the pool.
Strategy went out the window in Athens for the champ, who admitted to having too much on his mind as
he stood on the blocks.
Who could blame him?
If Thorpe’s title defence wasn’t already one of the biggest events of Australia’s Games campaign, it took on
a life of its own after the Olympic trials in March that year when he was disqualified after a false start in the
400m heats.
He was later granted a swim in his signature event after Craig Stevens gave up his place to his training
partner. The gesture meant Thorpe was no longer racing for just himself. Expectation had become a much larger
beast.
“Through circumstances ... my preparation did not include training for this event. (So) it was the first time
I swam purely on emotion. I could not really implement a strategy.”
Thorpe touched to win his second Olympic 400m gold in 3min43.10sec — 0.26sec ahead of teammate Grant
Hackett - then went on to win gold in the 200m and bronze in the 100m.
It took his overall Olympic haul to nine medals and past Dawn Fraser and Susie O’Neil as Australia’s most
successful Olympian.
Herald-Sun July 9*

LETTER OF THE MONTH
YOUTH OF TODAY
NICOLA
Year 8, SCHOOL WITHHELD
If you watch the news or read the newspaper the impression you would get of the youth of today
is that they are all out of control. They swear constantly, they are drunk half of the time, they have
no respect for their elders and they don’t stand up for the elderly on trains/buses. A lot of older
people have been complaining and taking about the ‘good old days’ when they were children and
were respectful.
Older people always think that youth are bad mannered and rude. In the 1970s, when most
people complaining now were young, a poet wrote about youth and how spoilt, stubborn and ill
mannered they were. A scripture from ancient Egypt has been found where a teacher was
complaining about youth.
Have the older people forgotten what it is like to be young and rebellious? Young people
always rebel and do the wrong thing; it’s the way they express themselves. They need to
experiment, gain some life experience and learn what is right and wrong. They have a lot to deal
with and by the time they have got a little older they will have settled down and probably started
complaining about youth as well.
...People are quick to blame the parents, but I only partially agree with this. Sure, kids might
pick up things at home, but parents can’t monitor their kids 24/7. A lot of people act totally
different at school or on public transport to the way they do at home.
They are good and bad things about every generation and it only takes a few people to ruin it
for all.
‘spress’ November 2008

Q&A
SEAMUS BYRNE
EDITOR OF GAMING GUIDE,
KOTAKU AUSTRALIA
What are the most popular video games and why?
There are the big name series like Halo, but also massive successes in casual games like
Bejeweled and big casual games for Nintendo Wii like WiiSports. If there is one thing
connecting most of today’s biggest games, it is the ability to play with friends.
How have games changed?
Graphics are the most obvious evolution for games, but multi-player has completely
revolutionised the industry when you compare it to the ‘80s and early ‘90s. While many
detractors still believe games are anti-social, the reality today is that they are incredibly social.
Whether sitting together on a couch or online against players from around the world, games
are now much more about shared entertainment experiences and challenges.
What does a typical ‘gamer’ look like?
The latest research shows a ‘typical’ gamer is about 28 years old (I’m 32) and almost half
are female. Certain kinds of games will appeal to different types of people, but there are so
many kinds of videogames now it would be hard to pin down a single ‘typical’ player.
Teenagers probably have more leisure time for games than adults, but more people are
foregoing TV in favour of keeping up their gaming hobby. | think the gamer stereotype of the
anti-social, teenage boy is only held by people who are over 40 and have only touched a
game once or twice in their life.
There’s been a lot of talk about games promoting sexism and violence — what’s your
opinion?
Compared with nightly news, Hollywood movies, and celebrity magazines, I’d suggest games
are hardly the worst offenders in any debate over sex and violence. Unlike more passive
forms of media, a game can also demonstrate consequences for certain actions. Some of
the best action games in recent years, such as the Metal Gear Solid series and the Splinter
Cell series, reward players for choosing to achieve goals through stealthy means rather than
all guns blazing. There’s plenty of violence in games, but games and sport are ultimately a
contest, and that brings conflict to the forefront — even chess is based on the idea of war. |
think gamers respond more to the quality of game play than the violence.
What do you think is the next big thing in video games?
Gaming as a professional sport. Already in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, there are gamers
making a very comfortable living playing videogames at an elite level. | think schools should
start to support kids who take their games seriously in the same way they support those who
take their football, or their chess, seriously. What are the odds of turning pro in tennis? Pretty
slim. | think there are better odds for young gamers to take games to a professional level.
They won't make millions — yet — but there are opportunities to make a good salary out of
gaming if you can make it into a big team overseas, and with good local support local
opportunities are likely to emerge in the decade ahead.
‘spress’ November 2008
