. i ARIES> Mar 21 — Apr 20
Some people love to take simple things and make them complicated. They use long words
when they could just as easily use short ones. Or they refer, mysteriously, to obscure rules
and regulations to support vague assertions and assumptions. All this is a convenient way to
claim authority or to maintain control. When, though, you are being given a bunch of reasons
why something very easy must become difficult, it can be very annoying. If you use your
psychological scissors, you can cut through a tangle of tape today.
© TAURUS> Apr 21 — May 21
When your heart says one thing and your mind another, a dangerous division emerges. The
two most crucial guiding forces in your life begin to wage war. It is always better to be open
about an inner conflict than to hide it from others or deny it to yourself. If you suppress it,
your heart will try to trick your head. It will allow it to think that it is in control, but it will
undermine it by causing you to overlook something crucial. Negotiate an inner truce. Make
peace with yourself this week and all relationships will improve.
GEMINI> May 22 — Jun 22
Every so often scientists set out to prove that psychic power don't exist. They collect
clairvoyants and stick them in laboratories where, under the flicker of fluorescent lights and
the constant suspicious gaze of prejudiced academics, they try to make them summon
spontaneous insight. If you now seek a full explanation for a powerful impulse, you won't find
it. Indeed, you will squash an inspired, instinctive idea if you subject it to too much analysis.
But if you just trust it and act on it, you will work wonders.
Herald-Sun January 5 2008

sections.title: Questions 27-30
sections.passage:
THE TOYMAKER
Jeremy de Quidt, ills. Gary Blythe
Random House, $32.95
The usually benign art of toy-making takes a sinister twist in this book about
Menschenmacher, a German artisan who brings his toys to life by removing the beating
hearts of small birds and nestling them in the cavities of his creations, with disturbing results.
At the heart of this story is a boy named Mathias. Not yet a teenager, he already has a life of
misery. When his miserable grandfather dies, the former conjuror passes on a secret that
forces Mathias to outwit a collection of ghastly characters. One early scene has Mathias and
his new friend Katta chased down a tunnel that’s thoroughly scary. Jeremy de Quidt’s novel
for older readers is not for the faint-hearted. Gothic in style, there are hints of fantasy, horror
and a bit of Grimms’ fairytales, too. Gary Blythe’s literal black and white drawings help you
visualise some of the most disturbing characters, which is not always a good thing! Don't let
the flowery cover mislead you; this is a finely crafted read that explores big questions about
life and death and what it is to be truly alive. A thrilling read that lingers in the mind.

Canberra's hills shimmered above the road as Angela left the city centre. Round bald hills with
grass like short brown fur, long sloping hills baking in the sunshine. The far-off gums on Tidbinbilla
Peak and Mt Tidbinbilla shone like blue-green armour. The Wallaces’ house was on the outskirts
of Canberra, a new suburb with only a few houses finished, backing onto hot paddocks. The long
dry grass rippled like feathers in the breeze. The blue ranges rose above the Murrumbidgee River.
It was a small house, and very new. The grass grew in patches over the clay, a few shrubs
were tied to stakes and a couple of roses grew by the front door. They looked stunted and badly
pruned. Angela smiled. Maybe they had been nibbled by a dinosaur. She knocked on the door. It
opened slightly. A face peered out.
‘Hello. Michael? I’m Dr Angela Boardman.’
The door opened wider. ‘I rang Mum,’ said Michael. ‘She said | could talk to you.’
‘| thought you asked her when | rang,’ said Angela, as she walked into the hall.
Michael shook his head. ‘Mum says to pretend she’s home if anyone rings when she’s at
work,’ he said, ‘in case it’s a burglar or something. Then | ring her up straightaway. She doesn’t
get home till after five.’ He led the way into the kitchen. Angela followed him.
‘What time does your daddy get home?’
‘He doesn't,’ said Michael. ‘He doesn’t live here any more.’
‘Oh,’ said Angela.
Michael Wallace was thin, with wide dark eyes and spiky black hair. He had a habit of watching
you closely that Angela found disconcerting. ‘Would you like a cup of coffee?’ he asked. ‘| make
Mum one when she gets home from work. Or there’s orange juice.’
Angela shook her head. ‘I just came to talk to you about your picture of the dinosaurs,’ she
said. ‘It was very good, Michael.’
‘Have | won?’ asked Michael hopefully.
‘Well, no. But | liked them a lot.’
‘| didn't think | would,’ said Michael. ‘It was Miss Watson who wanted to send them. She's my
teacher. She liked them too. But they weren't real dinosaurs. Not like tyrannosauruses or
brontosauruses.’
‘Of course they were real,’ said Angela, ‘just as real as the big ones. Where did you get the
idea from?’
Michael looked out the window, then back at Angela. ‘Oh, | just did,’ he said.
There was a pause. A fly buzzed through the open window, landed on Angela’s face. She
brushed it away, It came back again with sticky summer feet. Through the window she could see
a new house going up next door, wooden frame and piles of bricks. There must have been a
lovely view of the hills before they started building, she thought.
‘Maybe some orange juice would be nice,’ said Angela.
Excerpt from ‘Dancing Dinosaurs’ By Jackie French

whose achievements to date rank him among the most successful golfers of all time. Currently

Woods has won fourteen professional major golf championships, the second highest of any male

tournament where no black player competed until 1975 and a club that didn’t admit a black
member until 1990.

major championships and the 2008 Ryder Cup, in order to rehabilitate his injured left knee.

The Game of Cricket
Cricket is a bat and ball game. It was played in England before the end of the sixteenth century.
It is now the leading summer game in Britain, most of the countries of the British
Commonwealth and also in South Africa.
Cricket is similar in many ways to baseball. In cricket, there is a bowler who bowls (pitches
a ball made of cork and twine encased in leather). A player from the opposing team tries to
hit the ball with a narrow, flat-faced wooden bat. The batsman’s object is to score runs. The
team that scores most runs wins the game.
A cricket field may be of any size. Near the centre of the field is the pitch, a special strip of
level ground that measures 66 feet [20.12 metres] in length. The pitch is marked out with
white lines called creases. At both ends of the pitch are the wickets, which consist of three
short stumps. The wickets are 9 inches [22.86 centimetres] wide and 28 inches [71.1
centimetres] high. The batsman has to guard the wicket against the bowler when he is trying
to make runs.

S O U NDER by W.H. Armstrong.
Sounder was already across the road into the stalk land, whining, moving his head from one
side to the other, looking back to be sure the boy was following.
Across the stalk land, into the pine woods, into the climbing, brightening glow of dawn, the boy
followed the dog, whose anxious pace slowed from age as they went. “By a dog’s age, Sounder
is past dying time,” the boy said half aloud. Fear had always prompted him to talk to himself.
Deep in the pine woods, along a deserted logging road the boy and dog came to a small open
space where there had once been a log ramp. The sun was just beginning to drive its first
splinters of light through the pines, bouncing against the tree trunks and the earth. At the foot
of one of the trees the boy’s father sat, the lantern still burning by his side.
“So tuckered out he fell asleep,” the boy said to himself.
But the figure did not move when Sounder licked his hand. The boy put his hand on his father’s
good shoulder and shook ever so gently. The chin did not lift itself; no eyes turned up to meet
the boy. “‘Tired, so tired.”
When the boy returned to the cabin and told his mother, her lips grew long and thin and pale.
But when she finally spoke, they were warm and soft as when she sang. “When life is so
tiresome, there ain’t no peace like the greatest peace - the peace of the Lord’s hand holding you.
And he’I1 have a store-bought box for his burial ‘cause all these years I paid close attention to
his burial insurance.”
They buried the boy’s father in the unfenced lot behind the meeting’ house. The preacher stood
amid the sumac and the running briars before the mound of fresh red earth and read:

An extract from William Taylor’s book “Circles”
My mother died of sick madness. She died of this sick madness and of grief and fear. She
died in a strange and alien place, so far from what she thought of as home, a home she
would never, ever see again.
If a story may be said to have a beginning, this is the beginning of mine. In truth, I know,
the story of no one really does have a beginning. There must always be something that has
just gone on before and there were, naturally, a lot of somethings that happened before my
mother’s death that indeed led to that cursed and dreadful moment. It is true, though, that
the dying of the poor sad woman I loved so dearly really did provide the marker, the turning
point to my subsequent existence.
It was fifty years ago to the day, the day on which I choose to begin to write these words,
fifty years ago that my father, my brother and I dug her grave, dressed Mother in her own
gown, wrapped her remains, poor thin little soul she had become, in the linen that had once
been her mother’s, and laid her to rest among those trees. At rest in those trees, beneath the
trees she had so greatly feared. She rests there today, a scant half mile from where I sit
writing these words, words that I write surrounded by a comfort and splendor that she never
experienced and of which, likely, simple soul, she never dreamed.
Today I pushed my way through the undergrowth, doing my best to follow the ill-formed
track to the spot beneath the giant rimu tree where a slab of marble says: ‘Elizabeth
Costello 1840-1876 and John Costello 1839-1876’. My father, foolish man, lost spirit,
survived his wife by no more than a handful of hours. Robert and I dug his grave and then
we left this place with, in reality, little hope of ever seeing it again.

The Black Rat
He lived in a tin hut with a hard dirt floor,
He had bags sewn together that was his door.
He was a Rat of Tobruk until forty-five,
He was one of the few that came back alive.
Battered and scared he fought for this land,
And on his return they all shook his hand.
The price of fighting for the freedom of man,
Did not make any difference to this Blackman.
He returned to the outback, no mates did he find,
If he had a beer he was jailed and then fined.
He sold all his medals he once proudly wore:
They were of no use to him any more.
Confused and alone he wandered around,
Looking for work though none could be found.
The Anzac marches he badly neglected,
Would show to his comrades how he was rejected.
He fought for this land so he could be free,
Yet he could not vote after his desert melée.
And those years in that desert they really took their toll,
He went there quite young and came home so old.
This once tall man came from a proud Black tribe,
Died all alone — no one at his side.
lris Clayton

I am a 17-year-old year 11 at a boys’ school. I sat through the past week of politics
astounded. I have no political bias, nor am I excusing the comments of Alan Jones and Peter
Slipper, which I find insensitive and disgusting, or the occasional sexist and backwards 1970s
view of Tony Abbott.
However, to quote our Prime Minister, “I will not be lectured about misogyny or sexism”.
At school, I have attended numerous lectures regarding respect for women. At these lectures,
we are constantly reminded we are all possible future perpetrators of violence towards women,
forgetting to mentions this male is not alone in loving and respecting his mother, his
grandmother and all other females in his life.
Some — far too many — men do terrible thing to women, but that does not mean I will too. I
refuse to be tarnished with the same brush.
While I do not condone the actions of sexist, misogynist men, nor the opportunities too
many women have been denied, I take offence at the double standards and the insinuation I
will mature to become a sexist, misogynist, violent male.
Gordon Meggs, Heidelberg
Herald Sun, 17/10/2012

sections.passage:
“You have your arms!”
“Sorry?”
It was a particularly humid late afternoon in sixth grade and I had been left for dead at school. Teachers,
maintenance staff, even the sanitary-disposal van had left the grounds, leaving me in the company of
a peer that I had spoken to only once throughout the entire year (and that was only to ask if she could
please stop using my treasured connector pens). She was prematurely developed, buxom girl who
spoke in a deep, husky voice and had sun-bleached hair from over-tanning.
Let’s just say she was the antithesis of me.
She repeated her revelation, this time with more gusto.
“You shave them! That’s so gross... I can’t believe you’d do that!”
“T don’t shave them!”
I tried to explain to her that I was just born that way and that most Chinese girls don’t have much hair
on their arms, save for a fine fuzz. However, she had already lost herself in a state of cackling delirium
— clearly overwhelmed by her own hilarity and the freakish nature of my body.
I crossed my arms in defiance, but after realising this would probably expose their hairlessness more,
made to hide them under my Lion King swimming bag, which contained chlorine soaked hand-me-
down togs that literally hung off me if I didn’t knot them up at the back. It had not been a good sports
lesson; once again I was isolated in the sixth lane with a pair of flippers and a kick-board, while my
friends mastered tumble-turns and learnt to open their eyes underwater. I watched them through my
blurry, steamed-up, over-sized goggles, and saw their hair floating around them with an ethereal
quality that mine, tightly contained in a cap full of baby powder, simply could not achieve. I had
pleaded for hours with my mum about the cap, but she had remained adamant:
“When you put the powder in, it makes the can come off so much easier! Like magic!” she explained.
“But it looks like dandruff... or nits.”
“Ai-ya! You know what the herbalists say. You'll get a headache with wet hair. Do you want to get
sick from having a wet head all day?”
“Tt it’s normal, yeah!”
Extract from A Call To Arms by Michelle Law

sections.title: Questions 8-10
sections.passage:
SKATING STEREOTYPES
JACKSON WIERINGA
Year 9, CBC FREMANTLE
As a member of the skating community, I’m sick of looking in the letterbox and seeing a
picture of a skateboarder with some writing next to it. Excitedly thinking it’s about skating, I
start reading only to discover in disgust that it’s about youth crime. I’m tired of the unfair
stereotype which people have got for skaters.
This really annoys me and I’m sure this applies to hundreds of thousands of skaters around
Australia. Yes, there are some skaters who contribute to youth crime, but most don’t! Why
take a picture of a skater just doing his thing, when there could have been a drug deal going
on right behind them! But no, he’s a skater — he must be associated with youth crime! It’s
totally biased and what has skating to do with youth crime anyway? From what I can see,
nothing.
It’s crazy. You would think in this day and age, skateboarding would be more understood.
People and the government are always complaining that kids don’t exercise enough, yet
people continue to bag skating! A survey done on the internet found that 87 per cent of people
aged 18-60 associated skating with youth crime.
So next time you see an article with a skater next to it about youth crime, write and tell
them how stupid they are. People need to have a hard look at themselves. GOOD media
coverage is the only way to fix this!
Spress October 2008

The Sanctuary
Colin Thiele, 1992
When Storm Boy went walking along the beach, or over the sandhills, or in the sanctuary, the
birds were not afraid. They knew he was a friend. The pelicans sat in a row, like a lot of important
old men with their heavy paunches sagging, and rattled their beaks drily in greeting; the moor-
hens fussed and chattered; the ibises Gul the air into Strips as they jerked their curved beaks up
and down; and the blue crane stood in silent dignity like a tall thin statue as Storm Boy went past.
But one morning Storm Boy found everything in iproaPand contusion. Three or four men had
gone into the sanctuary. They had found some pelican nests- wide, rough nests of sticks, grass,
and pelican feathers as big as turkey quills — and they had killed two of the big birds nesting
there. After that they had scattered everything wildly with their boots, kicking and shouting and
picking up the white eggs and throwing them about until they were all broken. Then they had
gone off laughing.
Storm Boy crept forward in fear and anger. From behind a tussock he looked round sadly at the
ruin and destruction. Then, just as he was about to run back to tell Fingerbone to fill his
blunderbuss with salt, he heard a faint rustling and crying, and there under the broken nests were
three tiny pelicans — still alive. Storm Boy picked them up and carefully hurried back with them.

Phulan and I step gingerly through the prickly grey camel thorn, each of us balancing a red clay pot
half-filled with water on our heads. It was all the water we could get from the toba, the basin that is our
main water supply.
Our underground mud cisterns are infested with worms. We’ll dig new ones when the monsoon rains
come — if they come.
The winter sky is hazed with dust. There has been no rain in nearly two years, and the heat of the
Cholistan Desert is as wicked as if it were summer.
Phulan walks with her eyes down, her feet shuffling, kicking up puffs of sand that is light as dust. Her
name means ‘flower’, and she is beautiful when she smiles.
I am Shabanu. Mama says it’s the name of a princess, but my red wool shawl has worn so thin I can
see through it. I pull it tighter around me and pretend it’s a shatoosh. It’s said that real princesses wear
shatoosh shawls so fine they can pass through a lady’s ring..
In the courtyard that circles our round, thatched huts, Mama and Auntie have made a fire, and a kettle
keeps warm beside it for tea. Even when we are down to the last of our water we have tea. Grandfather
leans against the courtyard wall, chin on his chest, his turban nodding in rhythm to his snores.
Mama sits with yards of yellow silk in her lap, stitching one of Phulan’s wedding dresses. She has
embroidered silver and gold threads, mirrors and tassels into the bodice. You’d think Phulan was the
princess!
‘Daughter of the wind’ by Suzanne Fischer — Staples

What Is a Mirage?
Amirage is an optical illusion. This illusion is something that we see, but is not really there. It occurs
mostly when the air is very hot.
In deserts there are places where there is water, and trees grow. Travellers sometimes think they are
coming to an oasis only a few kilometers away, where they can find water and shade. Then, as they
travel on, the oasis disappears. It had been a mirage! The oasis was not pure imagination. When the
travellers saw the oasis, and it receded, they really had seen an oasis. It was much further on and
below the horizon. The light from the real oasis had been reflected from a layer of air. The travellers
had seen it as if a huge mirror had been placed in the sky to give them this panorama.
The explanation for this is that there are layers of ait of different temperatures. These layers are of
different thickness of density. Whenever light passes from one thing to another of different density,
part of it is deflected back.
Appearances due to a similar cause are often seen at sea. A ship near the horizon may seem to have.
another ship, exactly like itself, perched upside down upon it.

Bushfire Weather by Jeri Kroll
It’s cool in the hills,
breezes dart through houses like trapped birds
beating glass till they’re free
It’s clean up there. Smog doesn’t rain
across the garden, smudging the birds of paradise,
fingerprinting the windowsills.
It’s calm in the hills when the frenzied heat
in the town bullies pedestrians.
The north wind eggs it on:
cotton wrapped like a second skin
loosens and billows, even sunglasses can’t screen the grit,
the earth in the driveway’s blown off,
vegetables wilt in the garden,
the city lies like an old dog.
In century heat, in the tinder-dry hills,
Air has an edge, too, But shade is kinder.
Children swing across the Onkaparinga
into cool green slime. Cats pant under water tanks,
horses munch prickly grass under rattling trees.
By one o’clock the city has a compress on its head,
no longer looks at the hills
as if they meant afterlife.
The north-east wind dries sweat running down the spine,
belches out yellow clouds, pummeling cyclists,
rocks the lucky sheep trucked from the hills
Down in the mall the dogged buskers play
till a string snaps.

H.M.S. BELLEROPHON
On June 1 1815 an attempt was made by the French to break the blockade of Europe
imposed by the British navy. France under Napoleon had already conquered most of
Europe but was short of food. A convoy of American grain ships escorted by fleet of French
warships attempted to penetrate the blockade and unload at the, French port of Brest. The
convoy was intercepted however by the British fleet commanded by Admiral Howe. Agreat
engagement ensued and for many hours the battles raged. Although some of the grain
ships managed f@llimp into harbour, eventually the ue sr ce inflicting
heavy losses on the French. | | | :
One of the British warships participating in the battle was Bellerophon. With 74 guns,
Bellerophon, the flagship of the Fleet, was possibly the finest warship afloat at the time.
The ship was in the thick of the battle for some hours, taking a bad battering, and her
causalities included the captain, Rear Admiral Parsley, who lost a leg to a cannon shot. On
board Bellerophon at the time was a young officer, scarcely more than a boy, acting as
Aide-de-camp to the Admiral. His name was Mathew Flinders.
In between bouts of destruction caused by French broadsides and the noise and chaos
of the Bellerophon’s own guns being fired as the battle raged back and forth, Flinders was
able to find time to jot down notes on the course of the battle for the Admiral. This was one
of his official duties. The description in his journal, copied up at the end of the battle, runs
to 40 pages and is regarded by naval historians as the best account of this most famous
battle. From it they are able to judge exactly the course of the engagement.
Flinders survived the ‘Battle of the Glorious First’ and, at a later date of course, became
quite famous in a different way as a navigator and explorer although still serving as an
officer in the Royal Navy. The Bellerophon too \ived on to carry out at least one more
famous voyage when she carried Napoleon from France to Portsmouth before he was
transported as a prisoner to the Island of St Helena in the Atlantic Ocean.

she added, fiddling with the strap of her cherry-red Fender Stratocaster. “But | figured in the

questions.stem: Among them were the singer-songwriters Jesse Harris, Richard Julian and Sasha Dobson, whose separate sets involved generous overlap in personnel and style. options: With so many collaborators on hand, her solo set didn’t last long. She sang “Cold, Cold

The ultimate test for life’s priorities
David Suzuki
(David Suzuki is a Canadian-based environmentalist, scientist, author and broadcaster. This
is an edited version of a speech he gave at the Seymour Centre in Sydney.
In Mews 1992, more than half of all living Nobel Prize winners signed a document called
‘Warning to Ht ty. that began with this stark statement: ‘Human beings
and the natural world are on a collision course. Human activities inflict harsh and often
irreversible damage on the environment. If not checked, many of our practices put at serious
risk the future we wish for human society.’ Scientists are extremely cautious when making
pronouncements to the general public, so this was a most unusual alarm call. In biological
terms, the globe is experiencing an 6Co-holocaust, as more than 50,000 species vanish
annually and air, water and soil are poisoned with civilisation’ s effluents.
The great challenge of the millennium is recognising the reality of impending ecological
collapse, and the urgent need to get on with taking the steps to avoid it. But our obsession
with economics has become an impediment to taking appropriate action. | have often been
told: ‘Listen Suzuki, we have to pay for all those parks and environmental clean-ups. We
can't afford to protect the environment if we don’t have a strong, growing economy.’ That
sentiment flows from a belief that the economy provides us with all of our products, from
food to oil to manufactured goods. This is nonsense. Everything we depend on, whether it
is Cars, popcorn or computers, comes from the earth and will eventually end up going back
to it. It is the biosphere, that thin layer of air, water and soil within which life exists, that
creates the earth’s productivity and abundance that, in turn, make economies and our lives
possible.
| suggest the following exercise can help to get our priorities in order. Imagine that you have
lived a full and rich life and are now on your death-bed. As you reflect on life, what memories
fill you with happiness, pride and satisfaction? | suspect it will not be the latest designer
clothing, a huge house, a sport utility vehicle or a high tech entertainment centre. What
makes life worthwhile and joyful is not ‘stuff that can be bought with money. The most
important things are family, friends, community and the sharing that enhances the quality of
all of our lives. There are several reasons we are failing to see the urgency of what is
happening, including:
e Most people alive today were born after 1950 and thus have lived all their lives during
a period of spectacular unprecedented and unsustainable growth and change. But
for most of us, this is all we’ve ever known and it seems normal. Rapid change also
brings rapid collective forgetfulness, and memories of what the world once was
quickly fade.
e Most people now live in the human-created environment of big cities where it’s easy
to believe the illusion that we have escaped our biological dependence on the natural
world.
7 page 8
e The explosive increase in information shatters the world into fragments devoid of the
history or context that might explain their relevance, importance or significance. In
order to attract attention, stories or reports become shorter and increasingly shrill,
sensational or violent.
e The great public faith that ‘they’ — scientists and technologists — will resolve our
problems is simply unwarranted. While technology -can be impressive, our
knowledge of the complexity of the real world is so limited. For example, we have no
idea how to replace thousands of species now extinct or repair the ozone layer.
What are our real basic needs in order to live rich and fulfilling lives? | believe you can not
separate environmental and social needs. Hungry people will-not care if their actions
endanger an edible species or an important habitat. Unemployment, injustice or insecurity
lead to desperation and the need to survive at all costs. To protect an environment for future
generations, we have to build a society on a foundation of clean air, water, soil and energy
to fulfil our needs; we have to ensure full employment, justice and security for all
communities to serve our social needs; and we have to retain sacred places, a sense of
belonging and connectedness with nature and a knowledge that there are cosmic forces
beyond our comprehension or control, to satisfy our spiritual requirements. Then, we can
work on the best kind of economy to construct from there. Right now, we seem to be trying
to squeeze everything into the constraints dictated by the economy without establishing the
fundamental bottom line. ;

sections.passage:
There are novel ways of getting teenage boys reading and girls into
IT, writes Blanche Clark
THE accepted wisdom is that boys and girls learn differently, but that doesn’t mean educators
are accepting gender differences as a fait accompli.
Moves are afoot to make reading as speccy as footy and computer games for adolescent
boys and IT as fabulous as fashion and social networking for girls.
Concern that boys are lagging behind girls in reading tests has led to numerous primary
and secondary programs.
But the State Library of Victoria’s Boys, Blokes, Books and Bytes program concentrates
on years 5-8, a period when many boys give up reading for pleasure.
Developed by the library’s Centre of Youth Literature, it promotes boys, their families,
schools and libraries talking about books.
The library’s reader development and onsite learning manager, Paula Kelly, says a toolkit
has been sent to every co-ed and boys’ school in Victoria. The program includes a website
with advice on great reads for boys and a blog for boys to discuss books.
“It’s not so much that boys can’t read, as they choose not to read. They don’t see it as
cool and acceptable,” Kelly says.
“There’s also a distinct lack of male role models actually reading. When they see their
dads reading or other men reading it is usually for purposes of work. They equate the idea of
reading as work; it’s not fun.”
Schools are encouraged to run boys’ book clubs, invite fathers and other male role models
to the school and form partnerships with local libraries.
Kelly says boys need a choice about what they read, and novels, non-fiction, graphic
novels, books that have an audio component, and comics should all be offered.
“Sure reading a novel raises your chances of school achievement, but ultimately reading
is good for you; it’s about your wellbeing.”
She says the library is often asked if it will offer a similar program for girls.
“Girls come to reading much more easily. No one looks at a girl and goes, ‘You’re a bit
of nerd because you’re a reader’. There is no issue with girls, but there is with boys.”
At the launch of the program on Thursday, University of Melbourne vice chancellor Prof
Glyn Davis said the program was a positive way to encourage children to read without getting
bogged down in political debates about methods of teaching literacy.
“There are important things about cultural literacy and basic reading skills in this program,
but the end result is designed to get boys reading and to enjoy reading,” he said.
Davis said it was hard to explain why it had become difficult to encourage boys to read.
“But a key part of the explanation lies in the electronic world and all the current
alternatives to books,” he said.
Herald-Sun October 14 2008

Descent from the Summit
by John Murray.
Simon felt the temperature dropping on the summit. For the first time, the sun disappeared
completely, plunging them into a dusky gloom. Simon knew that they did not have any
more time. He was not sure how fit Brechner was, but knew that they would have to go,
and take a chance. He didn’t have to speak to Gilbert. “Going. Going now,” Gilbert said,
lumbering over to the edge.
They shortened the safety lines to twenty feet. Gilbert was the lead and they put Brechner
between him and Simon. Between them, he reasoned, they would be able to hold him if he
slipped. “Happy birthday, Brechner,” Simon said as they pulled on their oxygen masks
again and stopped speaking. Simon knew that he had to find a rhythm and concentrate on
the ground in front of him. He was thinking too much about Brechner. He was too anxious,
too eager to get down. Climbers killed elimbers, he knew. It was the thin air, the tiredness,
and the cold that were doing it to him. He took long deep breaths of oxygen. He checked
his gloves and jackets again and tried to relax his abdomen and calves. And then he
lumbered around and eased himself back off the edge after Gilbert and Brechner. Simon
heard the metallic rattle of pegs and clips around Gilbert’s waist as he lowered himself
down the slope ahead of him.
They descended down the buttress and were moving along the first ridge when the cold
front hit them. The wind picked up to a steady fifteen Knots and walls of cloud began
blowing over the mountain. The air filled with curtains of grey fog. The cloud in front of
Simon’s face was wispy and glutinous. Ahead of him, he saw the dark form of Brechner,
hunched forward, walking with wide swings of his arms. The safety line was limp between

ICE SPIKES
Dr Alice Caseleyr 2005,
What are ice spikes?
Ice spikes are unusual structures that occasionally grow out of the ice cube trays in your
freezer. They look like the limestone stalagmites that are sometimes found in caves.
How do ice spikes form?
Ice spikes grow as the water in an ice cube tray turns to ice. Beginning on the top of each
cube, the water freézes inwards until only a small hole is left unfrozen in the centre. At the
same time as the surface solidifies, ice also starts to form under it, at the sides and on the
bottom of the cube. Since water expands as it freezes, the ice forming below the hardened
surface starts to push some water up through the hole. This water begins to form the ice
spike’s tubular shape. As water continues to be pushed out, it travels up the tube, freezing
around the rim and adding to its length. The spike will continue growing until all the water
in the cube becomes frozen or until the mouth of the tube ices over. Ice spikes have been
known to grow to a length of 56mm.
What helps ice spikes grow?
Experiments show that spikes are more likely to form when distilled water is used in the trays
and the temperature is just below freezing point (0° Celsius). If the temperature is too low,
the ice cube will freeze solid before the tube can begin to grow. Ice spikes will also form
more often if a fan is installed in the freezer to circulate the air. This is because the moving
air cools the top of the ice cube more rapidly. At the optimum temperature, and with air
blowing over the ice tray, approximately half of the cubes should develop ice spikes.

Recent film versions of The Importance Of Being Earnest and An Ideal Husband have
faithfully retained Oscar Wilde's view of snobbish 19th-century society. Kudos, then, to A
Good Woman helmer Mike Barker for moving Wilde's play Lady Windermere's Fan to 1930s
Italy, where the author's pithy aphorisms compete for our attention with gorgeous
Mediterranean scenery. The dialogue proves a mouthful for society gals Helen Hunt and
Scarlett Johansson, so Tom Wilkinson shines brightest as an ageing toff with a heart of gold.
Hunt plays Mrs Erlynne, a penniless New York socialite who travels to Europe to squeeze
cash out of young newlyweds Robert and Meg Windermere (Mark Umbers and Scarlett
Johansson) and find herself a new man. The notorious seductress is soon enjoying secret
liaisons with Robert while Meg, convinced that her new husband is having an affair, falls into
the arms of the caddish Lord Darlington (Bright Young Things' Stephen Campbell Moore).
"SKILLFULLY BANISHES THEATRICALITY"
Wilde's 1892 play was his first stage success and set the template for his other studies of class
and human nature. But while Barker keeps faith with the author's classy wit and waspish
repartee, he skillfully banishes theatricality by taking the action out of the salon and into the
bustling beauty of the Amalfi coast. The result may be reminiscent of The Talented Mr Ripley
and A Room With A View, but it's still a classy diversion that, like Bright Young Things before
it, evokes a bygone age of deliciously divine decadence.

sections.title: Questions 11-17
sections.passage:
ANCIENT MURDER MYSTERY SOLVED?
TUTANKHAMEN was only ten years old when he became the Pharaoh of Egypt around
3300 years ago. The cause of his death, at a young age, has been an enduring mystery that
has puzzled historians, archaeologists, forensic scientists and even police detectives ever
since his mummified body was uncovered in 1922.
The discovery of Tutankhamen’s tomb fllelléd "speculation about the possible cause of his
death. Unlike most other Egyptian tombs, although the antechamber and annex had been
disturbed, Tutankhamen’s burial chamber had been untouched by tomb raiders or vandals.
it was filled with fabulous treasures, including a priceless gold funeral mask. However the
tomb was small and clearly unfinished in parts, which gave rise to the theory that the young
pharaoh had died suddenly and the tomb had been hastily prepared. This led experts to
surmise that Tutankhamen had been murdered.
Tutankhamen’s mummy was first examined by Dr Douglas Derry. Derry established that the
king had been about eighteen when he died. In 1963 Tutankhamen’s body was x-rayed by
R.G.Harrison, an anatomist and an authority on mummies. The x-ray revealed a possible
skull fracture suggesting that Tutankhamen may have been killed by a blow to the back of
the head. This finding was strongly supported by further tests in the mid-1990s which led to
a hunt for a long-dead murderer.
Bob Brier, a researcher from Long Island University and two former US police officers, Greg
Cooper and Mike King, were just some of the people who became obsessed with identifying
King Tutankhamen’s killer. Using modern forensic and profiling techniques they began their
own investigation. There were several suspects: Ay, Tutankhamen’s chief adviser who
succeeded him as Pharaoh; Maya, his treasurer; Horemheb, his general who also became
Pharaoh after Ay’s death; and Ankhesenamen, Tutankhamen’s wife, who later named Ay.
The investigator agreed that Ay had the most to gain from Tutankhamen’s death and felt
satisfied that they had correctly identified the ancient assassin. However, many
Egyptologists remained sceptical and subsequent tests have suggested a completely new
scenario: King Tutankhamen may have died from an infection in a badly broken leg.
A research team, led by Zahi Hawass, the Chairman of Egypt’s Supreme Council of
Antiquities, examined images of the mummy taken from a CT scan and concluded that there
was no evidence of a blow to the back of the head, and therefore no indication of foul play.
The most recent theory that Tutankhamen died as a result of a broken leg may help to solve
another, smaller mystery: why, among the glorious treasures in Tutankhamen’s tomb, there
were also 130 walking sticks!
- READING page 5

The Music Lesson
On Saturday, Dad was waiting in the car to pick me up from my violin lesson. My lesson
would proceed in this same dependable fashion: I’d try to spend as much time as possible
with Ms. King on my musicianship, make lengthy technical queries, and thus forestall the
agony of actually having to play those wretched pieces.
‘Mina, did you practice at all this week?’ she might lower her wire frame glasses and gently
enquire only at the end of the lesson.
‘Oh, yes,’ I'd tell her. ‘But | had a bit of difficulty with the tempo of the serenade. Could you
perhaps play it for me again, Ms. King?’
Here she would smile knowingly, sigh, and take her own bow in her hand; then, reveling in
the face of profound admiration that | had over the years cultivated specifically for my
transactions with her, she’d play the serenade beautifully.
On this particular Saturday, though, we played our roles the same way; | paid her the tuition
fee and then proceeded to the front door, where, instead of waving good-bye to me,
entreating me to ‘practise hard’, she began to accompany me down the sandstone porch
steps toward my waiting father. | thought perhaps she was simply going to greet him, but
seeing her approach, Dad genially rolled down the window.
‘| thought you might like to come in for a cup of coffee.’ This was the phrase that | had etched
into my mind, the clincher. Canny dad eyed me as we followed Ms. King back in to her
studio.‘What would you like, Mina?’

SKATE WORLD
Push. Glide. Push. Glide. Push. Glide. Push.
Sorry, mate. You have absolutely no idea. None at all. Not unless you have strapped onto
your feet a pair of Italian roller blades, snapped on a helmet so firm that the strap clamps
you jaw shut — and then stretched a pair of racing gloves over your hands so snug that they
suck the sweat from your palms.
Then you start to get the rush. The pump. You’re at Skate World and the music is jumping
out of the loudspeakers and the hot summery smell of buttered popcorn is floating in the air.
And it’s Saturday night and your mates are there. Goofing around. But not you mate. Not
tonight.
READING page 9
For fourteen weeks you've been working towards this one. The regional sprint finals. Every
afternoon after school you go down to the gym for an hour and a half. And for fifteen minutes
straight you sit on the mean black rowing machine and pull and pull and make that machine
hum.
Fifteen minutes that start easy and then by minute six your stomach is cramping and your
leg muscles are beginning to swear.
By minutes eight you’re sweating all over. Your back. Your neck. And your tee-shirt is dripping
and you keep on pulling because you're not on a rowing machine, you're on the skating rink
and you're picturing in your mind your best mate Ronnie — big tall Ronnie — and he’s still
ahead of you like he’s been all year and you'll do anything — you'll dig deeper, you'll push
harder — just to beat him.
By minute twelve your brain is saying enough! Give up! But you focus on Ronnie, you're
gaining on him and nothing is going to beat you, and Ronnie — he’s starting to wilt too — and
now it’s you or him. Who can hang on longer? Who can dig the deepest? Thirty strokes a
minute. You lift the pace again.
You concentrate on the little black meter as it counts down the last 60 seconds. Pulling,
pulling. Your calf muscles are on fire and your lungs are heaving on the edge of meltdown.
And you'll do anything to beat your best mate. First the Regionals. Pull! Pull! Next the
Nationals. Harder! Harder!
Fourteen weeks at the gym. The rowing machine. The weights. I’ve got a trainer who tells
me, “You've got the speed Kirk, but you need to work on your power and your concentration.
You've got to focus, mate.’
You build concentration all right. You’re focused on one thing alone. There’s no time for
games or for mucking around. You are Captain Sensible.

FAIRY TALE: A TRUE STORY
Fairies....... pixies....elves....and a knowledge of Peter Pan wouldn’t go astray here. And
where do fairies live? Ask any child spellbound by their mythical nature and they will. answer:
At the cinemas everywhere. It is rated G and is appropriate for young audiences, while
appealing to adults as well.
The story is set in Cottingley Glen. Lush, green English glades, sparkling streams and
waterfalls create a magical effect. Here, the symbolism is overtly pure, good, wholesome. A
tree fairy takes flight over the countryside. At once the audience is invited to enter the world
of Elsie and Frances, two girls who believe, with all their heart, that fairies are real. The two
girls bring hope and enchantment to others like Polly, Elsie’s mother, who is dealing with
overwhelming grief for her son. They also bring optimism to a war-weary nation-it is 1917,
a dark year in the height of the Great War. Elsie and Frances are instrumental in breathing the
wonder of life back into a lifeless world.
Their feat is not easy. By taking photographs, that appear to capture a group of fairies
living in the garden, they need to convince hardened cynics. At first no one believes the girls,
but as the photographs are passed on from one notable to the next-Kodak, Sir Arthur Conan
Doyle, Harry Houdini — the magic begins to transform the thinking of a nation.
Considering this is a film for children, it deals with fantasy and reality, spirituality, death,
loss and grief. The search for meaning is a predominant theme and it is explored through
Elsie, who treasures her fairy house that her brother made with her. It is furthered by Frances
who copes with her missing gather by earnestly believing in fairies. It is a touching film and
the success of Fairy Tale: A True Story lies in its ability to cause us to suspend our disbelief
in fairies. This is achieved in part by juxtaposing events in the film which seem plausible,
because they occur in ways which seem quite natural, with elements of fantasy. For example,
the film producers can make the audience believe that anything 1s possible. Imagine a child’s
reaction when they are involved in Houdini’s magic and are then drawn into the marvel of
Peter Pan. Ten-year-old Frances is entranced as Peter Pan flies across the stage. Tinkerbell is
then created by a stage hand manipulating a mirror, reflecting a real image creating fantasy!
Fairy Tale: A True Story stars Florence Hoath, Elizabeth Earl, Paul McGann and
Phoebe Nicholls. Old film great Peter O’ Toole makes an appearance, as well as Harvey Keitel
(yes, he was in Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction).
= Thinking Skills page 1

sections.title: Questions 7-13
sections.passage:
Seymour
Seymour had been awake since sunrise and was watching the stumbling hands of the clock
so he could legitimately get out of bed. Seven-fifteen to the exact second was when Thelma
began her day, and she’d made it clear that his being there mustn’t interfere with her routine.
She’d give him the back room, which wasn’t really a proper one, just a small fibro-cement
extension tacked on to the kitchen. Summer clung like cellulose wrapping to its iron roof,
and even at this early hour he was sweating. Yesterday’s stored heat undulated from the
concrete yard outside, and he lay in clammy pyjamas and outstared the clock, At ten minutes
past seven he sprang thankfully out of bed and went into the kitchen to make Thelma a
morming cup of tea. He wasn’t being ingratiating — it was just something his mother had told
him to do before she left, and Seymour had a quiet and biddable nature.
“Thelma’s not young and she’s got that full-time job,” his mother had said. “It’s very kind of
her to help us out like this, so you mustn’t give her any cause to regret it. You be a big help
round the house while you’re there, Seymour. There’s no need to tell you to watch your
manners, I can say that for you. Take her a cup of tea first thing in the mornings, she’s never
had anyone to do that for her. I’m sure she’d appreciate it.”
He didn’t mind making anyone an early morning cup of tea, but it was a nerve-wracking
business in this particular kitchen, where even inanimate objects like canisters seemed
capable of disapproval if you put them back in the wrong places. Here there was a place for
everything and everything in its rightful place. The tea, for instance, was kept in a green
plastic caddy with its own little measuring ladle, and you somehow didn’t dare use any other
spoon. He took the cup of tea along the hall and knocked on Thelma’s door.

LETTER OF THE DAY
IT seems William Cameron (“At loss over frock shock”, September 16) up holds the view that women
can only be feminine when they are dressed up all pretty in a frock. ,
When are people going to realise that femininity and masculinity can be expressed and explored in
many more ways than just appearance?
Women and men should feel open to express themselves aesthetically based on what makes them
feel confident, happy and spiritually free, not confined by the rigid constraints of the terms masculine
and feminine.
Femininity is more than clothes, make-up, sanitary products and fancy weddings.
How do we expect to go forward and look after the things that really matter, such as the environment,
family and global peace, when all we are worried about is how someone dresses?
I’m hoping that summer trends for 2008 are intelligence and enlightenment.
Shallow and obtuse is so 2007. .
Pep Phelan, Macleod

of Parker..

ANIMALS OF THE GREAT BARRIER REEF
An incredible variety of marine animals live on and around the Great Barrier Reef. The
wildlife species range from the minute drifting jellyfish to huge predatory sharks. Sea turtles
breed in greater numbers at the Great Barrier Reef than anywhere else in the world. Gentle
dugongs which are marine relatives of the elephant, swim languidly among the sea grasses,
and birds such as the reef heron catch fish in the shallows by spearing them.
The reef is made up of some 400 species of coral. It also supports approximately 200
species of cowrie shell, and probably as many as 2000 species of fish (about one tenth of all
known fish species). Up to 200 species of fish may live in a single area of reef that is about
the same size as a soccer pitch.
Numerous primitive animals burrow into the very coral of the reef itself. These include
boring sponges, worm, mollusks and sea urchins, as well as snails and sea slugs that eat the
coral.
Various fish eat living coral. The brightly coloured parrotfish nips off small chunks with
its sharp, beak-like front teeth. It then grinds up this gritty mouthful with its rounded back
teeth to extract the fleshy insides of the coral.
And what about the coral itself? Much of the coral of the reef is white. This is the skeleton
of the dead polyps, which are tiny anemone-like creatures. In contrast, live polyps are
typically very brightly coloured. Sea fans and sea whips, as well as other creatures of the reef,
also display brilliant hues of red, yellow, orange, purple, pink and green. As well as providing
a spectacular home to marine life, the colours of the reef act as a way of identifying species,
helping species to find a mate. It also helps confuse predators in the region, which are on the
hunt for food.

Wealth data tells a tale of two cities
Tim Colebatch
TWO towers symbolise the gap between affluence and deprivation in Melbourne. Barely three
kilometres apart, fringing the city in opposite directions, the 2006 Census shows them as polar
opposites of socio-economic advantage and disadvantage in our state.
The desirable tower is Yarra's Edge, the award-winning "urban village" developed by Mirvac ‘on
the old site of South Wharf, in Docklands. On a wide-ranging index of measures, the Bureau of
Statistics ranks it the most socioeconomically advantaged community in Victoria.
The tough tower is an old Housing Commission block of flats, on the corner of Melrose and
Canning Streets in North Melbourne, down from Racecourse Road. Many of its residents are
refugees, Islam is the main religion, and only 39 people have a job.
From census data collected in more than 9000 districts throughout Victoria, the Bureau has
constructed an index of socioeconomic advantage and disadvantage, ranking each district —
ranging in size from city blocks to large areas of farmland and forest — from 1 to 9055.
The index covers 21 variables, such as the proportion of households with high or low incomes,
the proportion with broadband or no internet access, how many people work as professionals
or labourers, the size of mortgages and rent payments, the number of bedrooms, and
occupants’ qualifications.
At both ends, the extremes are clustered in towers edging the city. Six of the 10 most
advantaged districts are new apartment blocks in Docklands, Southbank, Port Melbourne and
the CBD. And nine of the 10 most disadvantaged are old Housing Commission towers in North
Melbourne, Ascot Vale, Kensington and Collingwood.
One difference leaps out: at the Melrose Street flats, only 25% of people were born in Australia,
as against 65% at Yarra's Edge. And, at Yarra's Edge, the migrants come mostly from the US,
Malaysia and England; at Melrose Street, from Vietnam, China, Somalia and Eritrea.
While tax data last week showed the taxman still makes his biggest hauls in Portsea, Toorak,
and Brighton, the Bureau's index, finds the new towers along the Yarra and the waterfront have
Melbourne's greatest concentration of well-off people.
The second best collection of Melburnians lives in Southbank just behind the National Gallery.
Southbank and Docklands each have two collectors' districts in the top 10, which also include
Beacon Cove in Port Melbourne (sixth) and the city block bounded by La Trobe, Queen,
Lonsdale and William streets.
Reading Skills page 5
Of the traditional homes of wealthy Melburnians, the river end of St Georges Road, Toorak,
remains pre-eminent. The Bureau ranks it the third, closely followed by another riverside area
along Alexandra Avenue, South Yarra. The Monomeath Avenue area of Canterbury was also
in the top 10, as was the part of Kew heading to the river along Molesworth Street.
The top 10 areas by postcode were Docklands, the World Trade Centre, Canterbury, East
Melbourne, Southbank, Brighton, Toorak, Malvern, Queens Road and Portsea.
The poorest postcodes were mostly in the bush: Korong Vale and Nyah West in the north-west,
Cressy in the Western District, and Nowa Nowa and Longwarry in Gippsland. Melbourne's most
disadvantaged suburbs are Braybrook, Frankston and Broadmeadows.
The Age, March 27 2008

Road Toll’s Harsh Reality
On Tuesday police launched their Car Crash Reality’ Check in Federation Square.
A concept hatched by Herald Sun columnists Anan Howe and Neil Mitchell, it features the
wrecks of two cars involved in accidents that left their drivers with horrendous injuries:
Launched by the Premier, John Brumby, the CCRC aims to cut the road toll by confronting
visitors, particularly 18 to 25-year-old drivers, with the devastating really of motor vehicle
accidents.
It may yet achieve its goal. But tragically and ironically, it didn’t prevent the crash that shattered
eight young lives when a car hit a power pole in Clayton yesterday. pom
Police called to a scene of carnage had to drive one of the eight ambulances taking the
critically injured to hospital because paramedics could not leave one of the occupants. The 20-
year-old woman was trapped amid the twisted metal and bloody glass.
Passengers with broken bones were still curled around each other in the a from the force
of the high-speed impact.
Others were lying by the side of the road. Two staggered towards police and emipulenicg
officers from where they had been thrown from the careering car. we
It is every parent’s worst nightmare. How many fear the midnight knock to tell them their son
or daughter has been killed or maimed in a senseless accident caused by speed and booze?
The Herald Sun hopes the horror of this accident will stick in the minds of schoolchildren, as
well as the kids already out on the roads.
Too many of them are driving too fast, risking not only their lives but the lives of others. Too
many are drinking and driving, something the Herald Sun has campaigned against so vigorously
for nearly 40 years.
Declare War On 1034 began after that number of people died on Victorian roads in 1969.
Young people, particularly, are still ignoring the safe-driving message.
The TAC has run numerous campaigns against the deadly cocktail of speed, alcohol and drugs.
There has been much headway.
But last year, 333 people still died on our roads and each death is one too many.
Then there is the hidden toll. Hundreds more are injured. They are the maimed and the
disfigured from accidents that in so many cases are preventable.
The State Government has reacted quickly to yesterday’s accident by pledging to change seat
belt laws. That’s a good thing, long overdue.
Ultimately our battle to lower the road toll, particularly among the young, will only succeed if
we accept individual and collective responsibility. How many more reality checks do we need?

The following passage, written in 1893, is from the diary of twelve-year-old Helena Morley.
Helena’s father was English and her mother Brazilian. The family lived in the remote Brazilian
town of Diamantina, whose economy was based on diamond mining. The diary is translated
from Portuguese (Brazil’s national language).
Monday, April 17°
Ever since | was little I’ve been hearing my father say, ‘I must teach this girl English. She’s a
perfect little English girl, but she can’t be one without knowing the language.’ He only talked
about it and then he went off to mine and forgot all about it. Now that he’s teaching English at
the high school he said to me, ‘Let's begin classes Monday.’ Today was Monday and |
presented myself for my lesson.
My father thinks that | have unequalled intelligence. No one can even speak of anyone’s
intelligence when he’s around without his coming out with the same remark: ‘Daughter, if you’d
just settle down and study one hour every day, I’d like to see the person who could get ahead
of you.’ | listen to this the same way | listen when they say I’m pretty, because | know the story
of the owl.* But today | felt | disappointed him and | feel sad about it. What makes my father go
on thinking such nonsense? I’ve only received two prizes at school. Just in music and
gymnastics. Why does he keep on thinking I’m intelligent? It serves him right!
Today he began by saying that English is easier than Portuguese because the verbs aren’t
complicated in the way they are in Portuguese; there are very few rules. And everything
depends on the pronunciation, and | must have inherited that. We were going to begin by
reading a book. He read first. | didn’t understand a thing and he said that didn’t matter and told
me to repeat it. | couldn’t. He read it a second time and told me to say the word ‘THE’ the way
he wanted. | said it about a number of times and he kept saying it wasn’t right. | saw it was
impossible to get it right and | told him | didn’t want to learn English any more, he says it's
easier than Portuguese, and maybe it is for other heads, but not mine. Mine is very hard;
English can’t get in. My father looked at me in amazement and said that we’d try again
tomorrow. Shall | have to go through this every day?

Questions for 20 to 25. Half-Truths Beware of those who use the truth to deceive. When someone tells you something that is true, but leaves out important information that should be included, he can create a false impression. For example, someone might say, “I just won a hundred dollars on the lottery. It was great. | took that dollar ticket back to the store and turned it in for one hundred dollars!” This guy’s a winner, right? Maybe, maybe not. We then discover that he bought two hundred tickets, and only one was a winner. He’s really a big loser! He didn’t say anything that was false, but he deliberately omitted important information. That's called a half-truth. Half-truths are not technically lies, but they are just as dishonest. Untrustworthy candidates in political campaigns often use this tactic. Let’s say that during Governor Smith’s last term, her state lost one million jobs and gained three million jobs. Then she seeks another term. One of her opponents runs an ad saying, “During Governor Smith’s term, the state lost one million jobs!” that’s true. However an honest statement would have been, During Governor Smith’s term, the state had a net gain of two million jobs.”

beware Questions for 26 to 30. URANUS Uranus, the seventh planet from the Sun, enjoys very long seasons. Forty-two years of sunlight is followed by forty-two years of darkness. The reason for this is that the planet’s, rings and moons are all tilted at an angle of 98 degrees, and so Uranus travels around the Sun on its side. Scientists do not have a definite answer for why the planet lies in this way, but one reason postulated is a collision with some other heavy body many millennia ago. Uranus can be just barely seen with the naked eye, but it was not until it was examined by telescope, that it was identified as a planet. This happened in 1781, when Sir William Herschel found it while mapping the constellation of Gemini. Its faint ring system was not discovered until 1977. There are eleven rings in total. It was once thought that Uranus only had five moons: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon, but Voyager Two revealed at least twenty-one, and there may even be more. All the moons revolve around the plane of the planet’s equator. Uranus, rotates on its axis in about seventeen hours, and takes eighty-four earth years to orbit the sun. The atmosphere is made up of 83% hydrogen, 15% helium and 2% methane. It is this methane which gives the planet its characteristic blue appearance. The actual planet is composed of a solid rock fragments that are up to a meter thick. This rock is some of the densest material ever encountered in the universe.

For them, constant change is the air they breathe, the Water they swim in. It is simply the way the world is. They are the generation for whom the women’s movement was an established historical fact; the generation who take equality between the sexes for granted (and who are infuriated by older people — especially older men in senior positions — who still don’t understand that personhood is a gender- neutral concept, and still haven’t grasped the essential difference between yesterday's view of women and today’ Ss). They know that more than 50 per cent of university students are women, that 45 per cent (and rising) of the workforce are female and that girls can do anything they choose. They know that most mothers have paid work outside the home because that’s how it is for their own mothers. They don’t expect Mum to be there making peanut butter sandwiches when they get home from school, and they vaguely wonder why she even bothers mentioning the fact that that’s what her mother used to do. ($3) On the other hand, roughly 750,000 members of this generation live in a household where no one is currently earning any wages, so the reality of unemployment is pretty stark. Even if their parents have work, at least 30 per cent of young Australians are facing the bleak prospect of a labour market that doesn’t want them . . . at least not yet. (If you had applied unsuccessfully for 200 jobs, as a respondent in one of my recent research projects had, what would you do next?) ($4)To older Australians, the sharp rise in the divorce rate over the past 20 years seems cataclysmic, shaking the very foundations of the institution of marriage. But to the rising generation, nothing has changed: from the time they became aware of the nature of marriage and divorce, they had known that lots of their friends live with one parent, so what's the big deal? Do you imagine that contemporary children and adolescents exchange information about their parents’ marital status in darkly whispered confessions behind their hands? Do you think that living in a one-parent family feels like a heavy burden for kids to bear? Think again: almost one million dependent children are in precisely that situation, which doesn’t mean that it’s always fun for them, but it does mean that it’s hardly worth mentioning. (In any case, having one parent at home might sometimes feel like half the burden of having two.) To the intense irritation of their parents, the members of this generation are able to program the VCR without even reading the manual. Having grown up in the thick of the information revolution (‘What revolution?’) they know today’s technology is already obsolete by the time they get their hands on it, and that smarter things are constantly coming over the horizon. They know there’s an accessible drug culture in every town and suburb, and that ‘street kids’ are part of the scene. (No wonder they've embraced the Gritty realism of the new writing for young people.) (S5) Paradoxically, they're also our most dependent generation, staying at home for longer and relying on social security in larger numbers than any previous group of young Australians. Like every generation before them, they are responding to the world as they find it. (To what other world could they possibly respond?) Not surprisingly, their experience of impermanence and unpredictability has taught them one big, central lesson: keep your options open. So they are inclined to hang loose; to postpone commitment to a career, a sexual partner, a political party, a set of religious beliefs, a brand... or even to whether. they'll be home for dinner tonight. For many of them, that is an exciting, liberating approach to life. Those flapping shoelaces can be a sign of confidence, freedom, flexibility and. adaptability. But not for all: the lack of a clear focus and the absence of a stable framework can also.breed insecurity, uncertainty and an n aching sense of alienation. In the wait-and- see world of the young, even the symbol of Untied laces is ambiguous.

In the hall her heart sank. The front door was open — Lucy had gone outside. It was a cold night, and
Mina knew that her friend was wearing just a thin nightdress. Hurriedly throwing a shawl around her
own shoulders, she went to look for her.
The church clock was striking one as Mina ran through the streets of Whitby. She kept a sharp
lookout, but there was no sign of the white figure she had expected to see. She ran along the Crescent,
then she explored along the North Terrace — nothing. Searching farther and farther away from the
house, she made her way up to the West Cliff.
At the edge of the West Cliff she looked across the bay to the East Cliff. There was a bright full
moon but also lots of swift-moving clouds, so a dappled light was moving across the sea and the town.
For some time she couldn’t distinguish very much at all. Then the moon emerged fully, casting a
narrow strip of cold blue light over the East Cliff.
Mina could see the tombstones of the old graveyard, leaning over at crazy angles, making dark
silhouettes against the wild night sky. The strip of light moved steadily along the tombstones and
memorials. And there on their seat, was the half-reclining, snowy-white figure of Lucy.
Almost as soon as she spotted her friend, the moon went in. But it seemed to Mina that something
dark had been standing behind Lucy, or leaning over her. Whether it was man or beast Mina wasn’t
sure.
She started running down the slope of the West Cliff as fast as she could. It seemed to take forever.
Eventually she was leaping up the endless steps of the East Cliff, her legs shaky with tiredness. As she
neared the graveyard on the cliff top she gasped. She had been right. A dark shape was leaning over
her friend.
“Tucy! Lucy!” she called in fright.
At the sound of her voice, the dark figure raised its head. Mina saw a pale face and red, gleaming
eyes. For a moment they flashed at her. Then, as Mina got closer, the dark figure seemed to melt into
the surrounding blackness.
“Lucy!” Mina cried, throwing herself next to her friend on the bench.
Lucy was still asleep. Her lips were parted, and she was breathing in long, heavy gasps. She put
her hand to her throat and moaned. Mina wrapped her shawl around her friend’s shoulders. Lucy
seemed unusually cold and gave a shudder. Using a safety pin, Mina fastened the shawl at Lucy’s
throat. But she must have been clumsy, because Lucy’s hand went to her throat again, and Mina noticed
that there were two little red marks on her neck. Mina thought that she must have pricked her
accidentally.
Excerpt from ‘Dracula’ (Usborne Classics Retold) By Bram Stoker

sections.passage:
Underworld: Rise of the Lycans (MA15+)
Director: Patrick Tatopoulos (feature debut)
Starring: Bill Nighy, Michael Sheen, Phona Mitra, Kevin Grevioux
>Gone to howl and never coming back
OH, THE vagaries of franchise filmmaking. When the going is good, the talent will happily
front up for a sequel. When the talent goes elsewhere, the only option is to persuade
whoever is left to do a prequel. Such is the sorry fate which has befallen the Underworld
series. You remember the first two flicks, right? You don’t? OK, here’s what you missed.
Kate Beckinsale in a rubber catsuit. Scott Speedman and a posse of greasy-haired dudes
with coloured contact lenses. An ancient blood feud between fashion-victim vampires and
not-so-stylish werewolves.
Whew. Classic stuff, huh? Well, it used to fill the time between visits from Wesley Snipes
and the Blade gang. However, now that Beckinsale and Speedman have better things to do
with their time, former support players Bill Nighy and Michael Sheen have been bumped up
the billing. For their trouble, these stalwart British thesps have been saddled with a cheap
and cheerless cash-in that should bury the whole underworld thing once and for all. In Rise
of the Lycans, the narrative clock is wound back a century or five to explain how vampires
and werewolves came to hate each other so. Unremarkably, what follows sucks and bites
in equal measure. Big-boss vamp Viktor (Nighy) gets his black velvet cape in a twist when
he discovers his headstrong daughter Sonia (Rhona Mitra, prepared to show a little more
and emote a lot less than her predecessor Beckinsale) has been canoodling with the hairy
he-man hellhound Lucian (Sheen). After building up this Transylvanian standoff with a pile
of claptrap about keeping all spooky species strictly separated, the film then devolves into a
wonky Braveheart for werewolves.
Sadly, Sheen is no Mel Gibson. Now, Sheen is a fine actor. On the strength of his work as
David Frost in Frost/Nixon and Tony Blair in The Queen, you could easily argue he is one of
the best in the business at the moment. However, no amount of growling, howling or baby
oil on his biceps can establish Sheen’s credentials as a rough ’n’ tumble man of action.
Nothing else of note to mention here, save for a hulking man-mountain named Kevin
Grevioux, whose voice is so unbelievably deep he could short-circuit a
subwoofer merely by clearing his throat.
Herald-Sun January 22"7 2009

He crouches, and buries his face on his knees,
And hides in the dark of his hair;

On the Darling River
The Darling - which is either a muddy gutter or a second Mississippi - is about six
times as long as the distance, in a straight line, from its head to its mouth. The state of the
river is vaguely, but generally understood to depend on some distant and foreign phenomena,
to which bushmen refer in an offhand tone of voice as "the Queenslan' rains", which seem to
be held responsible, in a general way, for most of the outback trouble.
It takes less than a year to go upstream by boat to Walgett or Bourke in a dry season
because the river is then a string of waterholes. After a while the passengers get sick of
climbing out of the boat while it is carried to the next long waterhole. They get sick of being
stuck in the same sort of place, in the same old way; they grow weary of seeing the same old
timer drop his swag on the bank opposite whenever the boat ties up for wood; they get tired
of lending him tobacco, and listening to his ideas, which are limited in number and narrow
in conception.
It shortens the journey to get out and walk; but then you will have to wait so long for
your luggage - unless you hump it with you.
We heard of a man who determined to stick to a Darling boat and travel the whole
length of the river. He was a newspaper man. He started on his voyage of discovery one
Easter in flood-time, and a month later the captain got bushed between the Darling and the
South Australian border. The water went away before he could find the river again, and he
left his boat in a scrub. They had a cargo of rations, and the crew stuck to the craft while the
tucker lasted; when it gave out they rolled up their swags and went to look for a station, but
didn't find one. The captain would study his watch and the sun, rig up dials and make out
courses, and follow them without success. They ran short of water, and didn't smell any for
weeks; they suffered terrible privations, and lost three of their number, not including the
newspaper man. There were even dark hints of considering the drawing of lots in connection
with something too terrible to mention. They crossed a thirty-mile plain at last, and sighted a
young Aboriginal girl. She led them to a boundary-rider's hut where they were taken in and
provided with rations.
Later on a syndicate was formed to explore the country and recover the boat; but
they found her thirty miles from the river and about eighteen from the nearest waterhole deep
enough to float her so they left her there.

sections.title: Questions 11-16
sections.passage:
Environmental Dangers
Two introduced animals have created a danger to our environment and continue to
do so despite government efforts to overcome the problems they are causing.
The buffalo was introduced from Indonesia between 1825 and 1843. It bred
successfully in regions of the Northern Territory which perfectly suited its needs. The wetland
areas of the Northern Territory are at risk from these animals. They have caused
considerable damage and it is estimated that over 6,000 hectares of paper bark forests have
been utterly destroyed. When these animals move from place to place they create deep
channels in the water-logged areas. The banks of the water courses are damaged. This
means that the natural banks can no longer function effectively. In the dry season water from
the ocean breaks into these areas. The plant and animal life that cannot tolerate the increase
in salinity can no longer survive or are greatly reduced. Although steps are being taken to
minimise the damage, there are still an estimated 80,000 of these animals. The damage
they continue to cause to swamps, fresh water springs and nesting sites of water birds is
considerable.
Introduced with the arrival of the First Fleet, the feral goat causes problems over a
much wider area than the buffalo. Early settlers used them for meat and milk. Today it is
estimated that there are 7 million feral goats in Australia. They are found in approximately
half the area of Australia. Control of feral goats is almost impossible as they can exist on
virtually all types of vegetation. Properties and National Parks are at risk as mobs of feral
goats ravage the natural vegetation to such an extent that areas are reduced to a barren
landscape. Water supplies for stock and native animals are often reduced to muddy bogs,
and, in the extreme heat can be completely dry. Their habit of stripping trees and grasses
causes severe erosion of vast tracts of land, wind erosion in the dry months and erosion by
water when flooding rains occur.
Both these pests require a prolonged and expensive eradication program to avoid
the environmental damage which will continue.

sections.passage:
The United Nations flag
The United Nations emblem features a map of the world as seen from the North Pole cupped by
olive branches, a symbol of peace dating back to Ancient Greece. When set on a light blue
background it forms the United Nations flag.
The emblem originated in 1945, when a button design was sought for the San Francisco
conference at which the United Nations charter was drafted and approved. The Presentation
Branch of the United Sates Office of Strategic Services prepared the design and on 7 December
1946 the General Assembly accepted a modified design as the official seal and emblem of the
United Nations flag, using the emblem on a light blue background.
The United Nations flag is not an Australian flag, but it is flown in Australia and elsewhere
according to special rules set out in the United Nations Flag Code. In accordance with a
proclamation made by the Governor-General on 19 August 1948, 24 October each year is
observed throughout Australia and its Territories as United Nations. The United Nations flag is
flown on this day in the position of honour. If only one flag pole is available, the United Nations
flag should be the flag flown on that day.
The United Nations flag

Australia
The Age Newspaper
Jim Schembri, reviewer, December 2, 2008
There are moments while watching Baz Luhrmann’s over-sized, over-long Outback weepie
Australia when one wonders if there are any tablecloth clichés about Australia that have been
missed.
No, it all seems to be there. The horses. The cattle. The dust. The rugged Aussie loner. The
Aborigine standing on one leg in a loincloth. The beer. The roos. About the only thing missing
is a bloke named Bruce.
It may not be the stuff from which classic films are typically born but such clichés provide a
great featherbed of easy-to-digest references for the type of sweeping melodramatic saga
designed to appeal to the lucrative “chick flick” market and to foreign audiences eager for an
attractive holiday destination.
By these measures Australia cannot be seriously faulted. With its open links to the tourism
industry, the film is a great ad. As entertainment, the saga, cringe-inducing as it often is,
eventually delivers the type of big, crowd-pleasing, teary emotional pay-off that makes its
many longueurs and overcooked characters worth enduring, even if the film is 30 minutes
too long.
Set in the Northern Territory in 1939 on a remote cattle station with the fairytale name of
Faraway Downs, Australia tells of the forging of a family. Lady Sarah Ashley (Nicole Kidman)
is the prissy English aristocrat who arrives to make a go of the station after the murder of her
husband, allegedly by a blackfella called King George (David Gulpilil). Helping her take her
cattle to Darwin is the enigmatic Drover (Hugh Jackman), a no-nonsense piece of calendar-
worthy, girl-baiting Aussie beefcake.
Glueing the story together is Nullah (Brandon Walters), a sweet-faced little boy of mixed
blood whose stateless status and dubious parentage serves as the lightning rod for the film’s
overarching themes of racism, responsibility, love and reconciliation.

Dead Worried
This comedy, which was written by M. Simmons, centres on the adventures of the
main character, Danny, his family and friends. From the beginning there is one
embarrassment after another, until finally Danny suffers concussion in a fall and loses his
memory. His little sister helps him rediscover it in a most unusual way.
Danny, who wants desperately to be a hero, believes he is adopted. No-one else in
the family has such stinky feet, not even his sister, who, Danny fears, will be the only child
at school not toilet trained. He is madly in love with Mandy who owns a dog that has
adopted a kitten.
In the introduction, Danny is embarrassed when his sister bites the judge of her
baby beauty contest. The difficulties continue through every chapter. When Danny reports
an armed robber to a bank clerk, three cucumbers fall out of the man's bag. When he calls
the police to a crime scene, the "Criminals" are rehearsing a play. When he mistakenly acts
as a human shield for the school bully, he decides it is safer to stay out of the way.
Then, when Danny, dressed as a hero, falls from the monkey bar and loses his
memory, it's all too much. Danny can't even remember his parents. All he can remember is
"salami".
