The ultimate test for life’s priorities
David Suzuki
(David Suzuki is a Canadian-based environmentalist, scientist, author and broadcaster. This
is an edited version of a speech he gave at the Seymour Centre in Sydney.
In November 1992, more than half of all living Nobel Prize winners signed a document called
‘World Scientists’ Warning to Humanity’ that began with this stark statement: ‘Human beings
and the natural world are on a collision course. Human activities inflict harsh and often
irreversible damage on the environment. If not checked, many of our practices put at serious
risk the future we wish for human society.’ Scientists are extremely cautious when making
pronouncements to the general public, so this was a most unusual alarm call. In biological
terms, the globe is experiencing an eco-holocaust, as more than 50,000 species vanish
annually and air, water and soil are poisoned with civilisation’s effluents.
The great challenge of the millennium is recognising the reality of impending ecological
collapse, and the urgent need to get on with taking the steps to avoid it. But our obsession
with economics has become an impediment to taking appropriate action. | have often been
told: ‘Listen Suzuki, we have to pay for all those parks and environmental clean-ups. We
can’t afford to protect the environment if we don’t have a strong, growing economy.’ That
sentiment flows from a belief that the economy provides us with all of our products, from
food to oil to manufactured goods. This is nonsense. Everything we depend on, whether it
is cars, popcorn or computers, comes from the earth and will eventually end up going back
to it. It is the biosphere, that thin layer of air, water and soil within which life exists, that
creates the earth’s productivity and abundance that, in turn, make economies and our lives
possible.
| suggest the following exercise can help to get our priorities in order. Imagine that you have
lived a full and rich life and are now on your death-bed. As you reflect on life, what memories
fill you with happiness, pride and satisfaction? | suspect it will not be the latest designer
clothing, a huge house, a sport utility vehicle or a high tech entertainment centre. What
makes life worthwhile and joyful is not ‘stuff that can be bought with money. The most
important things are family, friends, community and the sharing that enhances the quality of
all of our lives. There are several reasons we are failing to see the urgency of what is
happening, including:
e Most people alive today were born after 1950 and thus have lived all their lives during
a period of spectacular unprecedented and unsustainable growth and change. But
for most of us, this is all we’ve ever Known and it seems normal. Rapid change also
brings rapid collective forgetfulness, and memories of what the world once was
quickly fade.
e Most people now live in the human-created environment of big cities where it’s easy
to believe the illusion that we have escaped our biological dependence on the natural
world.
ee page 8
e The explosive increase in information shatters the world into fragments devoid of the
history or context that might explain their relevance, importance or significance. In
order to attract attention, stories or reports become shorter and increasingly shrill,
sensational or violent.
e The great public faith that ‘they’ — scientists and technologists — will resolve our
problems is simply unwarranted. While technology can be impressive, our
knowledge of the complexity of the real world is so limited. For example, we have no
idea how to replace thousands of species now extinct or repair the ozone layer.
What are our real basic needs in order to live rich and fulfilling lives? | believe you can not
separate environmental and social needs. Hungry people will not care if their actions
endanger an edible species or an important habitat. Unemployment, injustice or insecurity
lead to desperation and the need to survive at all costs. To protect an environment for future
generations, we have to build a society on a foundation of clean air, water, soil and energy
to fulfil our needs; we have to ensure full employment, justice and security for all
communities to serve our social needs; and we have to retain sacred places, a sense of
belonging and connectedness with nature and a knowledge that there are cosmic forces
beyond our comprehension or control, to satisfy our spiritual requirements. Then, we can
work on the best kind of economy to construct from there. Right now, we seem to be trying
to squeeze everything into the constraints dictated by the economy without establishing the

Brumby’s Run
It lies beyond the Western Pines
Towards the sinking sun,
And not a survey mark defines
The bounds of “Brumby’s Run’.
On odds and ends of mountain land,
On tracks of range and rock
Where no one else can make a stand,
Old Brumby rears his stock.
Awild, unhandled lot they are
Of every shape and breed.
They venture out ‘neath moon and star
Along the flats to feed;
But when the dawn makes pink the sky
And steals along the plain,
The Brumby horses turn and fly
Towards the hills again.
The traveller by the mountain-track
May hear their hoof-beats pass,
And catch a glimpse of brown and black
Dim shadows on the grass.
The eager stockhorse pricks his ears
And lifts his head on high
In wild excitement when he hears
The Brumby mob go by.
Old Brumby asks no price or fee
O’er all his wide domains:
The man who yards his stock is free
To keep them for his pains.
So, off to:scour the mountain-side
With eager eyes aglow,
To strongholds where the wild mobs hide
The gully-rakers go.
Arush of horses through the trees,
A red shirt making play;
A sound of stockwhips on the breeze,
They vanish far away!
Ah, me! before our day is done
We long with bitter pain
To ride once more on Brumby’s Run
And yard his mob again.

sections.title: Questions 1-5
sections.passage:
READY TO RUMBLE!
by Dr Karl Kruszeinicki in Good Weekend, The Sydney Morning Herald Magazine, June
12, 2004.
Domestic cats have lived with people for many thousands of years. It’s a simple and
happy relationship — we take care of them, and they catch rodents for us. They let us
know that we have kept our side of the bargain by purring — a sure sign of contentment.
Or is it?
The sound of a cat's purr is very distinctive. It starts when they’re about a week old. They
can do it while either breathing in or breathing out, and with their mouths closed. If you
try, you can make a kind of rumble while you breathe out, but the rumble generated while
breathing in sounds rather strangled. Oddly, cats that purr (domestic cats, mountain lions,
pumas, etc.) can’t roar all that well, and cats that have a terrifying roar (tigers, lions, etc.)
aren’t too good at purring.
The mechanics of a cat’s purr are still a bit of a mystery. A cute version of a human’s
snore, perhaps? We now know that the cat’s throat emits short bursts of sound between
25 and 200 times each second. There’s a very short interruption to this regular pattern
as the cat changes from breathing in to breathing out, and vice versa. Over the years
there have been many theories, but the most popular one is that the pipe through which
the air passes to and from the cat’s lungs changes its diameter abruptly 25 to 200 times
each second. No one is quite sure where the change in diameter happens, or what drives
it, although it has been found that electrical signals change 25 to 200 times each seconds
in some of the muscles in the cat's air pipe.
So when do cats purr? Indeed, they do purr when they are contented, but they may also
purr when they are in pain, or giving birth, or being threatened.
A cat's purr is a bit like a human smile. Sure, we smile when we are happy, but we might
also smile nervously when we feel threatened, or if somebody is being catty towards us.
- Reading Skills page 1

sections.title: Questions 6-10
sections.passage:
There are novel ways of getting teenage boys reading and girls
into IT, writes Blanche Clark
THE accepted wisdom is that boys and girls learn differently, but that doesn’t mean
educators are accepting gender differences as a fait accompli.
Moves are afoot to make reading as speccy as footy and computer games for adolescent
boys and IT as fabulous as fashion and social networking for girls.
Concern that boys are lagging behind girls in reading tests has led to numerous primary
and secondary programs.
But the State Library of Victoria’s Boys, Blokes, Books and Bytes program concentrates
on years 5-8, a period when many boys give up reading for pleasure.
Developed by the library’s Centre of Youth Literature, it promotes boys, their families,
schools and libraries talking about books.
The library’s reader development and onsite learning manager, Paula Kelly, says a toolkit
has been sent to every co-ed and boys’ school in Victoria. The program includes a website
with advice on great reads for boys and a blog for boys to discuss books.
“It's not so much that boys can’t read, as they choose not to read. They don’t see it as
cool and acceptable,” Kelly says.
“There’s also a distinct lack of male role models actually reading. When they see their
dads reading or other men reading it is usually for purposes of work. They equate the idea
of reading as work; it’s not fun.”
Schools are encouraged to run boys’ book clubs, invite fathers and other male role
models to the school and form partnerships with local libraries.
Kelly says boys need a choice about what they read, and novels, non-fiction, graphic
novels, books that have an audio component, and comics should all be offered.
“Sure reading a novel raises your chances of school achievement, but ultimately reading
is good for you; it’s about your wellbeing.”
She says the library is often asked if it will offer a similar program for girls.
“Girls come to reading much more easily. No one looks at a girl and goes, ‘You're a bit of
nerd because you're a reader’. There is no issue with girls, but there is with boys.”
At the launch of the program on Thursday, University of Melbourne vice chancellor Prof
Glyn Davis said the program was a positive way to encourage children to read without
getting bogged down in political debates about methods of teaching literacy.
“There are important things about cultural literacy and basic reading skills in this program,
but the end result is designed to get boys reading and to enjoy reading,” he said.
Davis said it was hard to explain why it had become difficult to encourage boys to read.
“But a key part of the explanation lies in the electronic world and all the current
alternatives to books,” he said.
Herald-Sun October 14 2008

sections.title: Questions 11-17
sections.passage:
Descent from the Summit
by John Murray.
Simon felt the temperature dropping on the summit. For the first time, the sun disappeared
completely, plunging them into a dusky gloom. Simon knew that they did not have any
more time. He was not sure how fit Brechner was, but knew that they would have to go,
and take a chance. He didn’t have to speak to Gilbert. “Going. Going now,” Gilbert said,
lumbering over to the edge.
They shortened the safety lines to twenty feet. Gilbert was the lead and they put Brechner
between him and Simon. Between them, he reasoned, they would be able to hold him if he
slipped. “Happy birthday, Brechner,” Simon said as they pulled on their oxygen masks
again and stopped speaking. Simon knew that he had to find a rhythm and concentrate on
the ground in front of him. He was thinking too much about Brechner. He was too anxious,
too eager to get down. Climbers killed climbers, he knew. It was the thin air, the tiredness,
and the cold that were doing it to him. He took long deep breaths of oxygen. He checked
his gloves and jackets again and tried to relax his abdomen and calves. And then he
lumbered around and eased himself back off the edge after Gilbert and Brechner. Simon
heard the metallic rattle of pegs and clips around Gilbert's waist as he lowered himself
down the slope ahead of him.
They descended down the buttress and were moving along the first ridge when the cold
front hit them. The wind picked up to a steady fifteen Knots and walls of cloud began
blowing over the mountain. The air filled with curtains of grey fog. The cloud in front of
Simon’s face was wispy and glutinous. Ahead of him, he saw the dark form of Brechner,
hunched forward, walking with wide swings of his arms. The safety line was limp between
them and lay on the snow like a crack on a white cement wall. Simon could still just make
out Gilbert up front, walking smoothly and with long high steps down the incline. Their
footholds were still clearly visible in the snow, and Simon concentrated on placing his
boots in the centre of each to minimise his effort and to reduce the chance of slipping. He
felt the muscles in his forehead clenching. His eyes were dry and gritty. Simon knew that
they would need about an hour to traverse this top ridge, which angled to the south. It was
most vulnerable they would be on the descent. He imagined the three of them in his mind
as bobbing specks, like currants swirling in milk.

On the Rocks
By John Foulcher
Accrab, spurting from the water,
dangling its legs over shells. It lugs its body
sideways, like a survivor dragged clear,
then shudders into speed
a hovercraft’s height from the rocks, sidestepping
periwinkles
with the ease of a waiter through tables,

till its belly grinds into the pattern of polyps;
its pincers twist in, legs become ridges in the stone.

The sea snatching up loose life,
leaving in a crossfire of foam.
Not with the crab though. The crab
Waits, jerks into limbs and extremities
And runs through the instant of the water’s withdrawal,
wedges
between rocks
like a lost coin.

A Good Woman (2005)
Reviewed by Neil Smith PG
Updated 08 May 2005 Contains mild language and sex references
Recent film versions of The Importance Of Being Earnest and An Ideal Husband have
faithfully retained Oscar Wilde's view of snobbish 19th-century society. Kudos, then, to A
Good Woman helmer Mike Barker for moving Wilde's play Lady Windermere's Fan to 1930s
Italy, where the author's pithy aphorisms compete for our attention with gorgeous
Mediterranean scenery. The dialogue proves a mouthful for society gals Helen Hunt and
Scarlett Johansson, so Tom Wilkinson shines brightest as an ageing toff with a heart of gold.
Hunt plays Mrs Erlynne, a penniless New York socialite who travels to Europe to squeeze
cash out of young newlyweds Robert and Meg Windermere (Mark Umbers and Scarlett
Johansson) and find herself a new man. The notorious seductress is soon enjoying secret
liaisons with Robert while Meg, convinced that her new husband is having an affair, falls into
the arms of the caddish Lord Darlington (Bright Young Things’ Stephen Campbell Moore).
"SKILLFULLY BANISHES THEATRICALITY“
Wilde's 1892 play was his first stage success and set the template for his other studies of
class and human nature. But while Barker keeps faith with the author's classy wit and
waspish repartee, he skillfully banishes theatricality by taking the action out of the salon and
into the bustling beauty of the Amalfi coast. The result may be reminiscent of The Talented
Mr Ripley and A Room With A View, but it's still a classy diversion that, like Bright Young
Things before it, evokes a bygone age of deliciously divine decadence.

Old Man Platypus
From The Animals Noah Forgot
By A.B.Patterson
Far from the trouble and toil of town,
Where the reed-beds sweep and shiver.
Look at the fragment of velvet brown
Old Man Platypus drifting down,
Drifting along the river.
And her plays and divers in the river bends,
In a style that’s most elusive;
With few relations and fewer friends,
For Old Man Platypus descends
From a family most exclusive.
He shares his burrow beneath the bank
With his wife and his son and daughter
At the roots of the reeds and the grasses rank;
And the bubbles show where our hero sank
To its entrance under water.
Safe in their burrow below the falls,
They live in a world of wonder,
Where no one visits and no one calls,
They sleep like little brown billiard balls
With their beaks tucked neatly under.
And he talks in a deep unfriendly growl
As he goes on his journey lonely;
For he’s no relation to fish or fowl.
Nor to bird nor beast, nor to horned owl;
In fact, he’s the one and only!

Album Of The Month
This is an impossibly good album. The third release from the Verve — a UK band who split
up after two albums and several turbulent years of unfulfilled promise, only to come back
with this really makes “Be here Now” look a little directionless. The two bands have very

The Beatles. Starting out with their first single “Bittersweet Symphony”, the album drips
monster hits. Sonnet is a masterpiece, as is One Day and any number of others. It’s the kind

sections.title: Questions 11-15
sections.passage:
ANCIENT MURDER MYSTERY SOLVED?
TUTANKHAMEN was only ten years old when he became the Pharaoh of Egypt around
3300 years ago. The cause of his death, at a young age, has been an enduring mystery
that has puzzled historians, archaeologists, forensic scientists and even police detectives
ever since his mummified body was uncovered in 1922.
The discovery of Tutankhamen’s tomb fuelled speculation about the possible cause of his
death. Unlike most other Egyptian tombs, although the antechamber and annex had been
disturbed, Tutankhamen’s burial chamber had been untouched by tomb raiders or vandals.
It was filled with fabulous treasures, including a priceless gold funeral mask. However the
tomb was small and clearly unfinished in parts, which gave rise to the theory that the
young pharaoh had died suddenly and the tomb had been hastily prepared. This led
experts to surmise that Tutankhamen had been murdered.
Tutankhamen’s mummy was first examined by Dr Douglas Derry. Derry established that
the king had been about eighteen when he died. In 1963 Tutankhamen’s body was x-rayed
by R.G.Harrison, an anatomist and an authority on mummies. The x-ray revealed a
possible skull fracture suggesting that Tutankhamen may have been killed by a blow to the
back of the head. This finding was strongly supported by further tests in the mid-1990s
which led to a hunt for a long-dead murderer.
Bob Brier, a researcher from Long Island University and two former US police officers,
Greg Cooper and Mike King, were just some of the people who became obsessed with
identifying King Tutankhamen’s killer. Using modern forensic and profiling techniques they
began their own investigation. There were several suspects: Ay, Tutankhamen’s chief
adviser who succeeded him as Pharaoh; Maya, his treasurer; Horemheb, his general who
also became Pharaoh after Ay’s death; and Ankhesenamen, Tutankhamen’s wife, who
later named Ay. The investigator agreed that Ay had the most to gain from Tutankhamen’s
death and felt satisfied that they had correctly identified the ancient assassin. However,
many Egyptologists remained skeptical and subsequent tests have suggested a
completely new scenario: King Tutankhamen may have died from an infection in a badly
broken leg.
Aresearch team, led by Zahi Hawass, the Chairman of Egypt's Supreme Council of
Antiquities, examined images of the mummy taken from a CT scan and concluded that
there was no evidence of a blow to the back of the head, and therefore no indication of foul
play. The most recent theory that Tutankhamen died as a result of a broken leg may help
to solve another, smaller mystery: why, among the glorious treasures in Tutankhamen’s
tomb, there were also 130 walking sticks!
= Reading Skills page 5

The Music Lesson
On Saturday, Dad was waiting in the car to pick me up from my violin lesson. My lesson
would proceed in this same dependable fashion: I'd try to spend as much time as possible
with Ms. King on my musicianship, make lengthy technical queries, and thus forestall the
agony of actually having to play those wretched pieces.
‘Mina, did you practice at all this week?’ she might lower her wire frame glasses and gently
enquire only at the end of the lesson.
‘Oh, yes,’ I’d tell her. ‘But | had a bit of difficulty with the tempo of the serenade. Could you
perhaps play it for me again, Ms. King?’
Here she would smile knowingly, sigh, and take her own bow in her hand; then, reveling in
the face of profound admiration that | had over the years cultivated specifically for my
transactions with her, she’d play the serenade beautifully.
On this particular Saturday, though, we played our roles the same way; | paid her the tuition
fee and then proceeded to the front door, where, instead of waving good-bye to me,
entreating me to ‘practise hard’, she began to accompany me down the sandstone porch
steps toward my waiting father. | thought perhaps she was simply going to greet him, but
seeing her approach, Dad genially rolled down the window.
‘| thought you might like to come in for a cup of coffee.’ This was the phrase that | had etched
into my mind, the clincher. Canny dad eyed me as we followed Ms. King back in to her
studio. ‘What would you like, Mina?’
‘Oh, I'll have a cup of coffee, too,’ | affected with my grown-up voice. ‘Look, Dad! | said,
reaching for Ms. King’s quaint metronome, which lay on a shelf in her studio, a souvenir (I
could use this word any time in a sentence now) from Budapest.
‘Don’t touch that, Mina,’ he said gruffly.

SKATE WORLD
Push. Glide. Push. Glide. Push. Glide. Push.
Sorry, mate. You have absolutely no idea. None at all. Not unless you have strapped onto
your feet a pair of Italian roller blades, snapped on a helmet so firm that the strap clamps
you jaw shut — and then stretched a pair of racing gloves over your hands so snug that they
suck the sweat from your palms.
Then you start to get the rush. The pump. You’re at Skate World and the music is jumping
out of the loudspeakers and the hot summery smell of buttered popcorn is floating in the air.
And it’s Saturday night and your mates are there. Goofing around. But not you mate. Not
tonight.
For fourteen weeks you’ve been working towards this one. The regional sprint finals. Every
afternoon after school you go down to the gym for an hour and a half. And for fifteen minutes
straight you sit on the mean black rowing machine and pull and pull and make that machine
hum.
Fifteen minutes that start easy and then by minute six your stomach is cramping and your
leg muscles are beginning to swear.
By minutes eight you’re sweating all over. Your back. Your neck. And your tee-shirt is dripping
and you keep on pulling because you’re not on a rowing machine, you're on the skating rink
and you’re picturing in your mind your best mate Ronnie. — big tall Ronnie — and he’s still
ahead of you like he’s been all year and you'll do anything — you'll dig deeper, you'll push
harder — just to beat him.
By minute twelve your brain is saying enough! Give up! But you focus on Ronnie, you're
gaining on him and nothing is going to beat you, and Ronnie — he’s starting to wilt too — and
now it’s you or him. Who can hang on longer? Who can dig the deepest? Thirty strokes a
minute. You lift the pace again.
You concentrate on the little black meter as it counts down the last 60 seconds. Pulling,
pulling. Your calf muscles are on fire and your lungs are heaving on the edge of meltdown.
And you'll do anything to beat your best mate. First the Regionals. Pull! Pull! Next the
Nationals. Harder! Harder!
Fourteen weeks at the gym. The rowing machine. The weights. I’ve got a trainer who tells
me, ‘You’ve got the speed Kirk, but you need to work on your power and your concentration.
You've got to focus, mate.’
You build concentration al! right. You’re focused on one thing alone. There’s no time for
games or for mucking around. You are Captain Sensible.

sections.title: Questions 1-6
sections.passage:
FAIRY TALE: A TRUE STORY
Fairies pixies....elves....and a knowledge of Peter Pan wouldn't go astray here. And
where do fairies live? Ask any child spellbound by their mythical nature and they will answer:
At the cinemas everywhere. It is rated G and is appropriate for young audiences, while
appealing to adults as well.
The story is set in Cottingley Glen. Lush, green English glades, sparkling streams and
waterfalls create a magical effect. Here, the symbolism is overtly pure, good, wholesome. A
tree fairy takes flight over the countryside. At once the audience is invited to enter the world
of Elsie and Frances, two girls who believe, with all their heart, that fairies are real. The two
girls bring hope and enchantment to others like Polly, Elsie’s mother, who is dealing with
overwhelming grief for her son. They also bring optimism to a war-weary nation-it is 1917, a
dark year in the height of the Great War. Elsie and Frances are instrumental in breathing the
wonder of life back into a lifeless world.
Their feat is not easy. By taking photographs, that appear to capture a group of fairies
living in the garden, they need to convince hardened cynics. At first no one believes the girls,
but as the photographs are passed on from one notable to the next-Kodak, Sir Arthur Conan
Doyle, Harry Houdini — the magic begins to transform the thinking of a nation.
Considering this is a film for children, it deals with fantasy and reality, spirituality, death,
loss and grief. The search for meaning is a predominant theme and it is explored through
Elsie, who treasures her fairy house that her brother made with her. It is furthered by Frances
who copes with her missing gather by earnestly believing in fairies. It is a touching film and
the success of Fairy Tale: A True Story lies in its ability to cause us to suspend our disbelief
in fairies. This is achieved in part by juxtaposing events in the film which seem plausible,
because they occur in ways which seem quite natural, with elements of fantasy. For example,
the film producers can make the audience believe that anything is possible. Imagine a child’s
reaction when they are involved in Houdini’s magic and are then drawn into the marvel of
Peter Pan. Ten-year-old Frances is entranced as Peter Pan flies across the stage. Tinkerbell
is then created by a stage hand manipulating a mirror, reflecting a real image creating
fantasy!
Fairy Tale: A True Story stars Florence Hoath, Elizabeth Earl, Paul McGann and
Phoebe Nicholls. Old film great Peter O’Toole makes an appearance, as well as Harvey
Keitel (yes, he was in Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction).

Seymour
Seymour had been awake since sunrise and was watching the stumbling hands of the clock
so he could legitimately get out of bed. Seven-fifteen to the exact second was when Thelma
began her day, and she’d made it clear that his being there mustn't interfere with her routine.
She’d give him the back room, which wasn’t really a proper one, just a small fibro-cement
extension tacked on to the kitchen. Summer clung like cellulose wrapping to its iron roof,
and even at this early hour he was sweating. Yesterday's stored heat undulated from the
concrete yard outside, and he lay in clammy pyjamas and outstared the clock, At ten minutes
past seven he sprang thankfully out of bed and went into the kitchen to make Thelma a
morning cup of tea. He wasn’t being ingratiating — it was just something his mother had told
him to do before she left, and Seymour had a quiet and biddable nature.
“Thelma’s not young and she’s got that full-time job,” his mother had said. “It’s very kind of
her to help us out like this, so you mustn’t give her any cause to regret it. You be a big help
round the house while you’re there, Seymour. There’s no need to tell you to watch your
manners, | can say that for you. Take her a cup of tea first thing in the mornings, she’s never
had anyone to do that for her. I’m sure she’d appreciate it.”
He didn’t mind making anyone an early morning cup of tea, but it was a nerve-wracking
business in this particular kitchen, where even inanimate objects like canisters seemed
capable of disapproval if you put them back in the wrong places. Here there was a place for
everything and everything in its rightful place. The tea, for instance, was kept in a green
plastic caddy with its own little measuring ladle, and you somehow didn’t dare use any other
spoon. He took the cup of tea along the hall and knocked on Thelma’s door.

ANIMALS OF THE GREAT BARRIER REEF
An incredible variety of marine animals live on and around the Great Barrier Reef. The
wildlife species range from the minute drifting jellyfish to huge predatory sharks. Sea turtles
breed in greater numbers at the Great Barrier Reef than anywhere else in the world. Gentle
dugongs which are marine relatives of the elephant, swim languidly among the sea grasses,
and birds such as the reef heron catch fish in the shallows by spearing them.
The reef is made up of some 400 species of coral. It also supports approximately 200
species of cowrie shell, and probably as many as 2000 species of fish (about one tenth of
all known fish species). Up to 200 species of fish may live in a single area of reef that is
about the same size as a soccer pitch.
Numerous primitive animals burrow into the very coral of the reef itself. These include
boring sponges, worm, mollusks and sea urchins, as well as snails and sea slugs that eat
the coral.
Various fish eat living coral. The brightly coloured parrotfish nips off small chunks with its
sharp, beak-like front teeth. It then grinds up this gritty mouthful with its rounded back teeth
to extract the fleshy insides of the coral.
And what about the coral itself? Much of the coral of the reef is white. This is the skeleton
of the dead polyps, which are tiny anemone-like creatures. In contrast, live polyps are
typically very brightly coloured. Sea fans and sea whips, as well as other creatures of the
reef, also display brilliant hues of red, yellow, orange, purple, pink and green. As well as
providing a spectacular home to marine life, the colours of the reef act as a way of identifying
species, helping species to find a mate. It also helps confuse predators in the region, which
are on the hunt for food.
- Reading Skills page 1
© Copvriaht: EX Edu-Kinadom Colleae

Of A Boy
By Sonya Hartnett
He returns the brush carefully to the tray, bristles down, beside the mirror, but his fingers linger,
balancing on the pyramid tips. ‘You never use this brush and mirror, do you, Gran?’
She doesn’t look up from the knot she’s discovered. ‘It’s too good to use.’
‘Then why do you have it? Why do you keep it on the table?’
His chin is jerked up as she wrenches the knot, and he hears his hair tearing. ‘If we only kept what
had a use’, she says, ‘there would be a lot less junk lying round.’
He contemplates her image in the dresser mirror, wondering what she means. He's never
seen much junk lying anywhere around the stolid neighbourhood, but he imagines tottering tangles
of doll heads, bike tyres and foil milk bottle caps rising as creaky mountains from the middle of
footpaths. He scrambles like a mouse to the peak of a rubbish hill and as far as he can see is inviting
flotsam and curious dregs, a child’s utopia. He returns his gaze to the silvery mirror: his gran is
wearing a cream dress splashed with flowers so red they might be bleeding.
‘Crystal looks the same as glass,’ he muses. ‘What's the difference?’
His grandmother doesn’t answer. He shifts his balance to the other foot. ‘I don’t know why
there’s two things that look the same but get called different names.’
‘Adrian stand still!’ She cuffs the side of his head and he straightens obediently, dropping
his hands to his sides. In the mirror she’s frowning furiously at his hair. His hair is dense and yellow
and strangely, stiffly wild, an armload of hay dumped helter-skelter on his head. It tangles like it has
a_lunatic mind of its own. ‘Where on earth did he get this hair? His gran asks no one, and strand
after strand of it breaks beneath her ploughing comb. ‘It didn’t come from our side of the family. The
McPhees haven't got this impossible straw. It's come from the father’s side.’

sections.title: Questions 13-20
sections.passage:
Wealth data tells a tale of two cities
Tim Colebatch
TWO towers symbolise the gap between affluence and deprivation in Melbourne. Barely
three kilometres apart, fringing the city in opposite directions, the 2006 Census shows them
as polar opposites of socio-economic advantage and disadvantage in our state.
The desirable tower is Yarra’s Edge, the award-winning "urban village" developed by Mirvac
on the old site of South Wharf, in Docklands. On a wide-ranging index of measures, the
Bureau of Statistics ranks it the most socioeconomically advantaged community in Victoria.
The tough tower is an old Housing Commission block of flats, on the corner of Melrose and
Canning Streets in North Melbourne, down from Racecourse Road. Many of its residents
are refugees, Islam is the main religion, and only 39 people have a job.
From census data collected in more than 9000 districts throughout Victoria, the Bureau has
constructed an index of socioeconomic advantage and disadvantage, ranking each district
— ranging in size from city blocks to large areas of farmland and forest — from 1 to 9055.
The index covers 21 variables, such as the proportion of households with high or low
incomes, the proportion with broadband or no internet access, how many people work as
professionals or labourers, the size of mortgages and rent payments, the number of
bedrooms, and occupants' qualifications.
At both ends, the extremes are clustered in towers edging the city. Six of the 10 most
advantaged districts are new apartment blocks in Docklands, Southbank, Port Melbourne
and the CBD. And nine of the 10 most disadvantaged are old Housing Commission towers
in North Melbourne, Ascot Vale, Kensington and Collingwood.
One difference leaps out: at the Melrose Street flats, only 25% of people were born in
Australia, as against 65% at Yarra's Edge. And, at Yarra's Edge, the migrants come mostly
from the US, Malaysia and England; at Melrose Street, from Vietnam, China, Somalia and
Eritrea.
While tax data last week showed the taxman still makes his biggest hauls in Portsea, Toorak,
and Brighton, the Bureau's index, finds the new towers along the Yarra and the waterfront
have Melbourne's greatest concentration of well-off people.
The second best collection of Melburnians lives in Southbank just behind the National
Gallery. Southbank and Docklands each have two collectors’ districts in the top 10, which
also include Beacon Cove in Port Melbourne (sixth) and the city block bounded by La Trobe,
Queen, Lonsdale and William streets.
Reading Skills page 5
© Copvriaht: £X Edu-Kinadom Colleae
Of the traditional homes of wealthy Melburnians, the river end of St Georges Road, Toorak,
remains pre-eminent. The Bureau ranks it the third, closely followed by another riverside
area along Alexandra Avenue, South Yarra. The Monomeath Avenue area of Canterbury
was also in the top 10, as was the part of Kew heading to the river along Molesworth Street.
The top 10 areas by postcode were Docklands, the World Trade Centre, Canterbury, East
Melbourne, Southbank, Brighton, Toorak, Malvern, Queens Road and Portsea.
The poorest postcodes were mostly in the bush: Korong Vale and Nyah West in the north-
west, Cressy in the Western District, and Nowa Nowa and Longwarry in Gippsland.
Melbourne's most disadvantaged suburbs are Braybrook, Frankston and Broadmeadows.

Erring on the side of ‘er’
THEY are seen as a mark of poor communication, and can be ... um ... simply
maddening for anyone waiting for a punchline.
But the utterances that slow down our sentence actually make us better understood,
according to scientists.
They found that “ums”, “ers” and “ahs” — known as “disfluencies” — force a listener to
pay attention.
The experts at Stirling and Edinburgh universities in Scotland asked volunteers to listen
to a series of sentences, including a number that had disfluencies.
They then tested how much the listeners could remember.
Inserting the “ers” apparently had a significant effect on recall.
Up to an hour after hearing typical sentences, volunteers got 62 per cent of words
correct where there had been a dissiliency in the sentence. That compared with 55 per
cent for sentences where there had not been any stumbles, the team said. :
Dr Martin Corley, of Edinburgh University, said: “A disfluency is an interruption to the
predicted ritual of things. It’s like we are saying to ourselves ‘I’d better pay attention, ;
because what I thought was going to happen isn’t going to happen’.”

What’s the Inference? — The Lady in Black
Winter.
One in the morning, Monday 9 June.
Night has leeched life from the suburbs on the surrounding hills and from the
wharves around the Backwater Bay. The bus is a vulnerable glow-worm of light
crawling along the wet, back road.
Brett stares absentmindedly through the window glare into the damp gloom. All
he can see is the pool of yellow light racing along the road as if accompanying the
bus on its silent mission. The road could well be part of the black surface of still water
of the nearby bay. The scattered lights of the city centre are lost in the cold mist that
drifts across the water and seeps into the surrounding locked suburbs.
The bus stops for some T intersection lights that carry on their relentless cycle of
amber, red, green though the bus is the only traffic at this hour. It could be a ghost
town. Brett stares out into the buses growing along the roadside. A sign states that
the landscaping is a government project to green the environment with natural
vegetation.
Behind the saplings and bushes are the vague skeletal structures of a silent
railway goods yard. Brett shivers and thinks how great it will be to get into bed.
Selling hamburgers on the late-night shift was not a great challenge but it gave him
some holiday cash.
The bus shudders gently forward as the lights change to green. Out of the corner
of his eye Brett catches sight of amovement in a gap in the shrubbery. For a moment
he thinks it his reflection in the lightly misted glass. He hadn’t seen the person until
she had moved and he almost called out to the driver to stop then suddenly realised
she probably didn’t want to catch the bus. It wasn’t a regular bus stop.

The following passage, written in 1893, is from the diary of twelve-year-old Helena Morley.
Helena’s father was English and her mother Brazilian. The family lived in the remote
Brazilian town of Diamantina, whose economy was based on diamond mining. The diary is
translated from Portuguese (Brazil’s national language).
Monday, April 17%
Ever since | was little I've been hearing my father say, ‘l must teach this girl English. She’s
a perfect little English girl, but she can’t be one without knowing the language.’ He only
talked about it and then he went off to mine and forgot all about it. Now that he’s teaching
English at the high school he said to me, ‘Let’s begin classes Monday.’ Today was Monday
and | presented myself for my lesson.
My father thinks that | have unequalled intelligence. No one can even speak of anyone’s
intelligence when he’s around without his coming out with the same remark: ‘Daughter, if
you’d just settle down and study one hour every day, I’d like to see the person who could
get ahead of you.’ | listen to this the same way | listen when they say I’m pretty, because |
know the story of the owl.* But today | felt | disappointed him and | feel sad about it. What
makes my father go on thinking such nonsense? I’ve only received two prizes at school.
Just in music and gymnastics. Why does he keep on thinking !’m intelligent? It serves him
right!
Today he began by saying that English is easier than Portuguese because the verbs aren't
complicated in the way they are in Portuguese; there are very few rules. And everything
depends on the pronunciation, and | must have inherited that. We were going to begin by
reading a book. He read first. | didn’t understand a thing and he said that didn’t matter and

the way he wanted. | said it about a number of times and he kept saying it wasn’t right. |
saw it was impossible to get it right and | told him | didn’t want to learn English any more,
he says it’s easier than Portuguese, and maybe it is for other heads, but not mine. Mine is
very hard; English can’t get in. My father looked at me in amazement and said that we’d try

Dream on Cedar
“Dream on Cedar” text from The Slightly True Story of Cedar B. Hartley
by Martine Murray.
There’s a long way between an idea and a real thing. Inside your mind there is a boundless
view. You can imagine whatever you want.
For example, you can plan exactly how you would like your house to be.
You close your eyes and picture spiral staircases with slippery banisters and blue wooden
floors and stars stuck on the ceilings, and a grass carpet for rabbits in the rabbit room.
Sometimes there might be a white cow on the couch or a herd of wild wandering albatrosses,
wearing new hats and recently returned all the way from Russia to tell you tales, waiting in
your bathtub which is a big as a bus and always perfectly warm with honey-scented bubbles.
And through the diamond shapes on the windows, all you can see is every kind of tree, even
mountain ash, and some with swinging ropes and the warbling of lemon-bellied fly ~ catchers
and laughing kookaburras and some festooned with rare spotted birds that sing like Stevie
Wonder.
And then, just at the moment when you're in the trees swinging from a rope and going all
Tarzan, your mum yells out and you have to open your eyes. ‘Cedar! Dinner’s ready.’
So you open them, and lo and behold, there you are just lying on your back facing the
cracked ceiling above you.
That’s how it really is. Real life is a bit like a used tea towel. And you can’t get even one
single albatross to wear a hat and tell you tales in the bath, no matter what you do. Some
ideas just have to remain as ideas.

The sport of competitive or race walking is believed to
have started in the last part of the 19th century. The first
ever championships of the Amateur Athletic Club of
England in 1866 included an 11 km walking event.
Professional indoor walking races were held in New
York City in the 1870s and 1880s, where competitors

winning prize went to the competitor who had walked
the greatest distance in six full days.
Competitive walking is also known as ‘heel - and - toe’
racing. This is because walkers must make sure their
leading foot touches the walking surface before the
trailing foot leaves it. In most walking events around the
world (except for England and wherever the Olympic
Games are held), the leading foot must be straightened
briefly while it touches the ground.

sections.title: Questions 21-30
sections.passage:
‘Hang Loose’ youth keep options open
(S1) Hugh Mackay is a social commentator and journalist who writes articles for the
Weekend Australian and the Sydney Morning Herald newspapers. He is a social researcher,
author and newspaper columnist.
lf you are looking for a symbol of contemporary youth culture, look no further than the laces
left untied on Doc Martens shoes. It’s as if the kids are saying, ‘I’m prepared to wear these
things, but | wouldn’t want you to think | was totally committed to the idea.’ As usual, the
rising generation are sending us a message from our future, so we’d better listen.
($2) Australians born since the mid-70s don’t share their parents’ and grandparents’ anxiety
about the rapid rate of change and its destabilising effect on our society. For them, constant
change is the air they breathe, the water they swim in. It is simply the way the world is. They
are the generation for whom the women’s movement was an established historical fact; the
generation who take equality between the sexes for granted (and who are infuriated by older
people — especially older men in senior positions — who still don’t understand that
personhood is a gender- neutral concept, and still haven’t grasped the essential difference
between yesterday's view of women and today’s). They know that more than 50 per cent of
university students are women, that 45 per cent (and rising) of the workforce are female and
that girls can do anything they choose. They know that most mothers have paid work outside
the home because that’s how it is for their own mothers. They don’t expect Mum to be there
making peanut butter sandwiches when they get home from school, and they vaguely
wonder why she even bothers mentioning the fact that that’s what her mother used to do.
($3) On the other hand, roughly 750,000 members of this generation live in a household
where no one is currently earning any wages, so the reality of unemployment is pretty stark.
Even if their parents have work, at least 30 per cent of young Australians are facing the bleak
prospect of a labour market that doesn’t want them . . . at least not yet. (If you had applied
unsuccessfully for 200 jobs, as a respondent in one of my recent research projects had,
what would you do next?)
(S4) To older Australians, the sharp rise in the divorce rate over the past 20 years seems
cataclysmic, shaking the very foundations of the institution of marriage. But to the rising
generation, nothing has changed: from the time they became aware of the nature of
marriage and divorce, they had known that lots of their friends live with one parent, so what’s
the big deal? Do you imagine that contemporary children and adolescents exchange
information about their parents’ marital status in darkly whispered confessions behind their
hands? Do you think that living in a one-parent family feels like a heavy burden for kids to
bear? Think again: almost one million dependent children are in precisely that situation,
which doesn’t mean that it’s always fun for them, but it does mean that it’s hardly worth
mentioning. (In any case, having one parent at home might sometimes feel like half the
burden of having two.) To the intense irritation of their parents, the members of this
generation are able to program the VCR without even reading the manual. Having grown up
in the thick of the information revolution (‘What revolution?’) they know today’s technology
is already obsolete by the time they get their hands on it, and that smarter things are
constantly coming over the horizon. They know there’s an accessible drug culture in every
town and suburb, and that ‘street kids’ are part of the scene. (No wonder they’ve embraced
the gritty realism of the new writing for young people.)
($5) Paradoxically, they’re also our most dependent generation, staying at home for longer
and relying on social security in larger numbers than any previous group of young
Australians. Like every generation before them, they are responding to the world as they
find it. (To what other world could they possibly respond?) Not surprisingly, their experience
of impermanence and unpredictability has taught them one big, central lesson: keep your
options open. So they are inclined to hang loose; to postpone commitment to a career, a
sexual partner, a political party, a set of religious beliefs, a brand . . . or even to whether
they'll be home for dinner tonight. For many of them, that is an exciting, liberating approach
to life. Those flapping shoelaces can be a sign of confidence, freedom, flexibility and
adaptability. But not for all: the lack of a clear focus and the absence of a stable framework
can also breed insecurity, uncertainty and an aching sense of alienation. In the wait-and-see
world of the young, even the symbol of untied laces is ambiguous.
By Hugh Mackay

More carriages called for
By John Darke
Why can’t Connex run extra carriages on trains instead of removing seats to make more
room for passengers?
In the 1970s, both the red and the blue trains consisted of seven carriages. These were
made up of three motor (power) carriages and four trailer (non-powered) carriages. Today,
Connex operates six-carriage trains consisting of four motors and two trailers, so adding an
extra two trailers to each train should not affect performance. It would, of course, require
building these extra carriages. There are still railway workshops at Newport, Ballarat and
Bendigo as well as a number of private railway equipment builders. The other thing that
would be required would be extending platforms by about 50m. As well as increasing the
passenger capacity by 30 per cent, it would also provide increased employment. Taking out
seats does nothing but force people to stand.
John Darke, of Frankston, drove suburban trains in Melbourne in the 1970s
Herald Sun October, 30 2008

The End of the Beginning
Ray Bradbury
P1 He stopped the lawn mower in the middle of the yard, because he felt that the sun at just
that moment had gone down and the stars had come out. The fresh-cut grass that had
showered his face and body died softly away. Yes, the stars were there, faint at first, but
brightening in the clear desert sky. He heard the porch screen door tap shut and felt his wife
watching him as he watched the night.
‘Almost time,’ she said.
P2 He nodded; he did not have to check his watch. In the passing moments he felt very old,
then very young, very cold, then very warm, now this, now that. Suddenly he was miles away.
He imagined he was his own son talking steadily, moving briskly to cover his pounding heart
and the resurgent panics as he felt himself slip into fresh uniform, check food supplies,
oxygen flasks, pressure helmet, space-suiting, and turn as every man on Earth tonight
turned, to gaze at the swiftly filling sky.
P3 Then, quickly, he was back, once more the father of the son, hands gripped to the lawn-
mower handle. His wife called, ‘Come sit on the porch.’ ‘I've got to keep busy!’ She came
down the steps and across the lawn. ‘Don’t worry about Robert; he'll be all right. But it’s all
so new,’ he heard himself say. ‘It’s never been done before. Think of it — a manned rocket
going up tonight to build the first space station. Good Lord, it can’t be done, it doesn’t exist,
there’s no rocket, no proving ground, no take-off time, no technicians. For that matter, | don’t
even have a son named Bob. The whole thing’s too much for me!’ ‘Then what are you doing
out here, staring?’
P4 He shook his head. ‘Well, late this morning, walking to the office, | heard someone laugh
out loud. It shocked me, so | froze in the middle of the street. It was me, laughing! Why?
Because finally | really knew what Bob was going to do tonight; at last | believed it. “Holy” is
a word | never use, but that’s how | felt stranded in all that traffic. Then, middle of the
afternoon, | caught myself humming. You know the song. “A wheel in a wheel. Way in the
middle of the air.” | laughed again. The space station, of course, | thought. The big wheel
with hollow spokes where Bob'll live six or eight months, then get along to the Moon.
Walking home, | remembered more of the song. “Little wheel run by faith, big wheel run by
the grace of God.” | wanted to jump, yell, and flame-out myself!’

This week, when the Tokyo housewife visited her local Ito-Yokado supermarket to buy butter to make a cake, she found the shelves bare. "! went to another supermarket, and then another, and there was no butter at those either. Everywhere | went there were notices saying Japan has run out of butter. | couldn't believe it — this is the first time in my life I've wanted to try baking cakes and | can't get any butter," said the frustrated cook. Japan's acute butter shortage, which has confounded bakeries, restaurants and now families across the country, is the latest unforeseen result of the global agricultural commodities crisis.

sharp increase in the cost of imported cattle feed and a decline in milk imports, both of which are typically provided in large part by Australia, have prevented dairy farmers from keeping pace with demand. While soaring food prices have triggered rioting among the starving millions of the third world, in wealthy Japan they have forced a pampered population to contemplate the shocking possibility of a long-term — perhaps permanent — reduction in the quality and quantity of its food.

sections.title: Questions 26-30
sections.passage:
Seven Impossible Interviews Before Breakfast #31: Recent Printz Honor Recipient
Sonya Hartnett (an Exclusive Summer Blog Blast Tour Interview)
P1 7-Imp: We find your writing so lyrical and evocative and graceful and exquisite and
precise and introspective and damn near teetering on poetry (whew — oh, and also haunting,
though we think that word gets overused in book reviewing). Have you ever written poetry?
How did you become such a master of (beautiful) metaphors? We suspect writers like that
were quiet, observant children and remain quiet, observant people (quiet, as in listens well
and takes in a lot). Are we right?
P2 Sonya: | guess | was a quiet, observant child — | was extremely shy, and | think that is
often an underlying reason for being both quiet and observant. | don’t think !’m that way any
more. | am still intrinsically shy, but for most of my life | have had to get up on stage, face
audiences, answer questions, put on the show required of an author by the media and the
publisher and the readers. So I’m actually pretty difficult to shut up, these days. Although the
shy person inside me always listens in to my inane prattle, and hates me.
P3 | don’t write poetry — | don’t particularly even like poetry (poems about dogs excepted,
for some reason). When | write, | listen for the tune of the words — | can hear the ‘music’ of
the book very clearly. | try to match the rhythm of the words to the tune | hear. | can always
tell if a sentence is wrong, because it jars the flow of the music. And | guess this is what
poets do — construct their words to match a particular beat.
P4 I’m not sure why I’m so drawn to metaphors — | am often criticized for using them too
often. They are a defining characteristic of my style, although | sometimes try to keep them
to a minimum (and fail). | have always noticed the interconnectedness of the world -— how
things relate to and echo and influence each other, in appearance and behaviour and nature
-— and this might be the reason | so frequently draw similarities between various things. |
also think it helps fix, quite precisely, the image or emotion | want a reader to absorb.
P5 Jules: What the Birds See is devastatingly, obscenely good writing, probably one of my
top-five favorite books ever. | find it striking how you — as Robert Cormier did — nail the
sometimes cruel world of children, the part of their world that gets glossed over when we
sentimentalize childhood (in What the Birds See you wrote, “Adrian has never thought that
what happened to him had been cruel — children inhabit an animalistic world and accept
with grace its harsh rules’). You also really capture the emotional fragility and fears of
childhood (in a way that makes me think of Maurice Sendak’s take on the themes of his
books). How do you do that? Do you remember childhood vividly?
P6 Sonya: | don’t remember childhood vividly -—— indeed, | have very few clear recollections
of things said and done and seen in my life until the age of about twenty. But | do remember
the feelings of childhood: | remember how it felt to flounder so helplessly in a world that was
impossible to understand or control; | remember the terror that small disasters, like lost
library books, inspired in me; | remember the shattering loneliness of losing a best friend. |
remember, too, the great simple pleasures of being a kid: riding a bike on a newly-made
road, eating ice cream and chocolate topping, watching the morning cartoons in a silent
house, my feet up on the heater.
P7 | find it interesting that people really love Adrian, and feel so deeply for him. To many
readers, he’s more alive and real than any other character I’ve created. | have had women
get amazingly angry with me for ill-treating him. | think people relate to him because we all
remember and recognize those hard, bright emotions from childhood — they burn into us,
we never forget their ache, or their giddy joy. When readers encounter Adrian, they see
something of the child they were. He makes them worry for their own children. He makes
everyone cry.
P8 7-Imp: /n this country, people tend to place you, as an author, into the Young Adult fiction
category (though your titles are also seen as cross-over ones — stepping over into adult
fiction, that is). How do you feel about that label? Do you think it’s accurate? Do you get tired
of all the labeling and trying to figure out into which category a country is going to place you,
tired of the confusion over your intended audience?
P9 Sonya: | get extremely tired of it. It is an issue that has haunted almost my entire career,
and it never gets solved, and somehow | seem to get blamed for it, and have to be the one
who explains it, when it’s nothing at all to do with me. By and large, it’s the publishers who
decide where a book gets placed in the market. | write whatever comes to me, and | write
whatever the book requires. My first responsibility is to the work — not to the reader, not to
the reader’s mother, not to a school teacher, not to a librarian: to the book. If what | write
offends someone, | have no qualms about telling that person to look elsewhere for their
literary satisfaction.
P10 For some of the books, “YA” is an appropriate label. And | like the idea of teenagers
reading my books. They are non-judgmental, forgiving readers, and they don’t get all
squeaky and hysterical about things. But the labelling of my books has been a ball and chain
I've dragged forever, and I’ve seen ridiculous things happen in attempts to place the work
where it ‘belongs.’ I’ve seen What The Birds See promoted as a book for nine-year-olds,
because it has a child of that age in it. And | suffer the general scorn with which children’s/YA
writers are treated by the media, by festival, etc. (at least, that is the case in Australia). Then
| see the work being compared to Faulkner, Steinbeck, Harper Lee — all these writers who
are certainly not writers for the young. These days, the issue is so stupid and annoying and
old — it’s cost me so much respect and recognition, let alone money — that | rarely let myself
be drawn into discussing it.

Half-Truths
Beware of those who use the truth to deceive. When someone tells you something
that is true, but leaves out important information that should be included, he can
create a false impression.
For example, someone might say, “I just won a hundred dollars on the lottery. It
was great. | took that dollar ticket back to the store and turned it in for one hundred
dollars!”
This guy’s a winner, right? Maybe, maybe not. We then discover that he bought
two hundred tickets, and only one was a winner. He’s really a big loser!
He didn’t say anything that was false, but he deliberately omitted important
information. That’s called a half-truth. Half-truths are not technically lies, but they
are just as dishonest.
Untrustworthy candidates in political campaigns often use this tactic. Let’s say that
during Governor Smith’s last term, her state lost one million jobs and gained three
million jobs. Then she seeks another term. One of her opponents runs an ad
saying, “During Governor Smith’s term, the state lost one million jobs!” that’s true.
However an honest statement would have been, During Governor Smith’s term,
the state had a net gain of two million jobs.”

URANUS
Uranus, the seventh planet from the Sun, enjoys two distinct and long seasons. Forty-
two years of sunlight is followed by forty-two years of darkness. The reason for this is
that the planet, rings and moons are all tilted at an angle of 98 degrees, while other
planets look like spinning tops as they make their journey around the Sun, Uranus is
flipped on its side, and appears to be rolling around the Sun. Scientists do not have a
definite answer for why the planet lies in this way, but one reason postulated is a collision
with some other heavy body many millennia ago.
Uranus can be just barely seen with the naked eye, but it was not until it was examined
by telescope, that it was identified as a planet. This happened in 1781, when Sir William
Herschel found it while mapping the constellation of Gemini. Its faint ring system was
not discovered until 1977. There are eleven rings in total. It was once thought that
Uranus only had five moons: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon, but Voyager
Two along with various other telescopes revealed at least twenty-two new bodies. All
the moons revolve around the plane of the planet’s equator.
Uranus, rotates on its axis in about seventeen hours. The atmosphere is made up of
83% hydrogen, 15% helium and 2% methane. It is this methane which gives the planet
its characteristic blue appearance. The actual planet is composed of a solid rock
fragments that are up to a meter thick. This rock is some of the densest material ever
encountered in the universe.

Why Do Some People Call Football “Soccer”?
One of the best-known differences between British and American English is the fact that
the sport known as football in Great Britain is usually called soccer in the United States.

questions.stem: In fact, the word is thoroughly British in origin. So why is it that Americans
options: (not to mention Canadians, Australians, and others) are likelier to use the word than Brits
are? The answer lies in how the sport developed in each country.
Although football-type games have been around for centuries, the sport we know today is
often said to have begun in 1863, when England’s newly formed Football Association

wrote down a set of rules. 2 . Rugby football, named after an English boarding school, was a variation that allowed players to carry and run with the ball to advance it toward the goal. The game played under the Football Association’s rules thus became known as association football. Inevitably, the names would be shortened. 3 . The latter term was further shortened to “soccer” (sometimes spelled “socker”), and the name quickly spread beyond the campus. However, “soccer” never became much more than a nickname in Great Britain. By the 20th century, rugby football was more commonly called rugby, while association football had earned the right to be known as just plain football. Meanwhile, in the United States, a sport emerged in the late 19th century that borrowed elements of both rugby and association football. 4 . As a result, American association-football players increasingly adopted soccer to refer to their sport. The United States Football Association, which had formed in the 1910s as the official organising body of American soccer, changed its name to the United States Soccer Football Association in 1945, and it later dispensed with the “Football” altogether. The Flute
This passage is from The Bamboo Flute written by Gary Disher.
Mr. Riggs says, ‘l want you to explain this, Paul.” He’s holding a length of bamboo -
the confiscated, unfinished flute. | look up. There is kindness in his face. It transforms
his terrible (blind) eye. | feel confused. ‘Sir, | was making a flute, sir.’
He nods. ‘I can see that.’ He offers it to me. ‘You’d better take it home and finish it.’
| take it from him. For a while, neither of us speaks. | gather myself and look at his
eye and say, ‘Sir, | made another one.’
An expression of regret passes over his face. ‘Did you? | would have given this one
back to you, but | thought it was just a stick. When | was burning the rubbish
yesterday, | realised what it was.’ ‘That’s all right, sir.’ We stand there, feeling
awkward.
He looks at me curiously. ‘Can you play?’
‘Yes, sir.’ ‘Then you must show me on Monday.’
Another one of those long pauses. ‘Sir,’ | say, ‘| can show you now. I’ve got the other
one in my kitbag.’
He folds his arms and leans against the edge of his desk and says, ‘All right then,
let’s hear you.’
| take out the flute, my fingers fluttery in the gaze of his shiny eye. Then | position
myself and begin to play, and the magic takes over. He’s smiling.
Mr. Riggs is listening and smiling. | finish, feeling hot-faced and shy.

Underworld: Rise of the Lycans (MA15+)
Director: Patrick Tatopoulos (feature debut)
Starring: Bill Nighy, Michael Sheen, Phona Mitra, Kevin Grevioux
>Gone to howl and never coming back
OH, THE vagaries of franchise filmmaking. When the going is good, the talent will happily
front up for a sequel. When the talent goes elsewhere, the only option is to persuade
whoever is left to do a prequel. Such is the sorry fate which has befallen the Underworld
series. You remember the first two flicks, right? You don’t? OK, here’s what you missed.
Kate Beckinsale in a rubber catsuit. Scott Speedman and a posse of greasy-haired dudes
with coloured contact lenses. An ancient blood feud between fashion-victim vampires and
not-so-stylish werewolves.
Whew. Classic stuff, hun? Well, it used to fill the time between visits from Wesley Snipes
and the Blade gang. However, now that Beckinsale and Speedman have better things to
do with their time, former support players Bill Nighy and Michael Sheen have been
bumped up the billing. For their trouble, these stalwart British thesps have been saddled
with a cheap and cheerless cash-in that should bury the whole underworld thing once and
for all. In Rise of the Lycans, the narrative clock is wound back a century or five to explain
how vampires and werewolves came to hate each other so. Unremarkably, what follows
sucks and bites in equal measure. Big-boss vamp Viktor (Nighy) gets his black velvet cape
in a twist when he discovers his headstrong daughter Sonia (Rhona Mitra, prepared to
show a little more and emote a lot less than her predecessor Beckinsale) has been
canoodling with the hairy he-man hellhound Lucian (Sheen). After building up this
Transylvanian standoff with a pile of claptrap about keeping all spooky species strictly
separated, the film then devolves into a wonky Braveheart for werewolves.
Sadly, Sheen is no Mel Gibson. Now, Sheen is a fine actor. On the strength of his work as
David Frost in Frost/Nixon and Tony Blair in The Queen, you could easily argue he is one
of the best in the business at the moment. However, no amount of growling, howling or

ELEMENTS OF THE AUSTRALIAN FLAG
THE UNION JACK
The Australian national flag has the Union Jack in the upper left-hand quarter nearest the
flagpole (‘canton’) and the rest of the background (the ‘field’) coloured dark blue. The Union
Jack, the commonly used name for the Union flag, is the flag of the United Kingdom and has
its own history.
The first Union flag was created in 1606 and consisted of the red cross of St George
(England) on a white background and the white diagonal cross of St Andrew (Scotland) on
a dark blue background. This flag was first raised in Australia on 29 April 1770 by Captain
Cook at Stingray Harbour (later renamed Botany Bay). Cook raised it again at Possession
Island, off Cape York when he claimed the east coast of Australia in the name of King George
the Third. Governor Phillip hoisted this flag again on 26 January 1788 at Sydney Cove,
marking the first European settlement. ,
When Ireland became a part of the United Kingdom in 1801, the red
diagonal cross of St Patrick was added to the Union Jack. This flag Mw AA
was flown by European settlers and explorers across Australia until
Federation in 1901, when the Commonwealth of Australia was ie | bw
formed and the Australia national flag flew.
THE COMMONWEALTH STAR
The Commonwealth Star on the Australian national flag created in 1901
had six points representing the States (formerly colonies); the seventh point
was added in 1908 to represent Commonwealth Territories. Another reason
for this change was for the star to match the crest of the Commonwealth
Coat of Arms, the first version of which was created in 1908. The
Commonwealth Star is sometimes referred to as the Federation Star.
THE SOUTHERN CROSS
Four seven-pointed stars arranged in a cross, together with a smaller five-pointed star
appear on the right-hand side (‘fly’) of the flag to represent the Southern Cross. The
Southern Cross is a constellation that can be seen only in the night skies of the Southern
Hemisphere. It was a common feature of many of the early unofficial Australia flags. The
formal name of the Southern Cross is Crux Australis and the individual stars are named by
the first five letters of the Greek alphabet in order of brightness—{clockwise from the bottom
star) Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta and Epsilon.
The original competition-winning design had each star with a different *
number of points, ranging from nine to five to reflect their brightness. The *
number of points was simplified by the British Admiralty, and the official ¥*
x
drawing in the Commonwealth of Australia Gazette of 23 February 1903
showed the four larger stars of the same size with seven points each and *
the smaller one with five.
From ‘Australian Flags’ 1998

POKEMANIACS can attest that the urge to “catch’em all” in some games can be irresistible.
Yet while Spectrobes has strong instant appeal, this fossil-fuelled sequel still does not have
the same long-term allure as Nintendo’s pocket monster series.
Youngsters again guide a cocky young space cadet who can command Spectrobes, the
only creatures that can save the universe from a powerful new threat that can consume
entire planets. The critters are found in fossils deep underground, requiring trainers to
excavate, awaken and evolve them before they can be useful in battle.
Newcomers will initially enjoy the process of scouring planets for precious underground
booty, then carefully chipping away layers of rock, sand, lava and ice using the touch screen
while harnessing tools such as drills and vacuums to remove the treasure without shattering
its precious contents. The procedure can be tense and exciting, but eventually becomes a
tiresome chore as repetition sets in.
There are 185 Spectrobes to collect. While they still lack the charismatic charm of
Pokemon, it is fun to discover new creatures because of their unique attacks. Work has been
invested in the battle system, which remains simple and cumbersome but now offers some
much-needed depth.
Two Spectrobes are taken into each scuffle and players can instantly switch between
them. Unfortunately, players will struggle to always get the best view of the action as they
try to quickly pummel foes using melee and projectile-based attacks.
Although the rock-paper-scissors dynamic does little to prevent trainers from using the
same warriors every time, incubators encourage the development of a diverse squad. Mined
minerals can be fed to the creatures to improve their combat skills, rewarding those who
invest significant time in scavenger hunts. The game also supports multi-player battles and
creature trading.
The Age January 227 2009

FOLLOWING an astonishing 2008, Nintendo is confident that its hugely successful Wii and

Buoyed by record Christmas sales, including $37 million worth of Nintendo product in

He turned away the good old horse that served him many days;
He dressed himself in cycling clothes, resplendent to be seen;

The United Nations Flag
The United Nations emblem features a map of the world as seen from the North Pole cupped
by olive branches, a symbol of peace dating back to Ancient Greece. When set on a light
blue background it forms the United Nations flag.
The emblem originated in 1945, when a button design was sought for the San Francisco
conference at which the United Nations charter was drafted and approved to take effect on
24 October. The Presentation Branch of the United Sates Office of Strategic Services
prepared the design and on 7 December 1946 the General Assembly accepted a modified
design as the official seal and emblem of the United Nations flag, using the emblem on a
light blue background.
The United Nations flag is not an Australian flag, but it is flown in Australia and elsewhere
according to special rules set out in the United Nations Flag Code. In accordance with a
proclamation made by the Governor-General on 19 August 1948, 24 October each year is
observed throughout Australia and its Territories as United Nations Day. If there are two or
more flagpoles of equal height the United Nations Flag is flown on this day alongside the
Australian National Flag. If only one flagpole is available, the Australian National Flag should
be the flag flown on that day.

The Last of His Tribe
Henry Kendall
He crouches, and buries his face on his knees,
And hides in the dark of his hair;
For he cannot look up to the storm-smitten trees.
Or think of the loneliness there --
Of the loss and the loneliness there.
The wallaroos grope through the tufts of the grass,
And turn to their coverts for fear:
But he sits in the ashes and lets them pass
Where the boomerangs sleep with the spear --
With the nullah, the sling, and the spear.
Uloola, behold him! The thunder that breaks
On the top of the rocks with the rain,
And the wind which drives up with the salt of the lakes
Have made him a hunter again --
A hunter and fisher again.
For his eyes have been full with a smouldering thought;
But he dreams of the hunts of yore,
And of foes that he sought, and of fights that he fought
With those who will battle no more
Who will go to the battle no more.

On the Darling River
The Darling - which is either a muddy gutter or a second Mississippi - is about six
times as long as the distance, in a straight line, from its head to its mouth. The state of the
river is vaguely, but generally understood to depend on some distant and foreign phenomena,
to which bushmen refer in an offhand tone of voice as "the Queenslan' rains", which seem to
be held responsible, in a general way, for most of the outback trouble.
It takes less than a year to go upstream by boat to Walgett or Bourke in a dry season
because the river is then a string of waterholes. After a while the passengers get sick of
climbing out of the boat while it is carried to the next long waterhole. They get sick of being
stuck in the same sort of place, in the same old way; they grow weary of seeing the same old
timer drop his swag on the bank opposite whenever the boat ties up for wood; they get tired
of lending him tobacco, and listening to his ideas, which are limited in number and narrow
in conception.
It shortens the journey to get out and walk; but then you will have to wait so long for
your luggage - unless you hump it with you.
We heard of a man who determined to stick to a Darling boat and travel the whole
length of the river. He was a newspaper man. He started on his voyage of discovery one
Easter in flood-time, and a month later the captain got bushed between the Darling and the
South Australian border. The water went away before he could find the river again, and he
left his boat in a scrub. They had a cargo of rations, and the crew stuck to the craft while the
tucker lasted; when it gave out they rolled up their swags and went to look for a station, but
didn't find one. The captain would study his watch and the sun, rig up dials and make out
courses, and follow them without success. They ran short of water, and didn't smell any for
weeks; they suffered terrible privations, and lost three of their number, not including the
newspaper man. There were even dark hints of considering the drawing of lots in connection
with something too terrible to mention. They crossed a thirty-mile plain at last, and sighted a
young Aboriginal girl. She led them to a boundary-rider's hut where they were taken in and
provided with rations.
Later on a syndicate was formed to explore the country and recover the boat; but
they found her thirty miles from the river and about eighteen from the nearest waterhole deep
enough to float her so they left her there.

Environmental Dangers
Two introduced animals have created a danger to our environment and continue to
do so despite government efforts to overcome the problems they are causing.
The buffalo was introduced from Indonesia between 1825 and 1843. It bred
successfully in regions of the Northern Territory which perfectly suited its needs. The wetland
areas of the Northern Territory are at risk from these animals. They have caused
considerable damage and it is estimated that over 6,000 hectares of paper bark forests have
been utterly destroyed. When these animals move from place to place they create deep
channels in the water-logged areas. The banks of the water courses are damaged. This
means that the natural banks can no longer function effectively. In the dry season water from
the ocean breaks into these areas. The plant and animal life that cannot tolerate the increase
in salinity can no longer survive or are greatly reduced. Although steps are being taken to
minimise the damage, there are still an estimated 80,000 of these animals. The damage
they continue to cause to swamps, fresh water springs and nesting sites of water birds is
considerable.
Introduced with the arrival of the First Fleet, the feral goat causes problems over a
much wider area than the buffalo. Early settlers used them for meat and milk. Today it is
estimated that there are 7 million feral goats in Australia. They are found in approximately
half the area of Australia. Control of feral goats is almost impossible as they can exist on
virtually all types of vegetation. Properties and National Parks are at risk as mobs of feral
goats ravage the natural vegetation to such an extent that areas are reduced to a barren
landscape. Water supplies for stock and native animals are often reduced to muddy bogs,
and, in the extreme heat can be completely dry. Their habit of stripping trees and grasses
causes severe erosion of vast tracts of land, wind erosion in the dry months and erosion by
water when flooding rains occur.
Both these pests require a prolonged and expensive eradication program to avoid
the environmental damage which will continue.
