sections.title: Questions 12-16
sections.passage:
Early Forms of Parliament
The evolution of the parliamentary system used in Australia can be traced back to
the United Kingdom. Long before the term United Kingdom was used, the Anglo-Saxons and
Jutes from mainland Europe were settling in England. They brought with them a type of self-
government that suited the needs of the scattered tribes. There was a meeting held regularly
to make and enforce laws, settle quarrels and decide on suitable punishment. This was
called a ‘folk moot' with the leading freemen of the tribe or village making the decisions.
As the population increased and dispersed throughout England, kingdoms were set
up, but it was not until the tenth century that the country was united under one ruler.
Distances made it impossible for all the freemen to assemble as in the older ‘folk moot’ days,
and there gradually developed a simple form of representation of chosen men from each
district to regularly attend meetings. The group was called the 'Witan’, or the meeting of wise
men.
The main objectives of the Witan were to advise the King on matters of law-making,
the levying of taxes and the defence of the kingdom. All the Saxon rulers used the Witan
system, and, although it held little resemblance to the later developed parliamentary system,
it nevertheless created in the minds of the people the view that the King should not be an
absolute ruler.
With the invasion of England by William, Duke of Normandy, there were swift and
radical changes. The Witan was abolished and a Great Council was established, made up
of the great barons and leading churchmen. William was an autocratic ruler and called the
Great Council together quite infrequently. There remained, however, the strong feeling that
the Great Council should become an important voice of the people, so that Kings should rule
in the interests of all the King's subjects.

Sea Safety
The Editor,
East Coast Advertising,
PO Box 717,
Eastview.
Dear Ms Alford,
Once again another sea rescue that was completely unnecessary has taken place.
Small craft, sailing vessels and helicopters have been involved in a four-day search of our
coastline, often in appalling weather and dangerous seas because of human stupidity.
| am very pleased that the Haslan family was finally rescued from the serious danger
they were in, but the danger was of their own making. Reports indicate that the minimum
safety requirement and safety kits were not on board. Not to have the correct safety
equipment, sufficient safety floatation devices and communicating equipment and setting off
past Barr's Point into the open sea, can only be described as almost criminal negligence.
The weather forecast on the morning the family set out indicated rising seas and
steadily increasing winds, though only freshening during the afternoon to 17 - 21 knots.
The area outside Barr's Point is well known as a place where the current can run in the
opposite direction to the waves. When this happens the waves can overrun each other and
this in turn generates steep and dangerous rogue waves. In this part of the world, the
weather forecasts for fishermen and the general conditions north and south of Eastview are
well known, widely advertised and most people take the necessary precautions to ensure
the safety of the lives of their family.
What did this rescue cost in terms of official police, rescue personnel and volunteers?
A large sum of money no doubt. It is time people who, through their own ignorance, lack of
responsibility and common sense, were made to pay to our local council at least part of the
overall cost of their rescue.
Yours Sincerely,
Arthur Sanding
(President - Eastview Yacht Squadron)

Magna Carta
During the period 1100 to 1300 there were actions taken that contributed to the
development of the Westminster system of government. There had been a token _
parliament previously, where the King set up a Great Council to give advice on matters of
taxation, governance and national security. Quite frequently the Kings chose to act
completely autocratically and paid only lip service to the advice of this small but powerful
group of nobles and bishops.
It was this total disregard of the Great Council that brought about a situation,
where there was great unrest in England. King John took no heed of laws that had been
promulgated, and increased taxes without recourse to discussions with the Great Council.
The barons and the bishops were incensed by the King's conduct and acting on the advice
of the Archbishop of Canterbury, determined to force the King to rule justly. A famous
document was drawn up and King John was forced to sign this first great charter of English
liberty.
Although the document benefited most by the terms of Magna Carta, it led to
further extensions of rights and responsibilities for the common people. It contained three
very significant clauses, which even today are a cornerstone of our legal and governmental
system.
e No man shall be imprisoned except by the lawful judgement of his equals.
° To none shall justice be sold, denied or delayed.
These two clauses were included to ensure that persons could not be imprisoned on the
whim of a king, and that there must be an honest and accountable justice system.
@ The King shall impose no tax without the consent of the Great Council.
Although later kings did not always honour these three clauses, it was the beginning of an
era where the monarchy ruled through a parliamentary system that empowered the
citizens of England to have some input into the governance of the country.

On the Parapet
The officer riding alone in the midst of the column was the other attraction. His head
was bare; otherwise he was in full armour. At his left hip he wore a short sword; in his
hand, however, he carried a truncheon, which looked like a roll of white paper. He sat upon
a purple cloth instead of a saddle, and that, and a bridle with a forestall of gold and reins of
yellow silk broadly fringed at the lower edge, completed the housings of the horse.
While the man was yet in the distance, Judah observed that his presence was
sufficient to throw the people looking at him into angry excitement. They would lean over
the parapets or stand boldly out and shake their fists at him; they followed him with loud
cries, and spit at him as he passed under the bridges; the women even flung their sandals,
sometimes with such good effect as to hit him. When he was nearer, the yells became
distinguishable - "Robber, tyrant, dog of a Roman! Leave us be!"
When quite near, Judah could see that, as was but natural, the man did not share
the indifference so superbly shown by the soldiers; his face was dark and sullen, and the
glances he occasionally cast at his persecutors were full of menace; the very timid shrank
from them. It was Valerius Gratus, the new governor of the country.
To say truth now, the Roman under the unprovoked storm had Judah's sympathy; so
that when he reached the corner of the house, the latter leaned yet farther over the
parapet to see him go by, and in the act rested a hand upon a tile which had been a long
time cracked and allowed to go unnoticed. The pressure was strong enough to displace
the outer piece, which started to fall. A thrill of horror shot through him. He reached out to
catch the missile. In appearance the motion was exactly that of one pitching something
from him. The effort failed - nay, it served to push the descending fragment farther out over
the wall. He shouted with all his might. The soldiers of the guard looked up, so did the
great man, and that moment the missile struck him, and he fell from his seat as dead.
= -—— Reading page5

It was dark when Edward awoke. At first he didn’t know where he was. And then he
remembered. He was in bed. In his bedroom. It was the middle of the night. And he
remembered, too, Julie’s twisted face and the things she said. The face and the words had
kept him awake, and had haunted his dreams when at last he slept.
It was ridiculous, really. All this fuss about an imaginary ghost. Why did he get in such a
state over Julie? She was only a little kid, after all. His baby sister. You were supposed to
love your sister, not — not fear her. But no, he wasn’t really afraid of her. How could he be?
Such a sweet little girl with blue eyes and fair bouncing curls who was half his age. A little
girl who played games and imagined things. Who imagined ghosts. A ghost in her bedroom.
But he was frightened. He knew that now. And as his fear mounted again, the room
seemed to get colder. He shut his eyes and snuggled down under the blankets, shutting out
the room and the cold. But not the fear.
And then he heard it. A sound. A faint scraping sound, as though something heavy was
being dragged along the landing. A sound that came closer and grew louder. A wet, slithering
sound. And with it came a smell, a sickening smell of, oh, drains and dead leaves and decay.
And the sound grew louder and he could hear breathing, harsh breathing, long choking
breaths coming closer.
“Julie?” Edward said, and then he repeated it, louder. “Julie!”
But there was no answer. All he heard was the scraping, dragging sound coming closer,
closer. Near his door now. Closer.
“| know it’s you!” Edward shouted, and heard the fear in his voice. “You're playing ghosts
again, aren't you? Aren’t you?”
And then there was silence. No sound at all. Edward sat up in bed and listened. The awful
slithering noise had stopped. It had gone. The ghost had gone.
He hugged himself with relief. It had been a dream, that’s all. He’d imagined it. Just as
Julie imagined things. Imagined ghosts.
Then he heard the breathing again. The shuddering, choking breaths. And he knew that
the thing hadn't gone. That it was still there. Outside his door. Waiting. Waiting.
And Edward screamed, “Julie! Stop it! Stop it! Please stop it! | believe you! | believe in the
ghost!”
The door opened. The shuddering breaths seemed to fill the room, and the smell, and the
slithering wet sound of a shape, something, coming towards him, something huge and dark
and —

The second book was a School History textbook. The two thousand years of England's
story were neatly parcelled into compartments for ready reference. The compartments, as
usual, were reigns. It was no wonder that one pinned a personality to a reign, forgetful that
that personality had known and lived under other kings. One put them in pigeon-holes
automatically. Pepys: Charles Il. Shakespeare: Elizabeth. Marlborough: Queen Anne. It
never crossed one's mind that someone who had seen Queen Elizabeth could also have
seen George I. One had been conditioned to the reign idea from childhood. However, it did
simplify things when you were just a policeman with an injured leg and a concussed spine
hunting up some information on dead and gone royalties to keep yourself from going crazy.
He was surprised to find the reign of Richard Ill so short. To have made oneself one of the
best-known rulers in all those two thousand years of England's history, and to have had
only two years to do it in, surely augured a towering personality. If Richard had not made
friends he had certainly influenced people.
The history book, too, thought that he had personality: Richard was a man of great ability,
but quite unscrupulous as to his means. He boldly claimed the crown on the absurd ground
that his brother's marriage with Elizabeth Woodville had been illegal and the children of it
illegitimate. He was accepted by the people who dreaded a minority and began his reign
by making a progress through the south, where he was well received. During this progress,
however, the two young Princes who were living in the Tower, disappeared, and were
believed to have been murdered. A serious rebellion followed, which Richard put down with
great ferocity. In order to recover some of his lost popularity he held a Parliament, which
passed useful statutes against Benevolences, Maintenance, and Livery. But a second
rebellion followed. This took the form of an invasion, with French troops, by the head of the
Lancaster branch, Henry Tudor. He encountered Richard at Bosworth, near Leicester,
where the treachery of the Stanleys gave the day to Henry. Richard was killed in the battle,
fighting courageously, leaving behind him a name hardly less infamous than that of John.

Pictures from the Deserted Village
O. Goldsmith
Near yonder copse, where once the garden smiled,
And still where many a garden flower grows wild;
There, where a few torn shrubs the place disclose,
The village preacher's modest mansion rose.
Aman he was to all the country dear,
And passing rich with forty pounds a year;
Remote from towns he ran his godly race,
Nor e'er had changed, nor wished to change his place;
Unpractised he to fawn, or seek for power,
By doctrines fashioned to the varying hour;
Far other aims his heart had learned to prize,
More skilled to raise the wretched than to rise.
His house was known to all the vagrant train,
He chid their wanderings, but relieved their pain:
The long-remembered beggar was his guest,
Whose beard descending swept his aged breast;
The ruined spendthrift, now no longer proud,
Claimed kindred there, and had his claims allowed;
The broken soldier, kindly bade to stay,
Sat by his fire, and talked the night away;
Wept o'er his wounds, or tales of sorrow done,
Shouldered his crutch, and showed how fields were won.
Pleased with his guests, the good man learned to glow,
And quite forgot their vices in their woe;
Careless their merits or their faults to scan,
His pity gave ere charity began.

Australia's First Great Administrator
Imagine you are back in the eighteenth century, without the benefit of modern
technology and machinery, and you are given a task of this magnitude.
Your task is to proceed to a remote corner of the globe and establish a settlement.
A fleet of wooden sailing ships will be provided. There will be 750 convicts, and four
companies of marines to control the colony. On the three store ships, food for two years,
clothing, building and farming tools and trading goods for the indigenous people will be
transported. Some cattle, pigs, horses, sheep and plant seeds will be obtained at
Capetown in South Africa. It will take the fleet eight months to reach its destination.
This then was the task of the founder of the first European settlement in Australia,
Captain Arthur Phillip. He was appointed to this task in 1776. This energetic, colonial
administrator began his task with great enthusiasm, and, such was his ability and his
superb organisational skills, that he managed to overcome a list of difficulties that would
have broken a Jesser man. The settlement was made at Sydney Cove in 1788.
Phillip had a huge number of problems to overcome. Though some of these were
caused by the unwillingness of the authorities in England to pay sufficient attention to
assisting in the planning, many could probably not have been foreseen.
The convicts who were to help establish the settlement were lazy and
troublesome. Few had any useful skills, particularly the farming and animal raising
aspects. The officers were frequently quarrelsome and did not often display a diligent
attitude to what was a monumental task. To add to this list, problems arose with the
indigenous population despite Phillips’ attempts to keep the peace. Food was in short
supply and more convicts, often in poor health, continued to arrive.
Despite these difficulties, Captain Phillip succeeded in establishing the first
European settlement and firmly believed that his early work would allow the settlement to
thrive, and that the country had a wonderful future in store.

We return to Captain Haldane and his friends, who had been meditating escape from the
first day of their arrival at the Staats Model School. The difficulty was, of course, the
guards, and Mr. Churchill's exploit made the Boer Government redouble its vigilance. It
was found impossible to bribe the sentries; a plan for a rising of the prisoners was soon
given up; and the scheme of sinking a shaft and then tunnelling to an adjacent kitchen
garden proved impracticable, since the diggers very soon struck water. For three miserable
months Captain Haldane cogitated in vain, and the best he could do was to get hold of a
tourist map of South Africa and study the country east of Pretoria in case some way of
escape should present itself. Meantime an incident cheered the prisoners. A man
accompanied by a St. Bernard dog took to walking outside the school and signalling by the
Morse code with his stick. He was warned off by the guards, but he found another means
of communication and sent messages from an adjacent house giving the news of the war.
In the middle of February 1900 there was a rumour that the officers were to be moved to a
new building from which escape would be impossible. This gave Captain Haldane an idea.
He resolved to go into hiding beneath the floor, so that the Boers should think he had
escaped, and then, when the officers were moved and the building was left empty, to
emerge and get out of the town. His companions in the attempt were Lieutenant Neil Le
Mesurier of the Dublin Fusiliers and Sergeant-Major A. Brockie of the Imperial Light Horse.
They collected a few necessary articles, opened the trap-door, and went to earth.
It was a horrible place in which they found themselves. The floor of the building was about
2 feet above the ground, and the space below was divided into five narrow compartments
by four stone walls, on which the cross beams rested. Each of these compartments was
about 18 feet long and 30 feet wide, and there were manholes between them. The air,
what there was of it, came through a small ventilator somewhere on the veranda. The
place was pitch dark, and the atmosphere was stuffy to the last degree. The three thought
that their imprisonment there would only last for twenty-four hours. They went to earth on
26th February, and next day there was a great to-do about their disappearance.
Descriptions of them were circulated over the whole country. One of their friends above,
Lieutenant Frankland of the Dublin Fusiliers, arranged a small daily supply of provisions.
Excerpt from ‘A Book of Escapes And Hurried Journeys’ by John Buchan

One morning shortly after breakfast, Captain Ahab, as was his wont, ascended the cabin
gangway to the deck. There most sea-captains usually walk at that hour, as country
gentlemen, after the same meal, take a few turns in the garden.
Soon his steady stride was heard, as ta and fro he paced his old rounds, upon planks so
familiar to his tread, that they were all over dented, like geological times, with the peculiar
mark of his walk. Did you fixedly gaze, too, upon that ribbed and dented brow; there also,
you would see still stranger footprints - the footprints of his one unsleeping, ever pacing
thought.
But on the occasion in question, these dents looked deeper, even as his nervous step that
morning left a deeper mark. And, so full of his thought was Ahab, that at every uniform turn
that he made, now at the mainmast and now at the binnacle, you could almost see that
thought turn in him as he turned, and pace in him as he paced; so completely possessing
him, indeed, that it all but seemed the inward mould of every outer movement.
"D'ye mark him, Flask?" whispered Stubb, "The chick that's in him pecks the shell. Twill
soon be out."
The hours wore on - Ahab now shut up within his cabin; anon, pacing the deck,. with the
same intensity of purpose in his aspect.
It drew near the close of day. Suddenly he came to a halt by the bulwarks and inserting his
boney leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand grasping a shroud, he ordered
Starbuck to send everybody aft.
"Sir!" said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on shipboard except in
some extraordinary case.
"Send everybody ait," repeated Ahab. "Mastheads, there! Come down!"
Then the entire ship's company were assembled, and with curious and not wholly
unapprehensive faces, were eyeing him, for he looked not unlike the weather horizon
when a storm is coming up. Ahab, after rapidly glancing over the bulwarks, and then
darting his eyes among the crew, started from his standpoint; and as though not a soul
were nigh him, resumed his heavy turns upon the deck. With bent head and half-slouched
hat he continued to pace.

The Day is Done
By Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
The day is done, and the darkness
Falls from the wings of night
As a feather is wafted downward
From an eagle in its flight.
| see the lights of the village
Gleam through the rain and the mist,
And a felling of sadness comes o'er me,
That my soul cannot resist.
A feeling of sadness and longing,
That is not akin to pain,
And resembles sorrow only
As the mist resembles the rain.
Come, read to me some poem,
Some simple and heart-felt lay,
That shall soothe this restless feeling,
And banish the thoughts of day.
Not from the grand old masters,
Not from the bards sublime
Whose distant footsteps echo
Through the corridors of time.
For, like strains of martial music,
Their mighty thoughts suggest
Life’s endless toil and endeavour,
And to-night | long for rest.
Read from some humbler poet,
Whose songs gushed from his heart,
As showers from the clouds of summer,
Or tears from the eyelids start.

2004 ATHENS IAN THORPE
Hilt REBECCA WILLIAMS
IAN Thorpe boasted many strengths as a swimmer. But until his 400m freestyle final in 2004,
emotion had never been a weapon he’d used in the pool.
Strategy went out the window in Athens for the champ, who admitted to having too much
on his mind as he stood on the blocks.
Who could blame him?
If Thorpe’s title defence wasn’t already one of the biggest events of Australia’s Games
campaign, it took on a life of its own after the Olympic trials in March that year when he was
disqualified after a false start in the 400m heats.
He was later granted a swim in his signature event after Craig Stevens gave up his place
to his training partner. The gesture meant Thorpe was no longer racing for just himself.
Expectation had become a much larger beast.
“Through circumstances ... my preparation did not include training for this event. (So) it
was the first time | swam purely on emotion. | could not really implement a strategy.”
Thorpe touched to win his second Olympic 400m gold in 3min43.10sec — 0.26sec ahead
of teammate Grant Hackett — then went on to win gold in the 200m and bronze in the 100m.
It took his overall Olympic haul to nine medals and past Dawn Fraser and Susie O’Neil
as Australia’s most successful Olympian.

What is a Mirage?
A mirage is an optical illusion. This illusion is something that we see, but is not really
there. It occurs mostly when the air is very hot.
in deserts there are places where there is water, and trees grow. Travellers sometimes
think they are coming to an oasis only a few kilometers away, where they can find water
and shade. Then, as they travel on, the oasis disappears. It had been a mirage! The
oasis was not pure imagination. When the travellers saw the oasis, and it receded, they
really had seen an oasis. It was much further on and below the horizon. The light from
the real oasis had been reflected from a layer of air. The travellers had seen it as if a
huge mirror had been placed in the sky to give them this panorama.
The explanation for this is that there are layers of air of different temperatures. These
layers are of different density. Whenever light passes from one thing to another of
different density, part of it is deflected back.
Appearances due to a similar cause are often seen at sea. Aship near the horizon may
seem to have another ship, exactly like itself, perched upside down upon it.

Ancient Fashions
Clothing in ancient Greece was a very simple affair. Everyone wore a variation on the same
theme; rich and poor; adults and children; and men and women. The garment of choice
was the chiton, a type of long, loose robe which fastened on the shoulders with pins and
clasps.
The variations on the ‘chiton’ theme depended on the age, gender, social status and
occupation of the wearer. Women wore long chitons covering their ankles, but men’s were
shorter. Poor people had garments of rough wool or linen while those of the upper classes
were of imported silk. Rich ladies could follow the current fashion with red, blue, yellow or
purple robes but those who were less affluent had to content themselves with undyed ones.
Children and tradesmen had short, plain chitons which permitted them to be active.
People in ancient Greece did not have different clothes for different seasons. In colder
weather, they simply added more layers. If there was a particularly cold spell, or if they
were travelling somewhere, they might top everything with a cloak called a himation.
Ancient Greeks did not wear shoes indoors but needed leather sandals to walk on rough
roads or cobblestones outside. Sometimes, ladies wore very high-heeled sandals to assist
height.
Women in ancient Greece always wore their hair long, and piled it up in complicated
arrangements, sometimes decorating it with ornaments or jewellery. Light coloured hair
was esteemed so women used bleach to acquire the desired look. Likewise, fair skin was
valued so hats were always worn in the outdoors on sunny days.

There is a time, in Japan, when cherry trees briefly dress the countryside with boughs of
pale pink blossoms and spring is welcomed. It was at such a time that a farmer took his son
to a temple where he might learn to become a priest.
From that day the boy rose early each moming to begin the tasks which the priests set
for him. He rang the bell to awaken the yellow-robed ones from their slumbers. He rolled’ up
their sleeping-mats. He cleaned their sandals and he filled their bowls with rice. He did all of
that and he did it well. He also studied his lessons, and then, he spent his spare time drawing
cats. He drew nothing but cats! Cats sleeping, cats stretching, cats eating, cats hunting, cats
yawning, cats snarling, cats stalking, cats lapping, cats slinking, cats walking, cats running!
Cats! Cats! Cats! And kittens, too! The boy owned no paints. He drew on parchment and on
ricepaper with a piece of charcoal. He drew in the dust on the ground and once, he scratched
on a large fleshy lotus leaf with a thorn.
The Priests of the Yellow Robes noted his drawings. They saw that they were excellent.
They decided that he would make a better artist than one of them and they asked him to
leave the temple.
The boy, who was named Yoda, did not want to shame his father because he had failed
to become a priest. So, he did not return to his home, but wandered down the mountainside,
going from village to village.

She went out of her front door into the sunshine and was surprised to find a spring day
waiting for her. The weather had turned warm while she had stayed indoors; February was
over and March had come in, as they say, like a lamb. There was a smell of dampness in
the air as the frosted ground thawed, a smell of things getting ready to grow. It made her
feel even more cheerful than before, and she walked almost gaily across the garden.
And yet despite the fine warmth of the day — indeed, in a way, because of it — Mrs Frisby
could not quite get rid of a nagging worry that kept flickering in her mind; it was the kind of
worry that, if you push it out of this corner of your thoughts, pops up in that corner, and finally
in the middle, where it has to be faced. It was the thought of Moving Day.
Everybody knows that the ground hog comes up from the deep hole where he has slept
away the winter, looks around, and if he decides the cold weather is not over, goes back
down to sleep for another six weeks. Field mice like Mrs Frisby are not so lucky. When winter
is over, they must move out of the garden and back to the meadow or the pasture. For as
soon as the weather allows, Farmer Fitzgibbon’s tractor comes rumbling through, pulling the
sharp-bladed plough through the soil, turning over every foot of it. No animal caught in the
garden that day is likely to escape alive, and all the winter homes, all the tunnels and holes
and nests and cocoons, are torn up. After the plough comes the harrow, with its heavy
creaking discs, and then the people with hoes and seeds.

Raccoon
The Raccoon (Procyon /otor), also known as Raccoon, North American Raccoon,
Northern Raccoon, Washing Bear or informal Coon, is a medium-sized mammal native to
North America and the most widespread species of the family Procyonidae. Since the mid-
20" century they have also been introduced to the European mainland and in the Caucasus
region after having escaped from fur farms or being deliberately released to the wild.
Two of the most distinctive characteristics of the raccoon are its facial mask around the eyes
and extremely sensitive front paws; they are also know for their good memory. Often
raccoons live together in small, loose groups. Their original habitats are deciduous or mixed
forests, but due to their adaptability, they are also found in urban areas where some house
owners consider them to be pests. Furthermore, raccoons are omnivorous and usually most
active during the night.

Start to finish: 144 hours

1 tbs dried chives

Noodle soup mix

Organic boom sparks farm shortage
Mike Edmonds
VICTORIAN shoppers are turning to organic food in their droves.
Nationwide the demand for organic produce has leapt by more than 80 percent since 2004.
Organic processors have even issued a plea for more farmers to adopt the techniques
needed to meet the demand.
A national study by New England University shows organic farm numbers have increased
by more than 5 per cent a year over the past five years. Australia has almost 12 million
hectares of certified organic farmland, the largest of any food-producing nation.
Organic farmer Jo Whitsed, of Corryong, believes customer recognition of the logos used
by testing authorities is an important factor in the growth rate.
“Demand has really taken off in the last few years,” she said.
“Consumers are learning about certified organic, and looking for the logo.
“They’re concerned about the health benefits, the environment and animal welfare issues.”
Organic farming has been the norm for three generations of the Whitsed family on their
150 ha property in a lush valley on the upper reaches of the Murray River. Jo and Steve
Whitsed are continuing the family tradition.
There’s a chance too that Jo’s daughter, Tahnia, could become a fourth-generation
organic farmer, but at 7 she hasn’t decided.
No pesticides or chemicals are used, and cattle feed on pasture rich in treated-waste
products from within farm boundaries or on silage grown and prepared on the farm.
The family runs 160 dairy cows to produce organically certified milk.
“The cows are milking the best they ever have,” said Jo Whitsed.
“We make up our own licks from cider vinegar, dolomite and molasses, and we certainly
don’t get the vet out very often.”
There are seven organic certification groups in Australia, using standards established by
the Quarantine Inspection Service.
Australian Certified Organic, with its sprouting-bud logo, claims to certify about two-thirds
of the genuine organic produce.
“Shoppers need to look for the certification logo,” said Dr Andrew Monk, of Biological
Farmers Australia. “It is harder to farm organically and the product will cost more.
“Consumers make a conscious decision to choose organic. But don’t buy if it’s not
certified.”
Herald-Sun 2008

THE ball fell to Ben Cousins in the middle of the incongruously lush oval at Gosch’s Paddock.
He gathered, arched his back in that familiar way and ran in a wide semi-circle. Now in space,
he paused momentarily, then accelerated again, on a new course, straight towards goal.
Ahead, other players hastily rearranged themselves. “Watch the dish,” urged a man in
the crowd of around 1500, standing three-deep around the fence.
Cousins’ “dish” (that is, pass) began wide, but curved as if on an unseen wind, unerringly
onto the chest of the helmeted Graham Polak, leading hard into the forward pocket.
It would be gilding the lily to say that the crowd roared, but it certainly clapped
appreciatively.
Cousins and Polak played together for Richmond yesterday. It was an irresistible turn of
events since one was a drug addict out in the football cold three months ago and the other
was — and still is — rehabilitating from head injuries after being wrong-footed by a tram last
June.
But it was qualified by all these certainties: it was February 5, too early even for March
championship; it was 27 degrees, too sultry for football; the Nylex clock that formed part of
the backdrop said so.
Cousins played half a game, then was whisked away by car, his now customary blaze of
secrecy. Polak played about 40 minutes. Matthew Richardson was long gone, back, bare-
chested, across the scorched parkland to the Tiger’s Punt Road HQ; one, dominant quarter

Then it fell like huge hot drops of metal, heavy like the sap of trees or globules of honey.
It was even the colour of honey, sometimes burnt honey, sometimes golden.
The juices of the forest so greedily sucked up, the heady juices of gum and pine and
acacia, and the wind-blown salts of the earth and the sweat of men and the blood of beasts
and the steam of ditches and ponds and creeks and rivers and reservoirs, of tanks and
hoses, of irrigated fields and mud puddles, seemed to have become too heavy a load for the
sated heavens to bear, and having weakened, having allowed the first drops to fall, they
seemed to be spilling the lot over.
Black rain, red rain, golden rain, steaming rain, crashed on to the earth, and the sound
was real thunder and the jagged light was real lighting and the giants of north wind and south
wind, of the inferno and of the breadth of the wide cool sea, were locked in conflict.
Peter and Gran Fairhall dragged themselves from the spring, away from the snakes and
the other swimming creatures, and the mammoth flare in the sky had dissolved, had
vanished, had become a tempestuous brown fog.
Gran, confused but revived, awfully battered but conscious, wrapped her huge fleshy arms
about her grandson, as she was often apt to do, and hugged him tight. For years Peter had
detested it, had endured it with a set face and pounding heart; but that had been the way of
a boy, not the way of a man. Gran even sensed the difference herself and faintly heard his
voice: ‘It’s all right, Gran. Everything's all right now.’
Pippa felt it beating on to her body. At first it came hot like her morning shower and she
thought it was fire; but it did not consume her; it grew cooler; and cooler still.

Q Why do the tops of some Christmas cakes crack?
| use a fan-forced oven. - Val
A Because Christmas cakes are usually dense with fruit, they take a
long time to cook, therefore the top of the cake is exposed to more
direct heat than the rest of the cake.
To prevent this, sprinkle or finely mist water over the top of the cake
before putting it in the oven. After the first 30 minutes baking, cover
the top of the cake with foil or brown paper and place a container of
water in the oven to create a little steam during the cooking.
Make sure you refill it during the cooking process. Fan-forced ovens
tend to dry rich fruit cakes more than conventional cooking.
Cook at a moderately slow temperature and let the cake cool in the
tin for 30 minutes or more before turning out. As the cake cools, any
cracks usually close over.

In the great deserts of Egypt, where the hot and golden-grained sands stretch on and on
towards the shimmering, far away ends of the earth, miracles are said still to happen.
Everything out here is wide open and lonely. Nearly all of the desert land is dry, the
sand baked almost rock-hard in places by the sun. Sometimes, if you are travelling
through this furnace of a place, you might come across an oasis — a small patch where
there is a water-hole, with palm trees and small plants called Lilies of the Nile growing
around it. Here you will find shade, and you will be able to fill you water-bottle and wet your
handkerchief and tie it around your neck to cool yourself. If you find an oasis in the desert,
you will be very lucky, as they are few and most definitely far between.
Not many people live in the desert. Those who do usually travel around a lot, not
staying in the one place for a very long time at all. Sometimes they will camp at an oasis
for a few weeks, but they will always move on, for they are usually fearful of meeting up
with a certain tribe — a tribe which has dwelt under the Egyptian sun for thousands of
years. The people who live out in the desert will do anything to avoid coming into contact
with this tribe (one man, long ago, was said to have glued ibis feathers to his body and a
long curved stick to his mouth, and then stood on one leg in the sand, crowing loudly, just
so the tribe would think he was a bird and maybe leave him alone), and so they keep
constantly on the move.
The reason why everyone avoids this particular tribe has nothing to do with
dastardliness, or with their being murderers or thieves or taxation cheats — because they’re
not. Nor do the tribe members make rude sounds or push people to the ground and sit on
them, actions which would automatically make them disagreeable. As a matter of fact, the
tribe is fairly harmless. As another matter of fact, they’re not even human beings. They are,
as everybody who has journeyed through these wide sandy plains and hills knows, one of
the oldest wayfaring groups in all of the African continent: camels.
Excerpt from ‘Brenda is the Night’ by Geoffrey McSkimming

FANTA drinks sold in Britain contain pesticides at up to 300 times the level allowed in tap
or bottled water, according to research.
A Spanish study of 15 countries found pesticide levels in orange and lemon drinks sold by
Coca-Cola under the Fanta brand were at their highest in Britain. The lowest were in

remove the chemicals, and called for new safety standards to regulate the soft drinks
market. The industry denies children are at risk and insists the levels found by researchers
at the University of Jaen are not harmful. The researchers tested 102 cans and bottles of
soft drinks, bought from 15 countries, for the presence of 100 pesticides.

under the maximum residue levels allowed for fruit, but they were “very high” and “up to
300 times” the figure permitted for bottled or tap water. The chemicals detected included
carbendazim, thiabendazole, imazalil, prochloraz, malathion and iprodione.
A Coca-Cola spokesman said: “The generally minuscule levels that were detected were
well within the acceptable daily intake levels and these findings should reassure
consumers there is no safety issue here.”

sections.passage:
Hating Alison Ashley (PG)
Directed by Geoff Bennett
Screenplay by Christine Madafferi from the novel by Robin Klein
Rated PG
Cinemas Everywhere
Adapting a well-loved book is a tricky business. Watching this one, you think inevitably of
Kate Woods's beguiling film of Melina Marchetta's Looking for Alibrandi. Admittedly,
Marchetta's is a more sophisticated story about an older age group, but the biggest
difference between the films lies in their method of construction. Marchetta wrote the
Alibrandi script herself, radically altering her book's architecture while leaving its tone intact.
But Ashley director Geoff Bennett and writer Christine Madafferi have contented themselves
with a painting-and-decorating job.
They use design and costumes to flesh out the characters, which means that Erika and her
9C classmates present a full catalogue of teen fashions, while the Yurkens live in a riot of
leopard-print fabric and fluoro-coloured plastic. Try searching for a sign of emotional
engagement and you're soon lost in the scenery.
| had trouble, too, with the script's constant stream of voice-over narration. | think it's being
employed as a sort of back-to-base security system to make Klein fans feel as if they're still
in touch with the novel, but such verbosity is dangerous coming from someone as self-
absorbed as Erica. On the page, she's taking you into her confidence. On screen, she's
nagging you to the point of numbness.
Relieved of the obligation to tell you what you're looking at, Burmeister could be very funny.
It's impossible to tell since she has nobody to play off. Beatific Alison and bristling Erica have
the makings of the quintessential odd couple, but their friendship never fires because they
scarcely connect. Even when we get to the heart of Alison's problems - an absent father and
an indifferent mother - Goodrem seems to be floating above the action, possibly because
the script has no way of flagging her down to meet its requirements.
Much of the story takes place at school camp, where 9C follows the ritual of every school
camp movie and stages a show for visiting parents. Kittson's commanding but basically
benign Miss Belmont shines here as the mechanics of the plot creak under the pressure of
reaching a denouement that makes sense; Craig McLachlan pulls off some neat pratfalls as
the bumbling PT teacher, Mr Kennard ("I put the fizz into phys ed"), and | liked Alexander
Cappelli as Erica's nemesis, Barry Hollis, the evil genius of 9C. There is, too, one Castle-
like moment when Richard Carter's Lennie finally succeeds in getting through to Erica with
the story's main theme - that appearances aren't everything. But a lot of wasted opportunities
have to be endured before you get to it.
By Sandra Hall
March 19, 2005, Sydney Morning Herald

HOMEWORK WOES
VANESSA CLELLAND
Year 8, GLADSTONE PARK SC
There is too much homework for students. Students should be at movies, over at friends’
houses, etc, but instead they are spending hours cooped up in their room, researching
what they should have done at school. Schools last from between 6-7 hours; surely that is
long enough. My little sister is in Grade 1 and spends on average nearly two hours a night
doing homework. Is that really acceptable for a six-year-old? There has been no evidence
to support the argument that homework improves achievement. Students’ mental health is
at risk. Remember children are the future and we will be looking at a bleak future if the
pressure and endless amounts of homework continue. We need to stop, or reduce,

Q&A
SEAMUS BYRNE
EDITOR OF GAMING GUIDE, KOTAKU AUSTRALIA
What are the most popular video games and why?
There are the big-name series like Halo, but also massive successes in casual games like
Bejeweled and big casual games for Nintendo Wii like WiiSports. If there is one thing
connecting most of today’s biggest games, it is the ability to play with friends.
How have games changed?
Graphics are the most obvious evolution for games, but multi-player has completely
revolutionised the industry when you compare it to the ‘80s and early ‘90s. While many
detractors still believe games are anti-social, the reality today is that they are incredibly
social. Whether sitting together on a couch or online against players from around the world,
games are now much more about shared entertainment experiences and challenges.
What does a typical ‘gamer’ look like?
The latest research shows a ‘typical’ gamer is about 28 years old (I’m 32) and almost half
are female. Certain kinds of games will appeal to different types of people, but there are so
many kinds of videogames now it would be hard to pin down a single ‘typical’ player.
Teenagers probably have more leisure time for games than adults, but more people are
foregoing TV in favour of keeping up their gaming hobby. | think the gamer stereotype of the
anti-social, teenage boy is only held by people who are over 40 and have only touched a
game once or twice in their life.
There’s been a lot of talk about games promoting sexism and violence — what’s your
opinion?
Compared with nightly news, Hollywood movies, and celebrity magazines, i'd suggest
games are hardly the worst offenders in any debate over sex and violence. Unlike more
passive forms of media, a game can also demonstrate consequences for certairr actions.
Some of the best action games in recent years, such as the Metal Gear Solid series and the
Splinter Cell series, reward players for choosing to achieve goals through stealthy means
rather than all guns blazing. There’s plenty of violence in games, but games and sport are
ultimately a contest, and that brings conflict to the forefront — even chess is based on the
idea of war. | think gamers respond more to the quality of game play than the violence.
What do you think is the next big thing in video games?
Gaming as a professional sport. Already in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, there are
gamers making a very comfortable living playing videogames at an elite level. | think schools
should start to support kids who take their games seriously in the same way they support
those who take their football, or their chess, seriously. What are the odds of turning pro in
tennis? Pretty slim. | think there are beiter odds for young gamers to take games to a
professional level. They won’t make millions — yet — but there are opportunities to make a
good salary out of gaming if you can make it into a big team overseas, and with good local
support local opportunities are likely to emerge in the decade ahead.

Some people love to take simple things and make them complicated. They use long words

two most crucial guiding forces in your life begin to wage war. It is always better to be open

your heart will try to trick your head. It will allow it to think that it is in control, but it will
undermine it by causing you to overlook something crucial. Negotiate an inner truce. Make
peace with yourself this week and all relationships will improve.

Every so often scientists set out to prove that psychic power don’t exist. They collect
clairvoyants and stick them in laboratories where, under the flicker of fluorescent lights and

THE TOYMAKER
Jeremy de Quidt, ills. Gary Blythe
Random House
The usually benign art of toy-making takes a sinister twist in this book about
Menschenmacher, a German artisan who brings his toys to life by removing the beating
hearts of small birds and nestling them in the cavities of his creations, with disturbing results.
At the heart of this story is a boy named Mathias. Not yet a teenager, he already has a life
of misery. When his miserable grandfather dies, the former conjuror passes on a secret that
forces Mathias to outwit a collection of ghastly characters. One early scene has Mathias and
his new friend Katta chased down a tunnel that’s thoroughly scary. Jeremy de Quidt’s novel
for older readers is not for the faint-hearted. Gothic in style, there are hints of fantasy, horror
and a bit of Grimms’ fairytales, too. Gary Blythe’s literal black and white drawings help you
visualise some of the most disturbing characters, which is not always a good thing! Don't let
the flowery cover mislead you; this is a finely crafted read that explores big questions about
life and death and what it is to be truly alive. A thrilling read that lingers in the mind.

The Game of Cricket
Cricket is a bat and ball game. It was played in England before the end of the sixteenth century.
It is now the leading summer game in Britain, most of the countries of the British
Commonwealth and also in South Africa.
Cricket is similar in many ways to baseball. In cricket, there is a bowler who bowls (pitches
a ball made of cork and twine encased in leather). A player from the opposing team tries to
hit the ball with a narrow, flat-faced wooden bat. The batsman’s object is to score runs. The
team that scores most runs wins the game.
A cricket field may be of any size. Near the centre of the field is the pitch, a special strip of
level ground that measures 66 feet [20.12 metres] in length. The pitch is marked out with
white lines called creases. At both ends of the pitch are the wickets, which consist of three
short stumps. The wickets are 9 inches [22.86 centimetres] wide and 28 inches [71.1
centimetres] high. The batsman has to guard the wicket against the bowler when he is trying
to make runs.

Eldrick Tont “Tiger” Woods (born December 30, 1975) is an American professional golfer
whose achievements to date rank him among the most successful golfers of all time.
Currently the World No. 1, he was the highest-paid professional athlete in 2007, having
earned an estimated $122 million from winnings and endorsements.
Woods has won fourteen professional major golf championships, the second highest of any
male player, and 65 PGA Tour events, third all time. He has more career major wins and
career PGA Tour wins than any other active golfer. He is the youngest player to achieve the
career Grand Slam, and the youngest and fastest to win 50 tournaments on tour.
Woods has held the number one position in the world rankings for the most consecutive
weeks and for the greatest total number of weeks. He has been awarded PGA Player of the
Year a record nine times, the Byron Nelson Award for lowest adjusted scoring average a
record eight times, and has tied Jack Nicklaus’ record of leading the money list in eight
different seasons. He has been named Associated Press Male Athlete of the Year a record-
tying four times, and is the only person to be named Sports Illustrated’s Sportsman of the
Year more than once.
Woods was the first African American to win the Masters in 1997 at Augusta National; a
tournament where no black player competed until 1975 and a club that didn’t admit a black
member until 1990.
After winning the 2008 U.S. Open, Woods missed the rest of the 2008 PGA Tour, missing
two major championships and the 2008 Ryder Cup, in order to rehabilitate his injured left
knee.
In 2002, scholar Molefi Kete Asante listed Woods on his list of 100 Greatest African
Americans.

a dark room, and you have to be quite imaginative about it all. So when I’m screaming and

Sideswipe
Claire Carmichael, Random House
People work out whether or not they want to read a novel by using all sorts of different cues
— the cover illustration, the blurb on the back, the length of the book and the size of the print.
More and more, however, | am seeing books which give mixed messages about their
intended readership and Clare Carmichael’s latest novel, Sideswipe, is one of them. Gregory
Roger’s cover illustration reflects the sinister nature of the plot and the blurb indicates
‘intense family drama’ dealing with adult concepts. Yet the wide print and the large spacing
between the lines are more appropriate to a junior primary school novel.
Setting aside the confusion, however, the story itself is likely to appeal to those who enjoy
murder mysteries with the emphasis on murder rather than mysteries.
Ed Wyatt is a computer whiz and on the verge of patenting a new time travel game,
Sideswipe. When he is found dead, electrocuted in his office, everyone assumes it was an
accident. Even his children, Ash and Kayla admit he could be very careless. It is only when
Stuart, Ed’s old partner, starts showing an interest in the kid’s mother and any plans Ed
might have left regarding Sideswipe that Ash becomes suspicious. When all the adult
authorities refuse to take him seriously Ash decides to take the matter into his own hands.
An improbable ending does not all together spoil what is otherwise an entertaining read.
Claire Renner

Hating Alison Ashley (PG)
By Sandra Hall
March 19, 2005, Sydney Morning Herald
It's a girls' world in this comic and colourful adaptation of a-much-loved children's novel,
writes Sandra Hall.
Directed by Geoff Bennett
Screenplay by Christine Madafferi form the novel by Robin Klein
Rated PG
Cinemas Everywhere
It should come as no surprise that Delta Goodrem doesn't convince as a 14-year-old
schoolgirl. Hiding under a Mona Lisa smile and a Goldilocks wig, she looks like a 20-year-
old pop star on the run from the paparazzi.
Not that it matters: The film of Hating Alison Ashley, Robin Klein's much-read children's novel
has little to do with the real world. It's set in Ockerdom, a place where we patriotic filmgoers
have spent a lot of time lately, thanks to the run of comedies which have been trying, with
raucous relentlessness, to make themselves loveable in the happy-go-lucky manner of The
Castle.
Hating Alison Ashley is not really Alison's story. As Klein's many fans know, its narrator is
_ Alison's classmate, Erica Yurken (Saskia Burmeister), a talented self-dramatist, who fancies
she's been stranded in the wrong life. Her refined sensibilities, she thinks, are more suited
to some ivy-covered temple of learning than scungy, working-class Barringa East, where
she's been dumped among the delinquents of 9C. Whenever she can, she escapes to the
sick bay, where her impressive list of imaginary ailments has gained her a reputation as a
creative hypochondriac.
And life at home is no better. Although her sweet-natured mum (Tracy Mann) does her best,
Erica can't forgive her for taking up with Lennie (Richard Carter), a truck driver she met at
Parents Without Partners, or for giving her such unbearable siblings. Her chief torturer is her
elder sister, boy-mad Valjoy (Rachael Carpani), whose boots and big hair are almost as
scary as her interest in martial arts.
School improves for Erica with the arrival of Miss Belmont (Jean Kittson), whose fishnet
stockings and gallows humour give her the air of a semi-respectable dominatrix. Miss
Belmont does the previously unthinkable and keeps 9C in order. She also gives Erica high
marks and makes her feel special - until the arrival of Goodrem's Alison Ashley.
Alison is perfection incarnate. For a minute or two, Erica fancies she has found a kindred
spirit. But Alison proves to be strangely aloof. And, even worse, the quality of her classwork
eclipses Erica's.

sections.passage:
1914 - 2014
As of 2014, it is 100 years since the first real global conflict - World War 1. It began
in 1914 and was concluded in 1918. Millions died on the battlefields of Europe as Germany
and its allies fought a four year trench warfare against the Allies led by Great Britain. Many
countries were aligned with Great Britain, particularly the Commonwealth countries,
including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and South Africa. This was a great patriotic
war and these countries were involved in the conflict early in 1914.
At the time of the outbreak of hostilities the British Government requested Australia's
assistance in men and materials. Just north of Australia lay Papua New Guinea. This area
was then German New Guinea. In this area there were a number of radio communication
stations. Their existence meant that German New Guinea would be in contact with the
powerful German fleet. The British Government wanted to isolate the area, so that no
information could pass from it to the German Fleet.
On 9 August a request was made for Australia to take on this task. The orders were
simple - a small contingent would need to be sent to destroy the radio communication
- centres in German New Guinea, and another group would bolster the small force of troops
on Thursday Island, just south of the German territory.
The first group, the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force, was made up
of 1,500 volunteers. The objective in destroying the radio communication towers was
completed in September of 1914. This was the first action of Australian troops in the Pacific
region, and it effectively isolated the German colony from contact with Berlin or the German
fleet. The group that was sent to Thursday Island spent much of their time managing the fort
and patrolling the island. Within a few months there was not even the remote possibility of
Australia being invaded from the north, and the troops were withdrawn.
- Australia had played a small but significant role in protecting our shores.

An extract from William Taylor’s book “Circles”
My mother died of sick madness. She died of this sick madness and of grief and fear. She
died in a strange and alien place, so far from what she thought of as home, a home she
would never, ever see again.
If a story may be said to have a beginning, this is the beginning of mine. In truth, I know,
the story of no one really does have a beginning. There must always be something that has
just gone on before and there were, naturally, a lot of somethings that happened before my
mother’s death that indeed led to that cursed and dreadful moment. It is true, though, that
the dying of the poor sad woman J loved so dearly really did provide the marker, the turning
point to my subsequent existence.
It was fifty years ago to the day, the day on which I choose to begin to write these words,
fifty years ago that my father, my brother and I dug her grave, dressed Mother in her own
gown, wrapped her remains, poor thin little soul she had become, in the linen that had once
been her mother’s, and laid her to rest among those trees. At rest in those trees, beneath the
trees she had so greatly feared. She rests there today, a scant half mile from where I sit
writing these words, words that I write surrounded by a comfort and splendor that she never
experienced and of which, likely, simple soul, she never dreamed.
Today I pushed my way through the undergrowth, doing my best to follow the ill-formed
track to the spot beneath the giant rimu tree where a slab of marble says: ‘Elizabeth
Costello 1840-1876 and John Costello 1839-1876’. My father, foolish man, lost spirit,
survived his wife by no more than a handful of hours. Robert and I dug his grave and then
we left this place with, in reality, little hope of ever seeing it again.

The Black Rat
He lived in a tin hut with a hard dirt floor,
He had bags sewn together that was his door.
He was a Rat of Tobruk until forty-five,
He was one of the few that came back alive.
Battered and scared he fought for this land,
And on his return they all shook his hand.
The price of fighting for the freedom of man,
Did not make any difference to this Blackman.
He returned to the outback, no mates did he find,
If he had a beer he was jailed and then fined.
He sold all his medals he once proudly wore:
They were of no use to him any more.
Confused and alone he wandered around,
Looking for work though none could be found.
The Anzac marches he badly neglected,
Would show to his comrades how he was rejected.
He fought for this land so he could be free,
Yet he could not vote after his desert melée.
And those years in that desert they really took their toll,
“He went there quite young and came home so old.
This once tall man came from a proud Black tribe,
Died all alone — no one at his side.
Iris Clayton

The Sanctuary
Colin Thiele, 1992
When Storm Boy went walking along the beach, or over the sandhills, or in the sanctuary,
the birds were not afraid. They knew he was a friend. The pelicans sat in a row, like a lot of
important old men with their heavy paunches sagging, and rattled their beaks drily in
greeting; the moor-hens fussed and chattered; the ibises cut the air into strips as they
jerked their curved beaks up and down; and the blue crane stood in silent dignity like a tall
thin statue as Storm Boy went past.
But one morning Storm Boy found everything in uproar and confusion. Three or four men
had gone into the sanctuary. They had found some pelican nests- wide, rough nests of
sticks, grass, and pelican feathers as big as turkey quills — and they had killed two of the
big birds nesting there. After that they had scattered everything wildly with their boots,
kicking and shouting and picking up the white eggs and throwing them about until they
were all broken. Then they had gone off laughing.
Storm Boy crept forward in fear and anger. From behind a tussock he looked round sadly
at the ruin and destruction. Then, just as he was about to run back to tell Fingerbone to fill
his blunderbuss with salt, he heard a faint rustling and crying, and there under the broken
nests were three tiny pelicans — still alive. Storm Boy picked them up and carefully hurried
back with them.

H.M.S. BELLEROPHON
On June 1% 1815 an attempt was made by the French to break the blockade of Europe
imposed by the British navy. France under Napoleon had already conquered most of
Europe but was short of food. A convoy of American grain ships escorted by fleet of French
warships attempted to penetrate the blockade and unload at the French port of Brest. The
convoy was intercepted however by the British fleet commanded by Admiral Howe. A great
engagement ensued and for many hours the battles raged. Although some of the grain
ships managed to limp into harbour, eventually the British emerged as victors inflicting
heavy losses on the French.
One of the British warships participating in the battle was Bellerophon. With 74 guns,
Bellerophon, the flagship of the Fleet, was possibly the finest warship afloat at the time.
The ship was in the thick of the battle for some hours, taking a bad battering, and her
causalities included the captain, Rear Admiral Parsley, who lost a leg to a cannon shot. On
board Bellerophon at the time was a young officer, scarcely more than a boy, acting as
Aide-de-camp to the Admiral. His name was Mathew Flinders.
In between bouts of destruction caused by French broadsides and the noise and chaos
of the Bellerophon’s own guns being fired as the battle raged back and forth, Flinders was
able to find time to jot down notes on the course of the battle for the Admiral. This was one
of his official duties. The description in his journal, copied up at the end of the battle, runs
to 40 pages and is regarded by naval historians as the best account of this most famous
battle. From it they are able to judge exactly the course of the engagement.
Flinders survived the ‘Battle of the Glorious First’ and, at a later date of course, became
quite famous in a different way as a navigator and explorer although still serving as an
officer in the Royal Navy. The Bellerophon too lived on to carry out at least one more
famous voyage when she carried Napoleon from France to Portsmouth before he was
transported as a prisoner to the Island of St Helena in the Atlantic Ocean.

The ultimate test for life’s priorities
David Suzuki
(David Suzuki is a Canadian-based environmentalist, scientist, author and broadcaster. This
is an edited version of a speech he gave at the Seymour Centre in Sydney.
In November 1992, more than half of all living Nobel Prize winners signed a document called
‘World Scientists’ Warning to Humanity’ that began with this stark statement: ‘Human beings
and the natural world are on a collision course. Human activities inflict harsh and often
irreversible damage on the environment. If not checked, many of our practices put at serious
risk the future we wish for human society.’ Scientists are extremely cautious when making
pronouncements to the general public, so this was a most unusual alarm call. In biological
terms, the globe is experiencing an eco-holocaust, as more than 50,000 species vanish
annually and air, water and soil are poisoned with civilisation’s effluents.
The great challenge of the millennium is recognising the reality of impending ecological
collapse, and the urgent need to get on with taking the steps to avoid it. But our obsession
with economics has become an impediment to taking appropriate action. | have often been
told: ‘Listen Suzuki, we have to pay for all those parks and environmental clean-ups. We
can't afford to protect the environment if we don’t have a strong, growing economy.’ That
sentiment flows from a belief that the economy provides us with all of our products, from
food to oil to manufactured goods. This is nonsense. Everything we depend on, whether it
is Cars, popcorn or computers, comes from the earth and will eventually end up going back
to it. It is the biosphere, that thin layer of air, water and soil within which life exists, that
creates the earth’s productivity and abundance that, in turn, make economies and our lives
possible.
| suggest the following exercise can help to get our priorities in order. Imagine that you have
lived a full and rich life and are now on your death-bed. As you reflect on life, what memories
fill you with happiness, pride and satisfaction? | suspect it will not be the latest designer
clothing, a huge house, a sport utility vehicle or a high tech entertainment centre. What
makes life worthwhile and joyful is not ‘stuff that can be bought with money. The most
important things are family, friends, community and the sharing that enhances the quality of
all of our lives. There are several reasons we are failing to see the urgency of what is
happening, including:
e Most people alive today were born after 1950 and thus have lived all their lives during
a period of spectacular unprecedented and unsustainable growth and change. But
for most of us, this is all we’ve ever known and it seems normal. Rapid change also
brings rapid collective forgetfulness, and memories of what the world once was
quickly fade.
e Most people now live in the human-created environment of big cities where it’s easy
to believe the illusion that we have escaped our biological dependence on the natural
world.
ve page 8
e The explosive increase in information shatters the world into fragments devoid of the
history or context that might explain their relevance, importance or significance. In
order to attract attention, stories or reports become shorter and increasingly shrill,
sensational or violent.
e The great public faith that ‘they’ — scientists and technologists — will resolve our
problems is simply unwarranted. While technology can be impressive, our
knowledge of the complexity of the real world is so limited. For example, we have no
idea how to replace thousands of species now extinct or repair the ozone layer.
What are our real basic needs in order to live rich and fulfilling lives? | believe you can not
separate environmental and social needs. Hungry people will not care if their actions
endanger an edible species or an important habitat. Unemployment, injustice or insecurity
lead to desperation and the need to survive at all costs. To protect an environment for future
generations, we have to build a society on a foundation of clean air, water, soil and energy
to fulfil our needs; we have to ensure full employment, justice and security for all
communities to serve our social needs; and we have to retain sacred places, a sense of
belonging and connectedness with nature and a knowledge that there are cosmic forces
beyond our comprehension or control, to satisfy our spiritual requirements. Then, we can
work on the best kind of economy to construct from there. Right now, we seem to be trying
to squeeze everything into the constraints dictated by the economy without establishing the
fundamental bottom line.

Brumby’s Run
It lies beyond the Western Pines
Towards the sinking sun,
And not a survey mark defines
The bounds of “Brumby’s Run’.
On odds and ends of mountain land,
On tracks of range and rock
Where no one else can make a stand,
Old Brumby rears his stock.
Awild, unhandled lot they are
Of every shape and breed.
They venture out ’neath moon and star
Along the flats to feed;
But when the dawn makes pink-the sky
And steals along the plain,
The Brumby horses turn and fly
Towards the hills again.
The traveller by the mountain-track
May hear their hoof-beats pass,
And catch a glimpse of brown.and black
Dim shadows on the grass.
The eager stockhorse pricks his ears
And lifts his head on high
In wild excitement when he hears
The Brumby mob go by.
Old Brumby asks no price or fee
O’er all his wide domains:
The man who yards his stock is free
To keep them for his pains.
So, off to scour the mountain-side
With eager eyes aglow,
To strongholds where the wild mobs hide
The gully-rakers go.
Arush of horses through the trees,
A red shirt making play;
A sound of stockwhips on the breeze,
They vanish far away!
Ah, me! before our day is done
We long with bitter pain
To ride once more on Brumby’s Run
And yard his mob again.

sections.passage:
READY TO RUMBLE!
by Dr Karl Kruszelnicki in Good Weekend, The Sydney Morning Herald Magazine, June
12, 2004.
Domestic cats have lived with people for many thousands of years. It’s a simple and
happy relationship — we take care of them, and they catch rodents for us. They let us
know that we have kept our side of the bargain by purring — a sure sign of contentment.
Or is it?
The sound of a cat’s purr is very distinctive. It starts when they're about a week old. They
can do it while either breathing in or breathing out, and with their mouths closed. If you
try, you can make a kind of rumble while you breathe out, but the rumble generated while
breathing in sounds rather strangled. Oddly, cats that purr (domestic cats, mountain lions,
pumas, etc.) can’t roar all that well, and cats that have a terrifying roar (tigers, lions, etc.)
aren't too good at purring.
The mechanics of a cat’s purr are still a bit of a mystery. A cute version of a human’s
snore, perhaps? We now know that the cat’s throat emits short bursts of sound between
25 and 200 times each second. There’s a very short interruption to this regular pattern
as the cat changes from breathing in to breathing out, and vice versa. Over the years
there have been many theories, but the most popular one is that the pipe through which
the air passes to and from the cat’s lungs changes its diameter abruptly 25 to 200 times
each second. No one is quite sure where the change in diameter happens, or what drives
it, although it has been found that electrical signals change 25 to 200 times each seconds
in some of the muscles in the cat’s air pipe.
So when do cats purr? Indeed, they do purr when they are contented, but they may also
purr when they are in pain, or giving birth, or being threatened.
A cat's purr is a bit like a human smile. Sure, we smile when we are happy, but we might
also smile nervously when we feel threatened, or if somebody is being catty towards us.

There are novel ways of getting teenage boys reading and girls
into IT, writes Blanche Clark
THE accepted wisdom is that boys and girls learn differently, but that doesn’t mean
educators are accepting gender differences as a fait accompli.
Moves are afoot to make reading as speccy as footy and computer games for adolescent
boys and IT as fabulous as fashion and social networking for girls.
Concern that boys are lagging behind girls in reading tests has led to numerous primary
and secondary programs.
But the State Library of Victoria’s Boys, Blokes, Books and Bytes program concentrates
on years 5-8, a period when many boys give up reading for pleasure.
Developed by the library’s Centre of Youth Literature, it promotes boys, their families,
schools and libraries talking about books.
The library’s reader development and onsite learning manager, Paula Kelly, says a toolkit
has been sent to every co-ed and boys’ school in Victoria. The program includes a website
with advice on great reads for boys and a blog for boys to discuss books.
“It's not so much that boys can’t read, as they choose not to read. They don't see it as
cool and acceptable,” Kelly says.
“There’s also a distinct lack of male role models actually reading. When they see their
dads reading or other men reading it is usually for purposes of work. They equate the idea
of reading as work; it’s not fun.”
Schools are encouraged to run boys’ book clubs, invite fathers and other male role
models to the school and form partnerships with local libraries.
Kelly says boys need a choice about what they read, and novels, non-fiction, graphic
novels, books that have an audio component, and comics should all be offered.
“Sure reading a novel raises your chances of school achievement, but ultimately reading
is good for you; it’s about your wellbeing.”
She says the library is often asked if it will offer a similar program for girls.
“Girls come to reading much more easily. No one looks at a girl and goes, ‘You're a bit of
nerd because you’re a reader’. There is no issue with girls, but there is with boys.”
At the launch of the program on Thursday, University of Melbourne vice chancellor Prof
Glyn Davis said the program was a positive way to encourage children to read without
getting bogged down in political debates about methods of teaching literacy.
“There are important things about cultural literacy and basic reading skills in this program,
but the end result is designed to get boys reading and to enjoy reading,” he said.
Davis said it was hard to explain why it had become difficult to encourage boys to read.
“But a key part of the explanation lies in the electronic world and all the current
alternatives to books,” he said.
Herald-Sun October 14“ 2008

ICE SPIKES
Dr Alice Caseleyr 2005.
What are ice spikes?
Ice spikes are unusual structures that occasionally grow out of the ice cube trays in your
freezer. They look like the limestone stalagmites that are sometimes found in caves.
How do ice spikes form?
Ice spikes grow as the water in an ice cube tray turns to ice. Beginning on the top of each
cube, the water freezes inwards until only a small hole is left unfrozen in the centre. At
the same time as the surface solidifies, ice also starts to form under it, at the sides and
on the bottom of the cube. Since water expands as it freezes, the ice forming below the
hardened surface starts to push some water up through the hole. This water begins to
form the ice spike’s tubular shape. As water continues to be pushed out, it travels up the
tube, freezing around the rim and adding to its length. The spike will continue growing
until all the water in the cube becomes frozen of until the mouth of the tube ices over. Ice
spikes have been known to grow to a length of 56mm.
What helps ice spikes grow?
Experiments show that spikes are more likely to form when distilled water is used in the
trays and the temperature is just below freezing point (0° Celsius). If the temperature is
too low, the ice cube will freeze solid before the tube can begin to grow. Ice spikes will
also form more often if a fan is installed in the freezer to circulate the air. This is because
the moving air cools the top of the ice cube more rapidly. At the optimum temperature,
and with air blowing over the ice tray, approximately half of the cubes should develop ice
spikes.

A Good Woman (2005)
Reviewed by Neil Smith PG
Updated 08 May 2005 Contains mild language and sex references
Recent film versions of The Importance Of Being Earnest and An Ideal Husband have
faithfully retained Oscar Wilde's view of snobbish 19th-century society. Kudos, then, to A
Good Woman helmer Mike Barker for moving Wilde's play Lady Windermere's Fan to 1930s
Italy, where the author's pithy aphorisms compete for our attention with gorgeous
Mediterranean scenery. The dialogue proves a mouthful for society gals Helen Hunt and
Scarlett Johansson, so Tom Wilkinson shines brightest as an ageing toff with a heart of gold.
Hunt plays Mrs Erlynne, a penniless New York socialite who travels to Europe to squeeze
cash out of young newlyweds Robert and Meg Windermere (Mark Umbers and Scarlett
Johansson) and find herself a new man. The notorious seductress is soon enjoying secret
liaisons with Robert while Meg, convinced that her new husband is having an affair, falls into
the arms of the caddish Lord Darlington (Bright Young Things’ Stephen Campbell Moore).
"SKILLFULLY BANISHES THEATRICALITY™
Wilde's 1892 play was his first stage success and set the template for his other studies of
class and human nature. But while Barker keeps faith with the author's classy wit and
waspish repartee, he skillfully banishes theatricality by taking the action out of the salon and
into the bustling beauty of the Amalfi coast. The result may be reminiscent of The Talented
Mr Ripley and A Room With A View, but it's still a classy diversion that, like Bright Young
Things before it, evokes a bygone age of deliciously divine decadence.

sections.passage:
Extract A: New Caledonia — A French Paradise in the South Pacific
New Caledonia is a French territory in the South Pacific. It is a magnificent group of islands
about four hours by air from Australia. Spectacular coral reefs, glistening blue-green
lagoons and palm-fringed areas make for an idyllic tourist destination. While the main
airport is located at the northern end of the island, the capital city, Nouméa, is positioned
some ninety minutes away at the southern extremity. The largest island is known as Grand
Terre. There are many spectacular islands and cays with pristine beaches of shimmering
white sand.
_The islands have a fascinating mix of two cultures; the French, who colonised the territory
in 1853, and the Kanaks, the indigenous Melanesian inhabitants. There are more than 300
tribes in New Caledonia and these are organised into large groups of families ruled over by
a chief.
For the tourists, there are fascinating and exciting areas to visit and enjoy. The Isle of
Pines, a half-hour flight from Nouméa, the capital city, has a number of beautifully
appointed bungalows on the beach with a resort-style hotel and facilities. The exquisite
palms form a backdrop to the dazzling azure-blue of the lagoons in the immediate area.
Sites such as the convict ruins of Nouville remind the visitor of the days when French
political prisoners were transported to New Caledonia. The Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural
Centre was set up in the 1990s to showcase the history and culture of the Kanak people.
There has been a move towards gradual independence since 1998. The impact of French
colonialism has irrevocably shaped the region. The fusion of the two French and Kanak
cultures makes for a fascinating mix and ensures that New Caledonia is an engaging
tourist destination.
Extract B: Fiji — The Heart of the South Pacific
Fiji is a tropical paradise located in the South Pacific, known for its stunning beaches,
crystal-clear waters, and vibrant marine life. Comprising over 330 islands, Fiji is a cultural
and natural wonderland. The two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, are home to
most of the population, with the capital city, Suva, located on Viti Levu. Fiji is a favourite
destination for honeymooners, adventure seekers, and families alike.
The islands boast some of the world’s most pristine coral reefs, making snorkelling and
scuba diving popular activities. Visitors are drawn to places like the Yasawa and
Mamanuca island chains, known for their white sandy beaches and turquoise lagoons.
Cultural sites, such as traditional Fijian villages, offer a glimpse into the rich heritage of the
indigenous iTaukei people, who have lived on the islands for over 3,000 years. Firewalking
ceremonies, kava rituals, and Meke performances are essential parts of the Fijian
experience.
Fiji became a British colony in 1874 and gained independence in 1970. The influence of
British colonialism remains evident, especially in the architecture and legal system.
However, Fiji’s culture is firmly rooted in its indigenous traditions, creating a unique blend
of old and new. Fiji's warmth extends beyond its tropical climate, with the Fijian people
renowned for their friendliness and hospitality, making every visitor feel at home.
