Rove Interviews Daniel Johns
These are excerpts from a television interview between Rove McManus and Daniel Johns,
the lead singer from Australian band, Silverchair. This is not the start of the interview. Prior
to this, Rove has greeted Daniel and asked him about his recent ill-health.
ROVE: Are things any easier for you now down the track, now that you know you've
progressed so far? Is it a bit easier for you to get out there and do the promotion for an
album?
DANIEL: Yeah, | think so. It’s a lot more comfortable | guess. We just wanted, on this album,
especially to do what we could to expose it. It’s the kind of album that if you don’t put it in
people’s faces, then it runs the risk of being ignored because it's not a ‘one listen’ kind of
album. You’ve really got to listen to it a few times to understand where it’s going, and even
then you might hate it. (Rove /aughs)
ROVE: But this is a really brilliant album for you guys. Sometimes | have to be complimentary
to quests, but this time | actually do mean it. (Audience laughs) This is a brilliant album. |
guess it’s not as dark, with all due respect, as some of the other stuff that you’ve done. Does
that indicate the way your life seems to be progressing at the moment?
DANIEL: Yeah, definitely. It was a conscious decision to move and approach a wider colour
spectrum. Whereas it’s kind of restricting to know that. . . you know . . . there’s only black
and shades of grey to work with and on once you kind of overcome that reliance on
depression, then | think there’s a lot more to work with.
ROVE: So what was it? Were you just going around at the time being really... you Know . . .
moody and brooding all the time. Going ‘gruff gruff’. . . nobody understands me . . . ‘gruff
gruff gruff’? (Audience and Rove laugh)
DANIEL: Yeah pretty much.
ROVE: Did you just wake up one morning and suddenly go ‘Hey, life’s good! I’ve just
changed . . . .’ like that or was it a series of events that just got you to where you are?
DANIEL: It was a series of events, but then it was a conscious decision to...um... write
positive music in order to try and manipulate how | was feeling because | think music is
underrated in terms of how powerful it can be on people’s emotions.
ROVE: Now, Silverchair started when you guys were around 14 or 15 so that’s around seven
eight years now?
DANIEL: Yeah, we actually started when we were 12 years old.
ROVE: The band actually started then?
DANIEL: Yeah, me and Ben were in bands even when we were in primary school, but we
couldn't play instruments, so we just used to rap and press on a keyboard where you’ve got
a little demo button...
ROVE: Oh, yeah.
DANIEL: .. . that plays a little beat and we’d press demo, then we’d quickly run up and start

Reading 6
ROVE: But even now you guys are still, | guess in industry terms, still very young. Ah, when
you were starting out and you were just teenagers, is it a real ‘baptism by fire’ to be thrown
right in the deep end of the music industry? One minute you know you’re just playing in your
own garage, and then the next day it’s your first concert and you’re the supporting act!
DANIEL: Yeah, it was strange actually. We literally went from the garage and we just
constantly played in the garage for years. We didn’t even think we’d progress. We didn't

DANIEL: It was just terrible. | don’t know how we won. They must have seen something that

FAIRY TALE: A TRUE STORY
Fairies pixies....elves....and a knowledge of Peter Pan wouldn't go astray here.
And where do fairies live? Ask any child spellbound by their mythical nature and they will
answer: At the cinemas everywhere. It is rated G and is appropriate for young audiences,
while appealing to adults as well.
The story is set in Cottingley Glen. Lush, green English glades, sparkling streams and
waterfalls create a magical effect. Here, the symbolism is overtly pure, good, wholesome.
A tree fairy takes flight over the countryside. At once the audience is invited to enter the
world of Elsie and Frances, two girls who believe, with all their heart, that fairies are real.
The two girls bring hope and enchantment to others like Polly, Elsie’s mother, who is
dealing with overwhelming grief for her son. They also bring optimism to a war-weary
nation-it is 1917, a dark year in the height of the Great War. Elsie and Frances are
instrumental in breathing the wonder of life back into a lifeless world.
Their feat is not easy. By taking photographs, that appear to capture a group of fairies
living in the garden, they need to convince hardened cynics. At first no one believes the
girls, but as the photographs are passed on from one notable to the next-Kodak, Sir Arthur
Conan Doyle, Harry Houdini — the magic begins to transform the thinking of a nation.
Considering this is a film for children, it deals with fantasy and reality, spirituality,
death, loss and grief. The search for meaning is a predominant theme and it is explored
through Elsie, who treasures her fairy house that her brother made with her. It is furthered
by Frances who copes with her missing gather by earnestly believing in fairies. It is a
touching film and the success of Fairy Tale: A True Story lies in its ability to cause us to_
suspend our disbelief in fairies. This is achieved in part by juxtaposing events in the film
which seem plausible, because they occur in ways which seem quite natural, with
elements of fantasy.
For example, the film producers can make the audience believe that anything is possible.
Imagine a child’s reaction when they are involved in Houdini’s magic and are then drawn
into the marvel of Peter Pan. Ten-year-old Frances is entranced as Peter Pan flies across
the stage. Tinkerbell is then created by a stagehand manipulating a mirror, reflecting a real
image creating fantasy!
Fairy Tale: A True Story stars Florence Hoath, Elizabeth Earl, Paul McGann and
Phoebe Nicholls. Old film great Peter O'Toole makes an appearance, as well as Harvey
Keitel (yes, he was in Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction).

Seymour
Seymour had been awake since sunrise and was watching the stumbling hands of the clock
so he could legitimately get out of bed. Seven-fifteen to the exact second was when Thelma
began her day, and she’d made it clear that his being there mustn't interfere with her routine.
She’d give him the back room, which wasn’t really a proper one, just a small fibro-cement
extension tacked on to the kitchen. Summer clung like cellulose wrapping to its iron roof,
and even at this early hour he was sweating. Yesterday’s stored heat undulated from the
concrete yard outside, and he lay in clammy pyjamas and outstared the clock, At ten minutes
past seven he sprang thankfully out of bed and went into the kitchen to make Thelma a
morning cup of tea. He wasn’t being ingratiating — it was just something his mother had told
him to do before she left, and Seymour had a quiet and biddable nature.
“Thelma’s not young and she’s got that full-time job,” his mother had said. “It’s very kind of
her to help us out like this, so you mustn't give her any cause to regret it. You be a big help
round the house while you’re there, Seymour. There’s no need to tell you to watch your
manners, | can say that for you. Take her a cup of tea first thing in the mornings, she’s never
had anyone to do that for her. I’m sure she’d appreciate it.”
He didn’t mind making anyone an early morning cup of tea, but it was a nerve-wracking
business in this particular kitchen, where even inanimate objects like canisters seemed
capable of disapproval if you put them back in the wrong places. Here there was a place for
everything and everything in its rightful place. The tea, for instance, was kept in a green
plastic caddy with its own little measuring ladle, and you somehow didn’t dare use any other
spoon. He took the cup of tea along the hall and knocked on Thelma’s door.

Wealth data tells a tale of two cities
Tim Colebatch
TWO towers symbolise the gap between affluence and deprivation in Melbourne. Barely
three kilometres apart, fringing the city in opposite directions, the 2006 Census shows them
as polar opposites of socio-economic advantage and disadvantage in our state.
The desirable tower is Yarra's Edge, the award-winning "urban village” developed by Mirvac
on the old site of South Wharf, in Docklands. On a wide-ranging index of measures, the
Bureau of Statistics ranks it the most socioeconomically advantaged community in Victoria.
The tough tower is an old Housing Commission block of flats, on the corner of Melrose and
Canning Streets in North Melbourne, down from Racecourse Road. Many of its residents
are refugees, Islam is the main religion, and only 39 people have a job.
From census data collected in more than 9000 districts throughout Victoria, the Bureau has
constructed an index of socioeconomic advantage and disadvantage, ranking each district
— ranging in size from city blocks to large areas of farmland and forest — from 1 to 9055.
The index covers 21 variables, such as the proportion of households with high or low
incomes, the proportion with broadband or no internet access, how many people work as
professionals or labourers, the size of mortgages and rent payments, the number of
bedrooms, and occupants’ qualifications.
At both ends, the extremes are clustered in towers edging the city. Six of the 10 most
advantaged districts are new apartment blocks in Docklands, Southbank, Port Melbourne
and the CBD. And nine of the 10 most disadvantaged are old Housing Commission towers
in North Melbourne, Ascot Vale, Kensington and Collingwood.
One difference leaps out: at the Melrose Street flats, only 25% of people were born in
Australia, as against 65% at Yarra's Edge. And, at Yarra's Edge, the migrants come mostly
from the US, Malaysia and England; at Melrose Street, from Vietnam, China, Somalia and
Eritrea.
While tax data last week showed the taxman still makes his biggest hauls in Portsea, Toorak,
and Brighton, the Bureau's index, finds the new towers along the Yarra and the waterfront
have Melbourne's greatest concentration of well-off people.
The second best collection of Melburnians lives in Southbank just behind the National
Gallery. Southbank and Docklands each have two collectors’ districts in the top 10, which
also include Beacon Cove in Port Melbourne (sixth) and the city block bounded by La Trobe,
Queen, Lonsdale and William streets.
Of the traditional homes of wealthy Melburnians, the river end of St Georges Road, Toorak,
remains pre-eminent. The Bureau ranks it the third, closely followed by another riverside
area along Alexandra Avenue, South Yarra. The Monomeath Avenue area of Canterbury
was also in the top 10, as was the part of Kew heading to the river along Molesworth Street.
The top 10 areas by postcode were Docklands, the World Trade Centre, Canterbury, East
Melbourne, Southbank, Brighton, Toorak, Malvern, Queens Road and Portsea.
The poorest postcodes were mostly in the bush: Korong Vale and Nyah West in the north-
west, Cressy in the Western District, and Nowa Nowa and Longwarry in Gippsland.
Melbourne's most disadvantaged suburbs are Braybrook, Frankston and Broadmeadows.
The Age, March 27 2008

The Blue Mountains
Henry Lawson
Above the ashes straight and tall,
Through ferns with moisture dripping,
| climb beneath the sandstone wall,
My feet on mosses slipping.
Like ramparts round the valley's edge
The tinted cliffs are standing,

Now pouring down, now lost in spray

The blue with crimson blending;

Extract A: Gibraltar: The Strategic Sentinel of the Mediterranean
Gibraltar is situated at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, bordering Spain, and
encompasses an area of approximately five square kilometres. Despite its modest size,
Gibraltar holds immense strategic importance, commanding the western entrance to the
Mediterranean Sea. This pivotal location has rendered Gibraltar a coveted prize
throughout history, making it the focal point of numerous sieges and military campaigns.
The narrow Strait of Gibraltar serves as the gateway between the Atlantic Ocean and the
Mediterranean, making control of this area crucial for naval dominance and trade routes.
After the Moors were expelled from Spain in the late 15th century, the territory remained
under Spanish control for several centuries. The rugged terrain, dominated by the iconic
Rock of Gibraltar, provided a formidable defence against invaders, allowing the Spanish to
maintain their hold despite external pressures. However, the strategic value of Gibraltar
could not be overlooked by other European powers.
The turning point came during the War of the Spanish Succession in the early 18th
century. In 1704, an Anglo-Dutch fleet seized Gibraltar from Spain, marking the beginning
of British involvement in the region. This military manoeuvre was part of a broader conflict
over the Spanish throne, and control of Gibraltar provided the British with a critical naval
base. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 formally ceded Gibraltar to Great Britain, solidifying its
status as a British Overseas Territory. Since then, Gibraltar has remained under British
administration, despite periodic attempts by Spain to reclaim it. In 1967, the people of
Gibraltar exercised their right to self-determination by voting overwhelmingly to retain their
connection with Great Britain. This referendum was a decisive moment in Gibraltar's
history, reinforcing the population's desire to remain British amidst ongoing disputes with
Spain over sovereignty.
Extract B: The Suez Canal: An Essential Artery of Global Trade
From its inception, the Suez Canal has been a linchpin in global commerce, by connecting
the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea it serves as a vital artery for the transportation of
oil, natural gas, and a myriad of other commodities. Bypassing the lengthy route around
the south of Africa, the canal provides a direct route between Europe and Asia. Major
shipping lines traverse the canal daily, accounting for approximately 10% of all global
trade. The efficiency and reliability of the Suez Canal continues to underpin global supply
chains, making it a cornerstone of modern trade.
The canal, however, has been a focal point of geopolitical tensions since its construction. It
was initially under French and Egyptian control, but British involvement soon followed due
to its significance for trade and military strategy. During the 1956 Suez Crisis, Egypt
nationalised the canal, leading to a military intervention by Britain, France, and Israel.
Although military intervention temporarily disrupted canal operations, international
pressure, particularly from the United States and the Soviet Union, ultimately compelled
the invading forces to withdraw. Today, it is managed by the Suez Canal Authority and
generates billions of dollars annually for Egypt.
Despite its robust economic contributions, the Suez Canal faces ongoing challenges that
threaten its operational stability and long-term viability. Periodic blockages, such as the
infamous 2021 incident involving the grounding of the container ship Ever Given, highlight
the canal’s vulnerability to disruptions. Such blockages can have cascading effects on
global supply chains, leading to delays, increased shipping costs, and economic losses for
businesses worldwide.

The Day is Done
By Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
The day is done, and the darkness
Falls from the wings of night
As a feather is wafted downward
From an eagle in its flight.
| see the lights of the village
Gleam through the rain and the mist,
And a felling of sadness comes o'er me,
That my soul cannot resist.
A feeling of sadness and longing,
That is not akin to pain,
And resembles sorrow only
As the mist resembles the rain.
Come, read to me some poem,
Some simple and heart-felt lay,
That shall soothe this restless feeling,
And banish the thoughts of day.
Not from the grand old masters,
Not from the bards sublime
Whose distant footsteps echo
Through the corridors of time.
For, like strains of martial music,
Their mighty thoughts suggest
Life's endless toil and endeavour,
And to-night | long for rest.
Read from some humbler poet,
Whose songs gushed from his heart,
As showers from the clouds of summer,
Or tears from the eyelids start.

Extract A: Sea Safety - Letter to the editor
Once again another sea rescue that was completely unnecessary has taken place. Small
craft, sailing vessels and helicopters have been involved in a four-day search of our
coastline, often in appalling weather and dangerous seas because of human stupidity.
| am very pleased that the Haslan family was finally rescued from the serious danger they
were in, but the danger was of their own making. Reports indicate that the minimum safety
requirement and safety kits were not on board. Not to have the correct safety equipment,
sufficient safety floatation devices and communicating equipment and setting off past
Barr's Point into the open sea, can only be described as almost criminal negligence.
The weather forecast on the morning the family set out indicated rising seas and steadily
increasing winds, though only freshening during the afternoon to 17 - 21 knots. The area
outside Barr's Point is well known as a place where the current can run in the opposite
direction to the waves. When this happens the waves can overrun each other and this in
turn generates steep and dangerous rogue waves. In this part of the world, the weather
forecasts for fishermen and the general conditions north and south of Eastview are well
known, widely advertised and most people take the necessary precautions to ensure the
safety of the lives of their family.
What did this rescue cost in terms of official police, rescue personnel and volunteers? A
large sum of money no doubt. It is time people who, through their own ignorance, lack of
responsibility and common sense, were made to pay to our local council at least part of the
overall cost of their rescue.
Extract B: Excerpt from ‘The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean’ by R.M.
Ballantyne
| shall say little about the first part of our voyage. We had the usual amount of rough
weather and calm; also we saw many strange fish rolling in the sea, and | was greatly
delighted one day by seeing a shoal of flying fish dart out of the water and skim through
the air about a foot above the surface. They were pursued by dolphins, which feed on
them, and one flying-fish in its terror flew over the ship, struck on the rigging, and fell upon
the deck. Its wings were just fins elongated, and we found that they could never fly far at a
time, and never mounted into the air like birds, but skimmed along the surface of the sea.
Jack and | had it for dinner, and found it remarkably good.
When we approached Cape Horn, at the southern extremity of America, the weather
became very cold and stormy, and the sailors began to tell stories about the furious gales
and the dangers of that terrible cape. Each story outdid the one before in conjuring fearful
possibilities.
Nevertheless, we passed the dreaded cape without much rough weather, and, in the
course of a few weeks afterwards, were sailing gently, before a warm tropical breeze, over
the Pacific Ocean. Thus we proceeded on our voyage, sometimes bounding merrily before
a fair breeze, at other times floating calmly on the glassy wave and fishing for the curious
inhabitants of the deep - all of which, although the sailors thought little of them, were
strange, and interesting, and very wonderful to me.

The Teams
Henry Lawson
A cloud of dust on the long, white road,
And the teams go creeping on
Inch by inch with the weary load;
And by the power of the green-hide goad
The distant goal is won.
With eyes half-shut to the blinding dust,
And necks to the yokes bent low,
The bests are pulling as bullocks must:
And the shining tires might almost rust
While the spokes are turning slow.
With face half-hid by a broad-brimmed hat,
That shades from the heat's white waves,
And shouldered whip, with its green-hide plait,
The driver plots with a gait like that
Of his weary, patient slaves.
He wipes his brow, for the day is hot,
And spits to the left with spite;
He shouts at Bally, and flicks at Scot,
And raises dust from the back of Spot,
And spits to the dusty right.
He'll sometimes pause as a thing of form
In front of a settler's door
And ask for a drink, and remark "It's warm,"
Or say "There's signs of a thunderstorm";
But he seldom utters more

‘Hang Loose’ youth keep options open
By Hugh Mackay
($1) Hugh Mackay is a social commentator and journalist who writes articles for the
Weekend Australian and the Sydney Morning Herald newspapers. He is a social!
researcher, author and newspaper columnist.
If you are looking for a symbol of contemporary youth culture, look no further than the
laces left untied on Doc Martens shoes. It’s as if the kids are saying, ‘I’m prepared to wear
these things, but | wouldn’t want you to think | was totally committed to the idea.’ As usual,
the rising generation are sending us a message from our future, so we'd better listen.
($2) Australians born since the mid-70s don’t share their parents’ and grandparents’
anxiety about the rapid rate of change and its destabilising effect on our society. For them,
constant change is the air they breathe, the water they swim in. It is simply the way the
world is. They are the generation for whom the women’s movement was an established
historical fact; the generation who take equality between the sexes for granted (and who
are infuriated by older people — especially older men in senior positions — who still don’t
understand that personhood is a gender- neutral concept, and still haven’t grasped the
essential difference between yesterday's view of women and today’s). They know that
more than 50 per cent of university students are women, that 45 per cent (and rising) of
the workforce are female and that girls can do anything they choose. They know that most
mothers have paid work outside the home because that’s how it is for their own mothers.
They don’t expect Mum to be there making peanut butter sandwiches when they get home
from school, and they vaguely wonder why she even bothers mentioning the fact that that’s
what her mother used to do.
(S3) On the other hand, roughly 750,000 members of this generation live in a household
where no one is currently earning any wages, so the reality of unemployment is pretty
stark. Even if their parents have work, at least 30 per cent of young Australians are facing
the bleak prospect of a labour market that doesn’t want them . . . at least not yet. (If you
had applied unsuccessfully for 200 jobs, as a respondent in one of my recent research
projects had, what would you do next?)
($4) To older Australians, the sharp rise in the divorce rate over the past 20 years seems
cataclysmic, shaking the very foundations of the institution of marriage. But to the rising
generation, nothing has changed: from the time they became aware of the nature of
marriage and divorce, they had known that lots of their friends live with one parent, so
what’s the big deal? Do you imagine that contemporary children and adolescents _
exchange information about their parents’ marital status in darkly whispered confessions
behind their hands?
Do you think that living in a one-parent family feels like a heavy burden for kids to bear?
Think again: almost one million dependent children are in precisely that situation, which
doesn’t mean that it’s always fun for them, but it does mean that it’s hardly worth
mentioning. (In any case, having one parent at home might sometimes feel like half the
burden of having two.) To the intense irritation of their parents, the members of this
generation are able to program the VCR without even reading the manual.
(S5) Having grown up in the thick of the information revolution (‘What revolution?’) they
know today’s technology is already obsolete by the time they get their hands on it, and that
smarter things are constantly coming over the horizon. They know there’s an accessible |
drug culture in every town and suburb, and that ‘street kids’ are part of the scene. (No_
wonder they've embraced the gritty realism of the new writing for young people.) |
Paradoxically, they're also our most dependent generation, staying at home for longer and
relying on social security in larger numbers than any previous group of young Australians.
Like every generation before them, they are responding to the world as they find it. (To
what other world could they possibly respond?) Not surprisingly, their experience of
impermanence and unpredictability has taught them one big, central lesson: keep your
options open. So they are inclined to hang loose; to postpone commitment to a career, a
sexual partner, a political party, a set of religious beliefs, a brand ... or even to whether
they’ll be home for dinner tonight. For many of them, that is an exciting, liberating
approach to life. Those flapping shoelaces can be a sign of confidence, freedom, flexibility
and adaptability. But not for all: the lack of a clear focus and the absence of a stable
framework can also breed insecurity, uncertainty and an aching sense of alienation. In the
wait-and-see world of the young, even the symbol of untied laces is ambiguous.

Seven Impossible Interviews Before Breakfast #31: Recent Printz Honor
Recipient Sonya Hartnett (an Exclusive Summer Blog Blast Tour Interview)
P1 7-Imp: We find your writing so lyrical and evocative and graceful and exquisite and
precise and introspective and damn near teetering on poetry (whew — oh, and also
haunting, though we think that word gets overused in book reviewing). Have you ever
written poetry? How did you become such a master of (beautiful) metaphors? We suspect
writers like that were quiet, observant children and remain quiet, observant people (quiet,
as in listens well and takes in a lot). Are we right?
P2 Sonya: | guess | was a quiet, observant child — | was extremely shy, and | think that is
often an underlying reason for being both quiet and observant. | don’t think I’m that way
any more. | am still intrinsically shy, but for most of my life | have had to get up on stage,
face audiences, answer questions, put on the show required of an author by the media
and the publisher and the readers. So I’m actually pretty difficult to shut up, these days.
Although the shy person inside me always listens in to my inane prattle, and hates me.
P3 | don't write poetry — | don't particularly even like poetry (poems about dogs excepted,
for some reason). When | write, | listen for the tune of the words — | can hear the ‘music’ of
the book very clearly. | try to match the rhythm of the words to the tune | hear. | can always
tell if a sentence is wrong, because it jars the flow of the music. And | guess this is what
poets do — construct their words to match a particular beat.
P4 I’m not sure why I’m so drawn to metaphors — | am often criticised for using them too
often. They are a defining characteristic of my style, although | sometimes try to keep them
to a minimum (and fail). | have always noticed the interconnectedness of the world — how
things relate to and echo and influence each other, in appearance and behaviour and
nature — and this might be the reason | so frequently draw similarities between various
things. | also think it helps fix, quite precisely, the image or emotion | want a reader to
absorb.
P5 Jules: What the Birds See is devastatingly, obscenely good writing, probably one of
my top-five favourite books ever. | find it striking how you — as Robert Cormier did — nail
the sometimes cruel world of children, the part of their world that gets glossed over when
we sentimentalise childhood (in What the Birds See you wrote, “Adrian has never thought
that what happened to him had been cruel — children inhabit an animalistic world and
accept with grace its harsh rules’). You also really capture the emotional fragility and fears
of childhood (in a way that makes me think of Maurice Sendak’s take on the themes of his
books). How do you do that? Do you remember childhood vividly?
P6 Sonya: | don’t remember childhood vividly — indeed, | have very few clear
recollections of things said and done and seen in my life until the age of about twenty. But |
do remember the feelings of childhood: | remember how it felt to flounder so helplessly in a
world that was impossible to understand or control; | remember the terror that small
disasters, like lost library books, inspired in me; | remember the shattering loneliness of
losing a best friend. | remember, too, the great simple pleasures of being a kid: riding a
bike on a newly-made road, eating ice cream and chocolate topping, watching the morning
cartoons in a silent house, my feet up on the heater.
P7 | find it interesting that people really love Adrian, and feel so deeply for him. To many
readers, he’s more alive and real than any other character I’ve created. | have had women
get amazingly angry with me for ill-treating him. | think people relate to him because we all
remember and recognise those hard, bright emotions from childhood —- they burn into us,
we never forget their ache, or their giddy joy. When readers encounter Adrian, they see
something of the child they were. He makes them worry for their own children. He makes
everyone Cry.
P8 7-Imp: /n this country, people tend fo place you, as an author, into the Young Adult
fiction category (though your titles are also seen as cross-over ones — stepping over into
adult fiction, that is). How do you feel about that label? Do you think it’s accurate? Do you
get tired of all the labelling and trying to figure out into which category a country is going to

Pictures from the Deserted Village
O. Goldsmith
Near yonder copse, where once the garden smiled,
And still where many a garden flower grows wild;
There, where a few torn shrubs the place disclose,
The village preacher's modest mansion rose.
Aman he was to all the country dear,
And passing rich with forty pounds a year;
Remote from towns he ran his godly race,
Nor e'er had changed, nor wished to change his place;
Unpractised he to fawn, or seek for power,
By doctrines fashioned to the varying hour;
Far other aims his heart had learned to prize,
More skilled to raise the wretched than to rise.
His house was known to all the vagrant train,
He chid their wanderings, but relieved their pain:
The long-remembered beggar was his guest,
Whose beard descending swept his aged breast;
The ruined spendthrift, now no longer proud,
Claimed kindred there, and had his claims allowed;
The broken soldier, kindly bade to stay,
Sat by his fire, and talked the night away;
Wept o'er his wounds, or tales of sorrow done,
Shouldered his crutch, and showed how fields were won.
Pleased with his guests, the good man learned to glow,
And quite forgot their vices in their woe;
Careless their merits or their faults to scan,
His pity gave ere charity began.
- Reading Skills

In the hall her heart sank. The front door was open — Lucy had gone outside. It was a cold
night, and Mina knew that her friend was wearing just a thin nightdress. Hurriedly throwing
a shawl around her own shoulders, she went to look for her.
The church clock was striking one as Mina ran through the streets of Whitby. She kept a
sharp lookout, but there was no sign of the white figure she had expected to see. She ran
along the Crescent, then she explored along the North Terrace — nothing. Searching farther
and farther away from the house, she made her way up to the West Cliff.
At the edge of the West Cliff she looked across the bay to the East Cliff. There was a
bright full moon but also lots of swift-moving clouds, so a dappled light was moving across
the sea and the town. For some time she couldn't distinguish very much at all. Then the
moon emerged fully, casting a narrow strip of cold blue light over the East Cliff.
Mina could see the tombstones of the old graveyard, leaning over at crazy angles,
making dark silhouettes against the wild night sky. The strip of light moved steadily along
the tombstones and memorials. And there on their seat, was the half-reclining, snowy-white
figure of Lucy.
Almost as soon as she spotted her friend, the moon went in. But it seemed to Mina that
something dark had been standing behind Lucy, or leaning over her. Whether it was man or
beast Mina wasn’t sure.
She started running down the slope of the West Cliff as fast as she could. It seemed to
take forever. Eventually she was leaping up the endless steps of the East Cliff, her legs
shaky with tiredness. As she neared the graveyard on the cliff top she gasped. She had
been right. A dark shape was leaning over her friend.
“Lucy! Lucy!” she called in fright.
At the sound of her voice, the dark figure raised its head. Mina saw a pale face and red,
gleaming eyes. For a moment they flashed at her. Then, as Mina got closer, the dark figure
seemed to melt into the surrounding blackness.
= Reading Skills 1
“Lucy!” Mina cried, throwing herself next to her friend on the bench.
Lucy was still asleep. Her lips were parted, and she was breathing in long, heavy gasps.
She put her hand to her throat and moaned. Mina wrapped her shawl around her friend’s
shoulders. Lucy seemed unusually cold and gave a shudder. Using a safety pin, Mina
fastened the shawl at Lucy’s throat. But she must have been clumsy, because Lucy’s hand
went to her throat again, and Mina noticed that there were two little red marks on her neck.
Mina thought that she must have pricked her accidentally.
Excerpt from ‘Dracula’ (Usborne Classics Retold) By Bram Stoker

Good Timber
by Douglas Malloch
The tree that never had to fight
For sun and sky and air and light,
But stood out in the open plain
And always got its share of rain,
Never became a forest king
But lived and died a scrubby thing.
The man who never had to toil
To gain and farm his patch of soil,
Who never had to win his share
Of sun and sky and light and air,
Never became a manly man
But lived and died as he began.
Good timber does not grow with ease,
The stronger wind, the stronger trees,
The further sky, the greater length,
The more the storm, the more the strength.
By sun and cold, by rain and snow,
In trees and men good timbers grow.
Where thickest lies the forest growth
We find the patriarchs of both.
And they hold counsel with the stars
Whose broken branches show the scars
Of many winds and much of strife.
This is the common law of life.

Extract A: Excerpt from ‘To Kill a Mockingbird’ By Harper Lee
Our father didn’t do anything. He worked in an office, not in a drugstore. Atticus did not
drive a dump-truck for the country, he was not the sheriff, he did not farm, work in a
garage, or do anything that could possibly arouse the admiration of anyone.
Besides that, he wore glasses. He was nearly blind in his left eye, and said left eyes were
the tribal curse of the Finches. Whenever he wanted to see something well, he turned his
head and looked from his right eye. He did not do the things our schoolmates’ fathers did:
he never went hunting, he did not play poker or fish or drink or smoke. He sat in the living
room and read.
With these attributes, however, he would not remain as inconspicuous as we wished him
to: that year, the school buzzed with talk about him defending Tom Robinson, none of
which was complimentary. After my bout with Cecil Jacobs when | committed myself to a
policy of cowardice, word got around that Scout Finch wouldn’t fight any more, her daddy
wouldn't let her. This was not entirely correct: | wouldn't fight publicly for Atticus, but the
family was private ground. | would fight anyone from a third cousin upwards tooth and nail.
Francis Hancock, for example, knew that.
When he gave us our air-rifles Atticus wouldn’t teach us to shoot. Uncle Jack instructed us
in the rudiments thereof; he said Atticus wasn’t interested in guns. Atticus said to Jem one
day, “I'd rather you shot at tin cans in the back yard, but | know you'll go after birds. Shoot
all the bluejays you want, if you can hit ‘em, but remember it’s a sin to kill a mockingbird.”
That was the only time | ever heard Atticus say it was a sin to do something, and | asked
Miss Maudie about it. “Your father’s right,” she said. “Mockingbirds don’t do one thing but
make music for us to enjoy. They don’t eat up people’s gardens, don’t nest in corncribs,
they don’t do one thing but sing their hearts out for us. That’s why it’s a sin to kill to
mockingbird.”
Extract B: Excerpt from ‘Lorna Doone: A Romance of Exmoor’ by R.D. Blackmore
My dear father had been killed by the Doones of Bagworthy, while riding home from
Porlock market, on the Saturday evening. With him were six brother-farmers, all of them
very sober; for father would have no company with any man who went beyond half a
gallon of beer, or a single gallon of cider. The robbers had no grudge against him; for he
had never flouted them, neither made overmuch of outcry, because they robbed other
people. For he was a man of such strict honesty, and due parish feeling, that he knew it to
be every man's own business to defend himself and his goods; unless he belonged to our
parish, and then we must look after him.
These seven good farmers were jogging along, helping one another in the troubles of the
road, and singing goodly hymns and songs to keep their courage moving, when suddenly
a horseman stopped in the starlight full across them.
By dress and arms they knew him well, and by his size and stature, shown against the
glimmer of the evening star; and though he seemed one man to seven, it was in truth one |
man to one. Out of the six who had been singing songs and psalms about the power of
God, and their own regeneration - such psalms as went the round, in those days, of the
public-houses - there was not one who did not pull out his money, for the Doones.
But father had been used to think that any man who was comfortable inside his own coat
and waistcoat deserved to have no other set, unless he would strike a blow for them.
And so, while his gossips doffed their hats, and shook with what was left of them, he set
his staff above his head, and rode at the Doone robber. With a trick of his horse, the wild
man escaped the sudden onset, although it must have amazed him sadly that anyone
resist him.

Why Do Some People Call Football “Soccer”?
One of the best-known differences between British and American English is the fact that
the sport known as football in Great Britain is usually called soccer in the United States.

questions.stem: In fact, the word is thoroughly British in origin. So why is it that Americans
options: (not to mention Canadians, Australians, and others) are likelier to use the word than Brits
are? The answer lies in how the sport developed in each country.
Although football-type games have been around for centuries, the sport we know today is
often said to have begun in 1863, when England’s newly formed Football Association

wrote down a set of rules. 16 . Rugby football, named after an English boarding school, was a variation that allowed players to carry and run with the ball to advance it toward the goal. The game played under the Football Association’s rules thus became known as association football. Inevitably, the names would be shortened. 17 . The latter term was further shortened to “soccer” (sometimes spelled “socker”), and the name quickly spread beyond the campus. However, “soccer” never became much more than a nickname in Great Britain. 18 Meanwhile, in the United States, a sport emerged in the late 19th century that borrowed elements of both rugby and association football. 19 .As a result, American association-football players increasingly adopted soccer to refer to their sport. The United States Football Association, which had formed in the 1910s as the official organising body of American soccer, changed its name to the United States Soccer Football Association in 1945, and it later dispensed with the “Football” altogether. No longer just a nickname, soccer had stuck. Other countries where the word soccer is common include those that, like the United States, have competing forms of football. For instance, Canada has its own version of gridiron football; Ireland is home to Gaelic football; and Australia is mad about Australian rules football (which is derived from rugby). 20 The text above has 4 sentences removed from it. Choose sentences from the list below the text (A - E), to fill the gaps which correspond to the numbers in the text (15 - 20). 4 options will be given for each gap. There will be one extra sentence that is not needed. Linguistically creative students at the University of Oxford in the 1880s distinguished between the sports of “rugger” and “assoccer” While early sports literature sometimes used alternative terms, these variations rarely gained the uniform acceptance needed By the 20th century, rugby football was more commonly called rugby, while association football had earned the right to be known as just plain football Because the sport originated in England, it is often assumed that soccer is an Americanism At the time, it was the most widely played game of its kind in the country, but it wasn’t the only one Before long, it had proved more popular than either of them. In full, it was known as gridiron football, but most people never bothered with the first word In places where football can be ambiguous, soccer is usefully precise.

sections.passage:
The Tea Ceremony
Most of Julie’s friends’ parents drank coffee. Some of them liked tea, too; but not like her
parents did. Jill's family, Billy’s family, and Tanya's family each had just two or three boxes
of tea ona shelf, but Julie’s had a whole cabinet dedicated to tea. No bags in boxes either;
her parents drank loose-leaf tea only. “The real stuff,” her dad called it.
Packed tightly in rich red and gold tins, the Tang’s collection included fragrant jasmine
green tea; Longjing tea, a pan-fried green tea Julie preferred to call by its nickname,
Dragon Well tea; roasted, curly-leaved oolong tea; lightly sweet white tea; and more.
Every New Year—the Chinese New Year that is—her parents would have a traditional tea
ceremony. That's the time when she would roll her eyes and slink out of the room. Her
mom said it was an important cultural tradition, but Julie just thought it was B-O-R-I-N-G.
(Or at least she assumed it would be if she ever stuck around for it.)
However, now that she was 13 (an official teenager at last! ), Julie felt different, more
mature, and she was beginning to really enjoy history, thanks to her great social studies
teacher. Julie decided it was time this New Year to take an interest in her own family and
cultural history once she realised, she actually knew very little. (She had only been to
China once when she visited her grandparents as a five-year-old and her classes devoted
equal time to studies of all the cultures of the world.)
“Why do we have to do this tea ceremony every year?” Julie asked her mother, who was
taking the clay teapots out of the cabinet reserved for special teapots and fancy dishes.
“I’m not in the mood for complaints,” her mother warned.
“No, but | really want to know! What is the tea ceremony really all about, and why do you
always say that drinking tea is part of your DNA?”
Julie’s mother gave her a sideways glance, her mouth turning from a suspicious smirk into
a gleeful smile.
“Well, the DNA thing is a figure of speech.”
“| know that, Mom,” Julie sighed. “How old do you think | am? Ten?”
“Okay then. Legend has it that Shennong, a Chinese emperor and herbalist—someone
who grows and sells herbs and uses them to treat illness—discovered tea way back in
2737 B.C. He liked his water boiled so it would be germ-free when he drank it. One day, as
a servant prepared the emperor's water, a dead leaf dropped into the water. The emperor
drank it and actually found it to be quite tasty.
“Another story says that Shennong, whose name translates to ‘Divine Farmer’ and is
known by many as the father of agriculture and herbal medicine, would test out many
different herbs each day. Whenever he came across a poisonous one, he would use tea as
an antidote.
So Reading Skills
“Chinese people continued to drink tea and use it as medicine throughout history, and by
the early Middle Ages, drinking tea was common practice in China. It was considered one
of the seven necessities alongside firewood, rice, oil, salt, sauce, and vinegar.”
Julie’s mother walked across the room to the bookshelf and pulled out a yellow and red
book titled The Classic of Tea: Origins & Rituals, written by Lu Yu. “This book, which was
written around 760 A.D. is all about how tea is grown, how the leaves are processed, and
things like that. | advise you read this instead of wasting your time with all that TV.”
“| watch nothing but Tea TV,” Julie joked.
“Right. Well, in case they didn’t cover this on Tea TV, in the book, Yu describes the tea
trees that grew in South China. Back in those days, they would compress tea leaves into
little cakes—not like a birthday cake, just a little brick of leaves—which they would grind in
a stone mortar. They'd add hot water to this tea powder to make the beverage we know as
tea, and the Chinese call...”
“Cha,” Julie responded to her mother's lifted eyebrows. Cha was one of a few Chinese
words Julie had memorised.
“As tea became popular, so did tea shops. They continued to prosper during the Song
Dynasty, and China’s tea culture started to spread a little bit to other lands as monks and
Zen masters brought tea seeds, drink ware, and knowledge to Japan.
“However, Chinese rulers imposed a strict ban on tea exports during the Song, Yuan, and
Ming Dynasties. The ban made it difficult for tea to grow popular around the world. Then,
soon after the Qing Dynasty was established in the 17th century, the ban was officially
lifted and merchants travelled, first by land, to export tea. Many went as far as Russia,
almost 4,000 miles, by horse, oxen, mules, and yaks. Just imagine!”
“Whoa,” Julie thought about how hard it had been for her to run a mile today in gym class.
Mule or no mule, 4,000 miles by anything but plane was impossible for her to imagine.
“And what about the ceremonies?” Julie was interested in learning more but knew that if
she didn't wrap things up soon, her mom would talk straight ‘til morning.
“Well, a Chinese tea ceremony is a way for families to connect, which is why it’s a wedding
tradition. It's also about cultivating peace, quiet, enjoyment, and strength. When you're
performing a ceremony, there are six things to keep in mind: attitude, tea selection, water
selection, tea ware selection, ambiance, and technique. Let’s start with attitude.”
Julie smiled.

MULGA BILL’S BICYCLE by A.B. “Banjo” Paterson
‘Twas Mulga Bill, from Eaglehawk, that caught the cycling craze;
He turned away the good old horse that served him many days;
He dressed himself in cycling clothes, resplendent to be seen:
He hurried off to town and bought a shining new machine;
And as he wheeled it through the door, with air of lordly pride,
The grinning shop assistant said, “Excuse me, can you ride?”
“See here, young man,” said Mulga Bill, “from Walgett to the sea,
From Conroy's Gap to Castlereagh, there’s none can ride like me.
I’m good all round at everything as everybody knows,
Although I'm not the one to talk — | hate a man that blows.
But riding is my special gift, my chiefest, sole delight;
Just ask a wild duck can it swim, a wildcat can it fight.
There's nothing clothed in hair or hide, or built of flesh or steel,
There’s nothing walks or jumps, or runs, on axle, hoof, or wheel,
But what I'll sit, while hide will hold and girths and straps are tight:
I'll ride this here two-wheeled concern right straight away at sight.”
‘Twas Mulga Bill, from Eaglehawk, that sought his own abode,
That perched above Dead Man’s Creek, beside the mountain road.
He turned the cycle down the hill and mounted for the fray,
But ‘ere he’d gone a dozen yards it bolted clean away.
It left the track, and through the trees, just like a silver streak,
It whistled down the awful slope towards the Dead Man’s Creek.
It shaved a stump by half an inch, it dodged a big white-box:
The very wallaroos in fright went scrambling up the rocks,
The wombats hiding in their caves dug deeper underground,
As Mulga Bill, as white as chalk, sat tight to every bound.
It struck a stone and gave a spring that cleared a fallen tree,
It raced beside a precipice as close as close could be;
And then as Mulga Bill let out one last despairing shriek
It made a leap of twenty feet into the Dead Man’s Creek.
‘Twas Mulga Bill, from Eaglehawk, that slowly swam ashore:
He said, “I've had some narrer shaves and lively rides before:
lve rode a wild bull round a yard to win a five-pound bet,
But this was the most awful ride that I've encountered yet.
I'll give that two-wheeled outlaw best; it’s shaken all my nerve
To feel it whistle through the air and plunge and buck and swerve.
It's safe at rest in Dead Man’s Creek, we'll leave it lying still;
A horse’s back is good enough henceforth for Mulga Bill.”
The Sydney Mail, 25 July 1896

Extract A:
| wandered across the vast desert, where the burning sun left the earth both harsh and
strangely beautiful. In that quiet, endless expanse, each parched stone and withering
wildflower whispered a secret of resilience—a silent testimony to nature’s unyielding spirit.
As | ambled along the sun-cracked path, the arid wind carried with it a tapestry of dust and
distant memories, reminding me that even the most barren lands possess their own subtle,
poetic grace.
The desert, with its scorching days and chilly nights, was not merely a wasteland but a
living canvas painted with the shifting hues of time. Each ripple in the sand seemed to
echo the footsteps of those who had traversed this unforgiving terrain long before me. The
sparse vegetation, clinging stubbornly to life in crevices -and along weathered rock faces,
told stories of survival against overwhelming odds. | paused before a solitary shrub, its
gnarled branches silhouetted against a molten sky, and felt a kinship with its silent
struggle—a reflection of humanity’s own persistent quest to find meaning in desolation.
In that moment, the desert transformed before my eyes. What once appeared as a stark
and lifeless void revealed itself to be a mosaic of wonder, where every grain of sand was a
piece of an ancient puzzle and every breeze carried whispers of forgotten lore. The subtle
interplay of light and shadow danced across the dunes, as if nature herself were
composing a quiet symphony of renewal. The heat, while oppressive, also nurtured a
unique form of beauty, one that was raw and unfiltered—a beauty that demanded
reverence and care.
! found myself drawn deeper into the landscape, compelled to explore not only the physical
vastness but the inner wilderness that it stirred within me. The desert was a mirror
reflecting the delicate balance between destruction and creation. Here, in this realm of
extremes, the human spirit could learn the art of letting go—of releasing the weight of
modern expectations and embracing a simpler, more authentic connection with the land.
This pilgrimage through the desert awakened in me an acute awareness of our shared
responsibility. Just as the resilient wildflower fought against the odds to bloom in the arid
soil, so too must we nurture our own fragile ecosystems against the encroachment of
neglect and exploitation. The landscape, etched by both the scars of human activity and
the enduring pulse of nature, called out for protection—a plea for us to remember that the
beauty of our world is interwoven with its hardships.
Extract B: Excerpt from ‘To protect New Yorkers from floods and droughts, protect
wetlands‘ by Pete Lopez and Alex Wolf
For centuries, wetlands were often viewed as swamps or waste grounds, land to be
‘improved’ by draining and clearing. Although draining wetlands resulted in productive
farmland in some areas, it also came with a price — one that grows costlier over time.
Wetlands, including marshes, swamps, bogs and vernal pools, are critical to absorbing
rainwater. As we experience increasingly severe storms, our lack of wetlands is hitting
home harder every year. Where wetlands remain, they help filter pollutants, control the
flow of water into our streams and rivers, and reduce storm surge impacts.
Recognising the importance of wetlands, new statewide protections went into effect on
Jan. 1 as amendments to New York’s Freshwater Wetlands Act, first enacted 50 years ago.
Importantly, the new amendments provide for higher levels of wetland protection in flood
zones recognised by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. They also focus on
wetlands in urban areas and those vital for drinking water, wildlife and recreation.
In places where we’ve replaced wetlands with drainage canals, ditches or pavement, the
water races along at high speed, overfilling our creeks, slamming into bridges and washing
away roads. In more populated areas, it gushes along streets and traps people in homes
and cars.
During Superstorm Sandy in 2012, coastal wetlands prevented nearly $1 million dollars of
damage in the Rockland County village of Piermont alone, and $625 million in damages
across the region. Those savings multiply across the state over many years and many
storms.
Wetlands are also crucial to combatting drought and wildfires, a fact that came into the
spotlight during last summer’s unprecedented Hudson Valley wildfires. Wetlands help
recharge our water supplies for the drier months. Floods and drought are opposite sides of
the coin. Wetlands help with both issues.

Extract A - Spectrobes: Beyond the portals
POKEMANIACS can attest that the urge to “catch’em all” in some games can be
irresistible. Yet while Spectrobes has strong instant appeal, this fossil-fuelled sequel still
does not have the same long-term allure as Nintendo’s pocket monster series.
Youngsters again guide a cocky young space cadet who can command Spectrobes, the
only creatures that can save the universe from a powerful new threat that can consume
entire planets. The critters are found in fossils deep underground, requiring trainers to
excavate, awaken and evolve them before they can be useful in battle.
Newcomers will initially enjoy the process of scouring planets for precious underground
booty, then carefully chipping away layers of rock, sand, lava and ice using the touch
screen while harnessing tools such as drills and vacuums to remove the treasure without
shattering its precious contents. The procedure can be tense and exciting, but eventually
becomes a tiresome chore as repetition sets in.
There are 185 Spectrobes to collect. While they still lack the charismatic charm of
Pokemon, it is fun to discover new creatures because of their unique attacks. Work has
been invested in the battle system, which remains simple and cumbersome but now offers
some much-needed depth.
Two Spectrobes are taken into each scuffle and players can instantly switch between
them. Unfortunately, players will struggle to always get the best view of the action as they
try to quickly pummel foes using melee and projectile-based attacks.
Although the rock-paper-scissors dynamic does little to prevent trainers from using the
same warriors every time, incubators encourage the development of a diverse squad.
Mined minerals can be fed to the creatures to improve their combat skills, rewarding those
who invest significant time in scavenger hunts. The game also supports multi-player
battles and creature trading.
Extract B - Underworld: Rise of the Lycans
OH, THE vagaries of franchise filmmaking. When the going is good, the talent will happily
front up for a sequel. When the talent goes elsewhere, the only option is to persuade
whoever is left to do a prequel. Such is the sorry fate which has befallen the Underworld
series. You remember the first two flicks, right? You don’t? OK, here’s what you missed.
Kate Beckinsale in a rubber catsuit. Scott Speedman and a posse of greasy-haired dudes
with coloured contact lenses. An ancient blood feud between fashion-victim vampires and
not-so-stylish werewolves.
Whew. Classic stuff, huh? Well, it used to fill the time between visits from Wesley Snipes
and the Blade gang. However, now that Beckinsale and Speedman have better things to
do with their time, former support players Bill Nighy and Michael Sheen have been _
bumped up the billing. For their trouble, these stalwart British thesps have been saddled
with a cheap and cheerless cash-in that should bury the whole underworld thing once and
for all. In Rise of the Lycans, the narrative clock is wound back a century or five to explain
how vampires and werewolves came to hate each other so. Unremarkably, what follows
sucks and bites in equal measure. Big-boss vamp Viktor (Nighy) gets his black velvet cape
in a twist when he discovers his headstrong daughter Sonia (Rhona Mitra, prepared to
show a little more and emote a lot less than her predecessor Beckinsale) has been
canoodling with the hairy he-man hellhound Lucian (Sheen). After building up this
Transylvanian standoff with a pile of claptrap about keeping all spooky species strictly
separated, the film then devolves into a wonky Braveheart for werewolves.
Sadly, Sheen is no Mel Gibson. Now, Sheen is a fine actor. On the strength of his work as
David Frost in Frost/Nixon and Tony Blair in The Queen, you could easily argue he is one
of the best in the business at the moment. However, no amount of growling, howling or
baby oil on his biceps can establish Sheen’s credentials as a rough ’n’ tumble man of
action. Nothing else of note to mention here, save for a hulking man-mountain named
Kevin Grevioux, whose voice is so unbelievably deep he could short-circuit a subwoofer
merely by clearing his throat.

The Last of His Tribe
By Henry Kendall
He crouches, and buries his face on his knees,
And hides in the dark of his hair;
For he cannot look up to the storm-smitten trees.
Or think of the loneliness there --
Of the loss and the loneliness there.
The wallaroos grope through the tufts of the grass,
And turn to their coverts for fear:
But he sits in the ashes and lets them pass
Where the boomerangs sleep with the spear --
With the nullah, the sling, and the spear.
Uloola, behold him! The thunder that breaks
On the top of the rocks with the rain,
And the wind which drives up with the salt of the lakes
Have made him a hunter again --
A hunter and fisher again.
For his eyes have been full with a smouldering thought;
But he dreams of the hunts of yore,
And of foes that he sought, and of fights that he fought
With those who will battle no more
Who will go to the battle no more.
It is well that the water which tumbles and fills
Goes moaning and moaning along;
For an echo rolls out from the sides of the hills,
And he starts at a wonderful song -
At the sound of a wonderful song.
And he sees through the rents of the scattering fogs
The corroboree warlike and grim,
And the lubra who sat by the fire on the logs,
To watch, like a mourner, for him -
Like a mother and mourner for him.
Will he go in his sleep from these desolate lands,
Like a chief, to the rest of his race,
With the honey-voiced woman who beckons and stands,
And gleams like a dream in his face -
Like a marvellous dream in his face?

sections.title: Questions 1-8
sections.passage:
Taken By Suprise
Tim loved working in the subway.
Loved it.
If you pushed him, he’d admit he loved it more than his father. Not more than his mother, but
definitely more than his old man.
The subway, its tracks, tunnels, rails, and switches were his. Dirty and run-down to most
everyone else, but magnificent and sprawling to Tim.
The strangest part is that Tim loved the subway most when it rained. When it poured, it didn’t
matter if Tim was even on the clock. He would check in, grab his vest, hard-hat, and lantern
and walk the tracks.
It was just such a night.
Off the clock, but still on the job.
Thunder crashed overhead. The tunnel was a cool, wet 10 degrees.
Rain dripped through the grates overhead. Little streams flowed underneath the railroad ties.
For Tim, this was when the subway really came alive and showed the world its true self-——
the greatest cavern ever built; the greatest network of caves ever used by man.
Tim missed the next tie, and his boot fell hard into the river running between the rails. A
critter squealed at Tim’s inconsiderate splashing, and he smiled to himself. The last bit of
humidity from the 32-degree day moved across his face, pushed by a cool breeze behind.
Tim turned into it and looked down the tunnel at the long curving way, flecks of light glancing
off the steel. He took a deep, satisfied breath, and walked on.
Tim did not always walk the subway; he did not always work for it. He used to have a job
behind a cramped desk, in a cramped office, working with cramped people who couldn't
imagine much beyond their cubicles. Needless to say, they did not share Tim’s enthusiastic
dreams of urban spelunking.
But Tim made those dreams a reality and left his cubically-caged mates for subterranean
trusses, I-beams, and engineered slopes.
Moving further along the tracks, Tim grew aware of something completely unexpected out
in front of him. With each step, the void ahead seemed to quiet more. After another 30 yards,
Tim was standing in a completely silent stretch of tunnel. Water did not drip, critters did not
scurry, and street traffic overhead was muffled beyond recognition. Tim felt anxiety grip him,
and he immediately switched on his lantern. He needed more light than what laced off the
tracks to investigate this exception.
The I-beams were the first sight to set his stomach seizing. There was not a single, rusted,
wrought iron pillar as far as his lantern could stretch. Instead, the beams had been covered—
or replaced entirely, he could not tell—by concrete columns, grey and sterile to the touch.
The concrete had been purposefully pockmarked to absorb vibrations as trains passed
through. While the iron beams had acted as tuning forks, allowing the clanging chorus of
steel wheels on steel rails to resonate around a bend, the new pillars seemed capable of
soaking up any din like a sponge.
Tim let his hand run over each geometric dimple and shuddered at the thought of every ding
or clang already trapped, unable to dance along, weaving in and out of subway cars.
It was in that moment Tim realised also that there was no water dripping down onto his
helmet from overhead. He looked up and was confronted by a modern ventilation duct,
gently circulating the air. If his journey had begun here in this part of the tunnel he would not
have known that rain was coming down in buckets up above.
Tim rested his chin on his chest, shook his head, and cursed to himself, what have they
done to this place? His eyes turned downward, Tim realised that the streams between the
rails had dried up. The ties were made of pre-poured concrete, the channel was carved with
smooth right angles and drainage points all along the way. There was no sign of the ragged,
splintered wooden ties that would give way under a car's weight and send a wobble through
each passenger’s legs.
What have they done to this place?
The anxiety started to creep back into Tim’s mind. The pockmarked concrete pillars started
to resemble the pressed fireproof boards used as part of his old cubicle walls. The space in
between tracks looked like linoleum office flooring underfoot, the pre-poured railroad ties
were like simple inlayed design work. The vent and clean truss work overhead resembled
the ceiling and air conditioning grates that hung lifelessly over his old desk.
What have they done to my place?
Tim wasn’t spelunking anymore. He was moving past the standard forms of an office. He
was walking down rows of cubicles on his way to the water cooler, and he hated it. He wanted
to go back to the rundown caverns he loved so dearly. He wanted to run his hands over a
man-made creation that could not resist the pull of a more natural order.
It was in this moment that a train horn sounded, steady and deep. Tim lifted his head to
watch twin eyes about 300 yards down the track moving toward him. He quickly stepped out
from between the rails, off to the side between two columns. Making sure he was far enough
back, Tim braced up against the pillar and waited for the train to pass.

sections.title: Questions 7-8
sections.passage:
Extract A - Early Forms of Parliament
The evolution of the parliamentary system used in Australia can be traced back to the
United Kingdom. Long before the term United Kingdom was used, the Anglo-Saxons and
Jutes from mainland Europe were settling in England. They brought with them a type of
self-government that suited the needs of the scattered tribes. There was a meeting held
regularly to make and enforce laws, settle quarrels and decide on suitable punishment.
This was called a ‘folk moot' with the leading freemen of the tribe or village making the
decisions.
As the population increased and dispersed throughout England, kingdoms were set up, but
it was not until the tenth century that the country was united under one ruler. Distances
made it impossible for all the freemen to assemble as in the older ‘folk moot' days, and
there gradually developed a simple form of representation of chosen men from each
district to regularly attend meetings. The group was called the 'Witan', or the meeting of
wise men.
The main objectives of the Witan were to advise the King on matters of law-making, the
levying of taxes and the defence of the kingdom. All the Saxon rulers used the Witan
system, and, although it held little resemblance to the later developed parliamentary
system, it nevertheless created in the minds of the people the view that the King should
not be an absolute ruler.
With the invasion of England by William, Duke of Normandy, there were swift and radical
changes. The Witan was abolished, and a Great Council was established, made up of the
great barons and leading churchmen. William was an autocratic ruler and called the Great
Council together quite infrequently. There remained, however, the strong feeling that the
Great Council should become an important voice of the people, so that Kings should rule
in the interests of all the King's subjects.
Extract B - Excerpt from ‘The Daughter of Time’ by Josephine Tey
The second book was a School History textbook. The two thousand years of England's
story were neatly parcelled into compartments for ready reference. The compartments, as
usual, were reigns. It was no wonder that one pinned a personality to a reign, forgetful that
that personality had known and lived under other kings. One put them in pigeon-holes
automatically. Pepys: Charles II. Shakespeare: Elizabeth. Marlborough: Queen Anne. It
never crossed one's mind that someone who had seen Queen Elizabeth could also have
seen George I. One had been conditioned to the reign idea from childhood. However, it did
simplify things when you were just a policeman with an injured leg and a concussed spine
hunting up some information on dead and gone royalties to keep yourself from going
crazy. He was surprised to find the reign of Richard III so short. To have made oneself
one of the best-known rulers in all those two thousand years of England's history, and to
have had only two years to do it in, surely augured a towering personality. If Richard had
not made friends he had certainly influenced people.
The history book, too, thought that he had personality: Richard was a man of great ability,
but quite unscrupulous as to his means. He boldly claimed the crown on the absurd ground
that his brother's marriage with Elizabeth Woodville had been illegal and the children of it
illegitimate. He was accepted by the people who dreaded a minority and began his reign
by making a progress through the south, where he was well received. During this progress,
however, the two young Princes who were living in the Tower, disappeared, and were
believed to have been murdered. A serious rebellion followed, which Richard put down
with great ferocity. In order to recover some of his lost popularity he held a Parliament,
which passed useful statutes against Benevolences, Maintenance, and Livery. But a
second rebellion followed. This took the form of an invasion, with French troops, by the
head of the Lancaster branch, Henry Tudor. He encountered Richard at Bosworth, near
Leicester, where the treachery of the Stanleys gave the day to Henry. Richard was killed in
the battle, fighting courageously, leaving behind him a name hardly less infamous than that
of John.

sections.title: Questions 9-14
sections.passage:
The Tyger
by William Blake
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?
In what distant deeps or skies.
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?
And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?
What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp!
When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?
Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?
